summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the lal mirheschi powder was adulterated. The Trial Court acquitted the respondent on two grounds, namely (i) that the prosecution had failed to prove that the Lal mirchi film was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted him; and (ii) that it was unfit for human consumption on account of the presence of the meal wyorms as neither the Food Inspector nor the Public Prosecutor in support thereof. On appeal by special leave, the Supreme Court had held that the definition of 'adulterated ' under section 2(1)(f) of the Act was wide enough to include within its sweep two distinct and separate cclass altogether. Hence this appeal by Special Leave of the Delhi Administration. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The term "or otherwise unfit for" is residuary provision which would apply to a case not covered by or falling squarely within the clauses preceding it. If the phrase is to be read disjunctively, the mere proof of the article of food being "filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or because it is insectable on account Of any other cause". [466C E] 2. The second construction of section 2 (1)(a) of that Act would be a mixed question of law and fact whether the insect infestation was of such a nature, degree and extent as renders the article unfit for life.[470G H; 470A B] 3. In the instant case the Public analyst has found in the sample only nine living meals worm which were found present and that in our view, does not satisfy the requirements of the definition "adulteration" under section2(1) (f) because it consists wholly or in part of any filthy, put up, dis ggusted, roting, decomposing or insect affected while other two others are also mentioned.

The appellant was a dealer in foodgrains. On the date of taking possession of certain foodgrains he was prosecuted under section 7 Of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of clause 3 of the order. He was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. He appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas as well as to the High Court. The appellant then moved the Sessions judge for revision which was summarily dismissed. In appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there because storage has reference to 'business as a "dealer and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub para must be carried to its logical conclusion. In the present case the appellant has successfully proved that he was an agriculturist and the presumption under section 4(2) could, therefore,not be drawn against him. [901 C] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh, ; , referred to. (ii) It would not be correct for him to say that the words 'carrying on the business ' in the context of the Act postulate a course of conduct and continuity of transactions. Theruling maynof be applicable in certain circumstances as for example where, even a single transaction can be demonstrated to be in the course of business. [801 D] (iii) It was obvious that there could not be discry about thecarrying of business because in our opinion the appellant had successfully proved his case that he is an agriculturist or the presumption tinder section 4 (2). [802 C E] Manipur administration vs M/s. Navi Chandra Singh ; , followed.

The question whether a monthly tenancy was created by payment and acceptance of rent in the years 1925 and 1926, depends upon its being determined by a notice to quit. In the present case on the expiry of that period from month to month under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act and the lease having been admittedly brought more than twelve years after the final termination of the second annual lease the defendant became a tenant from month in law to month for himself and, therefore, was not entitled to institute a suit in contravention of its terms. The fact that the rent paid there was an annual rent and he argues that by reason of his holding possession of the land on assertion of a perma nent tenancy right for a long period of time, he acquired a valid title to the property. Held further, that in view of section 116, Transfer of . Property Act the tenant held over, not merely by payment but also by acceptance of rents and payments made to the Receiver. The original term "assessment" is defined in the Transfer Of Property Act as meaning any transfer or communication (other than a permission for the use or occupation) for the enjoyment of a house; and a lease of immovable property for any other purpose. The relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties was not a mere but one of a kind which was recognised by section 107, Transfer o f Property Act. In re: Nazir Ahmad vs Alauddin Ahmad, A.I.R. 1929 Cal. 377 and Shiwal Amin vs Syed Noor Mohammad, I.L.R , referred to.

The respondents filed a suit for partition and possession of a 6/16 share each. As Katheesumma, the mother of Seinaba was not a legal guardian of the property of Seinsaba it was contended that when succession opened out on the death of Mammotty it was entitled to the enhanced shares of 1/4 as there was no issue and the remaining three/4 were divisible between 552 Kanakas and his two sisters, Kunhamu getting twice as much as each sister, she was unaffected by the invalid gift in faVour of Seesinaba and accepted on her behalf by her mother. Held that G who had inherited the property during her illness (the father) was running a business which is almost a small business. Held further that the right to the property conferred by section 6(1)(1) of the includes in respect of gifts by a guardian to his minor ward (ijab) and (ii) not for gifts made through the mother as required by section 3 of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1951. Under certain circumstances of the case the gift was valid. Consequently it must be accepted as valid and complete. The title to property in dispute was B admittedly a valid gift. Once G had vested an absolute interest in the properties, he could cease to have any such rights. Since G did not complete his gift in this way and his transfer included immovable properties and it was accepted by him as a gift, the gift must be treated as valid though full and complete as required under the Hindu religious Endowments Act 1951.

Under the Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951, a fee though levied for rendering services of a particular type is not to be, co related to the services performed for each individual who is intended to obtain the benefit of the service. The Commissioner had, under section 76(1) of the Act, to make rules applicable to each temple separately and prescribing the method for determining contribution found no support in the provisions of the Principal Act or its scheme. The Rules framed by the Government of Madras were challenged in a writ petition filed by the respondents contending that the Commissioner had no power to give him any opportunity to meet the cost of audit of the temple. Where, however, in respect of services rendered by the Govern ment and their officers for defraying the expenses incurred on account of such services every religious institution shall be deemed to have been included in its income for purposes of the levy of contribution under s.76(1). Held that, under the Madras Act 19 (2) of 1951), a fee although levied for performing rendering services for a particular kind is not a tax merely because of the absence of uniformity in its incidence or because of compulsion in the collection thereof nor because some of the contri butories do not obtain the same degree of service as others may. The amount of contribution payable by the petitioners temple should be prescribed by a rule which remained to be made which means that what was decided was by this Court was that no such contribution could be recovered from the temple until such a rule was made.

The appellant filed a writ petition under section 19(1) of the (hereinafter called the Act) against the order dated 2nd April, 1975 of the High Court, Punjab and Haryana directing the issue of notice to the appellant to show cause why he should not be proceeded against for committing con tempt of the appellant 's liability to punishment under section 15. A preliminary objection was raised by the respondents that no appeal lies to this court as a matter of right under section19. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD : (1) An appeal in a given case special leave may be granted under Article 136 of the Constitution from an order or decision of a bench of the Supreme Court if the order has been made in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. No appeal can lie as a matters of right from any kind of order made by the High court in the proceeding for contempt: [512 C F] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, ; , followed. (2) The application is not maintainable. There are no observations by this Court nor on the facts of that case there can be any. any to show that an appeal would lie to, this court from an Order of the Collector merely initiating the proceeding without anything further. [513 C D] Barkadakanta Misra vs JusticeGatikrunna Mishra ; , distinguished. Barad Dasanta Mishra v Justice Gogatikrutnna Mishra A.I.R. 1976 S.C. 1206, and Baradaksanta Mishra 's case, A. l. R. 1976, referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of sections 3 and 7 of the Act. The trial court convicted him and sentenced him to six months rigorous imprisonment. On appeal, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In the appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (1) Under section 1 6(i A), as amended by the 1952 Act of 1949, the repeal of the earlier Act does not affect the subsequent Act. [768 D] Section 4 Of the 1952 , is designed to provide for a different situation, namely, the repealing of an earlier Act which has been applied, incorporated or referred to in a later Act. Under that section the repeal by this Amending Act of any enactment shall not affect any other enactment in which the repealed enactment has been made applicable incorporated or refers to. [761 D] (2) The word " text ", in its dictionary meaning means " subject or theme ". When an enactment amends the text of another it amends the subject or participate of it, though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. It is not possible to say that it disclosed an intention different from that envisaged by the said section. Indeed, the object of the 1952 Amending Act was not to give it any legislative effect but to excise dead matter from the statute book. The Legislature though, by the Act of 1948 inserted the said Section in the Act in the year 1952 as the said amendment was unnecessary and redundant. There is no foundation for this argument, and the entire premises is wrong.

The appellant, who was the managing Shebait of a deity, was appointed as a Receiver by the court in respect of certain properties and for recovering it from his office. He instituted two separate suits against him for recovery of moneys due in respect thereof which he had received advances from time to time from the latter. The trial judge dismissed both these applications and granted them relief in each suit. On appeal, by the judgment debtors, the High Court affirmed its decision and dismissed the appeals. Held, that on a proper construction of section 36(2) Of the Bengal Money Lenders Act which sets out the various powers which the court can exercise if it has reason to believe that the exercise of one or more of the powers will give relief to the borrower as contemplated by the Act, namely to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the Act. A new decree is passed only for the purpose of substituting the method of accounting sanctioned by the statute for the calculations upon which the original decree was passed and to give an opportunity to the judgment debtor to pay the decretal dues thus ascertained by instalments. But save and except for these, the old decree as well as the adjudications made thereunder are not wiped out and the parties are not relegated to their rights and liabilities under the original cause of action (2). The executing court merely deals with matters as to whether the decree holder was in fact a benamidar for another person and that the rights are to be adjusted in accordance with the provisions of the Bengal money Lenders act.

The respondent company brought a suit for recovery of the debt and interest on the ground that the respondents were allowed to continue as plaintiffs in respect of certain transactions in gold and silver effected by the firm as pucca adatias. The trial court passed an order directing the appellant company to execute the decree within 7 days from the date of judgment. On appeal, the High Court held that the transfer 'of the suit property was not transferred or agreed to be transferred to the respondent company by the document under consideration and consequently it was a transfer of the decree by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, further, that the respondent did not become a transferee of the original decree within the definition of 'decree holder ' contained in section 2(d) Of the , because, under the terms of the assignment, the appellant was entitled to transfer his share to the respondents and could therefore claim to have been substituted as plaintiff. The transaction was not one for the purchase or sale but for an outright purchase by a company which was subsequently transferred to it and had become the property of the appellant. The transferee of a decree cannot claim to be a transferee from the provisions of section 232 Of the Indian Penal Code, because (1) in their application for execution filed before the City Civil Court not mentioned any of these particulars but only stated that the court should declare them the assignees of the decrees as the decretal debt along with other debts were transferred by the appellant to him by the deed of assignment dated the 7th February, 1949 which was confirmed by the Custodian of Evacuee Property, Bombay and (2) that an application made by an assignee of a money decree must be under Order XXI Rule 16. The provisions of Order 21, rule 17(1) and Order XXII of the Civil Procedure Code were quite different from Order XXI , r. 11(2) and they did not affect any legal transfer or assignment of the suit to be passed in future by virtue of the distribution in writing executed before the decree came into existence and the only way in which the transferee could claim that the decree was transferred to him was by the operation of the equitable principle above enunciated. Kangati Mahanandi Reddi vs Panikalapati Venkatappa & another (I.L.R. [1939] 2 Calcutta 325, distinguished.

The respondent who carried on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows and windows, spices, etc. entered into a contract with the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, for "sale of some hung doors" in accordance with the specifications and conditions, in excess of certain rates provided by r. 1 hereof and in respect of the supply of goods, the price was to be revised in the light of cost revision of the controlled price of steel supplied to the respondent. The respondent paid a sum of money under the contract. He claimed that the contract was one for work, in the execution of which some movable property passed; and that it was not a contract for sale of windows and for rendering service in connection with the fixing of those windows. It was also contended by him that the terms of the tender were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and the "invoice" for payment made out by the respondent and that the High Court was in error in holding that the contracts were divisible between two parts representing the sale of the window, and labour charges in fixing the same and thus partly liable to sales tax. The question was whether on a consideration of all the circumstances, the contract between the parties could be evolved. HELD : (i) It is necessary for manufacturers or dealers in specialised articles to arrange to "fix" and "service" the articles. sold by them and on that account the contract does not acquire the character of a contract of service. [508 E] (ii) The object of the respondent was to enter into a works contract. That clearly appears from the terms Of the tender and its acceptance. The windows were to be fabricated according to the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge, and were to "fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance 'from the building with rawl plugs in cut stone work. [511 B] (iii) The service is not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves.

The prosecution case is that on November 8, 1967 Shankar Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla came to Ram Avtar Prasad complainant and told him that he (Shanker Lal) could arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The complainant agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plates at the rate of Rs. 38/ per piece, but on November 16, 1967 he had been purchased by Raj Kumar and was assured that this transaction would fetch him Rs. 3200/ . On November 15, 1967 his goods would be supplied on the following day. On November 16 the police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by Ram Avtar. A complaint against Shankar Lal was registered with the police after his suspicion having been aroused. Later on that day Shankar Lal sent a formal order to Ram Har Avtar and narrated to Raj Kumar Bhala who were present at the shop of Ram Avtar, as agent of M/s Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. The Trial Court convicted both the accused under sections 420, 468 and 471 I.P.C. There was no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High Court. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that there is no cogent reason for interference in the judgment and that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned, no case had been made out against him. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The report which was lodged by Shri Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Agarwalala respondent because it is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the F.I.R. and demanded the price of the goods washer plate plates from Ram Avtar and that circumstance, as pointed out by the High court, would hardly warrant an inference that Raj had himself been a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar.[279 C] It is no doubt true that in this case the part which is attributed to Raj Kishan is that he was present along with Shankar Lal when the latter brought washer advertisements in a taxi and demanded price of goods. However, as he was not present at there in connection with the said incident it would hardly be warrant an infer that Raj did not commit any conspiracy or cheat his own by any act done by him.

The petitioner, an allopathic doctor by profession, had himself drafted and filed a writ petition in the nature of public interest litigation alleging violation of fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. It was alleged that the Railways in this country were owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil their constitutional statutory obligations by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties was not available. The petitioner asserted that he had become a member of the Indian Railway Safety Work Fund, being run by the Indian Railways, and that on account failure to fulfill the constitutional obligation, adequate safety protective measures were provided mostly on roads where the volume of road and train traffic was low. It also alleged that unmanned level crossings were gradually being replaced by manned ones and improved technical gadgets are being provided for efficient operation. Relying on the Sikri Committee Report of 1978 it has been submitted that the State Governments appeared to be aware of their responsibilities in this matter and about 2/3 of the funds of the Safety Works had been utilised by March 31, 1982. While admitting that in the initial period utilisation of funds was poor and finalisation of schemes for over bridges and under bridges were slow, the situation is claimed to have improved and in 1982 83 as many as 14471 of them as on March 1,1982; unmanning level crosses with a volume of traffic of more than 6000 train vehicle units or poor approach visibility are being manned in a phased manner at the cost of the Railways and control at the gate is also being improved. It has been further pleaded that periodic review was undertaken about manning of unmaned level cross injuries and opening of new level crossages in consultation with appropriate State Governments. Earlier it used to be the obligation of the respective State Governments to provide for such level crossingings at their cost in view of the accepted position that at a level crossing the right of way is of the train in preference to traffic on the road. The Additional Director (Safety) had filed a counter affidavit stating that the recommendations of the Accidents Enquiry Committee were examined and implemented within the limits of financial and material resources. So far as manned level Crossings are concerned there were as many 14471 as on 3, 1982; unmenned levelrossings were provided largely on roads when the volume is high. It had been further stated that periodic reviewed was undertaken regarding manning inter lines with appropriate state Governments and that initially it used, to be 'the obligation of each State Governments in the post independence period, namely, the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees to investigate into the affairs of the Railway with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unmannerned level motor crossings on the Railways out of which 195 are important bridges and nearly 9400 are major bridges. It further alleged that periodic Review is undertaken about working of unmunned level crossexamination in consultation; with appropriate States Governments. The Joint Director (Technical), Engineering, has filed a Counter affidavit contending that the Report of the accidents Committees were examined, and implemented on within the limit of financial, material resources; so far as work manned crossings are concern, there was no necessity of rebuilding a bridge when its codal life is over. On behalf of the respondents it was contended: (1 ) The directions of the Accident Enquiry Committee should be examined and enforced strictly in accordance with law; (2) The Union Government should be free to collect the entire operational cost which would include the interest on the capital outlay out of the national exchequer, and (3) The transmission of the message by the Railway Authorities to the petitioner was neither arbitrary nor capricious. Allowing the writ petition, the Court, HELD: 1.

The appellants who had applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953, in respect of their proprietary jagirs. Against the award of compensation made by the Jagir Land Abolition Officer the appellants preferred appeals under section 16 of the Jagirs Abolition Act before the Revenue Tribunal constituted under the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Act, 1957 and all these appeals were ultimately dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal they were not "decide" as required by section 17 of the Act. Held: The language of section 17(1) of the jag Abolition Act, on its true interpretation, applies not only to a case where the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a ease where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing, the Tribunal may decide it on merits and to record its decision even though there is default on the part of the applicant to appear in the appeal. The legislature intended by the word "declared" in section 17 (1) to mean "dispose of the appeal 'or to put an end to the appeal". It was also open to the Tribunal in such a case to hear the respondent to the Appeal and decide it On merits. Regulation 19(2) contemplates a case wherein the appeal had been decided ex parte, and on a consideration of the language of s 17 (i) of Jagirs Abolition act the Tribunal was right in taking the view that the applications for restoration made by appellants were barred by limitation.

The appellants, who were descendants of a public temple brought the present suit under section 92 Code C.P.C., for removal of their respondent and another descendant of the deity for accounts. The question in the plaint was whether by the Punch Faisla Award of 1896 an absolute dedication of the village to the deities is made in favour of him or whether the disputed property belonged to the family either by Dinanath Sao himself or later on by his descendants. Held, that the use of the words "at that time" in the original necessarily meant " from the profits and income of mouza Telibandha which was maintained for general expenses of the family or that he made certain alienations of the property to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy and Ramsaran Lal absolutely with only a charge on it to meet the expenses of this temple and did not make an absolute endowment in respect of the dedication already made. The words "in that year " showed anabsolute dedication of this village to Shri Ramchandra Swami temple, which was recognised by the Privy Council in Ramsarain Lal vs Shanti Kumari Debi (1911) L. R. 75 I. A. 15 and C. P. Wavgouda vs Thakur Gulab Chand (1896) L Q.B. 316, distinguished. Held further, that there must be a separate and distinct intention between the parties to it, and that the mere use of words "haq uphod ' in para 2 of the Panch Faisala that by this award Teliasmuch had been dedicated for ever for the aforesaid purposes and it would not be right to take the indication of the word "Malik" was not correct.

A writ petition in the Allahabad High Court, challenging the orders of discharge of four persons who were members of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Lucknow Bar Association, was dismissed by a Single Judge. The appellants contended that: (1) no contempt of court had been committed; and (2) that contemners Nos. 1 & 2 were guilty of contumacious conduct, and the High Court held that they were responsible for the passing of the resolution. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. It is true that the High Courts referred to the contumacious behavior of the appellants but the High court did not intend to proceed against the appellants. [603B] 2. The language used by them was unfortunate; and Counsel for the appellants rightly said that was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. It could not, therefore be passed in this manner. [ 603F G] 3. The High Court overlooked the word 'criminal '. [ 604D] 4. In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the aforesaid observations. [ 607A B] 5. The matter becomes clear when the High High Court said 'we do not propose to punish contemners Nos 1 and 2 for the contumamiscious conduct for which we have adjudged them guilty though they express. [ 606E F] 6. The spirit used by him was unfortunate. Counsel for parties rightly said, that was inappropriate. [063G] 7. This is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. It would be undermining confidence to a small extent.

The three arbitrators took the assistance of appellant No. 8 and he functioned and acted as one of the arbitrators. On or about 2nd of July, 1977 the same agreement was re written on a fresh stamp paper and the same was registered by which the1985ciplinaryamed Arbitrators were given the option to take assistance of one, two or more persons. The dispute related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah. The disputes related to some properties among them in Chinusurah, the district of Hooghly at Hoohly in the State of West Bengal. The three arbitrators came to a conclusion that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting it for registration. On these grounds the learned Munsif passed an interim injunction in favour of the respondent restraining them from enforcing the orders of the court and if in compliance or obedience with court of doubtful jurisdiction, he could not be compelled to disobey the order of the Court and if he was in compliance thereof and disobedience or obedience to court of quo, he would have no right to take back such award from the custody of the defendant. On appeal by special leave to this court it was contended that the award having been presented for registration beyond time and as such was beyond time. It was further urged that the order made by the Court directing the arbitrators had to keep the award in the custody, of the trial court, was wrong and without jurisdiction, but no arbitrator could be compelled by him to disobey its interim orders. On behalf of the respondents it was argued that an award affecting immovable properties which was not registered and which was made outside the court could not form the basis of an award and an unregistered award in other words could not forms the basis for registration of the award. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. An award affecting the immovable property as in the instant case should be 125 registered. [121E] 2. The law itself and the administration of it, said Sir W. Scott, with reference to an alleged infraction of the revenue laws, must yield to that to which everything must bend, to necessity; the law, in its most positive and peremptory injunction, is understood to disclaim as it does in its general aphorisms, all intention of compelling impossibilities, and the Administration of justice must adopt that general exception in the consideration of all particular cases. [122F] 3. There was no dispute to the proposition that an arbitrator affecting immovable property should be registered. It is therefore not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A decision of the Full Bench which has been relied on by this Court in Nityananda M Joshi and Ors. vs Life Insurance Corporation of India and others, [1982] 3 SCR 869, that an order affecting immovable Properties as in a instant case shall be 125 registration. It would therefore not be necessary to deal with in detail this ratio of the A decision.

The appellant, a tenant for about 20 years in the premises known as " Fida Ali Villa" was fixed up by the respondent in some other place. There was some dispute as to date when these new premises were let to the appellant, the appellant alleged that they were let on June 1, 1948, and the respondent let out to him a portion of his new building which 219 was riot far from "fida Ali vsilla" and that he had four sub tenants three of them also shifted to the new premises which were let by the sub tenant. The trial court held that subletting was lawful in spite Of section 15 of the Act and, therefore, section 15 did not apply, but on appeal the Assistant Judge reversed the order of ejectment and dismissed the respondent 's suit for ejectment: Held, (per Sinha, j., dissenting), that section 15 Of the Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, is based on public policy and it has been held by this Court in P. D. Aswani vs Kavashah Mulla, (1957) 1 L.R. 49 I.A. 126, that even if any other law allowed subletting, e. g., section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, the sub letting would, because of section 15, be unlawful. The non obstante clause in section 10 of the Bombay Prevention of Adulteration Act and section 15 are applicable only to contracts for which a penalty is exigible in respect of matters covered by the Act. The plea of waiver is unsustainable only when the circumstances are such that the court will refuse to assist either party, the consequence must follow that the party in possession will not be disturbed". In other words the right of the respondent to sue for ejectment on the ground of subletting being a personal right for his benefit, the landlord must be taken to have waived it as by an express contract he had allowed the tenant to sub let and consequently he could not evict the appellant under section 13(1)(e) Of the Act : Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Co., (1947) L. R. 49 1. A. 126; P. C. 147, J., in Pentiah vs Vempell, , referred to. In the instant case the question is not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the Court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 as it stood before the amendment of 1955 and section 23 of the Contract Act and enforcement of the contract would produce the (1) A.I.R., 1949 Bom. 222, relied on.

% The Board conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990, whereat the marks awarded were found tampered with, and the appellant was declared on June 30,1990. Some writ petitions were filed in the High Court against non declaration of the results and the High Courts directed the Board to take expeditious action to declare the results of the examination within the specified time. In pursuance thereof, the Divisional Board proceeded to enquire into the use of unfair means at the final examinees of answer sheets. The appellants challenged the impugned notification on the ground that the procedure adopted by the Committee was to ensure purity of examination and if examinee is found to have used unfair means in answering questions then it is not open to the High court under Article 226 to itself evaluate the evidence as an appellate Court and to come to its own conclusions. The Division Bench rejected the writ petitions filed by the appellants. In these appeals, the appellants contended that since the procedure prescribed by the Act and Regulations made thereunder was a valid rule and not a reasonable regulation, it had no power under the Act to enquire in respect of irregularities committed at the stage of enquiry. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The examination committee, if relies upon such evidence to come before the conclusion that the examinees, their parents or guardians were parties to the fabrication and whether their complicity was established from record, and whether the evidence was sufficient to support such conclusion reached by the Standing Committee or the Enquiry Officer. Once a matter is established beyond reasonable doubt it must be taken for all purposes of law to be a fact, as there is no room for a distinction between what is found by inference from the evidence and what is alleged but as a positive face. [798F G] 1.2 In the instant case, the finding of the High Commissioner that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the examinee or the parent or guardian is justified on cogent evidence and in this case all the requirements are lacking, has been made not a relevant fact. The findings were based on no evidence and the conclusions were in different hand writings, which would show the non application of mind to the facts and it violates the principle of natural justice also does not apply to the factual situation. [774F] 1:3 It is well settled that under the scheme of the Act for the efficient and expeditious functioning of the concerned Boards, implementation of the provisions of the act, and to prevent use offair means at final examinations including fabrication of documents issued by the Board as an integral part of the power of the Divisional Boards. [779C] 1 :4 The examination fee prescribed by Section 33(3)(b) and (c) is not a statutory percentage which can be applied for in any particular case. However, at the same time, it cannot be said that each candidate has used unfair mean methods. When an inference of proof that a fact in dispute has been held established there must be some material facts or circumstances on record from which such an inference could be drawn. [765D E] State of U.P. vs Chet Ram & Ors., ; ; Shanti Prasad Jain vs The Director, of Enforcement, , referred to. 1.5 It may be open to a High Court to interfere with the order of the quasi judicial authority if it is found not supported by any evidence or if the order as passed in contravention of the statutory provisions of any law or in violation of the principles of natural Justice, the court has no jurisdiction to quash the order merely on the grounds that different view could possibly be taken on the evidence available on the record. [670C] State Of Uttar Pradesh vs ChetRam & Ors. , ; M/s. Indira Nehru Gandhi National Institute of Medical Sciences and Anr., AIR 1979 SC 295; V.B. Raju, AIR 1975 SC 2291; Dr.S.Sangamurthy v The Managing Committee, Madras & Ors.; ; ; and Smt. A.K.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the three accused who were staying at the Coronation Hotel were suspected of exporting potatoes at concessional rates on false declarations or certificates and they were seed potatoes. They were charged with an offence under the same section read with s 120 B. The Special Judge convicted them under both heads, but the High Court reduced their sentence to the term of imprisonment already undergone. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the object of the Act was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that it could come into play only when there was no offer to give an acceptance of gratification by a public servant and that the offence as defined in cl. (d)(2) did not come with. Held, further, that after the amendment all railway servants had become public servants not only for the limited purpose but generally under the Prevention Of Corruption Act. The words "corrupt or illegal means" find place in section 162. Even on this ground it cannot be held that there was any overlapping of offences. In one sense it can be made applicable there must be proof, it was said, that the public servant adopted corrupt or illegal device and thereby obtained for himself or for any other person any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. The word "obtains" is used in sections 161 and 165 of the Penal Code. A trap laid for catching the appellants and this circumstance according to the learned counsel for the appellants should be taken into account and it could not be held to be conclusive evidence that by so doing the offences there was a threat or inducement, or promise proceeding from the public servants or duress or extortion practised by him to obtain the pecuniary advantage The distinction between "corruption" and "disqualifying ' is one of the provisions intended for the protection of public 19 servants prosecuted under the Act while they are subjected also to increased disabilities. Ramjanam Singh vs The State of Bihar, [1952] S.C.R. 1071, considered.

The appellant State Bank of Saurashtra was the defendant in a suit for recovery of the amount advanced by it to the principal debtor. In pursuance of a demand promissory note, the surety executed a letter of guarantee with the Bank and he issued an allotment letter on September 16, 1957, offering to give security for the cash credit facility, giving security for cash credit by pledge of groundnut oil tins as also personal guarantee of defendant 2 Chitranjan Rangnath Raja. In the letter it was mentioned that the principal creditor would provide such quantity of goods as would provide full cover to the outstanding balance in the cash Credit account and the Bank was to be responsible for the safe custody and keeping of the pledged goods. The surety stated that the term of the surety would offer two securities, one the pledge of goods to be kept under the lock and key of the Bank to be supervised by the Bank 's employee, and secondly, the personal guarantee had to be taken on a reasonable price for the advances. The creditor and the surety agreed to give personal guarantee in the form Ext. 66 on September 10, 1957 and on the same day the principal defendant also executed a demand negotiable promissory note simultaneously. Thereafter, the principal buyer and the guarantor both took the cash credits facility by borrowing various amounts. Again, another amount of Rs. 84,828.07 P. was paid by the surety to the bank as security for further advances and on personal guarantee, of the sureties. The mortgage money in favour of the bank and the letter of Guarantee executed by the principal were handed over to the Bank by the appellant and the pursuant thereto, the other sum was advanced to the extent of Rs 75,000/ and the balance in cash credit account was required to be recovered from the surety. On September 16 the appellant sent a demand draft of Rs 24,320.04 P. against defendant 1 for payment of outstanding balance of Rs 65,879.04P. against defendants 1 to 7 together with interest thereon under the hypothecation bond executed by it in favour. The Bank thereafter filed a suit against the surety contending that the surety had agreed to grant cash credit facilities to the deceased principal debtor on the security of goods by way of pledge and that though the goods were to be stored in the godown in the compound of Vijay Oil Mills Pvt. Ltd., but the godown was to he kept under lock and keys of theBank, which it took was to remain under lock. The principal debtor also stated that since defendant No. 7 had agreed with the payment of the outstanding amount which was due according to the terms of the settlement between the parties, two security stood transferred to the appellant by Vijay oil Mills in the name of the deceased Principal debtor and they were treated as pledged with the bank. The trial Court judgment gave directions. In appeal, the High Court held that the sureties had agreed that the Bank would provide a quantity of foodgrains as would provided full cover for the Bank claim but since the contract of guarantee entered into by the tenant with the appellant was independent of the pledge, of goods given by the latter in favour, all on September 3, 1959, constituted one composite transaction and they evidence that the Principal debtor had offered two securities both at the time when entering into contract of Guarantee in which case he was deemed so to contract that both the securities would be available to the creditor (see Sanderson vs Aston) that if the two promissory notes executed by defendant No 7 were to form a part of the security, the appellant would not be discharged from his liability under the guarantee. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that in view of clauses 5,7 and 13 of the letter Of guarantee, Ext. 31 even if it is held proved that the security furnished by defendant NO 7 was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank, yet the surety could not be absolved from his responsibility undertaken under the letter dt. September 16.

The appellant 's family had two sons, called Amrit and Bhagwant, who were the son of Amritrao. The case of the appellant was that as a result of this partition the " patelki inam lands" fell in the resumed portion of the Jagir and the lands in suit were allotted to the share of the appel lant. As a result the jagir of Nawabagag was created and the appellant 'and his brother, Amritrao divided them among themselves. The other two plots came into being by the last settlement. Both the patel families went by them and they entered into an agreement with the Government to resume the lands. After some time before the expiry of the period of two years the jagirdars gave a notice of resumption to the appellant for passing a final order of resumption under section 18 Of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928. Objections were raised that the lands having been reserved as emoluments ceased to be co sharers they became entitled to resume and regrant the lands to respondent No. 1 on the ground that it was not a service grant, and secondly the orders of Government dated August 28, 1922, did not confer any new right nor did they deprive anybody of any subsisting right in respect of the "patelki Inam " lands and Government had no right to resume them and regain them to respondent 1. The appellant challenged the validity of these rules by a suit by the respondent 's decision before the High Court which was upheld by the High Courts. In appeal by special leave it was contended that under section 9 of the said Act the emoluments appertaining to the office of the p Patel and Patwaris Law, 1900 were subject to orders passed by the revenue authorities in respect Of the matters mentioned therein, and no right was given to a member of the family of the deceased to claim a share in the emoluments. Held, that under r. VI(2)read with r. V(2), the appellant had been entitled to his share in tho "p Patelki inam" lands as an undivided brother of Amritaji, Patel and it was open to Government to accept the revenue entries made by them which did not preclude respondent No 1 from exercising its authority under section 12 Of the Act. Venkata Jagannadha vs Veerabadrayya, I.L.R. , distinguished. The Raja Ramkrishna Ayyar vs Anjanmaya, I I. L. R. and Pataris Law (1917) 69 I.A. 518, relied on. Venkatasubbud vs Secretary of State for India in Council, [1962] 2 S.C.R 368, considered.

The question was whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the entire property held by the deceased valued at Rs. 1223,794/ , was chargeable to estate duty. The assessment in question related to the estate of Hajee Mohamed Zer Sailt, the father of two respondents, who died at Bangalore on March 22, 1955 leaving behind his properties and securities. His case was that despite their conversion, the Cutchi Memons retained a large part of Hindu law as their customary law including its concept& joint family property, the right of a son by birth in such pro perty and its devolution by survivorship constituted the customary law of Cutchi memons governed matters of succession and inheritance only. His contention was that there was no question of passing the said properties to them on the death of their father as envisaged by section 3 of the , Act or its being applicable to them or the said property, they having come to them under the Hindu Law rule devolution of joint family Property by survivorship. Held:(i) The rules of Hindu Law and custom applied to them did not provide that on the coming into force of the Hindu Succession Act, 1950, the appellants ' father would be governed by the Mahomedan law as to succession and succession with regard to matters other than those specified in section 2 of the Act. (ii)The High Court was right in its view that the test of "heirs" that they had accepted or laid down the customary Hindu Law for their adoption in the (1) A.I.R. (1948) Mad. 942, was whether the custom of adoption recognised in the(1) is not to adopt the text of the Koran as law a further than it has been adopted. There was no reason why an erroneous decision should be made after the commencement of the judgment of the High Court in respect of properties which were not governed by section 2 thereof, that if the parties as aforesaid were governed in matters of pro perti tions, succession and re ferred to them would be different from those specified by section (iii) there was also no question as to whether the Bombay view, as reflected in the decisions of the Courts since Beaman, J, in Elia Sait vs Dharanavva referred to above, must apply to a case where the question for consideration was whether such custom or usage had ever been proved and that it lay upon a party setting up a custom in derogation of that law to prove it strictly and (iv) that in matters matters of simple succession and inherited by survivorship, they would be subject to in matters relating to Muslims nor did it abrogate the custom or practice in respect Of matters other excepting those specified under section 2. In the present case, there was nothing wrong with the High opinion that the High view that no preference nor did the appellants have before it the matter, as suggested by the parties on the basis of the decisions since Goundas and the Cutch Memons had settled in Madras, had regulated their affairs, since they had settled down amidst Hindus according to Hindu law not only in matters Of succession and devolution but also in matters, of their property including the Hindu concept of coparcenary and survivorship. In fact, there were no reported decisions on the question whether the High court held any evidence as to the customary customary law which the Cutna Memons settled in Bangalore followed.

The appellant No. 1, J.K. Cotton Spinning & Weaving Mills Limited, has a composite mill wherein it manufactures fabrics of different types. The yarn so obtained is further processed in an integrated process in the said composite mill of the appellant No 1 for weaving the same into fabric. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill were liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not disputed their liability in respect of yarn which is also removed from the Factory. It was contended by the appellants that no duty of excise can be levied and collected in respect thereof on the manufacture of yarn obtained at an intermediate stage and thereafter subjected to an integrated processing process for the manufacture, of different fabrics, and that even after amendment there must be removal of the goods from one place to another for the purpose of collection of excise duties. It is contended for the appellants, that since no specification has been made by the Collector of such place or premises appurtenant thereto, the provision of deemed removal as contained in the Explanation to sub rule (2) of Rule 173A and proviso to Rule 173G, must be read along with the Explanation thereto. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The reasoning given by the High Court is set aside and that of the High Courts is restored. However, since after May 1968, rule 9 and rule 49 envisage the case of an integrated and continuous process of manufacture involving the use or utilisation of a commodity produced at an intermediary stage of an finished product, there is removal within the meaning of rule 9 & rule 49. [755E] 2. It does not contemplate any deemed removal, but a physical and actual removal of goods from a factory or any other place or Premises of production or manufacture or a warehouse etc. Under the definition "place of removal" may be a factory/all other place Or premises of production of the excisable goods. The Explanation to rule 173A & the proviso thereto provide that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place or under rule 9 or store room or other place of storage approved by the collector under sub rule(1), shall be deemed to have been removed from such place and premises as mentioned in sub rule.(l) of rule 49, [756H; 731A] 3. The explanation to rule 9 of Central Excise Rules is made in the licence and in the declaration that has to be furnished by the manufacturer in Form D 2, it was true that under rule 8(1) there is a provision for specification by the Collec tor but the question is what has to he specified by the Super intendent Collector. It cannot be made of the place of manufacture or production of excisable goods, and in our view, cannot be said of the places of manufacture and production of goods and not removal. [657C] 4.

% Section 68 D of the , provides that on publication of any scheme in the official Gazette any person already providing transport facilities by any means along or near the area or route proposed to be covered by the scheme lies, may within thirty days from the date of its publication in the Official Gazette file objections to it before the State Government. The petitioner was the holder of a permit issued under Chapter IV of the Act in the U.P. Gazette dated April 5, 1975 under Section 68 C of the . The petitioner filed his objection to the said Scheme along with several others. After a number of adjournments the Hearing Authority empowered under Section 69 C of Act was able to conclude the proceedings by April 26, 1979 and it is alleged that the Authority in the course of hearing ob served that it would finalise and approve the scheme by 21.5.1979. Before the Hearing authority could give its approval to the scheme under Section 46 D of Act the petitioner filed original suit No. 145 of 1979 on the file of Civil Judge Bulandshahr for a declaration that the above scheme published under section 68 C, of the was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the defendants in the suit from finalising and approving the scheme. The Civil Judge declined to grant the request of the petitioner and fixed the suit for arguments on November 8, 1985. Aggrieved by the order of the Civil Judge, the petitioner preferred a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the proceedings under Chapter III A of the Motor Vehicles Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the petitioner. Allowing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: (1) On the publication of the scheme in section 68 D, any person who is aggrieved by proposed introduction of the Scheme is entitled to file his representations and objections and to appear before the Hearing Authori ties under Section68 D of that Act and make his submissions in support of his objections or representation. Under S.68 C of Order I, r.11, the State Govern ment is authorised to make rules for the purpose of carrying into effect the provisions of this Chapter. The rules which are promulgated provide for the details relating to the manner in which objections or representations can be filed under Section 42D(i) and the procedure to be followed at the hearing of persons who have filed such objections and/or representations and the representatives of the State Transport Undertaking. [538C F] (2) The jurisdiction of the civil courts is impliedly barred from entertaining suits of the present nature. [541A] H. C. Narayanappa & Ors. vs The State of Mysore & Ors., ; at page 753 has observed that the jurisdiction of Civil Courts is impliedly excluded from entertaining suit of the maintainability of a suit in which the validity Of proceedings under chapter IV A of Motor VehiclesAct is called in question.

The appellant was charged of grossly abusing his position as a police officer and extorted money from the pocket of his neighbour. The prosecution case was that her daughter developed illicit connection with someone and became pregnant. In April 1963, she went to Ambala to her maternal aunt who was employed as a sister in the Ambala Air Force Hospital, and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. However, after the child was handed over to the appellant evidence was recorded. At about 7.30 or 7.45 P.m., the appellant met the girl, Miss Eylene and his wife expressed their reluctance to send Miss Einam with him. On September 4, 1963 when S.D.P. Mukatdhari Singh turned up the daughter of N. K. Lal went to the house of the appellant 's sister in law, who was working as a junior clerk in the New Delhi Air Force hospital, and told him that if they wanted to save themselves they should make some settlement with him and demanded a bribe of Rs. 1,000/ . On September 5, 1963, when S reached the house, MissEylene went there to her paternal aunt 's husband, who had no child of his own and wanted to adopt a child. Thereafter, on September 4. 1963, the appellant paid Rs. 90/ and agreed to pay later on a sum of Rs 700/ ; The appellant then compelled Russel Neniel and his daughter to execute a document in writing that they would pay him Rs. 700/ or agree to go to prison. It was alleged that S, who recorded his statement before the D.I.G., Ludhiana, gave a signai and took the same with him, to the police station and therefore the appellant arrested the girl at the resi dence of N 's brother in law. The appellant made her sign a paper and took it into possession by the Police on September 5. 1963. After the conclusion of the trial and after consideration of the evidence convicted the appellant of the charged and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs 5001/ or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 161 I.P . In appeal by special leave, the Court maintained the conviction. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Prevention of Corruption Act and, therefore, the conviction of the appel lant under section 5(2) was bad in law as all the relevant papers and materials were not placed before the police before whom the charge had been framed. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. When a public servant is charged under section 6(1)(d) of the Prevention with Corruption Act, it is alleged that the illegal grati fication was taken by him for doing or procuring an official act, it being not necessary for the Court to consider whether or not the accused public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act. [186 G] 2. When the appellant who was charged under s. 161 I P.C., and it is stated that he had never asked for bribe and that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to Russel, N had no source of income for doing any official act or for showing forbearing to show, in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son.

The appellant accepted a bribe of Rs. 100 from the respondent Railway officials and was charged with offences under section 161, I.P.C., for having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions favour to whomsoever in seeing that a speedy settlement of the claims cases preferred by him against the Bengal Nagpur Railway was subsequently the Eastern Railway. The charge was altered into one under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1), clause (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and was found guilty when the appellant was paid Rs.100 at the time of the sending of currency notes to the addressee for handing them over to the appellant. Held, that on the facts the sanction which the appellant accorded in this case is not a valid sanction. The sanction thus accorded was a valid one and could be revoked either by passing final orders himself or by making recommendations and such sanction would be necessary for the prosecution of the appellant under section 6(c) or by passing a final order, and that the sanctioning authority had no discretion to grant the sanction to the prosecution. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, A.I.R. (1948) L. R 75 I. A. 30, approved. Held further, that the sanction accorded was valid sanction as it was not a proper sanction and must have been given by the authority who made the order which had the sanction and to his satisfaction. Gokul Chand Dwarkadalas Moraraka vs King, (1947) L .R 75 I A. 31, held inapplicable.

The respondent landlord, who is the holder of life interest in a property, was allowed to enjoy the rents and profits for her life time subject to certain charges on account of his two sisters. After the life time of the settlor 's wife, his son, section M Gopalakrishna (appellant) shall enjoy the rent and profits of the said property. In support of the earlier order of eviction, the Rent Controller found that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction of the tenants. The High Court also refused to interfere in revision. On appeal by Special Leave, it was contended on behalf of the tenant that a single petition with regard to two different tenancies which though in the same premises, one for residential purpose and the other for nonresidential purpose was not maintainable. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: Under section 14(1)(b) if he is satisfied (a) that the building is bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction; (b) thatthe building is bonafide required by tho landlord for the immediate purpose of demolishing it and such demolition is to be made for the purpose of erecting a new building on the site of the building sought to be demolished, pass an order directing the tenant to deliver possession of the demised premises to the landlord before a specified date. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own ac count or on behalf or of another or on his behalf and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator receiver or guardian who would so receive the Rent or be entitled to receiving the rent if the building were let to a tenant". [276 F G] M/s Raval & Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramchandra, , relied on.

The respondent decree holder in the execution proceed es under section 6(a)(i) of U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 vested in the State of Uttar Pradesh free from all encumbrances. After coming into force of the Act, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these lands continued to vest in the intermediary. This Court rejected 's contention by holding that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the U. P. Zamindari (Amendment) Act (Act No. 17 of 1964), in the state of UttarP., new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the .. It also held that after the coming into effect of the enactment, what can still be done sold in executing a decree was not the right or title of the mortgagee. Dismissing the appeal of the respondent deposit dd The Court rial Judge having dismissed the execution proceedings against trees and holding that there was a distinction between; trees and a grove and grove land should have been upheld by a Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court, it was urged on behalf of the appellant that after fixation of the amount by the executing court under section 16(1)(a) (i) in the case of trees of standing uncut trees, which were part of grovees and groves and grove lands, it should have proceeded against trees in groves, and that the view taken by the execution Court, that there could not be upheld by the Division Bench. Dismissing his appeal, HELD: (1) The High Court 's view that after section 18(1) (a)(ii), the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force is not correct. [4 F] (2) In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncuts trees,which are parts of groving and grove lands and grove Land. The proposition is well settled that trees before they were cut, form parts of 'land '. And, an inseparable part is always included in the whole.

The six accused persons were charged with offences punishable under Sections 147, 148, 341, 323, 324 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC. After the acquittal of the four accused, two accused persons Nos. 2 to 6, namely, Rajan ( Preman),nataka (A1) Subran, (B2) Subarajan, (3) Subrateen, (4), Parameswaran) Sura (A7), Ambu (A8), Palan (A9) Palan, (A10) Palasi (A11) Palas (A12) Palam (A13) Palang (A14 Palas). The trial court convicted accused 2 to six under Section 326 IPC and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 1 2 to6 were also convicted for an offence under Section 147, 323/149, 324/34 IPC but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence recorded against the four appellants was set aside by the High court and they were acquitted. The convictions and sentences passed against them by the trial court were restored. In view of the limited notice issued by this Court, we are relieved of the necessity to reappreciate the prosecution evidence in extenso and shall confine ourselves to the determination of the nature of offence and the award of appropriate sentence to the four appellant appellants accepting, as established the prosecution case against the 4 four accused beyond a reasonable doubt. 90 According to the prosecution, all the six accused were armed with weapons like chopper, iron rod, cycle chain and sticks. It is the prosecution 's case that the accused had held PW2 George and while the first accused kicked him, the third accused inflicted injuries on him with a chopper and a knife. The assault took place in front of an arrack shop. According to PW4 Biju (PW5) and Anil (PW6), who have been believed by both the courts below and with which finding we have no reason to differ, all these six accused have caused injuries. It was the prosecution story that the appellants had held PWs 2 George and While the first appel lant 's father is alleged to have caught hold of him by the collar and inflicted injuries with a dagger, iron pipe, cycle chains, chain etc. The deceased succumbed to the injuries as a result of the assault during the occurrence, six accused Nos. I1, 2 to 5 were prosecuted for an offen cation under Sections 143, 147, 149, 148 IPC, but no such separate sentences awarded on the other counts. The trial Court acquitted all the four t accused and convicted them under Section 324/149 I.P.C.

The assessee 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September, 1966. The Income Tax Officer completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69 the assessee filed returns in which it stated that it was maintaining its accounts on mercantile basis. It did not dispute its liability to be taxed on the amounts disclosed and further that it Was maintaining its account on mercantile method alone and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax is payable by it. The assessee 'his case before the Income Tax officer was that it had maintained its accounts under assessment on mercantile and that it did not contest its liability nor did it take credit for the said amounts in the books at Coventry. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessment orders for the past years relating to the assessee reveal that the method of accounting was mercantile, that for the A.Y. 1967 68, a company which was finally filing the returns of income on behalf of the assessee by incorporating the figures as per its profit and loss account,that the Indian Company was not aware of the Income tax Department 's system of accounting in regard to royalty and that therefore it had committed a mistake in filing the return for the assessment year 1969 70 and 196869. The Tribunal, however, held that the question of method of account adopted by the assessee must be examined afresh and for that purpose allowed the appeals. In appeal before this Court, on behalf the appellant it was contended: 1. It was not following any particular method of accountancy regularly in the past year, that it been the Indian company which originally formed a co operative society in November 1939, that a distinction should have been made between non resident assessees and that (ii) the mere entry in the account books of the Indian Companies does not amount to receipt of income by the assesses. The argument was that the money was not actually received but the assessee firm was a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a) cannot apply. This was what the High Court held: (1) The question whether there is any conflict or inconsistency between Section 5(2) and Section 145(1) or not must depend on the facts of each case. Where a person competent to file an appeal against an order of assessment has merely asserted his claim it cannot be said that he has received the income in the country. [105 D] (2) The advantage of the law would be lost if the assessee succeeds in showing that he had received the tax and the amount so paid was one which could not be accepted by him in the earlier proceedings. [106 F B] Keshav Mills Ltd. vs CL T., Bombay, [1967] 60 I.T.R. 290; distinguished.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code read with s.34 for murder of one Lahu Vithu Patil on the night between May 23, and 24, 1960 at village Pasarde. Two persons Rama Krishna Patil accused No. 1 died and the fourth accused were acquitted and the 4th participant Deoba turned approver and was P.W. 5. The conviction was confirmed by the High Court. On appeal by special leave : HELD: (i) Though the conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence of such a witness without corroboration in material particulars. [835 G H] In the present case the approver 's evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction under section 34 of the Indian Penal code. Therefore though the conviction was based upon the uncorroborated testimony of An accomplice it could not be doubted that under section 133 of the Evidence Act a conviction based merely on the uncotorroborative testimony of the accomplice may not be illegal, the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Martin B in Res. vs Boyes ; , applied. Bhuboni Sahu vs The King (1947) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 309, referred to. 835 (ii) If the approver was given a true version of the occurrence he would have made no difference and that fact by itself will not corroborate the charge under section 300 read with section 34. [853 D F] Bhubnoni Sahu v The King, ; , followed.

The appellant was the servant of a public servant, who was not only a "public servant" but also a "section". He was guilty of a charge under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act. The Special judge accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted him under section 161 for offences punishable under section 120B, 161, I.P.C., on an accused count, but accepted the charge as true because he was not a " public servant" within the meaning of section 5.(2) and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. The appellant 's conviction and sentence were confirmed by the High Court, Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: (1)(a) The appellant being an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal Code, was not one who was appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty.[687 A] (b) there is a difference between "an office and an employment". The word "officer ' in the article includes a public officer. There is a distinction between "office and an " engagement" but it does not mean that a person must be an officer of the government. [688 G, 689 B C D] In the present case, the appellant was an officer who was at the time when he had entered into the service of the State Electricity Board which falls within the language of clause (12) to section 21 and therefore a "Public servant" would be an Officer within the connotation of that expression in section. [687 E F] (2) Whether sanction of the Government was required under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code is one who is appointed to a certain office for performance of any public duty, has to be decided by the judicial committee in accordance with the scheme and policy laid down by the Indian Penal code. Therefore, the sanction could not be deemed to be a public service servant within the expression "person" under the section because he had been taken the bribe money on behalf of the company [688 A B] (3) The fact that the appellant had objected to a trap as laid down in section 80 C.P., it cannot be brought within the scope of acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the . [688 F G] (4) An "officer in the Service or pay" of Government ' within the terms of section 21(6), Indian penal Code is a one who carries with the power to appoint the Secretary and such other officers as may be required to enable the Board to carry out its functions under this Act. Therefore,. the appellant cannot be deemed an officer within the said meaning in section 3, cl.(12) of section 2, I . [687 G] In any event he cannot be said to be "public servants" within clause (11) of s.21 and that is not correct. [681 E] (5) The High Court has found that the conviction was justified on a consideration of the evidence in that respect. There was no finding arrived at by the Special Judge in regard to the charge against the appellant because he found that there were other clerks attached to the office who occupied subordinate positions in relation to the Head Clerk and the duties of Head Clerk from the nature of things are bound to be immediately auxiliary to those of 'the Superintendent who is so armed.

The appellant was tried and convicted under r. 125(9) Defence of India Rules, 1962 for contravening cl. 4(b) of the Maharashtra Jowar (Restrictions on purchases and sale and Control of movement) Order 1964, read with r. 141(2). The Magistrate ordered confiscation to the Government. The appellant appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge. He also filed a revision before the High Court which dismissed the revision. In appeal by special leave the appellant contended that r. 142 (2) was ultra vires because it laid down a rule of evidence contrary to. the law contained in section 114 of the Evidence Act and that r . 141(1)(ii) fell within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the Defence ofIndia Rules. Allowing the appeal, HELD: The order of the High court maintaining the forfeiture of the seized stock of juar set aside and the rest of the order of confiscation was amounted to nothing less declared ultra vires, both in England and in India. [273B; 273H] The fact that contraband juar seized from the house belonging to a wandering tribe did not matter because section 43 of Defence of Indian Act provides perfectly valid because the rules must fall within the powers given under section 3(1). Section 3 gives very wide powers. It seems to us that r 's. 141 (2)(b) falls within section 2 because it was essential to that the rules may be inconsistent with existing legislation but by virtue of section 43, if otherwise valid they would have effect notwithstanding that they are inconsistent with the existing legislation.

The three brothers were tried by the Sessions Judge, Farrukhabad in connection with the murder of one Kunwar Singh. The trial court convicted Sia Ram under section 302 read with section 109 and sentenced him to death. One of the accused was acquitted by the Session Court but the High Court confirmed his conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that: (1) A person may, for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the murder Of the invite; and (2) even if the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate the commission of the murder, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD (1)(a) There is nothing at all to show that she was aware of the nefarious design of SiaRam and his associates. [628 B] (b) Inventation of one of the items attributed to a witness should be corroborated by evidence of identification. In fact, evidence of identity is itself a weak type of evidence. But the point of the matter is that the court which acquitted Shri Ram was justifiably influenced by the consideration that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification parade be held, the demand was opposed by the prosecution and the parade was there fore not held. [625 D E] (c) The argument on behalf the State, in regard to Sia Lal 's evidence, is unacceptable because the question of identity was essentially a matter which the court could assess and it was unsafe to convict the accused person for her failure to explain her utterance.[629 H; 627 A B] The prosecution has not discharged its burden. [ 625 C] (d) The High Court committed no error in holding on the complicity of S, particularly when the two witnesses had categorically stated that Sia had identified Sia son of one E and had emerged from behind the Shisham trees after Violet gave the call. Dubey is a practising lawyer and he would spare hard words.

The four accused were charged under section 302 read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code for committing murder of his deceased in furtherance of their common intention. All the accused pleaded not guilty to the charge. While the accused were acquitted by the Sessions judge, two accused were convicted under section302 read with 4 34 and 147. On appeal, the High Court set aside the acquittal of the four accused, but on a reference made at the instance of the State it was contended that there was no basis for his plea of private defence. Held: (i) The charge disclosed only named persons; it may also be that the prosecution witnesses named only the said accused; and there might be other evidence, such as that given by the court witnesses, defence witnesses or circumstantial pieces of evidence which may disclose the existence of new named or unnamed persons, other than those charged or deposed to by the prosecution witness. [682 H] (ii) The second illustration given by this Court was really based on evidence. The first illustration of section 34 had no application as it related to the four named accused who participated in the offence. Since it was possible that the story as given by a court witnesses could be covered by the third illustration the judgment should be set aside and convicted, giving benefit of doubt to all the accused; so sentenced.
