[681 C E] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, A. 1. R. , followed. (iii)The evidence was directed to establish that the said four persons participated in com plic ance with the four appellants who were charged with having committed the offence jointly. The High Court had no jurisdiction to convict the accused on the ground that it was doubtful whether a person other than the acquitted accused was also a participant in the assault.

% The Petitioner was a manufacturer of iron scrap, imported the goods and cleared them on various dates between September 1, 1966 and February 20, 1967. Under protest the goods arrived at the Bombay Port on December 22, 1965 were actually removed from the warehouse after the amending Ordinance had come into force, and that he came to know that the income tax authorities had imposed ban under section 132(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The petitioner asserted that he was never ready and willing, rather was anxious to get the material on payment of the then prevailing customs duty. However, due to circumstances beyond the control of the Petitioner, the goods could not be released. Dismissing the Writ Petition, this Court, ^ HELD: 1. Article 32 of the Constitution guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights. If there is breach of the fundamental rights, the petitioner can certainly have recourse to Article 32 and the writ petition is not maintainable. [626C D] Prakash Cotton Mills (P) Ltd. vs B. Sen & Ors., ; , distinguished. The proper remedy for correcting an error in such an order is to provide by way of appeal, or if the error is an error apparent on the face of the record, they by an application under Article 226 of the Constitu tion. [625G] Prakash Jute Mills ( P) Ltd vs B Sen & Anr., ; and Smt Ujjam Bai vs State of Uttar Pradesh, [1963] 2 SCR coast Hussain Begum Begum Begumuddin Begum Begum at page 843, referred to. 1.1 The petitioner cannot seek to remove the goods without payment of duties in accordance with the law. There is procedure provided by law for determination of the payment of customs duty.[625C D; 626A B] 1.2 In a particular situation whether customs duty is payable at the rate prevalent on a particular date or not has to be determined under the four corners of the .

The appellants were the managing director of a company (which went into liquidation) and in execution of the order of the Deputy Registrar of Co operative Societies, a bungalow belonging to the company was attached by the Collector under the Bombay Land Revenue Code on July 27 1942. Notice for sale was issued on November 24, 1942, and the proclamation was published under sections 165 and 166 of the Bombay Tenancy Act. The sale was fixed on February 2, 1943. On January 16, 1943, respondent No. 1 sold the property to defendants 8 to 10 who were respondents 2 to 4. On February 10, 1944, respondent Nos. 1 applied for postponing the sale which was rejected. In execution of this payment order a bungalow came into existence, and notice was issued under sections 166 and 166 Of the Bombay Act, 938, on December 24, 1943; but before the sale could be challenged as the sons were under a pious obligation under the Hindu Law to discharge the debts of their father. The suit was dismissed on June 23, 1944 and the Official Receiver was appointed for the recovery of the property. On November 24th, 1942 respondent No 1 sold another bungalow belonging not to him but to defendants 7 to 10 the respondents. The auction sale was held on February 5, 1943 and in the meantime the appellants sold a portion of the bungalow. On August 15, 1945, respondent 1 sold a part of the house to defendants Nos. 8 to 9 and the sale took place of the whole property without any protest or challenge by the sons and without notice to the Collector or the judgment creditor of the filing of the suit for partition. The Official Receiver purchased another bungalow from defendants 6 to 10 on August 16, 1945 and thereafter a sale deed was executed on September 24, 1946. On July 27, 1942 the purchaser sold another house on August 17, 1945 as he was in possession of the said bungalow till February 5. After the auction sale on August 18, 1945 respondent 1 brought a suit for permanent partition and possession by 'the Official Receiver against respondents Nos. 2 to 9 who were parties to the suit was impleaded as defendants nos.

Dismissing the Writ Petition and quashing of the orders of the Committee, this Court. HELD: 1. The petitioners Ms. Kiran Bedi and Jinder Singh are persons who fall under Section 8 B of the Act and have to be dealt with accordingly. According to the committee 's own opinion formed in the light of facts and circumstances of the case, all those persons to whom notices under Section8 B of Act have been issued to be examined at the end of the inquiry. The Committee should have considered whether the petitioners were entitled to be treated as persons governed by Section 8B of the . [522A C] 2.1 It is enough if at any stage the Commission considers it necessary to inquire into the conduct of any person. Such person would thereafter be governed by section 8 B and 8 C of the , who have to he examined at that end of a inquiry. [523C G] 2:2 In a case where the circumstances in which several incidents had taken place were not known to anybody else, the Committee would have asked them to give evidence along with others who were similarly placed at the rest of the enquiry. On behalf of both the petitioners it is submitted that they did not either wish to delay the proceedings or to show disrespect to the Committee but only wanted to protect their own interest by making the submission which they made before the Committee as per legal advice given to them. This is not a case wherein the circumstances have taken place are not known and to anybody, else.

The Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Rules, 1959, framed under section 21 of the Act provided that "the tax payable under the Act on fares or freights" shall be paid to the State Government in lump sum. Rule 8 (i) prescribes the method for levy and enjoins the issuance of a ticket showing the tax paid of a receipt showing the freight charged and the tax collected. The petitioners, who were seven in number, challenged the Act, and the notification from many angles, by filing a petition under article 32 of the Constitution. The main objection to the Act was that the tax has not been laid upon "passengers and goods" as authorised by Entry No. 56 but on "fares and freights", which were different entities, and in support of their contention that there is a difference, reference is made to Entry No., 89 of the Union List where power is conferred to tax "faass and freight". The petitioners contended that the Act in its pith, and substance, lays the tax upon income and not upon passengers and goods. HELD: (i). Rule 8(ii) of the Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation rules 1959, does not authorise the State Legislature to fix the amount of lump sum payment without guidance. Notification No discrimination between operators of public motor vehicles using roads has been pointed out, and all operators are equally affected by the Act. [532 E F] (2). The tax is for purposes of State and falls upon passengers & goods carried by motor vehicles within the State. No discrimination can be said to be made out. [525 A B] (3) Rule 8 in so far as material to this case, read with r. 8A and the Notification thereunder could not be said lo overreach the section to which they are subordinate and from which they must take their colour and meaning. The Act and the Rules must be read harmoniously and reading them so that it was plain that the apparent mandatory language of the Rules and the Notifications still retains the permissive character of the section, but only lays down what the amount must be, if lump sum paid is made in lieu of payment of the tax calculated on actual fares and freight charges. If the two Rules and notification are read harmoniously, and reading the plain intent is given to it that effect, the apparent official provision of the Rule and the notifications still retains their permissive character.

% The appellant, a private limited company having set up an industrial unit in engineering industry, served notice by retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity, power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week, and the mounting loss. Subsequently negotiations took place between the Union and the appellant leading to an agreement dated 1st April 1975 whereby the workmen who were sought to be retrenched were taken back in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures, and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. Simultaneously, the workmen demanded a revision of the wage scales and the appel lant pleaded its inability in view of the mountling losses, which resulted in the failure of the appellant to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April 1974 and, therefore, the retrenchment was illegal. The Labour Court by its award directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st August 1974 with full back wages, permitting the appellant, to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. the appellant challenged the Award in this appeal. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The relief of reinstatement has been granted and the award has been implemented and the retrenched workmen have been reinstated in serv ice. [567G] (2) Before dealing with the contentions in this case, it is necessary for this Court to exercise its discretionary jurisdiction only in cases where awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial and grave injustice to parties or raises an important principle of industrial law requiring elucidation and final decision by this Court or disclose such other exceptional or special circumstances which merit consideration of this Court (See Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Ltd., Calcutta vs Their Workman), [1959] Suppl. 2 SCR 136 at 140 and Susannah Sharm v.Workfild, ; Susannaha Sharm vsWorkfood AIR 1964 Madras 345; National Bank Employees ' Union vs The Workmen, and National Bank of India vs M/s. Protection Credit Trust Ltd., Bombay & Anr. [1974] i.L.J. 801 and Union of India and others v. M/S. Shyam Sunder & Sons, Delhi Dock Labour Board & Ors.[1975] 1 L.L J. 239, referred to. (3) The concern of common law doctrine that contract of personal service cannot be specifically enforced or the doctrine of remedial damages does not haunt in this branch of law. [569G H] (4) The reliefs of reinstatement with continuity 'of service can be granted where termination of service is found to be invalid. It would mean that the employer has taken away illegally the right to the work of the workman contrary to the relevant law or in breach of contract and simultaneously deprived deprived workmen of his earnings. If the services were not terminated the workmen ordinarily would have continued to work and would have earned their wages. When it was held that the termination of services was neither proper nor justified, it would not only show that the workman were always willing to serve but if they rendered service they would legitimately be entitled to the wages for the same. If, however, sacrifice on their parts is denial of the very means of livelihood.

In 1964 Churi was arrested on the night of September 16, 1969. The accused and his wife were seen together at the house. On search of the house of the accused a knife blows were recovered from him. The complainant 's case against him was that he had gone to the house on that evening and that while she went there at about 10 p.m. he did not return till about 8 p. m. when he went to the residence of the at his house, but it was also found that he lived alone in his house with the Khokhri and with which the injuries on the body of the deceased were received out from the inside. When the accused went up to the room of the complainant 'S where the deceased gave a beating to Churi, an accused in a murder case had come at the residence and told him that he bad killed his wife by giving her three Khokti blows, but since he refused to take Joginder with him there was no reference to the attempt at suicide in statement PH. The Sessions Judge accepted the prosecution case and convicted the appellant under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the confessional statement given by the accused to the police did not amount to confession made to a magistrate of a lower class and there was nothing on record to indicate that he was specially empowered by the State Government to record a confession. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : (1) The decision in Nazir Ahmed 's Case, also covers the case in hand and that on the principles there applied, here to oral evidence given by Shri Mahajan of the recorded statement as well as other circumstances of the case. Therefore, even after excluding the confession from consideration, the other material on record proves the guilt of the ac cused. [4H; 435A B] (2) The fact that the accused alone was with Churi deceased in the house when she was murdered there with the H Khokri and that the relations of the prose cution with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter, is not a fit case for which the extreme penalty need be exacted from the accused. [ 434B C] (3) The circumstances referred to above clearly establish beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of Churi had been recovered after the accused had visited the house and was found at their house on the day of occurrence. Mani Ram (PW 8) saw the accused together at their houses on the date of occurrence and at about 3 p. in., while Poshu Ram ( PW 7) saw him near the dead bodies. The fact, that the deceased along with Chur facto deceased resided in the near house of his brother, shows that the Accused also did not deny that he made any confessional statement on the fear of the villagers that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with them without the child. [ 435B C]. (4) The discovery and arrest of the suspected offender is one of the essential steps in the course of an investigation (see in this connection H. Rishbud & Inder Singh vs The State of Delhi, ; , referred to.

A mortgage was executed in 1938. This was done and 20 Round tank Lane for Rs. 5,000. The plaintiff sued for a sum of Rs. 89,485 12 including costs. On the 11th March, 1943, the plaintiff 's father applied to the Court for execution of a mortgage decree for sale. The Court ordered that the suit should be presented in the proper form and accompanied by an application to the High Court under Order XXXIV, Civil Procedure Code, but no such application was made. The High Court decided against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended: (i) in the absence of any other considerations the most equitable solution is really the second; (ii) section 82 must be read with section 82 and that of course would be the clear logical and simple conclusion i.e., there were no other provision of law to consider; but on those broad facts the case must be held to be one for which a subrogee would be entitled under the Transfer of Property Act. HELD : (i). The suit was not maintainable because it was filed beyond time, as section 81 of the Indian Contract Act could not apply on the ground that the question was never raised by the parties in the High court. [184 H] Mohammad Sher Khan vs Seth Swami Dayal ; , followed. (ii). It is well settled that where a mortgage deed is ambiguous and does not contain any provision which can be regarded as an unconscionable one, such recourse must be adopted to proper course of things; a suit for partition may have the same object in view of section 83 of the Transfer Of Property Act read with sections 82 and 84 of the , which deal wit nesses 234 to 106 the contrary. [185 H] (iii) It is open to a court to give a plaintiff such general or other relief as it deems just to the same extent as if it had been asked for provided that occasions no prejudice to the other side beyond what can be compensated for in costs. In the present case, although he has not used the word "subrogation" he has asked in substance for the relief to which a specific subrogatione would he entitled under section 92 of the Act and this Court is now only concerned with statutory rights and cannot in the face of the statu tory provisions have recourse to equitable principles.

The appellant was a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction got 69.96% marks in the qualifying examination. The Govt. of Karnataka by Notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engineers (Civil). The selection was to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the written test and marks secured in the interview were kept at 100 and 50 for interview. Thus the marks allotted for inter view amounted to 33.3% of the total marks. The appellants contended before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.S.C. were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court, the percentage learned Tribunal dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the decision have approached this Court by special leave. Disposing of the appeal and directing the respondent State Government to give appointment to the appellant Ashok alias Somanna Gowda on the post of Asstt., Engineer (Civil), and appel lant Rajendra, on the Post of Asstt, Engineer (Electrical) in Public Works Department within a period of two months of the communication of this order in case the appellants are found suitable in all other respects according to the Rules. The selection were to be effected on the strength of marks secured by them in interview calculated on the par ties obtained in viva voce out of 50 marks kept for this purpose, and were consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any mala fides in the matter of the impugned selections. However, the Rules are clearly in violation .of the ratio laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., J.T.J. 288, Mohinder Sain Garg vs State o r, J. T.N. 607 and Mohinder Sain Gupta vs State Of Punjab & Ors, J .T.R. On a direction given by this court on 4th September, 1991 the record of the Selection Committee was produced before this Court at the time of hearing. From a perusal of the marks awarded to the selected candidates it is clear that a large number of candidates have been selected though they had secured much higher marks than the appellants in case of the above criteria is applied for selection. In view of the fact that the result of the said selections was declared in 1987 and the selected ly candidates have already joined the posts, this Court do not consider it just and proper to quash the selection on the ground that the 75 marks for interview out of 150 are clearlyin violation in the observations of the judgment of this court in Ashok k Kumar Yadav and Ors. v State of J & Ors . ; , [1988] Sup. S.C R., 657, followed.

Kashmira singh & Anr. vs State, AIR 1981 SC 862; jai Prakash Sharma & Anr., ; referred to. Kash coupal Singh vs The State of M.P., ; and K.S. Appeal dis t posed of. The appellants workmen were directly engaged in the business of manufacturing textile goods. They were paid dearness allowance and gratuity uniform according to the basis laid down by the tripartite conference which suggested the wage scale on the same lines so that if an employee was dismissed or discharged for misconduct which caused financial loss to the employer, gratuity to the extent of that loss only will not be paid to him concerned. The Tribunal however fixed the maximum and the annual rate of increment and increased span of years in which the maximum would be reached. On a reference made by it at the instance of the appellants workmen under section 66(1) read with section 2(a) (b) of the , the Industrial Tribunal held that it was ordinarily desirable to have as much uniformity as possible in the wage scales of different concerns of the same industry working in the same region, as this puts similar industries more or less on an equal footing in their production struggle. The wage scales fixed for factory workmen must be set aside and the matter remanded to the Tribunal for fixing the wage structure including basic pay and dearness allowance with respect to clerical and subordinate staff. On remand the Tribunal took into account all comparable concerns in the matter of wages prevalent in comparable concerns, and finally fixed Rs. 20.50 as the maximum amount for employees belonging to clerical or subordinate staff was more than the highest in other comparable concerns; but it awarded generous annual increments reducing the total span within which a particular employee belonging to the clerical and subordi nate staff will reach the maximum. On reference, Held, that one does notdetermine any real difference unless one is shown by some produce on record. The second does not fix any time or fixed period in each case in fixing the time for making comparisons take into account the total wage packet, and dearness allowances. In the present case there was nothing in law to prevent the Industrial Tribunals from granting adjustments to the employees in the revised wage scales even in a case where previously pay scales were in existence; but this has to be done sparingly taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of each case. The change in wage scales prevalent in the companies was not justified by reason (i) that there was a trend towards uniformity in the matters of scales of dearness allowance as between clerical staff and other staff and factory workmen; and (ii) that it could not be said that the total wages packet fixed was abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total salary packet in the case of the other comparable concern.

The mortgagee 's interest in the property was extinguished by reason of the adverse possession exercised by the mortgagees. The mortgagors brought a suit for redemption, which was dismissed, but that application also was rejected on August 4, 1910. In 1911 the mortgagees executed usufructuary mortgage (Ex. D51) in favour of a person who executed a Kabuliyat for the same. The mortgagees contended that the surrender was valid and binding on the mortgagor as the mortgagee had the right to cancel the transfer in favour. Held that the facts of which are very similar to those of the instant case, quite clearly indicate the court 's understanding of the law applicable to them and that law was nothing but the provisions of section 74 of the Code. Where there are more occupants than one in respect of the same occupancy each has his own rights and the fact of registration of one of them as the registered occupant attracts the operation of the code and confers certain rights or imposes certain obligations on the registered occupants as laid down in the Code but does not take away the rights of other occupants. In dealing with this case the view taken by the High Court in the Letters Patent Appeals was correct and the principal contention urged before the High court must be repelled, The facts of that case show that the mortgagees came into possession of the property pursuant to the usufructuary mortgage. Therefore they had a lawful origin. A mere assertion of an adverse title on the part of the appellants cannot affect the subsisting right of redemption of the mortgagors or operate to shorten the period of limitation prescribed for a suitfor redemption.

The respondent company in the appeal is a com prising company incor pated under the Indian Companies Act dealing in carbon paper, typewriter, ribbon, stepler machines and steplers, despatches the said goods from its head office at Bombay to its branch office at Kanpur wherefrom sales there of are effected by the State of Uttar Pradesh. During the course of the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry No. 2 of List II of Schedule to the Notification and (2) whether ribbon was an accessory or a part of the typewriter. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the aforesaid claim. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10%. He however taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966 at 2%, and that of ribbon @ 10%. The validity of the order was challenged by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. Hence this appeal by certificate. Dismissing the appeal, the Court. ^ HELD: 1.01. From the definitions it is clear that in popular parlance, the word 'paper ' is understood as meaning a sub stance which is used for bearing, writing or printing, or for packing, or to cover the walls. Now carbon paper which is manu (1) [1831] 2) at 248. 840 factured by coating the tissue paper with a thermo setting ink (made to a liquid consistency) based mainly on wax, non drying oils, pigments and dyes by meansof a suitable coat ing roller and equalising rod and then passing it through chilled rolls cannot be used for the aforesaid purposes but is used according to 'the Randon House Dictionary of the English Language between two sheets of plain paper in order to reproduce on the lower sheet that which is written or typed on the upper sheet i.e. making replicated or carbon copies cannot properly be described as paper. It will, therefore, not come within the expression 'paper other than hand made paper ' as used in Notification No. ST 3124/X 1012(4) dated 1st July 1966, issued under section 3 A of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948" or the Rules made thereunder, it has to be understood according to the well established canon of construction in the sense in which persons dealing in and using the article understand it. [838B C] 2.02. It is well settled that a word which is not defined either in an enactment has to he construed in its popular and commer cial sense with reference to the context in which it occurs, but that it is to be construed in the popular understood and commerical sense with refer ence to the background in which that it occurs. [888F G] In law it is necessary also necessary to know what is paper as commonly or generally understood. The said word has been derived from the name of reedy plant papyrus and grows abundantly along the Nile river in Egypt is explained in 'The Shorter Oxford English Dictionary (Volume 2) (3rd Edition) as "a substance composed of fibres interlaced into a compact web, made from linen and cotton rags. straw wood" or other fibrous material, usually in thin sheets used to bear writing or making for wrapping things, decorating walls etc. ' [889C] 1.03. (2)(b) The word ' paper ' in the common parlance means paper which was used for printing, writing and p packing purposes. It was understood as a term in accordance with the commercial understanding. [877D] 2:3.1.

The respondents I to 4 were employed by the appellant Mills at the Sugar Mill in the District of Nainital in the year 1946. In 1951 the partners of the appellant Mill purchased the building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at a time when they were not proprietors of the Sugar Mills at Bulandshahr. The workmen who had acquired the building materials and other machinery belonging to them, closed it at Kirpalpur in the district of Nainital. At committal proceeding to his native place in different towns the partnership concern was set up by the concerned branch of the bank situated atawat in different villages with accounts separately maintained and governed under different service conditions. The respondents who were employed on the respondent Bank filed a suit for recovery damages from them, inter alia, on the ground that they had disobeyed their order of transfer and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). They were asked to submit their explanation as to why action should not be taken against them under the Standing Order. The trial Court held that the respondents were guilty of misconduct under standing order No. 1.of this standing order but the High Court in appeal set aside the finding and directed reinstatement of the workers. On appeal by special leave: Held, further, that there was no express agreement between the appellant and the respondents where under the appellant had the right to transfer the respondents to any of its concerns in any place and the respondent, therefore, without more, it would not be right to imply any such term between the contracting parties when the idea of starting new factories at different places was not in contemplation. The question raised was one of law, namely whether the appellant has the inherent right to make a new contract between them or whether it is merely in evidence that an imported workman at Amroha was entitled to house rent, fuel light and travelling expenses both ways, while at Bulandshahr the workmen are not entitled to any amenities. The questions involved in each case must be considered in relation to the said facts; When the respondents 1 to 4 had been employed by them they were running only one factory at Amroha. There is nothing on record to indicate that at that time it was intended to purchase factories at other places or to extend its activities in the same line at different place, and it was not necessary to multiply the citation for the other decisions relied on. The fact that a person joined such a service, must be deemed to be an implied condition of service. So too in Bata Shoe Company Ltd. vs Ali Hasan (Industrial Tribunal, Patna & Ors.) , transfer of an employee in the circumstances of that case from one post to another was held not to be any alteration of any service condition within the meaning of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. Rex vs Kemp & Co., Ltd., [1956] 1 L.L.J. 343; E. W. Woylelrart Company, Ltd. V. Ottoman Bank, [19561] , referred to.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the . The special contribution under section 2(1) of the , however, has ceased to have effect on and from July 1, 1973. That is the sequel to a notification issued under section 73 lI o the Act. Chapter VA provides for the establishment of the Employees ' State Insurance Corporation in accordance with the provisions contained in sections 33 and 34 of the Act, and the contribution payable by the employee called employees contribution and contribution payable to the employee as per the scheme. The appellant company challenged the validity of the above said notification through a writ petition in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that it contravened the provisions Of Chapter V I A of that Act. It was contended that the payment of special contribution directed to be made by the employer under the or other similar payments or benefits under various social welfare legislations must either be labelled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all and secondly that they are neither taxes nor fees. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on merits. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. When extending the Act to different establishments of the employees, the relevant Government (1) ; 6 SCR 913 1092 Government is given the power to constitute a Corporation for the administration of tho scheme of Employees 'State Insurance in accordancewith the provisions o the . [1091C] 2. Where a scheme of this kind, though very beneficent, could not be introduced in the whole of the country all at once, such beneficial measures which need careful experimentation have some times to be adopted by stages and in different phases, and so, inevitably, the question of extending the statutory benefits contemplated by the Act has to be left to the discretion of the appropriate Government. [1092D] 3. The scheme is analogous to a deferred insurance policy which parents often take out on the lives of their children, but which are to be effective only from a future date after the children attain a certain age, though premium is liable to be paid right from the start. Merely because the benefits to be received are postponed, it cannot be said that there is no quid pro quo. It is true that ordinarily a return in proe senti is generally present when fee is levied, but antiquaneity or contemporaneity of payment and benefit is not the most vital or crucial test to determine whether a levy is a fee or not. [1193H; 1094A B] 4. In fact, it may often happen that the rendering of a service or the conferment of a benefit may only follow after the consolidation of a fund from the fee levied. [1000E F] 5. It cannot be contended that there was no quid provision in this case. [ 1000C] 6. There is no reason to brand or stamp the contribution as a Tax or fee in Order to seek to legitimise it. Legitimation need not be sought fictionally from Entry 97 of List I or Entry 47 of List III when legitimation is directly derived for the charge from Entries 23 and 24 of List 111. Even if the charge is to be construed as a fee as the High court has done, it appears to us be justifiable on that basis too. It being not capable of any controversy that services and benefits are indeed meant to be and are bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer, in due course, when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. [1002C E] Holy Book covering all aspects of every question whether such questions or facets of such questions arose for consideration or not in that case.

The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls for several years even though there was no work for them. On these facts, the question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arise. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment `to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked out from him. The respondents are also running in heavy losses during the last three years and they have denied the petitioners ' claim. In spite of our above conclusion, keeping in view the offer made by respondent No. 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R V thereto, it was directed that all the 63 daily rated workmen including the 54 petitioners herein mentioned in the aforesaid Annexure RV to the counter affidavits be given the benefit of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme framed by respondent NO. 2 and they be paid the specified amounts In addition to the claim made by the respondents, the special leave petition is dismissed. [646B C] The principle that regularisation of daily rated workers and payment 'to him/her of the same pay equal pay to that Of a regular "regular workman arises merely when the ad hoc employee is doing his work as such.

The appellants claimed title to and the recovery of possession of a property from their co heirs, directly or mediately in execution of a decree obtained by them against the original owners. The referring defendants to their purchase by the appellants through Pir Baksh through Pirs of the share of survivorship, the High Court held that the transaction was valid and extended to the entire interest in the property and that in consequence the plaintiffs had no title to convey to them any interest in it, and passed a decree for possession of the same. The appeal to this Court by special leave arose out of a certificate granted by the Calcutta High Court under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution from the High Courts. HELD: Under section 41 of the , the bar is not attracted where the subsequent suit was by the heirs and assigns of that plaintiff. It is open to the parties to prove their title on disputed facts before it to rely on the sale deed or the other evidence which they could have taken in order to establish their title. The proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial Court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and for to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale was effected and the party claiming under him had failed to prove his title to it, the entire 16 as. share in the estate which belonged to PirBaksh would be entitled to a further 2 as. [207 E G] The proper course for such a case would be of ordering an appropriate order in the case. If the sale byyard were real and intended to pass title to Pisra baksh, the plaintiffs would be liable to deliver possession of that property and not those of their co sharers who obtained the 16 as share held by them through P. But no other evidence was adduced on behalf of the appellants to prove this fact. [208 H] The High Court had rightly rejected the second contention of the defendants based on this ground.

The appellant was put up for trial by the Sessions judge of Karimnagar, under section 302, Indian Penal Code, for murder of his brother Baga Rao. He was charged with having separated from his other brothers 's house and had partitioned the family lands. While returning to the village he found that two persons were related to three out of them. The appellant was tried by the trial judge and convicted under section 148 and sentenced to imprisonment for life by the Court of Sessions; but in appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) no request had been made for summoning the magistrate concerned, copies referred to in sub section (4) of section 173 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were supplied, and, as a necessary consequence thereof, he could not make a prayer for adjournment of the case in order to enable them to effectively cross examine those witnesses; and (ii) even when the accused persons were placed on their trial before the Sessions Judge any such grievance was made that they prayed for an adjournment of. the case but the learned Munsiff found that the provisions of section 207A had not been complied with. On appeal by special leave, Held : (i ) In cases exclusively triable by a court of Session it is the duty of the magistrate while holding a preliminary inquiry to satisfy himself that the documents referred in section 173 have been furnished to the accused and if he found, that the police officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf the Magistrate should see to it that is done. The omission complained of in the instant case was a mere irregularity which could be cured by the provisions Of section 537(a) of the . (ii). The omission alleged in the present case was an irregularity which did not render the entire proceedings and the trial null and void, but merely a irregularity which may have been concluded long ago. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor, [1958] S.C.R. 889), followed. In cases solely triable by the court of Sessions it is incumbent on each side to consider whether or not the accused had shown any prejudice. Section 537(1) does not help in appreciating the effect of non compliance with the provisions contained in section 162 or section 360, as the trial before a Sessions judge would be bad and no question of curing an irregularity arises. Abdul Majid vs The State of Punjab, [1954] S,.C. R. 621, followed.

On the report of the appellant, the Industrial Tribunal as well as the High Court gave its finding that the respondent had wilfully discharged the effluent by virtue of a.W. 2 's notice dated 14 6 1956 under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955 (hereinafter referred to as the Act), and held that it was proved that the effluents discharged by the factory of the respondent corrupt potable waters were one for the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality and that therefore the discharge of its effluent through a covered pucca drain was not in any way polluted by reason of the effluent being discharged through the existing channels, that all the papers and reports relating to the tests carried out periodically by the appellant were available for inspection by the respondent municipality and that they could be inspected by appointment. The High Court held against the appellant by special leave from the decision of this Court in M. C. Mehta vs District and Sessions Judge, Jhalawad, on the ground that the provisions of section 153 A(1), infringed his fundamental rights under Articles 14, 19 and 31 and that as it would be a reasonable restriction to the exercise of the fundamental right under article 19 (1)(C) to prevent a nuisance which would affect the public health and fertility of the soil, the protection of article 19 was not available to him. Held, that section 153 G(3) of Bombay District Municipalities Act 1901 as amended in 1955 (Act XI of 1956), contravenes article 19(1)( C) to (d) of 'the Constitution and that it would not be a unreasonable restriction to prevent such nuisance being imposed by section 153 C; that the sanction under section 295G of the Act was not conditional on any objection. A question of fact arises where the circumstances attract the provisions Of section 153 D are (i) when the person to whom the notice has been issued objects to it and the requisition contained therein absolutely, the objection is in substance to the issue of the notice itself which means he objects to the declaration of the municipality that a nuisance existed and (ii) where he consents to it subject to modification, the consent is not absolute. That is to say, some dispute between the person concerned and the Municipality remained outstanding as to the manner of carrying it out and that dispute would be the subject of an enquiry by the Special Officer. Since under section I(3), however, the appointment of a special judicial officer was considered necessary because the dispute between them and the party concerned required investigation and a report from the Officer, there is no need for the appointment to appoint a special judge as a special Judge if such reference has been made to him by the Municipality. The Special Officer apparently made no attempt to construe the provisions in sub section (3) either in substance or substance while he purported to act under section 154A of the said Act. The condition precedent for the exercise Of any power vested in the Municipality in a capricious manner, could not be regarded as the requisite qualification and that would attract the protection afforded by article 19 of the Constitution and was not satisfied.

The appellant was found to be unauctionable property and on the basis of a report by an expert, he was convicted under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act. The High Court dismissed his appeal holding that in order to prove that the articles belonging to a particular railway administration were the property of a railway administration but which had been discarded or rejected for further use would be outside the definition of railway stores; as such the question of punishment under section '3 did not arise, and the conviction was maintained by the Sessions Court. The appellant contended that the prosecution should have first adduced evidence to show that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. He also relied on a decision of the Orissa High Court in Udaya Dalai vs The State, , The High Courts were wrong in holding not proved that it had given an opportunity to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order of conviction, ^ HELD: (i) Though the prosecution is not called upon to prove the articles mentioned in his report, that the goods conformed to the Railway Standards, they held that they belonged to any particular railway Administration in India. The onus shifts to the prosecution to show satisfactorily of possession of railway property within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. [188A B] (ii)It was not possible to spell out any averment to the effect that the items mentioned in the report were used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a Railway. In the case of goods which had not been put to use evidence would have had to be led to establish that they had been manufactured for such us, [188E] (iii)The mere description of the goods as new would not fulfil the requirements of section2(b). Some evidence will have to be lead to the conclusion that the appellant 's goods conform ed to the specifications of the Indian Railway Standards Act. Their Lordships observed that the burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the articles not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Again, the mere description as new will would not fulfilled the requirements for section 2(b) [189C E] (iv)The burden of proving in this regard may be discharge by leading reasons about the identification marks on goods or any some, generality of them not to he found in case of non Railway goods.

The appellants, who were tenants of the demised premises in a short compass, contended before the Trial Court that Smt. Anandi and her mother had lease of the premises for 11 months from May 1, 1964 on payment of monthly rent of Rs. 18 which expired on March 31, 1965. Later, the Act was amended by an Act 14 of 1976 which was replaced by Act 14 1976. The definition of 'Tenant ' in section 3 sub clause (vii)(b) makes the legislative intent manifest that from the date of the Amendment Act came into force on the death of the tenant, his surviving spouse, son daughter and other heir in accordance with personal law as applica ble to him, who had been, in the case of premises leased out for commercial or business purposes, ordinarily carried on business with him/her in such premises as member of his family upto his death. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt Anandi paid and the respondent accepted the rent after determination of the lease. So she was a tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Rajasthan Rent Control Act, 1950 was amended through Ordinance 26 of 1975 which was repealed by Act14 1976 whereby the definition of "Tenant" was amended in place of clause (V). Aggrieved by this amendment, the appellants filed an application under Article 226 of the Consti tution claiming that Smt: Anandi had paid and accepted the lease after determination oth er the lease and so she was not a tenant in the premises. The trial Court dismissed her application on the view that as the appellants had not carried on the business with the tenant during her life time as family business they were not entitled to their benefit, the amended definition of the word 'Tenue ' contained in section 2(1) (iii) was amended and that the suit for eviction from a shop was laid in the Civil Court against the tenant. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that the lease hold right is an heritable estate and on death of Smt. A Goods Car Co. and as per the amendment Act, the commercial or tenancy was not heritable as held in J.C. The finding recorded by all the courts is that after the termination of the contractual tenancy the jural relationship of landlord and tenant between the respondent and Smt. The heritable property or interest in the lease holding right in the tenancy continued to subsist in the tenant Anandi. (2) that under the amended defined definition of tenant in section S.3(vii)(a) of the Act, if one seeks to make avail of the benefit of statu tory tenancy under the Act he must establish to the satis faction of the Court that the surviving spouse,, son or daughter and/or other heir, in case of residential purposes, he/she/they ordinarily had been carrying on business during the life time of the re spondent. (3) That the tenancy came to a terminus with its determination by issuance of notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act and the legal representatives do not succeed to the estate of the deceased tenant so as to prosecute the proceedings. (4) The respondents, who are management authorities in the demised two shops, started a shop on different premises which was governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1 of 1950 for carrying on small kirana business purposes and were entitled to the continuance of the tenancy. Therefore, under the unamended definition of Sec tion 2(2) of that Act, any tenancy is heritable. It is a personal right to the tenant and a reading of the amendment to the definition section would make it clear that so called statutory tenancy tenant has the right to sub let in common with a contrac tual tenant and this is because he also has an interest in it premises occupied by him/she. Therefore the suit cannot be dismissed on that ground alone.

An industrial dispute between the appellant Board and its employees was referred by the Government of Bihar to the Industrial Tribunal. The claim of the workmen that all workmen should have the same and similar benefits was rejected by the Industrial 'Tribunal as well as by the High Court. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (i) the State Government is the financier of the Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum; and (ii) no scheme run by the Board was running at a loss. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) The burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer that burden will have to be borne by the employer like the burden of wage structure in the interest of social justice. [46 D F] (b) In considering the question of provident funds and gratuity which stands more or less on the same footing as provident fund which is also a retiral benefit it will result in reduction of taxation in the shape of income tax. [47 C E] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, ; , referred to. (c) In view of the statutory obligations laid on the Board under various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the company to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident Fund or other amenities the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question. [48 E F] Gramphone Co., vs Its Workers and Workmen, , followed. Gramophonone Co 's Co. v Its Workmen; , (ii). It is a public service institution. It is not expected to make and profit. The contribution to the depreciation reserve is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the gratuity reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the appellant company.

The respondent who is the wife of the appellant filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by her on the ground that her husband was guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate rejected his application holding that there was no evidence to prove that she was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligation and dismissed the application filed by the respondent for maintenance. Thereafter, the matter was taken up in revision before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that the husband having been found to be impotant, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with her husband and hence she was entitled to grant of Maintenance. The High Court also took the view in Bundoo vs Smt. Mahrul Nisa, that the mere ground that the appellant husband was impecotent was not a just cause for refusal of the wife 's refusal to live alongwith her husband, and therefore, she was not entitled to maintenance if her refused to live w.e.f. July 11, 1978. The appellant came up in appeal by special leave against the High court 's order. Allowing the appeal ^ HELD: 1. It is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for theife to refuse live with the husband and therefore the wife is not entitled either to maintenance as he refused to reside with her deceased husband when it seems to him that the ground of impotence which had been held by a number of authorities under the Civil Law to be a good ground not only for restitution of conjugal rights but also for divorce. [706E G] 2. The learned Judge has taken and the principles adumbrated by the Judge apply fully to proceedings for maintenances because as there is no intention on the part of the husband to inflict that cruelty, she should suffer that predicament without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. [700E G; 705A] 3. The decision of the Madras High Court in Velayudhan vs Sukmari, ; , relied on by the learned Judge was purely obiter. It would appear that there is a clear finding cf fact by the trial court which had accepted the view of the Magistrate that the wife failed to prove by convincing evidence that her deceased father was impolent and was, therefore, unable to perform his marital duties, found himself bound by the decisions of the Bombay High Court. [607G] 4. In the instant case there is not a clear concurrent finding of fact by both the Courts below that the appel lant was implotent. The burden lies on the wife. Therefore, it would be pusillanimous to ignore such a valuable safeguard which has been provided by the legislature to a neglected wife. [ 705 A C] 5. It can not be said if there is evidence of cruelty on the par ties that where a husband contracts a marriage with another woman or keeps a mistress this would be deemed to be an " just ground" within the meaning of the second proviso so as to make the refusal of maintenance of the spouse to live With her husband fully justified and entitled to maintain.

The plaintiffs are the Union of India and, therefore, the State of Gujarat. The suit property is described in two parts in the schedule to the plaint which comprised two survey Nos. 162, 163, 164, 165 and 165 on which structures of old Lancer 's lines were standing or certain evacuees were Occupying at the time of the suit. By Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1984 published in the Bhavnagar Darbar Gazette dated 24th January 1948, the Government of India recognised the aforesaid Resolutions dated 19 th January, 1948 and 29th February, 1948. The land was under construction and occupation of a Bus Station and the buildings known as 761 Asharamganj, which were already occupied by the State Lancers and subsequently by refugees, and that the plaintiffs ' case was that by Resolution No 37 dated 1st January, 1964, the entire suit lands mentioned in part 2 of the schedule did not belong to the plain tiff, that the same were occupied by persons known as Rasala Lines and that consequent upon the Bhav nnagar State acceding to the Indian Union, and consequent on the Federal Financial Integrity of States, accommodation, lands and buildings in the use or occupation of the Ex Bhavnagar state forces were transferred to the Government o[ india and became its property. The plaintiffs ' claim was that the suit property was given by the Exaltsi tions to the Defence Department of the State for use but later by refugee, and therefore, they were entitled to recover rent or compensation in respect of this land for the period from 1st Jan. 1954 till delivery of possession. The Union of lndia contested the claim of the plaintiffs that so far as the suit was dismissed in respect thereof as barred by limitation it was not necessary either to deal with the argument of the defendants that the vesting was contem plated in the Resolution dated 19 January, 23, 1948 but it was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of State to dispose of the land. The trial Court decreed the suit in respect to the Parade Ground and dismissed in part on the ground that in respect offla tion of Rasala Line the plaintiff have admitted possession of the disputed plots on the basis that the whole assets of the Bhav Nagar town planning Department had been transferred to them by the orders of their Highness, Bhavnagar State in 1948 and they are collecting Revenue from the farmers.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshop. He was tried for an offence under section 161 Indian Penal Code read with sections 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947, and with abusing his position as a public servant, obtained on illegal gratification of Rs. 150 from one Nanak Singh before a Magistrate who convicted him under section I(1) (d) and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively in regard to the same. The appellant challenged his conviction and sentence before the High Court of Bombay which found favour with the Supreme Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that he was not an 'officer ' within the meaning of that term as used in section 21(9), Indian Penal code; and that the words "public servant" meant some person employed to exercise to some extent and in certain circumstances a delegated function of Government, it was argued that the appellant being a metal Examiner known as Chaser in the railway Carriage Workshops had not delegated to him by the supreme authority some portion of its regulating and coercive powers nor was he appointed to represent the State in its relations to individual subjects; and (2) that the conviction and sentences imposed upon him by these findings could not be challenged before this Court by way of a writ petition. Held, that the order passed by the High court of Bombay in 12 Bombay High Court Reports 1 must be held to have been affirmed and the appellant must succeed. Ram Krishan vs Delhi State ([1952] S C. R. 369) distinguished.

In a suit filed by the respondent for permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collector cum Deputy Excise and Taxation Commissioner from auctioning his half share, the contention of the respondent was that a part of the building standing on the said plot of land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and therefore his halfshare was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of proviso to sub section (l) of Section 60 of the Code Civil Procedure, 1908. The Trial Court upheld both these contentions, but dismissed the suit with costs. Hence this appeal on the question whether section 60 of Act applies to an attached attachments and sale in revenue recovery proceedings adopted under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 as being applicable to an attachment and salein execution of a decree. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: As per the opening words of sub sec.(1) of section 60, it is clear that section has no application to attachment and sell in any proceedings other than in execution of such a decree of a civil court. [848 B D] The respondents suit was liable to be dismissed on this ground alone. [881 E F] Section 60 does not apply to an seizure and sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said Act is concerned, it contains a complete code providing for the modes, and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the said act and the sale which was notified was also under the provi sions of the Punjab Act.

The appellant was the holder of two separate awards made on January 31, 1963 and January 18, 1962 under section 59(a) and the other under section 61 of the (the Act). Both were in respect of the lands acquired by the State Government. The Special Deputy Collector awarded a total compensation of Rs. 4,29,360. This was received in April, 1964 and by two separate guage awards dated January 31. 1963 and March 19, 1965 he awarded a sum of Rs . 20,45,000. In making the assessment also the respondent as in the case of estate duty assessment in respect thereof made an addition to the amount already determined under the award made by the Special Deputy Commissioner for those lands. He had paid this amount at the time of reassessment and the respondent filed returns with the assessing authority for the purposes of computation of the compensation payable, which included the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Collector in respect whereof the estate duty assessed was Rs. 18,29ions to be Rs. 20,46,360 as against Rs. 17,49,361. On February 11, 1964 the Special Dy. Collector awarded, a total sum of RS. 4.29, 60.57 as compensation and this amount was received by the heirs of Rashid, who had no interest in the disputed lands. The respondent as well as another person were not accepted by the authorities. Thereafter the appellant was called upon to deliver a further statement of Account. No objection was raised on behalf of the appellant that it had only one claim against the estates and nothing more and the right to claim further compensation was a precarious right, being merely a right to litigate a chancy and dicey right, which could not be elevated to the status of an asset or property and as such there was no question of any property having escaped assessment. The Assistant Controller of Estate Duty held that the fact that land references were filed against the awards of the Special Chief Deputy Collector under section 18 of the Land Acquisition Act and therefore it had escaped assessment to duty, but he rejected the same on the ground that the lands in question could not constitute property passing on the death of the deceased and that even assuming that any asset or asset chargeable to estate duty had escaped assess ment, the notice was illegal and without jurisdiction because such escapement was not due to any omission or failure on the part of the accountable person. The appeal filed by the appellant against the order of assessment was dismissed in limine by the Andhra Pradesh High Court which held that having regard to the enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands, such property could not form part of an estate of the respondents and consequently the order passed by the Assistant Controller under section 62(a), had no application. Hence these appeals. On behalf of Union of India it was contended: (1) that a fresh and independent right to 'receive extra compensation ' accrue to the heirs and that it was only right which the deceased had been the right had against the correctness of the awards and nothing other more; and (2) that in the instant case the respondent had issued it on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to tax because the lands had vested in the Government long prior to his death but he contended that upon such acquisition of lands, the right could not have accrued to the estate of deceased before the relevant date. Allowing the appeals and setting aside the order dated February 11. 1964, HELD: 1. The very issuance of the notice under section59(a)(i) which was done on a basis clearly unsustainable in law is liable to be quashed on this ground. [331B] 2.

The appellant 's election to the post of Director was challenged by him on various grounds. It was contended that section 73FF(1)(b) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 came into force on 12 5 1986. The Registrar of the Cooperative Societies by his order dated 7 12 1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors of the Bank holding that appellant was defaulter under section 73F(1) of . It was further contended that the expression 'makes default ' or 'stands disqualified ' occurring in section 73BFF(2) meant that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18 August 1986 to 21.10.1986 was extinguished and hence he was not at all eligible to contest the election. The Assistant Registrar, Cooperative Societies, Nagpur by his Order dated 7 December 1987 removed him from the committee of Directors holding that the appellant was defaulted in payment of loan instalments as referred to in section 74F(2). The order of the Assistant Registrar dated 7 July 12 1987 was served on the appellant on 8th December 1988. The appellant ' appeal against this order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar of Cooperative Societies. Thereafter, the appellant filed a writ petition challenging the order removing him from its Committee of directors, contending that section 74FF became applicable from 6.8.1986 as per Government Notification issued on 18 4 1986 and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21.11.86, on 18th August 1986 when he was elected as Director, he was defaulter by section 73 AB(1). The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that Section 73FF became operative from 6 8.1986 and that since he had repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section 78 of the Act on 18.886, it was for him to have made default until repayment of the loan and that in view of the fact that he repaid the loan before 7th December 1987, it would be invalid. Allowing the appeal by special leave the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant having failed to repay the entire amount before the notice under Section 78(1 ) of the Societies Act was issued, he is clearly not a defaulter in presenti on the date he contested the election and since he paid all the debts on 21st October 1986 and thereafter he could not be 'absolved of the disqualification. [683F G] 1.2 There was no room for holding that section 78(I) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act 1960 came to force from 6th August, 1986 when the appellant contested the elections; and that it would not exonerate the appellant ' from being in default on non payment of instalment on due date.

Rule 189 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules empowers Government to reduce or withdraw a pension. In order to avoid punishment the Government servant must be given opportunity of defence in accordance with the procedure specified in Note I to r 33 of the said rules. The State Government 's power to reduce the amount of pension payable to the respondent was interpreted and this Court held that merely because a Government servant retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation he could not escape the liability for misconduct and negligence or financial irregularities which he may have committed during the period of his service and the Government was entitled to withhold or reduce the pension granted to a government servant. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. Under Rule 189 expressly confers power on Government to withhold/ withdraw or withdraw any part of it if the pensioner be convicted of serious crime or be found to have been guilty of grave misconduct while he was in service or after completion of his Service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government Servant depend upon the good conduct of the Government servants. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 further provides that before any order reducing or withdrawing any part (of the pension is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be afforded opportunity of Defence in accordance to the procedure contained in Note 1 to r. 33 of Bombay Civil Service Rules, Conduct. Discipline and Appeal Rules has been initiated against the respondent after the respondent ceased to be in service of the State Government. [189 E F] 2.1 It is not correct to say that the reduction of pension by 50% was disproportionate to the charges proved against the Respondent.

Section 3(1) of the Orissa (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 provides that no order made under this Act by the State Government or the District Magistrate shall be called in question in any court. Section 3(4) enacts that if a landlord wants to bring a suit to eject his tenant he has to apply to the District magistrate for permission to do so. After the District Judge makes an order on the landlord 's application the party aggrieved by the order can apply in revision to the Commissioner within 30 days and the Commissioner, in exercise of his revisional jurisdiction, has to deal with the revision application under section 3(3). If he is satisfied that the District Court had acted illegally or with material irregularity or had wrongly refused to act, he may confirm or set aside. The appellant instituted a suit against the respondents for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that they needed the premises in suit to carry on their own business in the shop and they alleged that they had applied for permission under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act, but the Collector dismissed it by his order dated February 3, 1955. The respondent filed an appeal before the District judge but was allowed by the single Judge who found that the appellants ' suit was not maintainable because the notice given by the appellants under section 108 of the Evidence Act, which was also invalid in law. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 112(3) of , was invalid inasmuch as it did not show that the notice issued by them was received by the applicants and that the starting point of limitation under section 128 of the , had not been determined. ^ Held, (i) The jurisdiction conferred on the Commissioner by section 3 (1) is exactly similar to the jurisdiction conferred upon the High Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, and as such a nullity. In the instant case the order passed by the District Munsiff was not a nullity because it did go to the root of the matter and would, if upheld, lead to the conclusion that the impugned order was a nullity; (ii) The power conferred on an authority under section 7 F to revise the orders passed by him is very wide. In other words, whenever it is brought to the notice of the State Govt either by a party aggrieved ' by the Order passed by Commissioner or otherwise that the order is passed by a District Magistrate of one District when the property in question is situated in another district outside his jurisdiction, a party would be entitled to urge before a civil court that the application purported to have been granted by him was wholly invalid and a plea that an order had been passed by more than 30 days before the said date, even though it didsole come within the mischief of section 3 which applied only to cases where irregularity or illegality had been committed by the Magistrate in granting or refusing, to grant permission, could be raised in a civil proceeding.

The President of India appointed the Punjab Public Service Commission for the purpose of conducting examinations and procedure for the Court. After the examination was over by a Magistrate, he was removed from his office on May 24, 1983 from the office of the Member of the Selection Committee, which was then fixed as the date of hearing of the reference. The Chief Minister of Punjab joined this service in June, 1983. He later resigned and took charge of the post after about four years. In April, 1984 he filed an affidavit denying the allegations made against him. Thereafter, when he filed a writ petition before the High Court for quashing the said order, the same was dismissed by a learned single Judge who held that it was non compliance with Rule 2 of Order XLVII of the Supreme Court Rules, 1966. Against the judgment and order of dismissal the present appeal is filed under Article 136 of the Constitution before this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant in this Case: (1) The President 's opinion that a prima facie case exists for an enquiry and report by this Court should be given to discharge functions which ordinarily fall within the jurisdiction of a trial court, civil or criminal; (2) it would be impossible for him to prove his case unless he was allowed to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: ( 1 ) The President has made the Reference. [698 G] (a) It will not be conducive to justice to decide the reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. [643 E F] (b) Though the power of the President to make a reference to this Court under Article 317(1) is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority, the Court has the power to summon and examine witnesses but nothing contained therein can be read to mean that after deciding which witnesses should be summoned and examined, evidence must be recorded by this court itself. [sele sum] (c) The inquiry contemplated under the Article is into the facts themselves and facts also so as to enable this Court to pronounce upon the question whether the allegations against the Chairman or member are proved at all; and the purpose will be served by expending our own time in recording the evidence of various witnesses except for the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses. [470 G] The inquiry which this Court is required to hold is not into the limited question whether, on the basis of facts found by some another body establish misbehaviour in one case and misbehaviour or incapacity in those others. Their function is to find upon facts and their duty is to pronounce whether the facts found are established.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. 4 of 1939), on the allegation that the temple installed therein being a public endowment fell within the four corners of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. The Subordinate Judge decreed the appellants plaintiffs suit holding that the deity installed in the temple as a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The High Court reversed the decision of the subordinate Judge, and held that the Endowment was of a public nature and that a private endowment fell under the four boundaries of the statute and that the respondent had not application and that tile order passed by the respondent regarding the management was set aside. In appeal before this Court it was contended for the appellants that the High Court had overlooked the fact that (1) the endowment was of purely a private nature; (2) though (a) an idol installed in a temple, the worship of the deity is a necessary concomitant of the installation of the deities and therefore, the mere factum of worship would not determine the nature of the endowment, which could be of a private character; and (3) where the evidence showed that there was provision for a scheme to be framed by associating the members of the public at large and (b) where, however, a document is available to prove the nature and origin of the Endowment and the recitals of the document show that the control and management vests either in a large body body of persons or in the members or of the community, there is nothing to show that any contribution was called for from members of tho public. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) It is well settled that under the Hindu law, however it is not only permissible but also very common to have private endowments which though are meant for charitable purposes yet the dominant intention of the founder is to instal a family idol in the Temple and worship the same in order to effectuate the spiritual benefit to the family of the founders and his descendants and to perpetuate the memory of the object. [830C] (b). The primary distinction between private and public endowment, is that whereas in the former the beneficiaries are specified individuals, in the latter they are the general public or a class thereof. It follows that one of the important tests to determine the character of the dedication would be to find out if the management of the property dedicated is in the hands of the strangers or members of a community, then the endowment can only be regarded as public intended to benefit the general body of worshippers. In other words, the beneficiaries in a public trust are the [832E F] (c) If the mainisations were the members 'of the public who worship as a matter of right then the real purpose is to confer benefit on God; but where, therefore, it was proved that the intention of testator or the founder was to dedicate the temple merely for the benefit of the members Of the family or their descendants, the endowment would be of private nature. [883G H] (d) The question as to whether a religious endowment is a public or private one must depend on the application of legal concept of a deity and private endowment. It is manifest that whenever a dedication is made for religious purposes and a deity installed therein in a Temple, the belief of the temple is a mandatory consequence of the intention to dedicates the temple to public and not to the members thereof. [850A] (e) The provisions applicable to the case clearly show that sufficient care has been taken by the Pani family to see that the dedication to the society deity is not changed even if the family becomes extinct.

The appellant Bank entered into certain contracts and received monies for payment of money against the supplies under the contract. For the purpose of carrying out this arrangement, Malhotra executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The power of Attorney stated: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into various contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat Bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorneys have agreed to finance contracts and to advance moneys to Malhotra against his bills for payments under the contracts. For this purpose the appellant Bank executed irrevocable power Of attorney in their favour on July 12, 1948. The document appointed the appellant to be the attorney 's of Malhotra "to present and submit supply bill regarding our contracts to proper officer and/or authority of the Government Departments concerned. To obtain cheques for sums payable to the appellant under the said contract directly in their own name or in our names in payment of such bills or other amounts and to cash and to receive the amount thereof and appropriate such receipts towards repayment of the advances made or to be made hereafter and all other monies due from us to the attorney as aforesaid."
