The document was not a pay order. A pay order was revocable mandate. It gave the payee no interest in the fund. The appellant filed objections in the execution proceedings. On September 11, 1952, the objections were dismissed. On December 12, 1952. the appellant filed a suit in the Court of Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhatmal asking for a declaration that he was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhat had no right to attach it. The Trial Court held that the appellant was the assignee of his bill and decreed the suit. On appeal by the respondent, the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no transfer of the decree or of the claim which was the subject matter of the pending appeal as the borrower continued to be in the owner and the lender was merely authorised to act as his agent. Aggrieved by this decision of the High court, the appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The question whether a document amounts to an equitable assignment or not is primarily one of construction but we may mention a few decisions which throw light on the matter. [704 C] Palmer vs Carey , wherein it was held that an agreement to finance the borrower and a power of agent even date to receive monies due to the borrower under certain contracts had the effect of an equitable Assignment of the funds. In Loonkaran Sethiya vs State Bank of Jaipur, [1951] S.C.R.

The respondent was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The said company had a Provident Fund Scheme for its employees, but that provident fund was not recognised by the assessee. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. But on further appeal to the Tribunal by the respondent, the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ' it was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income tax Act, 1961 and thus exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3)(ii). The High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee, but on further appeals to this Court. HELD: (1) Section 17 has nothing to do either with deductions or with exemptions. It is merely a provision defining the expression 'salary ' '. [436E F] (2) Even assuming that the income in question is not salary and the same cannot be said to be either interest on the securities. income from house Pro perty; profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. it has to be considered as "income from other sources" and brought to tax under section 56. [441A B] (3) The expression 'profits in lieu of ' salary ' is plain and unambiguous but, therefore there is no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court.

The Bihar Legislature passed the Bihar Act, in so far as it prohibited the slaughter of cows and calves of cattle and of a specified age or not less than one year old. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the impugned Act violated articles 19(1)(g), 14(2) and 31(3); (ii) section 3 of the Bihar, and (iii) the provisions of article 19(5) offended article 19 (6). HELD: The ban on slaughter of buffaloes was reasonable but was of those which were useless. [688 F] The test laid down in article 48 is not a reasonable restriction imposed on the butchers who slaughter 25,02,000 bovine cattle and buffalo and strike down the ban on the slaughter. Section 3 of Bihar Act provides for the acquisition by appropriate authorities of the right to carry on their respective trades and section 4 prohibits the slaughter or slaughter of she buffaloes, bull, bullock or heifer and a new schedule specifying only (1) cows, (2) male and female buffaloes and (3) buffalo calves. There is no difference between her buffaloes, bulls and bullocks and it was not possible for the Legislature to have intended that the provisions contained in article 19 must be struck down as being unconstitutional. The question whether a total ban on slaughtering of a she buffaloes after the slaughter would fall within the purview of cl. (6) of article 31 is a matter for legislative determination and not one for legislative determina tion. [690 C,F G] The Bihar Act in so much as it prohibits the washing of bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) or running cattle (coking buffaloes and buffaloes) without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness is reasonable is also valid.

During the period July 1936, an explanation was called for from him under Standing Order 16(1) that his services will stand terminated as from 31st January. 1956; and on December 5, 1955, a memorandum was served on him by the respondent terminating his services with effect from January 31, 1956. The respondent submitted his explanation on December 3, 1955 in which he said that the charge was vague and that after 1949 he was not in any way concerned with the preparation of summaries and annual statements of accounts of the consumers department, and that as the charge contained a sum of Rs. 1,05894 7 which represented the amount of bills of the Central Railway had been deducted twice in the accounts. The company submitted his explanations on December 2, 1955 and December 3. 1955, to the Labour Commissioner, but no action was taken against him until further orders pending some investigation against the respondent. On January 2, 1956, the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court at Nagpur, for quashing the orders passed against him or for reinstatement etc. The preliminary objections taken were these: (i) that the Standing Orders did not apply to the respondent, though he was an employee within the meaning of that expression in section 2(1); and (ii) that as a result of the Standing Order, which provided for penalties for misconduct the respondent had a right to move the High court under article 32 of the Constitu tion for quashing such orders. Held, that the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act did not empower the Labour Court to interfere with its order in writ jurisdiction under Article 226 or article 227 of the constitution for correcting errors apparent on the face of it or erroneous or collateral errors. That the relief which was asked for is an equitable relief and the mere fact that a person has a ticket, particularly when the exercise of such an option is likely to defeat the very purpose for which tickets are issued in an industrial establishment did not make a person so employed an "employee" within the word " workman " as defined in section 3 (1) of the Act. Though the Standing order provided for penal consequences but no penalty was imposed, it was clear that there need not be one set of Standing Orders for all employees and the Standing orders in question being confined to those employees only to whom tickets had been issued would make employees synonymous with workmen a result negatived by two separate definitions given in Standing Order No. 2 (a) and (b).

The appellant is an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. The company went into production in the year 1964 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year 1967 68. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project had been a separate establishment in respect Of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year1964 63. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Plant could not be treated as a separate Establishment because under the Act, a company is itself an establishment, so that all units of a Company like Hindustan Steel Ltd will constitute one establishment. Since this Project had not been earning any profits the Tribunal directed payment of bonus at 4% of wages prescribed by the Act. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellant it was contended: (1) that the word "establishment" has been used in section 1(15), as an establishment owned, managed or controlled by a person or body other than a Government company or a corporation, and consequently, the , company is not entitled to claim bonus under section 16; (2) that even the establishment employing less than 20 persons will be a part of the parent establishment consisting of the factory. HELD: (i) While it would be a strange method for construction of language to hold that the establishment referred to in the main part of Section 3 will include all different departments, undertakings and branches which are owned controlled or managed by persons other than companies. It is difficult to say that, although the company, Hindustan Steel Limited has a number of undertakings, 635 separate accounts are kept for each separate undertaking, there was nothing wrong in calculation of bonus on this account. [631 C E] (ii) The Tribunal took into consideration the fact that separate balance sheet was prepared for each unit and separate profit and losses statement for all the units of the Company must be prepared and, for that purpose, quarterly statements of accounts have to be sent by each unit to the Head Office. There was nothing in the calculation of Bonus on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. The gross profits which could be earned or incurred by the company itself. The calculation of the bonus on the principle of " parity ' is justified because, the head office was working for all those units though as a distinct unit.

Section 3 of the Cess Act which provides for levy of cess on water consumed by persons carrying on certain industry and by the local authorities with a view to augment the resources of the Central Board and the State Boards constituted for the prevention and control of water pollution, provided that the cess is payable on the person carrying on the specified industry. The cess levied in both cases by the said assessing authori tys for demanding water cess from the sugar manufacturers on the ground that this industry falls under Item 15 of Schedule I to the Act. Sometime later, the Bihar and Haryana High Court have taken the view that sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 of the Sched ule I and therefore, they would come under Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products". On the other hand, the Andhra Pradesh State Board for Prevention and Control of Water Pollution vs Andhra Pradesh Rayons Ltd. & Ors. (supra) and Rajasthan State Electricity Board vs The Cess Appellate Committee & Anr., JT there fore, have to look merely at what is clearly said. There is no room for any intendment and there is not room for bringing within the provi sions of the Act anything by impli cation. Unless we give the botanical meaning to the word 'vegetable ' it is not possible to conclude sugar cane as vegetable. The High Court in Civil Writ Jurisdiction Case Nos. Ltd. vs State of Bihar & Ors., held that Sugar manufacturing industry was one of the main source of causing water pollu tion and since the object of the Pollution Act and the Cess act were intended to control water pollution and since they are to be given a wider meaning sugar industry would be covered by the Act, that sugar conse quently means what belongs to the plant kingdom as opposed to the animal kingdom, and it has a wider amplitude. It was further of the view of this Court that in interpreting the word "veget able" it is well settled that if a particular industry falls within the realm of taxation, must be judged by the predominant purpose and process and not by any ancillary or incidental process carried on by a particular Industry in running its business; that is to say, they are items of that industry and not those which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry fifteen. The word 'revegetrable ' has been defined in many ways. In the World Book it is defined as follows: "In the usual sense, the word vegetable is applied to those plants whose leaves, stalks, roots or tubers are used for food, such as lettuce,paragus, cabbage, beet and turnip. It also includes several plants whose fruits are the edible portions, as peas, beans, melons and tomatoes. " In the Concise Oxford Dictionary, 3rd Ed. p. 1365, it is described as: "Plant, esp. herbaceous plant, used for culi nary purposes or for feeding cattle, e.g., cabbages, potato bean, delion, etc." The term 'vequalification ' has also been defined as : "a general term used as an adjective in refer ring to any kind of plant life or plant product, viz. "vetgetable matter". " However, 'Were is no rere not merely a substantial expression but a combination of changes in form. The essential point thus is that in manufacture some thing is brought into existence which is different from that originally existed in the sense that the thing produced is by itself a commercially different commodity whereas in the case of processing it is only necessary to produce a commer cially different article. processing essentially effectuates a change in form, contour, physical appearance or chemical combination or otherwise by artificial or otherwise By artificial means and in its more complicated form involves progressive action in performing, producing or making something.

The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of his tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The Appellate Authority passed an order of eviction against the appellant. Before the High Court it was contended inter alia, (1) that the practice of the profession of an advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960; (2) that section 10(5)(a)(iii) used the expression 'business ' only and not the expression "profession". Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the "business" was 'business within the of that expression in Section 10 (3)(a) of Andhra Pradesh Building (Lease Rent & Eviction) Act, 1961. [14C] 2. It is not a sound principle of construction tn interpret expressions used in one Act with reference to their use in another Act; more so, if the two Acts in which the same word was used were not cognate Acts, it would be anamolous to hold that all the provisions of the Act including Section 4 which provides for the determination of fair rent and Section 10 which bars the eviction of tenants apply to nonresidential buildings owned by an Advocate but not Section 10 of the Rent Control legislation. [15D E] M.P. Sethurama Menon vs Thaiparambath Kunhukutty Amma, [1949] 2 K . B. D. 256; referred to.

The respondent deposited a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 with M/s India Supplies which the appellants were partners on the condition that interest would be payable @ 7/9 percent per month and that the respondent would be entitled to withdraw the deposit on demand. The suit was filed in the court of the First Civil Judge, Kanpur. The evidence was concluded before the civil judge, Kanpur, and by an order dated 12 May, 1964 the trial Court decreed the suit in favour of the respondent, but at the trial the issues were first whether it was a case where money was deposited under an agreement, that it was payable on demand and therefore the limitation would commence from the date of demand and the suit was instituted within three years from the demand. In appeal to this Court it was contended that Article 60 was the relevant Article because if was a ease of loan it was paid on demand; there could not be any payment of money in cash and adjustment entries were made in the books of the appellant, that when money in specie was not paid it would fall short of limitation, and that no payment of property in cash would depend merely on the terms of the document but had to be judged from the intention of the parties and the circumstances of the case. HELD: The appeal must fail. An award is something more than a mere loan of money. It will depend on the facts of each case whether the transaction is clothed with the character of a deposit of money, and the surrounding circumstances at the time of the transaction, the pecuniary position of the party are all overwhelming factors to antiquats the oral evidence as well as the documentary evidence of the Respondent that the amount was deposited with the appellant. [578 C E] V. E. A. Annamalai Chettiar & Anr., vs section V. section Veerappa Chettiar, , followed. Pipi and Subbaih Chetty & Ors. vs Visalakshgi Achi, I.L.R. , referred to. The mere fact that money in question was not said to be paid would not make the respondent a loan if money in difference to pay is made out or adjusted with the amount of consideration by the appellant but would not mean that money would be kept in deposit with the appel lant at the same time as the rest of the writing.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India. The petitioner made an application to this Court under Article 32 in Writ Petition (Crl). No. 292/86 challenging that order of detention. On 15th May, 1986 the Vacation Judge of this Court made an order for the release of the detenu on parole till further orders on the condition that he will report to the Directorate of Revenue, New Delhi every day and the Directorate would be at liberty to direct him to explain his fu ness during this time. In the mean time the respondents will be at li ber liberty to make an application for revocation of the parole if any misconduct or any other activity comes to their notice which requires the revocation of his parole. The prayer in the Writ Petition was that the period of parole, that is, from 15th of May, 1985 till February 22, 1987 should not be added to the period, of detention speci fied in the impugned order under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA and the period for one year had expired on February 20, 1987, that the impugned detention order had lapsed and the detenu became entitled to be freed from the order of deten tion. The writ petition was dismissed by saying that: "In the premises it must according ly be held that the periods of parole have to be excluded in recokning the period" of detention under sub section (1) section 3 of the . " The petitioner filed a Writ Petition in this Court challenging that Order of detention on various grounds. The main contentions raised were: (i) that the order had not been complied with as there are no written summons served on the detenu; and (ii) the petitioner was already in custody at the time the order was served and since the detenu was already In custody, the order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order would be necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the writ petition this Court, HELD: (1)(i) The fact remains that only one contention had been raised. There is absolutely no basis for the alle gation in paragraph 2 of the Writ peti tion that if the Court had indicated to Mr. Jethmalani in course of arguments that the submission on this limited point did not find favour with the Court, he would have proceeded to argue the other points. It was open to Mr., Jethmalani to make full submissions on all as pect arising in the writ Petition. That having not been done, it was improper on the part of Mr. Saran to raise these allegations in paragraph ly. [848D E] (ii). The fact that the detenu is already in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining au thority in making an order of preventive detention.

The semi skilled/skilled workers are working for a reasonably long period, on continuous basis. While the petitioners were not satisfied with the order of the Director General, Posts and Telegraphs Department in the Postal & Telecommunication Department, they filed petitions seeking regularisation of casual labourers, payment of interim relief, payment Of bonus, supply of dresses, leave and medical facilities etc. They claimed that they are being paid wages far less than the minimum pay payable under the pay scales applicable to regular employees and that even though some of them have been working for the last ten years as casual labourers they were very low and far less below the salary and allowances paid to the regular employees of the Posts and telegraphs Department belonging to each of the categories referred to above, and secondly no scheme has been prepared by the Union of India to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits, such as increments, pension, leave facilities etc which are enjoyed by those who had been recruited regularly. They stated that they were being exploited by the U.P. Government for quite sometime past, which was being granted to regular staff at the rate of 3/4th full of the minimum of the pay scale of semi skilled (Rs. 210 270) or skilled ( Rs.260 350 as the case may be and that there should not be any variation in the respective job con tent. The representations received by them were considered and rejected. Since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are not being regularly employed, they have filed the present petitions seeking similar reliefs, which were granted by this Court in Writ Petition No. 302 of 1986. Disposing of the matters, this Court, HELD: 1.1 On the facts and in the circumstances of the case, it is directed that the petitioners shall prepare a scheme on rational basis for absorbing as far as possible the casual labourers who have been continuously working continuously for more than one year in the Posts & Telegraphs and Department at the rates equivalent to the minimum wages in the pay of regularly employed workers in the corresponding cadres but without any increments with effect from 5th February, 1986 on which date the first of the two petitions, namely, Writ Petition NO. 302/86 was filed. The petitioners are entitled to corresponding Dearness Allowance and Addl. Dearness Allowance, if any, payable thereon. [610G] 1.2 On the fact that the Petitioners belong to category of causal labourers and are being not regularly employed and there is no justification for doing so. Such a classification is violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. It is also opposed to the spirit of Article 7 of the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, 1966 which exhorts all States parties to ensure fair wages and equal wages for equal work. [625C] 2.

In 1946 the assessee firm was levying interest. By Income tax, however, within four years of the expiry of his status as a partner, which could be taken only after he did not make a return in accordance with section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, but even before the end of the accounting year ending on March 31, 1950, the assessee filed a voluntary " return on January 5, 1950 showing year 's income for the assessment year 1945 46. The Income tax Officer included the sum of Rs. 59026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed him on it for the assess ment year 194546.59,026, which was the amount not chargeable to income tax but he added a footnote to the return to the following effect: " My wife has sold her old ornaments and deposited the sum Rs.59026 In the account year corresponding to the assessment years 1946 47 there were six cash credits aggregating to Rs. 4,935 in the name of the assesses 's wife. Before, however. the Income tax officer could take any action the assessee submitted a voluntary return on March 14, 1950 to which he replied that he was entitled under section 22(3) to make a " voluntary " returns on January May 5, 1945 of his income for that year. The Incometax Officer included this sum in the net income of Rs 5902,6 in his total income as correct, but on the question whether the notice issued under section 34 could be said to have been completed before March 31 , 1950, as required by section 34 (3) of Income tax (Amendment) Act and if no return was made within the time fixed by the notice, the department should have proceeded under section 23(4). The High Court on a reference, held that the Income Tax Officer had reason to believe that by reason of the omission or failure on the part of an assessee to make ' voluntary " declaration on January5, 1950 (after the assessee had filed a return which was not a complete one year after and since he did so he was precluded from issuing a notice under section 24(2) within the assessment Year, and that, therefore, there was no necessity to serve any notice under that section. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the answer given by the High Court of Bombay was correct in all the circumstances of this case. The High court was right in holding that it was a complete mistake to think that section 22 23(1) Of the Indian Incometax Act required filing of a voluntary ' return showing loss at any time before assessment. It could not be said that even a return filed in compliance with a notice tinder section 22 (2), if filed belatedly under section 20, would be a return showing an income below the taxable limit. The notice under s.22 was not invalid because it was not accompanied by a valid " return". Such a return could be filed under section 25(1). It was open to him to make his return in the present case as soon as he did and had done so, for this purpose no question could arise under section 33.

The first petitioner is a registered Central Trade Union claiming to represent about 85 per cent of its officers working in the various nationalised banks. The first petitioner 's grievance is that while the scheme under implementation postulates all appointments to be by nomi nation, some of its employees who are not workmen, is to be appoint ed by the Central Government. The second petitioner ' s contention is that whereas clause 3 of the Scheme does not justify or support the impugned circu lar. Dismissing the writ petitions and modifying the scheme as regards non workmen employees to warrant the same type of representation as in the case of the petitioners in transfer cases, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The object of the Act is to nationalise the banks in order to, as stated in the preamble to the Act, "control the heights of the economy and to meet progressively, and serve better, the needs of development of the Nation in conformi ty with the national policy and objectives". [855A] 1.2. The Act does not contemplate a manage ment unmindful of the true and legitimate interest of the employees. In a nationalised bank, everyone is as much an employee as he is an employer. There is no antithesis to be tween the management and the employees, and the distinction that traditionally existed prior to nationalisation is no longer applicable. The true management culture is indeed the cul ture that represents the various interests of all persons specified under section 9 as well as the larger and wider interest of national economy as postulated in the Preamble to theAct. [856E G] 1:3.

The assessee, who was the respondent, was imposed penalties imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for concealment of certain particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner, who declined to stay the recovery of penalty imposed. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution, and the High court allowed the petition holding that the Tribunal had the power to stay proceedings as also the collection of penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction, The Revenue came up in appeal by special leave against the judgment of the High COurt. Allowing the appeal this Court HELD: (1) By section 254(6), the power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal has been given to the Income tax Officer only when an appeal is presented under section 246 which and which would be to the appellate Assistant Commissioner and not to the Appel late Assistant Commissioner. [69 F G] (2) The powers which have been conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Tribunal with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental to make the exercise of those power, fully effective. In the instant case when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction it impliedly grants the powerof doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. [72 1 A] (3) The power of grant of stay is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It confers power on the High. Tribunal with wide possible amplitude. [76 G H, 77 A B] Union of India vs M/s. T. K. Motor Service, , followed.

The respondent was a constable. While posted as I.D. Police Station, intiathok district the Sub divisional Magistrate ordered the sub divisional magistrate to make an inquiry in respect of the charges which were the subject matter of the departmental trial and submitted a report to the District Magistrate recommending the transfer of the respondent for enquiry. On receipt of the said report the respondents filed the present petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging its dismissal from service and contending that the order of dismissal was invalid on account of serious irregularities in the discharge of his duties. Held, (per Subba Rao and Mudholkar, JJ.): (i) The power conferred upon the Superintendent of Police by para 486 of the Police Regulations is only administrative directions which are embodied in para 489(2). (ii) The various provisions of the Criminal Procedure Code read with section 483 of the Code indicate that para. 86 does not apply to a case where a magisterial inquiry is ordered; and (iii) the departmental enquiry was held subsequent to the completion of the magisterial enquiry and therefore it fell within the express terms of para 489 of the Regulations. [678 B] Per Hidayatullah, Subba Rao, J., dissenting). (i)(a) The order of suspension made by the High Court did not express its opinion on the other questions raised and argued before it. In view of that finding they found it unnecessary for them to express any opinion upon other arguments which had been advanced on behalf of the respondents.

Rule 8 of the Central Health Service Rules, 1963 ( '1963 Rules for short) provided that where the case of an officer appointed to any post in the grade of General Duty Officer Grade I or Specialists as the case may be, is considered for promotion to any posts in Supertime Grade II under this sub rule, the cases of all persons senior to such officer in the grades of General duty Officer, Grade I/or Specialists (Grade I) as the ease may be shall also be considered notwithstanding that they may not have rendered 10 years or 8 years of service respectively, in those grades. The appellant, who was the seniormost and otherwise qualified and was promoted as Director of Health Services, sought redress for his grievance praying inter alia on the ground that promotions were in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules. The principal contention was that their promotion were in violation of rule. Section 8(3) which provided for absorbing departmental candidates holding posts in categories 'A ' supertime scale Rs. 1600 2000 category 'B ' super time scale with grade I, fell in the category and make it obligatory on the State to treat them as equivalent to the strength of the speciality and the filling in of such post shall be governed by rule 8(2). The appellant contended that the promotion was in contravention Of Rule 8 of 1969 Rules. It was further urged that when a post is created in a certain grade, category or cadre, and it is to be filled in, some one who is already in that grade, a category or Cadre cannot be transferred to that post and the post so vacated by him can he filled in either by promotion or by direct recruitment as the situation warrants according to the rule and as determined by the quota rule. Allowing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant was not in any way concerned with the filling of a post in Super time grade II because he had not put in 8 years ' service in the speciality to which he belonged was ever promoted overriding his claim for supertime grade II from which date he claims as being eligible for promotion for promotion. This is clear from the 1966 Rules and when he declined to accept promotion, he was never superseded by any one junior to him in his speciality to whom he belongs was ever earlier promoted, overriding his claims to super time grade I. [53 E F; 55 B] 1.2 Rule 8(4) of the Rules provided that if the case is considered within a reasonable time it be provided that there would be a pool of 19 unspecified Specialists ' posts in supertime Grade Il and 9 unspecified posts also in super time Grade II. Once an unspecified specialists ' grade post was converted into a specified post and assigned to a speciality it can only be filled by promotion from amongst those originally belonging to generalists ' Grade only may be examined.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about an agrarian re ordering so pivotal to the progress of our rural economy. Haryana, happily a granary of our country is one of its States where land reform laws are likely to generate some great changes by banishing big concentration of Natur 's bounty in a few feudal hands creating an enthusiastic sense of distributive justice and exploiting the productive potential of land by the possessive passion of the landless many. So strategic is land reform that special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme, though its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time. has made for ambiguity, obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. Indeed, the conflict of opinion at the High Court level and the bone of contention before us arise from this drafting deficiency Legal Preface: A thumb nail sketch of the Act is a prefatory necessity. The defines 'small land owner ' as section 2(2) having in mind the optimum ownership in the given conditions. Permissible area ' Section 2(4) has in mind, the optimumness in the giving conditions. "Permissible area" [section 2(5)] is a cognate concept limiting the maximum permissible extent a person may hold and so long as he does not have any excess, he is a small landholder. He can evict the tenants from his holding and be in actual enjoyment as provided by the Act. If, however, he has lands beyond the permissible area, he becomes a large land owner and has to cough up the excess. However, he was given option to choose there best area he desires to keep, called 'reserved area ' ' ' [section 1(2)]. This creation of a surplus pool or reservoir is vital to the success of the statutory project since, by distribution of such lands, rehabilitation of ejected tenants and landless persons is to be "accomplished". Even if a person is amall holder, it is quite on the cards that, by inheritance or other operation of law, or by voluntary transfer he may acquire lands in excess of the permissible limit. In short, the legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible areas and the surplus in the hands of large holders whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of laws will go to feed the surplus pool. With this end in view, the Act has been amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High court has upheld certain patterns of alienations and oblique dealings by interpretative process. A study of the history of the legislation shows an unspoken criticism about judicial approach which three Judges were guided by historical process. [632C] The object and reasons of Punjab Act 14 of 1962, is to bring harmony between the law lords and the needs of a larger society; both the latter with a view to see whether it strikes at a gift made by, the respondent in favour of his sons whereby he sought to stow away some of his lands, shed some of their excess lands and look slim on as a small holder before the law Language permiting, the Court as interpretor, must fulfil, not frustrate the legislative mission. [532E F] The provisions of section 19 B are identical but the point involved is identical. In both cases the State of Haryana has come up to this Court in appeal, the former by certificate under article 133(1)(c) and the latter by special leave granted by this court. 2023 of 1972, respondent No. 1 after the commencement of the Punjab Security Of Land Tenures (Amendment) Act, 1962, continued to be a small land owner.

The appellants ' father executed a will, dated December 3, 1950, whereby Amarshah devised his estate in their favour. The other two branches of Sakru and Kajur were substituted by the word "Amarsha". The predecessors of the appellants ' son acquired certain properties including Malguzari lands on which they claimed to be the adopted son of Amarshijya upon the death of Amshah. They contended that the said land was joint family property, devolving by the rule of primogeniture and that the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malgu Zari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951 had become binding and conclusive against them because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof. The trial Court held that the land granted to Amarsabhagi was impartible and was governed by the rules of primimiture and Pratapshah father of the plaintiffs being the eldest member of the family. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the decree passed in respect of the Zamindari without giving any direction in the writ petition filed on behalf of the defendants. The High Court also found that the will set up by the appellants was not genuine because it devised the estate in favour of the testator 's widow Ratnabai, that the Will had not been produced before the Revenue Authorities and before the Com pensation Officer when disputes in relation to the estate of Am Narshah were pending before those authorities, and that it was produced for the first time nearly seven years after the death Of Amars advocate. The appellants contended that under the terms of the Chanda Patent and the terms recorded in the Wajib ul arz the Governor had the right to determine inheritance and the right thereto belonged to Amsastha, as devisees under his will. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) A suit to set aside a decision must be filed within two month from the order of succession if the Zamindar removed had died and the heir would get the right. The provision not approved as that on the deathof a zamindar it devolves upon his eldest son and in the absence of a legitimate or an adopted son it dev devolved upon the nearest male relative. But if the nearest in the line of succession is not selected, the estate must be given to the nearest heir who has the prescribed qualifications and is a successor to the Zamindar. [337 F G; 336 C] (ii) The declaration that Amarshipabha was impar tible and was covered by the rant of primemiture is not supported by the terms or by any entries in the sanad, nor by the history of the zamindari.

Section 12(3) (a) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 provides that where there is a dispute as to standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under the Act, the tenant shall be deemed to be ready and willing to pay such amount if before the expiry of the period of one month after notice referred to in sub section (2), he makes an application to the Court under section 11(3), and thereafter pays or tenders the amount of rent or allowed increases specified in the order made by the court. By a notice dated May 10, 1955, the respondent terminating the tenancy inter alia on the ground that the appellant were in arrears of rent for more than six months. The appellant 's suit was dismissed by the trial Court but on appeal, the High Court set aside the order of eviction and decreed the suit. In an application under article 227 of the Constitution the Bombay High Court held that when the respondent paid all arrears and costs of the suit on 23 December 1964 it could not be said that the respondent did not comply with the provisions of section 12 (3)(b). The High Court also took a contrary view. On appeal by special leave: HELD: The Gujarat High Court in Ambalal 's case held that the dispute is one which is in existence at the date of the notice or at any rate before the exiry of one months from the date when its service of the notices under section 12(2) ofthe Act. The Bombay High ' Court on appeal reversed the decision of the trial court. [637 A B] Ambalmal vs Badaldas, ; and Chhaganlallal 's Case (supra) distinguished. The provisions contained in sections 12(1)(b), 12, 13 and 14 of the Act deal with orders which may be passed by the Court during the pendency of an application disputing the rent. Provisions in section 11 (4) deal with order which may have been passed by a court during the hearing of the application disputing their rent. provisions in section II(3). of the [638 A, F] The Bombay Rents Control Act deal mainly with orders to which may he passed consequent upon dispute as regards standard rent. It is only when an application challenging rent is made within the time contemplated by Explanation 1 to section 12 of the that the provisions are attracted. In the present case, the respondents had not taken advantage of the limitation of time within which a dispute is to be raised as to amount to standard ' rent.

The respondent company company was a company incorporated in which it had a capital of Rs. 3,600 divided into 360,000 shares of Rs 10 each. The Aluminium Limited appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the respondent company. Two of these Directors ultimately retired and only one, namely, Mr. L. G. Bash was appointed to vote and/or from time to time appoint a special or general proxy to vote for and on behalf of the Aluminium Ltd. in respect of shares held by it in the respondent Company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the company. The respondent company was subsequently appointed as a director of the Company nominated by the Aluminium Limited. The question whether in computing the standard profits the statutory percentage should be taken at 10 per cent, was referred to the High Court which held that the directors who held the majority of the shares as trustees they were not 'a controlling interest ' in the company as contemplated by section 2(21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act. On appeal by special leave Held: The rule of interpretation of statutes is well settled and the question referred for decision to the Supreme Court was answered in the affirmative. The doctrine of law that decisions can have no application to the case before us, because, the same principle of those decisions could have no applicability to the present case. The analogy is inapt, because it cannot be said that the analogy was inapt for the principle of that decision can have any application to a case before this Court. In the instant case, the interpretation of law was erroneous and must be accepted.

The respondent was charged with an offence under section 79(c) of the Indian Electricity Act, 1948. In a writ petition filed by him before the High Court it was contended that the High COurt was in error in construing the relevant provisions of Regulations and Resolutions and holding that the allotment of posts of Accounts Superintendents should be made by promotion of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit. The High Court accepted this contention and quashed the resolution on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respond ent and therefore allowed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it is contended that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January 1970, it was no longer open to the respondent to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May 1969 for promotion. It is not possible to infer from the Resolution that the allottees were exempted from passing the S.A.S. Examination before qualifying for the promotion. Further it is not permissible to infer therefrom from the resolution that the allotee for promo tion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendent as before be insisted. Whatever might have been the purport of the Resolution on 19th5 1969, the Board by a subsequent Resolution had resolved on insisting on passing of the examination. The Single Judge who heard the Writ Petition dismissed it and the respondent preferred an appeal to a Bench of the Karnataka High Court which was allowed on 13th February 1973. It was contended before this Court that the said Resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the grounds of delay and/or laches on tile part of respondent and also on the view that in a case where the passing of S.S Examination was insisted prior to that Resolution in the same shall continue to be insisted in future also, and if passed of the S .A.T.

% The petitioner 's son, namely: Suman Behera was taken by the State of Orissa from his home in police custody at about 3 a.m. on 1.12.1987 when he came to know that the dead body of her son Suman was found on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraikela railway station. There were multiple injuries on the body of the deceased, while he was in police service; and ultimately his dead body was thrown on the Railway track. The allegation made is that it was a case of custodial death since Suman Behra died as a result of the multiple injuries inflicted to him while he is in police detention . The State of Uttar Pradesh and its police officers including Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur of Police Outpost Jeraikela Police Station were impleaded as respondents in this petition. During the inquiry it was found that Suman Behara was taken from his house on 1st December, 1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Kumar Barik with food for Home Sehra and he had been beaten for being detained at the police Outpost. At about 2 p.m., he came out of the Police Station OutpostDiscipline, from the Police Out Post Jeraikanpur to his house in village Chanpur under the police station Bisra, Distt. Sundergarh in Orissa; on 1 12.1987, the petitioner came to learn that his dead bodies had been thrown on railway track and that there were multiple diseases on the head of his son. On these basis the allegation of custodial deaths was denied as being detained by a driver. The Additional Solicitor General contended: (1) The evidence adduced during the inquiry did not support the defence of respondents and there is no reason to reject the finding of the District Judge that Suman be die in police operation because of injuries inflicted, to him; (2) The medical evidence did establish that the injuries had been caused to the deceased by lathi blows but it was asserted that the nature of injuries on his face and left temporal region could not have been caused by the lathis and, therefore, the death had occurred in the manner suggested by the police during a train accident; (3) The burden of proof which was heavily upon the respondent was on the State to prove that the death was unnatural or otherwise, taking this power to be settled by the decisions of this Court in a case where that is the only mode of redress available for the contravention made by the state or its servants in purported exercise of their powers and enforcement of the fundamental right is claimed by resort to the remedy in public law under the Constitution by recourse to Articles 32 and 226, but this aspect has not been adverted to. It is, therefore necessary to clear this doubt and to indicate the precise nature of this remedy which is distinct and in addition to the available ordinary processes, in case of violation of the constitutional right. [659H; 611A B] In the instant case on the finding reached by the District judge it was clear that it is a clear case for award of compensation to the petitioner for the custodial death of her boy. Verma J while dealing with the first question i.e. whether it was possible for the extreme contravention of fundamental right, yet it was also stated that "the petitioner could have been relegated to the ordinary remedy of a suit if his claim to compensation was factually controversial" and Article 32 cannot be used as a substitute for the enforcement of rights and obligations which can be enforced efficaciously through the ordinary processes '.

The two prisoners have been sentenced to death for an offence under Section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of their sentence are reported to have been rejected by the President recently. Before considering the merits of the application, it was, HELD: The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution which includes the freedom of Press is not an absolute right. [1186H] It is entitled to exercise its freedom of internal speech and be subject to the rules and regulations contained in the Jail Manual. There is no reason why newspapermen who can broadly, and we suppose without great fear of contradiction, be termed as friends of the society be denied the right of an interview under clause (4) of rule 549. [1107 F; 1008G] The constitutional validity of article 19(c)(a), which includes freedom of press is not a absolute right, nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information through the medium of an interviews of the two prisoners who are sentenced to imprisonment for life. No such right can be claimed by the Press unless in the first instance, the person sought to be interviewed is willing to be interview. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for us to say that the two seats are ready and willing to go on with all the facilities and regulations made in the jail Manual.

The appellant who was the Receiver of a tea garden mortgaged a tea estate in which he had insured the tea garden. The respondent instituted a suit against the respondent on the original side of the Tripura High Court for recovering the amount due under the mortgage. On an application made by the respondent, the Subordinate Judge appointed the Receiver as the Receiver subject to his furnishing security in the sum of Rs. 50,000. The appellant filed cross objections and enhanced the damages to the extent of Rs 32,525. The Judicial Commissioner allowed the respondent 's cross objection and enhanced damages to Rs. 4,525 which he did not accept. On appeal by special leave it was contended that under the terms of the bond, the appellant was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea gardens due to the Receiver 's default in relation to his duties as such Receiver was liable as a surety for the fulfilment of the conditions imposed on the Receiver under the order passed by the Court. Held: The fact that the bond was executed both be the Receiver and the appellant in favour of 'Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami the District Judge of Agartala, his successors in office and assigns respectively. The bond though executed two years after the tea plantation was damaged by the fire it was given retrospective operation with effect from January 22, 1950 being the date on which the Receiver had taken possession of the mortgaged property including the tea Plant. There is no substance in the second contention either. Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court. The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceeding including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate judge.

The appellants are dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by the appellant that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller, and that the State Government was competent to legislate for levy of tax only on transactions which were 'sales ' within the meaning of the . The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales Tax. The Additional Judge held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no sale ' within a the meaning. of the Act, and quashed the order inter alia on the ground that the transactions were 'a contract of sale. He further erred in holding that the sales were of goods not yet manufactured, whereas under cl . 5 he could authorise a producer or a stockholder to dispose of any iron or steel whether the same was in stock or not in accordance with the conditions contained or incorporated in the order of the Controller and that since there is liberty of contract between the parties, but subject to restrictions, the transaction could be regarded as a sale. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant : (1) the levy of sales tax by reason of cl. 3 did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax, because steel products were supplied pursuant to the directions of the Iron & Steel Controller made under cl. 10B of the Order; (2) the transactions did not resulted in sale, and were in respect of goods which were determined or determinable in the manner prescribed, and could not be taxed under a statute enacted in exercise of the powers in Entry 54 List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. HELD: The order passed by the High Court is set aside (1 ) The answer to the two questions referred by the Tribunal will be in the negative. [680 B] In the case before the Court there was evidence that what ever happened was left to be decided by mutual assent and the voluntary character of the transactions was not affected; (3) the High 'Court erred in its view, because even if the liberty of the contract in relation to the fundamentals of the transaction was completely excluded a transaction of supply of goods pursuant to directions issued under a Contrust Order might be regarded 'as a sale ; and such a transaction would be a sale; [680 G H] (4) It is not possible, therefore, to accept the contention that there was any contract between tile assessee and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the expression "sale of Goods" in section 2(h) of the Uttar Pradesh Sugarcane (Regulation of Supply and Purchase) Act, 1961.

The appellant Abdul Latif Wahab Sheikh, was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was due for release from prison on June 23, 1986. Though acquitted, he was not straightaway released from prison. The reasons were not clear to the Court from the record. Presumably he was required in connection with some other case. He is due for retirement on June 22, 1986 when an order for his detention was made under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act 1985. The mandate of Article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless the Advisory Board has reported within the period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. [209C E] In the instant case, the order of detention dated August 7, 1986 was revoked and a fresh order of deten tion was made on the same facts on the very day. The petition challenging one order of revocation was withdrawn as having become infructuous and another writ petition out of which the present appeal arises questioning the second order of Detention dated August 17, 1986 against which the instant appeal arose on the question whether a law may be made providing for successive orders for detention in a manner as to render the protection of Article 2(4). [211C D] Shibapada Mukher jee vs State of West Bengal, ; , and Shibapa Kr. Mukherjee & Anr. vs Union of India, ; referred to.

The petitioner, father of respondent No. 1, the father of the respondent (the husband), has established Vaidyas in Rajkot. They come from a well to do family. The petitioner is advanced in age and both the father and the son have been fighting between themselves since more than a decade. The High Court held that the First Appeal and Civil Revision Application were withdrawn in pursuance of an agreement reached between the parties on or about 14th August, 1978. The arbitrator had signed a clause that one of the parties would abide by the award dated 20th January, 1977 and that its interpretation should be left to the arbitrator himself. In this case, the petitioner challenged the award before the High Court and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act '). The question raised before the Judicial Committee was whether the suit was barred as res judicata) and they did decide it. It was further contended that there was no written agreement signed by both the parties to refer the disputes to arbitration. The Judicial Committee held that they had perfect jurisdiction to decide the question which was before them (namely, whether the Suit was barred under res judicata), and they decided it accordingly in terms thereof. The learned trial Judge made a decree in terms, whereby the award was agreed to and binding upon both the Parties. The Trial Court also made an decree in term of the order. Aggrieved by the judgment of the High court, the appellant preferred a Civil Revision application against the judgment and decree passed in Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977 whereupon he filed an appeal/revision. During the course of execution proceedings, the respondent applied on 20th June, 1977 for filing the award and sought stay of the operation of the previous award. A notice consequent upon filing of the awarded was issued to the petitioner. The application was converted into Special Civil suit No. 83 of 1977. It prayed for stay of operation of that order till further orders. During course of the execution proceedings the petitioner preferred a civil revision application against his judgment and order passed by the Civil Judge raising practically all the disputes raised by him in this civil revision applications. Both these legal proceedings were withdrawn by the appellant and thus the judgment rendered in Special civil Suit No 84 of 77 became final. The main objection to the award is that there had been no written arbitration agreement signed between the both parties to referring the dispute to arbitration, and since that application was decided against him he was compelled to rely upon a photo copy of the original award which was produced with the application. It also contended that as there was nothing written agreement in this context, it could not be said that the parties had agreed to refer to the arbitration. Dismissing the Civil Revision Petition, HELD: 1.

The respondent executed a registered lease of the estate in suit for 999 years, one in respect of 5/16 share of the Malias in Mouza Monohar Bahal and the other in regard to 5/ 16 share of his holding in 5/15 share of Malia in village Marich Kota to a firm then carrying on business under the name and style of Laik Banerjee & Company. On August 10, 1908, M executed an agreement for sale in respect thereof. The terms of the agreement provided that the respondent would pay the full costs of the execution case after the expiry of two years from that date. Under cl. (a) of sub s.(1) of section 28 of the Act the respondent was to deliver possession of the mortgaged properties to the appellant on the date specified in the agreement. The respondent paid the full cost of the execute candi dates and obtained a personal decree for Rs. Negotiations for settlement started and ultimately on January 30, 1937 a petition was filed before the Subordi nate Judge praying that under the circum stances mentioned therein he may be ordered to strike off this execution case keeping the attachment in force. Neither the original nor a certified copy of the order made on that date by the executing Court on the application for execution of decrees relating to execution cases relating to Execution Case No. 118 of 1936, was forthcoming but the parties had definite agreed that the order was substantially and correctly entered in column 20 of exhibit F which is a certified copies of extract from the Register of applications for executions of decrees pertaining to execution case No. 77/1938. The executing court dismissed the petition on the ground that the appellant having made special requests to the decree holder for an amicable settlement of the said execution case, it was not necessary to make detailed in the petition of June 2, 1939, as to day. Held, that there is no inconsistency between Promode Kumar Roy vs Tarun Kumar Roy, I.L.R. , Ram Kumar De vs Abhoya Pada Bhattacharjee. , approved. The order of January 30 1937 was a final order which brought the Execution Case NO 118/1938 and the attachment continued not because there was a pend ing execution proceeding but because a special order was made under Order XXI, rule 57 as amended by the High Court. Naturally, it is not necessary upon an application for execu tion of such a decree to apply for re attachment of the property. Ram Kumar Banerjee vs Gautam Ranjan Ghosh, I .L. R. , Razviah vs Parashram, I L.R , Champakchand Ltd., and Sago Boy vs Aswini Kumar Roy.I.L R. [1954] All. 894, referred to.

The first respondent was one of the principal points urged before him that in view of cl. (a) to section 29(2) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, which required a "appeal" for a period of 30 days prescribed by sec tion 12 of the Limitation Act and on that footing had held that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time if computed after making the deductions permitted by section 12 of that Act. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that for invoking sub section (2) Of section 29 of the , the requisite condition was that the First Schedule thereto shall prescribe a period for an appeal and that in computing the period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law, there would be no provision whereunder the party could at all file an appeal. HELD: (i) The procedure applicable in an appeal against an order made by a civil court under section 476 of the Code of Civil Procedure is that prescribed by the Code. whereas the period for which the limitation is prescribed in the first schedule is different from that prescribed therefor by the First Sch. from the date of the decree or order appealed from; and article 151 referred to in article 156. [148 A B] (ii) By the Amending Act of 1922, a conscious departure was made by the Legislature to impose a condition for the application of sub section(2). The words "appeal under this sub section" occurring in section 29, sub rule(2), mean that a period which is different between any period prescribed in tho first schedule. [147 C] (iii) It is not correct to say that the first limb of sub s.(2)of section 29 does not apply to an appeal under the Code on the ground that there would have been no provision whereby the party can at all filing an appeal, because, as a result, where a different period of time of limitation for appeal is expressly pro vided by a special law article 156 will not in terms be attracted. [145 C E] (iv) The fact that section 29 A of the Act does not prescribe a limitation of 30% which provides that an appeal shall be preferred within a period Of thirty days from the commencement of the cause of action or of any other case or application for special leave to appeal under sub section,(2.) will not affect the application to the second limb of section 29 (2). [143 G] (v) The words 'appeal" occurring by the Amending Acts in enacting section 29A and a reference to section 116C are intended to indicate that the absence of any positive period of Limitation for appeals would render the provisions of cl.(a) nugatory. But it will be useful to refer to the judgment of the High Court as well as the decision of this court reported in Ram Kishan vs State of Punjab, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 116; 446; and Ohmani vs Mohindar, A.I.R 1959 Mys. 11, referred to.

Section 76 of the Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 empowers the State Government to make rules regarding the maintenance and management of parking places and stands and the fees if any. Section 76 is also in Chapter IV dealing with 'control of traffic ' vesting in the State Govern ment. The first question which arose for consideration was whether the area in which the bus operators were asked to stop their buses was a bus stand or a halting place. Disposing of this appeal, it was, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was, therefore, in error in upholding the impugned order passed by the District Magistrate. [717G] T.B. Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Authority,Tanjore, ; and Municipal Board, Pushkar vs State Transport Authority., Rajasthan & Ors., ; , followed. 2.1 It is not disputed that in the instant case no order has been passed by tho Regional Transport Author ity as required under the Act to pass an order fixing the limits as a bus stands. Admittedly, the District Magis trate had passed the impugned ord er in question with the object of establishing a bus Stand in the area In question. That appears to be so from the order passed By the District Judge and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of Baldev Town Area Committee, Baldev to the President of the Union requiring the bus operator to stop his buses at the bus stand and to start from there and permit the passengers to get out their buses at that bus stand. It is open to the Regional Transport authority to take action immediately for determining any convenient place or places within the Town Area of Baldev (Mathura) as a Bus stand. The appeal is accordingly allowed, [718E F] 2.2 In T.P.

The appellants were charged with an offence under section 7 of the , and the trial Court convicted all the accused '. On appeal, the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction and sentence of the two appellants. The High Court dismissed the revision petition on November 4, 1965. In an appeal to this Court it was contended that upon the facts found by the lower courts no offence had been committed by the appellants; that there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export, and that there were no provisions in the Act which made a preparation to commit an offence punishable. Held: The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. The preparation consisted in devizing or arranging steps necessary for commission of offence. On the other hand, an attempt to commit a crime is a direct movement towards the commission after preparations are made. In order that a person may be convicted of an attempt ,to commit 'a crime, he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit it. If a man buys a box of matches, he cannot be convicted for attempted,arson his, however clearly it may be proved that he intended to set fire to a haystack at the time of the purchase. Nor can he be convicted under section7 of , because there is no provision in the . Act which makes a preparation for committing an offence pun. It follows therefore that the appellants should not have been convicted under s.7 of the .

The Sassoons were managing agents of the Sassoon Mills Ltd., which was in force from time to time. Under the agreement and if any remuneration for the broken period should be completely performed as a debt only at the end of each such period of service and that no remuneration or commission was payable to the Sassoonons under the terms of the Managing Agency Agreements, the transferees received from the company certain amounts of money in respect of which they were not liable to tax but the Sassuons. The Sassoors claimed before the Income Tax Officer that the Sasifons had not earned any part of the managing agency commission which had been paid by it to the transferees and were not exempt from tax in respect thereof. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the contention of the assessee. Held, that though under the contract of service between the Sasiffors and the Sashions on the completion of a certain year of their remuneration accrued on the 31st December, 1943 they had merely earned the commission or remuneration for it as set out herein above no part of their income could have accrued to them during the chargeable accounting period. In computing the taxable income of the assignee can it reasonably be said that the remuneration for that entire year is the income of an assignee and that it is the profits and gains of the business carried on by the assignee, when as a fact he stepped into the position of the servors only on some date in the course of the year by virtue of assignment. Commissioner of Income tax vs Lakshminarayan Ram Gopal and Son, Ltd., ; , 143 (1908) I.L.R. , followed.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. On appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave it was contended that a confession made by an accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the courts below held it to be. Held : (1) A confessional solil Audy is a direct piece of evidence. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. In 'A Treatise on the Law of Evidence ' by English Taylor, 11th Edn., Vol. I, p. 317 referred to. (2) Section 157 meant only "something that is stated" and the element of communication was not necessary before "s something else that is mentioned". Since in the present case, there was no difference between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it, the said confession is a confession which would depend upon its communication to another, though just like any other piece of Evidence, it can be admitted in evidence only on proof. This proof in the case of oral admission or confession could be offered only by witnesses who heard the admission or the confession, as, the case might be. K. Gopalan vs The State of Madras and Anr. [1959] Supp. 2 S.C R.

Rule 5 of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. Service Rules, 1972 as unconstitutional and void offending Article 14 of the Constitution of India, provides that every whole time officer or other employee of an existing insurer employed in connection with his General Insurance business immediately before the appointed day shall become an officer/employee of the Indian Insurance Co. In pursuance thereof the respondent Board of Directors was empowered to terminate the services of the appellant and others stood transferred and vested with the custodian. Under the Act, the service of the employees of the petitioner and others were transferred and vest in the custodian of New India Assurance Co. Ltd., the management of Orissa Insurance Cooperative Society Ltd., who was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972, vested in the Custodian of the New India Insurance Co., which the management was takenging its assets. The appellant challenged it in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed. Section 7 of the Act provides that for every wholetime officer or employee of another existing insurer in connection With his General insurance business, immediately before its appointed day, shall become a officer/ employee of the I.I.F.C., in which the undertaking of the insurer to which the service was relates has vested and would hold his office on the same terms and conditions as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such vesting and shall continue to do so unless and until his appointment is terminated. The respondent challenged it by way of additional grounds with leave, contending that in view of Rule 5 read thus: Termination of service: "An employee whether permanent or temporary, which shall be decided by the Board", the Board should have taken a decision, whether the need to continue the employee 's service subsist which would be based on the relevant material. Thereby, there would be objective consideration before taking a decision not only regarding the need for continuing the post but also the services and of the officer or the employee. Though the rule does not provide for prior notice, post decisional opportunity would be read into the rule. If so read it is not ultra vires Article 14. In this case, the impugned order terminating the services was illegal. Allowing the appeal by special leave, it was, HELD: (1) Rule 5 does not become arbitrary. unreasonable or void offending article 14. [225F] D.T.C. vs D. T.C Mazdoor Congress & Ors., 225 Judgment today today, approved. (2) The rule is valid. But from the facts, it is clear that the Board of Management did not abolish the post and put an end to the service. Obviously due to loss of confidence as the honesty and integrity became doubtful and his continuance in service was felt inexpedient and not in the interest of the business of the respondents.

Under section 22(1) of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915, every grantee of such privilege shall exercise in the same manner as provided by sub section (2) of that Section. A right or privilege under a contract shall not be barred either expressly or by implication from the granting of a license. The State Government and other respondents were granted licences for establishing 70 outstill Shops for 1970 71. The Collector issued an order on August 19, 1970 prohibiting the holders of any licence for running 30 shops for them. On February 3, 1971, the State Government issued a fresh order which he invited tenders from persons in respect of the seven shops. The High Court quashed the order dated September 6, 1971 for re auctioning the license and declared that rule 103(1). of the Board 's Excise Rules was ultra vires the Act. The appellants in CAs. 351/72 and the State appealed to this Court by special leave against the said decision. Allowing the appeals and setting aside the judgments of the High Court, ^ HELD: Section 22 enacts that a grantee of a privilege shall not exercise it unless or until he has received a license in that behalf from the Collector or Excise Commissioner. The power to accept or reject a tender without assigning any reason cannot be said to be arbitrary as Section 29(2) (a) does not authorise the exercise of such absolute and naked powers in determining the sum of money payable under sub section(1), because it empowers only the authority specified by the Statute. [818 F; 819 E] The power given to the State Legislature is "incompetent and ultra vires" the act. [411 G] In Narula 's case that there was no inherent right in a citizen to sell intoxicating liquors by retail, and that it is not a privilege of a citizen of the State, but a privilege which the State has conferred on the State legislature by the statute is "clearly an exclusive privilege" within the meaning of section 22. [879 A] Union of India vs Harinarayan Jaiswal ; ; C.I.T., Orissa vs Har inarayan Jaiswal and others , referred to.

The appellant was the domestic servant of Dr. Nanavati and accused No. 2 in a textile mill where he proposed to commit murder of Narendrakumar 's grand father, on the pretext of collecting clothes from a woman who was sitting nearby. The accused No 1 and 2 were charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with approver Dinkar Sakharam between 19 December 1967 and 4 January 1968 at Deolali Camp for the purpose of committing the murder of one Narendrakumar and committing murder of his grand father Dr. Champa Bhumanna Yadav and another, including accused No 3. The trial court found that there was corroboration in regard to the crime as well as the common intention. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that there had been corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar in material particulars by way of pre conceived plan to murder Narendra and, therefore the conviction could not be sustained. On the questions : (1) Whether there is corroboration in respect of accused No 2 and 3 being guilty of the offence; (2) whether there was capital sentence of accused NO 1 and 3. HELD: (1)(a) The evidence of the tailor was that of an accomplice. [618 B] (b) If a witness says that the accused and he stole the sheep and put the skin in a certain place, the discovery of the skins in that place would not corroborate the evidence Of the witness as against the accused.

The Surat Municipality declared its intention to make a town planning scheme under section 22 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954. The appellant claimed compensation for deprivation of his right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq. On November 4, 1971 the State Government granted sanction to the draft scheme with certain conditions. Before the Town Planning Officer the appellant claimed higher compensation. By his order dated November 4 1971 the Town planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq.; but the total compensation awarded was Rs. 3,31,455. Not satisfied with the decision of the Town development Officer the Appellant preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal which reduced his claim to Rs. 9.50 p. The Commissioner however dismissed the same.
