Before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in case the question whether the Act specifies a principle of compensation, it is observed in Shantilal 's case at page 357 of the report: "It is true that under the Act the market value of the land estimated without reference to improvements contemplated in the scheme has been completed. But on the question as to whether the act specifies a principles of compensation it is held in Shanchand vs The State of Gujarat that by virtue of the operation of the town planning Act a person is deprived of his land whether in whole or in part" and if the improvement contemplated in a scheme had stood completed on that date exceeds the marketvalue of the same plot when taken into account without improvements.

One K died in 1934. In 1950, he took the property of his family and provided that as soon as his minor daughters attained majority they should give to them per head one veli nanja land and one vela of punja land in vattam No. 149 in village Nagampadi 976 and further provided that the said Seetharama should deliver possession of the entire properties to the 90 children. After the death of K, his brother K filed a suit for partition claiming that they were entitled in law having regard to the provisions of the will to select their respective one vehi land and another veli fle tamar land from out of the lands in question on the ground of selection made by them, and the suit was resisted by the appellant who was prepared for a partition of land according to quality but was not prepared to accept his right of selection claimed by the daughters. The trial court dismissed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. Held: (i) The testator appointed Seethara as the guardian of his minor sons as well as of his foster son, namely, the appellant. There are two classes of cases which may orrise in cases where a will is so indefinite that it is not possible to give any definite intention to it at all; and if the intention of the testator was not to give the selection to his brother he would have given them a share in the vattayam, and (ii) the testator meant something different in the case of the daughters because he used the words " he shall deliver possession. The will cannot be read as intending that it should include from the entire land open to the heirs. When there are ways of partition available to parties in England also, the selection is with the legatee and the test is whether the testator intended that the daughters should get the area of land devised to them taking into account the good and bad quality of the land. In this case there were ways of a partition available in India to parties where the sons obtained their shares and the necessity for the adoption was not limited by the words used. [140 D G] (ii)(a) The will is not void for uncertainty because it is a policy provision evolved by English Courts in order that where the testator 's intention to make a gift was clear, even though there may be some difficulty because of the confusion arising out of such wills could be easily resolved without recourse to courts. In the instant case, the will has been clearly intended to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatees making the selection in order in which they were named in the will. This case does not in any way weaken the rule of benevolent construction by which the legatee is entitled in certain circumstances to make selection. [141 D] In the present case, it was clear from the face of the document that the testator did not intend that the properties should be partitioned by the court than that the legatee should have been left to make the selection and give the devised land to them. There were no words from which it can be inferred that the will intended that he would get their lands after taking into consideration the good & bad quality. [144 E] (b) The evidence, however clearly shows that in one case the testator himself indicated with sufficient clarity what he wanted his daughters to get.

A civil suit was filed by the appellant against the respondents in respect of a portion of plot nos. 156, 158, 164, 165, 167, 166, 168 etc., and plot No. 27 was carved out of plot Nos. 267, 268, 272, 273, 276, 277, 278, 279 and 280. The appellant 's case was that she was living with her sons at Lucknow and her husband 's cousins were looking after the lands which consisted of agricultural lands and groves and they were given them share by their father 's brother in law 's share, and that when they got her share they themselves mutated in the consolidation of holdings. The respondents resisted the suit contending that they acquired the plots through litigation and had absolutely no concern with them. It was further alleged that though at some time before the lands were joint but during the consolidation proceedings the plots in possession of the appellant were occupied by the defendants who having acquired the rights of a Sirdar under the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, the plaintiff lost her title by operation of law. The trial court decreed the suit for joint possession in respect thereof of Chakbandi plot nos, 201 and 274 only. As regards plot Nos., 93, 94 and 106, the dismissal of the plaintiff 's suit was upheld. In second appeal, the District Judge restored the judgment of the District Court but on appeal, a district judge held that some sort of fraud must have been committed by the respondents. The High Court also found that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. The area wise judgment of District Court was maintained because the clear evidence of PW Karbalai Begum, is to the effect that she had been not at all informed about the consolidation operations and was assured by the defendant that they would take proper care of her share in any proceedings that may be instituted. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The possession of these respondents apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees, would be in law the possession of a plaintiff. Apart from this, the fact remains that the District judge has come to a clear finding of fact after consideration of the evidence that a clear fraud was committed during the Consolidation operation either by the Respondents or by someone else as a result of which the rights were sought to be extinguished. [867A B] 2.1 In view of the clear decision of this Court, referred to above and the judgment in second appeal it is not open to the High Court to interfere with the finding of facts in second appeals. [881C D] 2:2 The suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act. Thus, the grounds on which the High court reversed the decision of the district judge regarding fraud having been committed in the Consolidation proceedings were not sustainable in law and the judgments of the High Courts cannot be allowed to stand. [88E G] 2 :3 Even assuming that there had been some evidence to prove that the respondents did obtain the plots by litigation, even then it could be said that the plaintiff "s rights extinguished.

Respondent No. 1, Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Prime Minister of India, was the Chief Minister of the Industries Department. About two decades back, the petitioner filed a writ petition challenging the appointment of Respondent No 1 in the Delhi High Court. The learned Single Judge dismissed the Writ Petition and dismissed the writ petition. In the review the Supreme Court referred to the decision in Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., ; , that the essential requirement of Article 173 read with Form VIIA was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. Allowing the review, this Court, HELD: The qualifications prescribed in the Third Schedule pursuant to the requirements of Article 75(4) of the Constitution is only for a Minister of tile Union and there was no separate form even for the Prime Minister. Since the Prime Ministers are also a member of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Chief Prime Minister, but the description of him as Deputy Cabinet Minister does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministry along with his other submis sions, this is the first contention raised by the petitioner in this writ petition, which has no force. So far as the second contention is con cerned, he himself does not press it. [3F H; 4A B] In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No . 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Union Council of Minis ters, though he had been described at as Deputy Ministers but the particulars of his nomination as a candidate; do not confer any power on him to any powers.

On 1st November, 1948, a strike ended completely. The apparent cause for the strike was that the management of the Mills had expressed its inability to comply with the request of workers to declare the forenoon of the 1st Nov., 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse, and on the 3rd November, the strike ended thereby. The contention of the Union was not accepted by the Madras Labour. His action was varied to this extent, but it was not said by them that stoppage of work did not fall within the definition of "strike" as given in section 2(q) of the . Held: (i) In view of the facts and circumstances detailed in the adjudicator 's award this contention cannot be seriously considered. It cannot be disputed that there was a cessation of work by a body of persons employed in any industry acting in combination, or in a concerted refusal or a lawful under a common understanding of any number of persons who are or have been so employed to continue to work or accept employment; (ii) The action of the workers on the night of 1st. November, was clearly illegal and the workers thus lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules. The decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal was set aside. In view Of the facts aforesaid it was clear, that the action of workers on a night of the Ist November did not come within the term "stkhivala" as provided in section 1(q)(I) of .

Section 292 of the Indian Penal Code, which deals with certification of films is violative of Articles 19(1)(g) and 301 of the Constitution. Section 79 makes an offence a non offence. When the offending act is actually justified by law in doing it there cannot be any activity which in the absence of such certification may constitute an offence under section 292 I.P.C. [516 C, 516 A B] Hari Vishnu Kamath vs Syed Ahmed Ali and Another ; , followed. The prosecution was unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and the certificate issued thereunder. [ 515 D E] In short, a special machinery and processual justice and a host of wholesome restrictions to protect State and society are woven into the fabric of the said Act. After 517 having carefully enacted such a legislation can it be that a certificate granted under it by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offenceunder section 292I.P C.C., driving the producer to satisfy a 'lay ' magistrate that the certificate of the Board of Censors notwithstanding, the film was offensive ? [517 A B E] The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified and it is just agreed to consider whether on balance the publication is proved to be justified as being for the public good. 1. Going to the basics, freedom of expression is fundamental. The censor is not the moral tailor setting his own fashions but a statutory gendarme policing films under Article 19(2) from the angle of public order decency or morality. These concepts are themselves dynamic and cannot be whittled down to stifle expression nor licentiously enlarged to promote a riot of sensual display. Anyway, the appeal must succeed and the Court extinguish the prosecution by the order. [ 516 B] 2.

One Mr Govindan Nair, appearing for him, has contended that (i) his client 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned; (ii) The Broachronomy of Government pleadingership which is a public office and the lucle loving appetite for law offices, in the absence of a wholesome ceiling on lawyer 's fees, are issues of moment in a developing society controlled by the politics of skill and enjoying a legal monopoly; and (iii) The petitioner was discriminated against by the State Government. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. Judicial grievance has been lost sight of by this Court. While considering this question, it is necessary to refer to the history of the Constitution on which the President and the Chief Justice have pronounced. [766G] 2. The importance of these wider observations is that avoidable litigation holds out money by way of fees and more fees if they are contested 763 cases and this lures a lawyer, like any other homo economics, to calculate income on a speculative basis, as this Government Pleader has done in hoping for a lakh of rupees. [769C] 3. Quashing the summary despatch deservedly given by the High Court to the writ petition whose main merit was daring novelty.

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Bank of India Ltd. At an extraordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the bank held on May 6, 1948 a resolution was passed increasing the share capital of the company and for that purpose offering new shares to the existing shareholders in the proportion of one new share for every three shares held by them in this company. In the present case the appellants as holders of shares of shares had become entitled to 1,62,000 shares of it at the rate of Rs. 100 per share. The question raised was whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the distribution of the right to apply for the shares amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. Held, that the High Court fell in error in holding that the distribution by the Mills amounted to distribution of dividend and was not Profit within the extended definition of that expression in section 2 (6A). The Tribunal had referred the question whether the receipts by the appellants amounted to dividend only within the limited definition of "public purpose" in section 1(6 A) of 'the Indian Income tax Act, as it did not intend to distribute any dividend. It could not accept the shares or decline to accept those shares or exercise the option of surrendering them in favour of its nominees. In nominating its shareholders to exercise the right of applying for the share had a market value of Rs., 100 per equity and in ascertaining whether distribution of dividends amounted to "so distributed" within section 2 the Act was intended to define the expression 'dividends ' as generally understood and includes in its connotation several other receipts set out in the definition. Further, when the legislature by section 2 A(6) sought to define a expression 'public purpose ' it added to the normal meaning of the expression several other categories of receipts which may not otherwise be included therein.

The appellant who was an elected candidate filed an election petition challenging the election of the first respondent from Jind Legislative Assembly constituency Jind Assembly Constituency. To this petition, the returned candidate as well as all other candidates were impleaded as parties and they contested the petition. After going through the pleadings of the parties, the Court ascertained the points on which parties were at variance and framed appropriate issues. The election petition reached the stage of recording evidence. It was an application filed by the appellant for permission to produce and examine witnesses whose names were set out in the Application. By order dated November 29, 1982, this Court made it clear that except Bahre son of Sher Singh, no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the afore mentioned witnesses was recorded, the court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned candidates; and thereafter the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the learned counsel of either side. It appears that again on January 11, 1983, petitioner submitted a list of witnesses intimating to the Court that he desires to examine them, but this was objected to by the returned respondent. When his application was rejected, appellant filed an appeal before the High Court against order of rejection of his prayer in limine, contending that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered was not mentioned in the List and therefore, the election petitioner could not be permitted to examine more witnesses whose name had not been mentioned in his list. A further contention was raised that the use for which respondent was asking did not mention the names of witnesses in the list; that even if the appellant bad a good cause for non supply of the list, before filing an appeal, the High court would have declined to permit him to examine such witnesses and thereafter, the matter could be set aside for hearing by oral arguments. The High Court observed that except Sher Singh one of the candidates had lost his deposits, the appellant was not permitted to produce more witnesses on the date fixed for recording his evidence; that merely because one of his nomination was rejected it did not give permission to examine him more than two other candidates whose names had not already been mentioned, and therefore the election petition should be dismissed. It accordingly allowed the appeal for hearing arguments of both sides. In the appeals before this Court, on behalf on behalf the appellant/writ petitioner, it was contended that the High Courts have introduced a proviso to sub section (4) of Rule 1 of order XVI and in exercise of the powers conferred by clauses 27 and 35 of the Letters Patent and Section 129 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the two rules operate.

% The appellant, a double M.A. and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement issued by the Committee of Management of the College for the post of Principal on the ground that he had assumed charge of the post and by publishing an order dated April 7, 1981 appointed the appellant as Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. The Selection Committee appointed the appel lant to the post on a regular basis. Pursuant to the said decision the Manager of the college issued an appointment order dated March 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee was appointed as Principal of the school on May 1, 1981 in the pay scale of 2000 at initial salary alongwith DA and admissible under Rules. The appellant challenged the aforesaid order before the High Court by a writ petition contending: (a) that the appointment of the appellant was not valid as the power to appoint was withdrawn by the State Government; (b) the appointment was not made without the knowledge of the order contained in the radiogram had suspended or withdrawn its power. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding, that the radiwalram dated April 27,1981 contained an order of the State Govt. in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of Principal and teachers; (c) the Committee had no power to make the appointment. There was difference between a general power and not a provision in any statute. All such recognised institutions must have a Scheme of Administration as envisaged by section 16A and the scheme of Administration envisages setting up a Selection Committee for selecting among candidates for appointment as Head of an Institution as provided in section 16F; (d) that while enacting the regulations prior sanction has been obtained of the Government, under sub section 4 of section 9 the State Govern ment enjoys the power of making appointments including the appointment to make appointment. The power is being regulated by the regulations, which has been extracted hereinbefore conferred power on the State government without making any reference to the Board to make an order or take such other action consistent with the provisions of the Act as it deems necessary and in particular, may by such order modify or rescind or make any regulation in respect of any matter; (e) that whereas the Government has power to sanction or not to sanction the regulation proposed by the Board. The terms "Procedure for selection of teachers and head of institutions" under section 16D of the Intermediate Education Act, 1921 are thus clear. The procedure for selection is regulated by section 17A and, the Scheme of Adminis tration envisaged thereunder envisages setting out of a Committee of management and the Committee has the power and to set up a selection committee for selecting the candidate for appointment to be appointed as head of an institution as provided under sec. 16 F; (f) that when appointing authority the appellant is satisfied that any person has been appointed as Head in contravention of the provisions Of the Act, the State Gov ernment was bound to hear the appellant before making any consequential order.

The respondent company sold the goods to manufacturers who use it for the purpose of impregnating it with rubber, fall under Entry 18 of the Schedule of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act 1954. The respondents challenged the assessment order on various grounds : (i) The goods were exempted from sales tax; and (ii) the notification issued by the Commercial Tax officer was without jurisdiction as no disputed question of fact arose. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The essential question to determine is the stage at which the goods under consideration become a 'textile fabric '. The meaning of the term "textiles" given in the Oxford Dictionary is: "A product of skilled workmanship". [502C D] 2. There is no absence of jurisdiction of the taxing authorities who had the power to decide the question either rightly or wrongly. [503D] 3. It is a question on which two views seem possible on apparent facts. And, neither of the two views can be rejected outright as untenable. [506E] 4. The view that on what appeared to the High Court to be a question of "fact, it should not decide whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to exemption. There was no appeal by the State of Assam. It did not, therefore, seem propel.] for us to finally decide on merits, the question argued before this court in the appeals by the Delhi Cloth Mills which are before this Court unless we could have decided the matter in favour of the appellant.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal which washeries on contract basis. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service but he filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the Government notification withdrawing and transferring the case to the Labour Court Patna. The High Court did not agree with the view of this Court in Management of Sri Rani Lakshmi Ginning & Weaving Mills Ltd. vs State of Punjab, [1984] II LLJ 122 that section 33 B of the . The High court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the Government before accepting the representa tion of the workman and transferring ted the case from the Labour court, Dhanbad should have given an opportunity to the management; and that in the absence of any indication by necessary implication the Government could not transfer a case on the basis of allega tions of one party without giving reasonable opportuni ty to other party to represent its point of view. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government was misled by the representation of the workmen that they are still residing in colony quarter at Dhanbad. Even the alleged recommendation of the Ward Commissioner referred in his counter affidavit had not been produced. [294G] 1.2 In the circumstances of the case, it would be unsafe to hold that under such circum stances Government could be called upon to give a notice to the parties before transferring the two cases from one Income Tax Officer to another without hearing the assessee. Denial of that opportunity is fatal flaw to the decision of Government. [298B C] 1:3 The non observance of natural justice is itself prejudice to any man and proof of prejudice is unnecessary. This takes us to the reasons given by the Govern ment in support of the order of transfer. The Government has stated that the workman is having his residence at Hajipur and it would he inconvenient for him to attend the labour court regularly at Dhanbad.[298G] 2.1 In the instant case, the State has withdrawn the pending reference from the High 'circumstances of the ease without getting it veri fied from the management. The State in fairness ought to have got it verified by giving an opportunity of being heard to the workman which is a party to the pending refer ence. Den equa tion is a fatal flaw, and that the principle of natural Justice being presumptive, it should be followed by the authorities unless it is excluded by express words of statute or by necessary impu dential implication.[298D E] 2:2 The procedural standards which are implied by the duty to act fairly has been explained by this Court. [295E F] 2(a) The procedure which are inherent in the exercise of a judicial power are merely those which facilitate if not ensure a just and fair decision. What is thus important in the modern administration is the fairness of procedure with elimination of element of arbitrariness. That is, however, not the same thing to state that they must act judicially or quasijudicially. The procedural standard which are implicit by the duties to act reasonably has been stated by Lord Pearson in Pearl berg vs Varty, , 548: "A tribunal to whom judicial or quasi judicial functions are entrusted is held to be required to apply those principles (i.e., the rules of natural ness in performing those functions unless there is a provision to the contrary. But where some person or body is entrusted by Parliament with administrative or executive functions there is no presump tion that compliance with the principles of natural ly is require although, as a 'Parliament is not to be presumed to act unfairly", the courts may be able in suitable cases (perhaps always) to imply an obligation to act with fair ness.

The question arising for determination in the appeal was whether the reference which was otherwise valid did not become incompetent merely because it did not specify how many of the workmen of thirty different categories were involved in the dispute. Held, that in view of the fact that more than three years passed since the reference was made, the Court was right in its favour and that therefore this appeal must be dismissed with costs to the respondent No. 3. Section 10(1) of the , provides that a workman who is party to a dispute shall be entitled to be represented in any proceeding under the Act by an officer of a trade union of which he is a member or (b) an officer o/any industrial union connected with, or by any other workman employed in, the industry in which the workman is employed. The expression "as represented by the Hotel Workers Union" in section 10(i) of , refers not only to dismissal but also to dismissal of particular workmen. In this case there was no force in the contention that the reference made was bad simply because in the order of reference it was mentioned that the Industrial Tribunal may, while considering the question whether the Tribunal could decide to dismiss a large number of workmen on the ground of vagueness, were concerned in it. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy [1953] S.C.R. 334, relied on. Held further that the challenge to the competence of a reference by the High Court on the grounds of vagueness also fails. The fact that there was only one composite strike which did not affect the competence and competency of the order Of reference cannot make the reference incompetent merely as it is mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the industrial dispute, and that the scope of the enquiry under section 10 (1) is entirely different from the purpose of a preliminary inquiry.

The appellant, a bushings and bearings imported by the appellant, for use in aeroplanes and parts ad valorem of such engines, was entitled to the benefit of the Notification No. 281 Cus/76, granting part exemption from payment of Customs duty in respect of these rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by them. The Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the appellant Company and affirmed the orders of the Customs authorities. According to the Appellate Tribunal, the bushments and bear ings are the same and as the bearings come under the Heading 84.06, they are not entitled to The benefit of exemption under the Notification. Hence this appeal by the Revenue. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. In the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption will be granted in respect Of parts of the engines, which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, they would get the benefit thereof of exemption as provided by the Notification irrespective of the fact that they or any or some of them have already been included under Heading No. 84. The Notification makes it clear that the Notification is inapplicable to parts of ships mentioned under Heading 8406, and there is no reason to exclude any of such parts simply because it is included under another heading. [226C E] 2. No doubt, the Notification does not purport to grant exemption to internal combustion piston engines but also to 'parts thereof '.[227G H; 228A B] 3. Assuming that Heading 84,06 will get the exemption under an earlier Notification, while in the context of the notification, it includes the parts of a engines mentioned under heading No.84.06.

The appellant plaintiffs are the son and daughter of Fathima Bee who had two sons, Respondent 1 had two children and a daughter. In the suit filed by them for declara tion that they were entitled to be in enjoyment and pos session of Saint Syed Moosa Shah Khadiri Dargah in Madras for a period of 27 days in all in the months of February, March, June, July and November each year. The plaintiffs alleged that after the death of Fathi ma Bee in 1957, Respondent No. 1 (Defendant 2) had 1/5 share in 6 months i.e., 36 days and 6 days respectively left surviving one son and two daughters. The plaintiff also alleged that since Respondent No 2 was alive but she was not a party to the suit, she served a notice on 23.3.1972 calling upon the defendants to recognise the right of management of the plaintiffs in the Dargah, contending that he was a Mujawar along with them as such were entitled under Muslim Law and therefore she was also a Mujawe along with Respondent No 's father for a certain period from February 1, 1978, to June 1, 6 and October 1, to 6 for the first plaintiff and 9 days from July 1 to September for the last one year. Respondents 1 (plaintiff) and 2 (Defendants) filed written statement taking the plea that their father had 1 /5 share of the Dargah in question for a term of 27 day in all the months i t e. February, June 20, 1969 to October 1st and 1st Defendants were entitled on the basis of Muslim Law. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in the operative part held that the plaintiffs were entitled as per Muslim Law to manage the Dargah for 27 days. In appeal the High Court took the view that the Courts below proceeded upon an erro neous assumption as if it was the duty of Respondent No 1 to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster has been established. It further held that even if really the rights of Fthima Bee had become barred by her not exercising the right, the plaintiffs themselves can have no independent right to claim. The High Court also took the same view in C.S. 116 of 1909 and another ground taken was that neither Fathna Bee nor the plaintiffs had at any time received a share in the hundi collection or offerings nor had posses sion or management of Respondent 1. Hence it was false to state that the females were totally excluded from the right or claim of any share in management or offerings in the Wakfs, and that even though Fathiman Bee had lost their right by ouster, there would arise a clear presumption of ouster. It was further observed that after coming into force of the Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1950 (the Act), the females who were not entitled to any right or management, must be evidence of open assertion of hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment by one of them to the knowledge of the other so as to construe ouster. The written statement filed by the defendants in the present case is totally lacking in the above particulars and thus apart from the want of evidence, there is no proper pleading of ouster in the instant case. It is an admitted case of the parties that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs any stand was taken that the right to management of Dargah or any claim in the offerings was neither raised for decided. Respondents Nos.

The 1st respondent, a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway (which previously used to be known as the G.I.P. Rly.), was granted house rent allowance by the Central Government under the Ministry of Railways 's letter dated January 2, 1947. The 1st Respondent challenged the validity of his claim claiming house rent allowances as part of his wages. The Authority condoned the delay and dismissed the respondent 's claim for house rent Allowance. The appellant then moved the Authority under section 4 of the , which rejected the claim on the ground that the house rent was "wages" as defined in the Act, that as a matter of fact, accommodation was offered to the 1st res pondent and he refused it, but even so, the appellant was not entitled to withhold the house Rent Allowance. Held, (per Sinha, C. J., FAZL ALI, PATANJALI SASTRI, MUKHERJEA and DAS JJ. dissenting). It is well settled that a contract of employment cannot be said to create an indefeasible right in the employee at all places wherever he may be posted and in all circumstances irrespective of whether or not he has been offered Government quarters. The rules clearly provide that the allowance will not be ad raissible to those who occupy government quarters or to those to whom such quarters have been offered but who have refused to take advantage of the offer. Rule 3(i) of the Railway Board 's order dated January 1, 1948 prohibits an employee from relinquishing any such right as is the subject matter of rule 3(1)(d), excluding "the value of any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee". The definition of "wages ' contained in section 2(vi) of . Sub section (2) of section 7 categorically indicates that the expression "value of any houses accommodation" clearly shows that house rent pay allowance is not "in terms of money but it is admissible only to such railway employees as are posted at specified places in order "to compensate Railway servants in certain costlier cities for excessive rents paid by them over and above what they might normally be expected to pay"; nor is such an allowance "intended to be a source of profit".

The detenu was one Indru 's Ramchand Bharvani; while in Writ Petition 435 of 1980, the detenu is one Indu 's son. While in writ petition 435 of 1981, the detention order purported to have been made under section 3(1) of COFEPOSA by the State Government was served on the detenus alongwith the order of detention on February 16, 1980. On March 25, 1980, an order of Detention, purporting to have be made under Section 3(2)(a) of the (for short called COFEPOSA) by the Central Government was also served on them alongwith the grounds of detention. The detenu accompanied with others were released on heavy bail subject to the condition that they would attend daily before the Customs Officers and cooperate in the investigation. This condition was later on related. On February 16 he received a letter from the Collector, addressed to the Secretary, Home Department, requesting him to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds for detention. On April 3, 1980 copies were received by the detenu on March 29, 1980 and February 18, 1980 respectively. The detention order was authenticated by the Under Secretary to the State Govt. of Maharashtra. The grounds of Detention were served on both the detenus along with the order dated March 31, 1980 which, in fact, was received by them on March 25. On July 16, 1983, the wife of the detenu addressed a letter to the first respondent (Under Secretary to Government of Maharashtra), requesting him (i) to furnish them with the materials relied upon; and (ii) to supply copies of the statements and documents relied upon in the 'grounds ' served on him after undue delay on the direction of the Central Govt., that the State Govern ment supplied copies of some of the statement to the detenus on April 3. 1980. The representation, dated March 24, 1980 made by the detenus to the detaining which, according to the information furnished at the Bar by the father of the detenus was still pending as it related. Hence, with a view to preventing them from giving an effective representation against their detention the Central government passed an order under section 11 of COFEPOSA on February 18. Dismissing both the petitions and directing the release of the detention, ^ HELD: 1. The right guaranteed by Article 22(5) of Constitution is two fold: (i). the detaining authorities must, as soon as may be, that is, as early as practicable after the detention communicate to the detenu the grounds on which the order has been made; (ii). the detained authority must afford the detenu earliest opportunity of making a representation against the detention. But it seems that the representation was never put up before the Minister; and in fact there was no physical difficulty in preparing and supplying the copies to the petitioners, of the material that had been relied upon or referred to in the ground of detention and the detenus could not make an effective representations. [352 C] Khudiram Das vs The State of West Bengal & Ors., , followed, (iii). The mere fact that the grounds were formulated by the Advisory Board without applying its mind to the nature of the documents, the copies of which were asked for by the petitioners had been incorporated in those 'ground 's which were served were more than sufficient to enable him to make an adequate representation at the earliest. Therefore, furnishing of copies of statements and also the documents relied on in the "grounds" of detention, would not be in public interest. [353 F G] Khurairam Das & Ors. vs The Union of India & Ors; , ; applied. (iv). There was no force in Contention (5), either. The first reason for non supply of copies given by the son to the habeas corpus detenu to enable them to make a full and effective representation at The earliest. [351 C] 2.

The Gujarat High Court recorded a very lengthily order though the reasoning in support of the non maintainability of the joint appeal was confined to a couple of pages only. The High Court in its order referred to ss 258, 410 and 423 of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Cr. P.C. as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 was against the lst maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting some persons tried jointly. It further held that r. 6 in Chapter XXVI of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960 was inconsistent with Ch XXXI of tile Code of Criminal Procedure, with the result that a joint re ferred appeal could not be entertained under section 537 Cr.P.C., and so holding rejected the appeal by respondent without going into the merits. The State appealed to this Court on the grounds (i) that r 6 in Ch XXVI of Bombay High Courts Appellate Side Act was inconsistent, with Chhanga of the code of Criminal Proce dure; (ii) that under section 417 Cr. C. P., which provided for an appeal in a case of acquittal empowered by the Code of criminal cases may like that of an appeal by State against several accused persons convicted at one trial must be upheld; and (iii) that such restricted order of admission being invalid, the appellant would be entitled to insist that his appeal should be heard on the merits, that is, the decision of this Court in Rabari Ghela Jadav 's case. HELD: Per Gajendragadkar. The power to frame a rule is specifically conferred on the High Court by section 554(2)(c) Cr. A.l.R., 1960 S.C, 746, and r.6 does not seem to be inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code.

Section 25(3) of the 1922 Act read with section 25(4) of 1961 Act provided that no tax shall be payable in respect of the income, profits and gains of the period between the end of the previous year and the date of such discontinuance. The assessee, a dealer in securities holding shares as its stock in trade, had been charging to tax under the 1918 Act and was assessed under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 (1918) read with the relevant Finance Act 1963 (21 of 1964). In the assessment for the year 1945 40 it was claimed by the assessee that it was liable to pay tax on the profits for the said period. The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer on March 7, 1956. The appellate Tribunal allowed the appeal in part. Both the assessee and the Department applied to the Appellate Tribunal for reference of the questions of law to the High Court. The High Court held that the foreign business of the assessee could not be deemed to have been charged under the provisions of 1918 Act. On appeal by certificate, HELD : From section 3 of the 1918Act the charge was made on the receipt of income in British India and as the income received by the joint family could not have been charge under the head 'profits derived from business ' but only as a receipt under section 3. The words "on which" in section 25 (4) were intended merely to indicate the classes of income. The heads did not exhaustively delimit sources from which income arises, and Business income was broken up under different heads only for the purpose of computation of the total income. By that breaking up the income does not cease to be the income of the business, the different heads of income being merely the classification prescribed by the Incometax Act for determination. [908 H] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M. Palaniappa Chettiar and Others; , followed.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks. The amount payable to the department was determined by the Assistant Commissioner of Sales Tax in terms of their running Bill No. XI dated 28th October 1967. The Electricity Board then referred the matter to the High Court contending that as the supplies were sales tax it would be difficult to hold in the light of the special features and characteristics of the contract with which the contract was entered into by the appellant with the public Works Department at the instance of the assessee. On reference, the High court held the transaction which was a works contract. In appeal before this Court, on behalf of the assesee it was contended that the principal terms governing the contract to which we will presently refer were: 1. The land should remain at the contractor`s risk till the date of final delivery; and in the event of the material being considered by the officer in the charge of the work to be inferior to that described in the specifications, the contractor shall on demand in writing forthwith to remove the same at his own cost and in case of his failure to do so within such period as may be named by the Executive Engineer or his Assistant. HELD: 1(a) The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not a works contracts. [162C] (b) According to the common features, the property was entirely of the assesses. He had not only to manufacture that but also to stack them for facilitating delivery. 1(c) It could not have been intended that the property in the earth would continue in the company despite its conversion into such a different thing as bricks. Further, there were several other terms which would ensure efficient production of the materials. [163F H] (d) The conclusion of the High 'Court was fully justified by the principal term governing the contracts to which the parties will presently referred. The contract was for sale of bricks and not works contract: [162E F] Chandra Bhan Gosain vs The State of orissa, referred to. In the present case, the building in the bricks was entirely separate of the appellant. He did not only manufacture that nor also to manufacture it, but also had to stacks them for facilitated delivery. [164C] 2(a). The contract provided that the bricks would remain at be the contractor 's risk until the date when final delivery. in Chandra Bhan Bas Gosain 's case (supra) the contractor could not sell the bricks at all unless they belonged to him. Then, he did not have any right to sell them and if he does sell it he will have to pay 10% of the value of the goods at the tender rates. [165E F; 166A B] Chandra Ban Gosain`s case and Chandra Bhan Girdharain vs State of Orissa, ; , relied on. (b)(a) There was nothing unreasonable in the contract in making the contract for the brick produced was transferred as a chattel for consideration and it would not be difficult for him unless they were his property. [166B C] (c) The decision of the Supreme Court in Chandra Ban Lal Pandain 'S case will govern the present ease where terms and conditions are almost identical so far as relating to the relevant subject matter.

Dismissing the writ petition, the Court ^ HELD: The two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were neither in operation on 4.2.1972 nor meant to have been published in the official Gazette. [475C] 2. (a) Article 352 does not prescribe that a Proclamation of Emergency should be published in an official gazette. Indeed it is seen that any public notification issued under Article 364(1) has to be published whenever the House of the People has been dissolved or the dissolution of the House is the business of Parliament of the Dominion of India and the proceedings of the legislatures by the journals of these bodies, or by newspapers purporting to be printed by order of the Government concerned. [386E G] (b) The State Legislature had power under section 102(2) of the 1971 Act to issue a Proclamation in pursuance of this Article. But it was open to the Governor General to publish a notification issued by him under Article 174(2), if he was satisfied that a grave emergency existed whereby the security of India or of any part thereof is threatened, whether by war or internal disturbance, he might by Proclamation make a declaration to that effect. [385E F] (c) The Constitution does not prescribes that a proclamation of Emergency must be published for the very same reason as condition precedent. The expressions "any public notification" and "a resolution approving the Proclamation are used in clause (2). The provisions of section 57 of the indicate that the course of proceeding of Parliament is to render judicial notice of the facts stated therein. [387F] 3. If a law issue under Article 356(1), the Governor shall cause to be prepared a full report of proceedings of both Houses of Parliament and of the State Legislatures, as the case may be, and publish it in such form and manner as the Chairman may from time to time direct." The Rules of Procedure of the both Houses are made under article 118(2)(a) of Article 143. [389B C] 4 (a). If a resolution approving a Proclamation has been passed by the Council of States, but no resolution with respect to such proclamation has been issued by the House or Houses of State Legislatures it is considered to be sufficient. But the real question in this case is whether the resolutions passed by both the Houses of parliament approving the two Pro clamations are ineffective. [390G] (d) The production of the Lok Sabha slips and newspapers containing proceedings of a two Houses of the Parliament, could not make them ineffective. Therefore mere non publication of the resolutions approving the Proclimations of emergency in the Official Gazette did not make it ineffective. If such publication is considered necessary in the public interest, there would be no need for the court to take judicial notice as laid down by section 57.

The appellants filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises constituted a temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. The claim was rejected by the District Judge on appeal. On further appeal the High Court reversed the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court, but held that the property did not constitute a temple and set aside the decision of the said authorities. Hence this appeal by special leave. It was contended for behalf of the appellant that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property of the family and was an alienable private property capable of alienation, and as such, was incapable of valuation; it could have in either case no market value. HELD: The claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the plaint, the property was the property of a public temple capable of alienations is not less than Rs. 20,000/ or more and (c) that the appeal did not involve any substantial question of law. [157 C F] Therefore, on the facts of the case it was difficult to hold that whether the property belonged to the Thoguluva family or was a public Temple, it was incapable for value of valuation as it could be had in either event no market values. [ 157 F G] The appellant 's case was that the premises were purely private and belonged to him and was not capable of valuation. Therefore, the suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application, being O.P. 3837, praying for a decree setting aside the said decision.

The respondents claimed their workmen Rs. 570/ per day and the subordinate staff as also in regard to tiffin arrangements made by them, while they were paid a much smaller salary for doing the same work than they were drawing before retirement. The appellant contended that the practice of employing retired persons should be discontinued, and for the reasons stated above, a cash allowance should be given to them. Held, that the Tribunal 's direction was either improper or unjustified, because there was some force in these contentions. When it appeared to the appel lant that some employees who had retired found it difficult to maintain themselves and their families, the appellant sympathetically considered their request for re employment and that is, the basis on which some of the re employments have been made. The decision to extend the relief would depend upon whether an employee is introducing a wage structure in respect of a reemployed personnel which is definitely inferior to the wage structure devised for the employees of the appellant by the award and that clearly cannot be permitted under industrial law. Chandi Charan Banerjee vs Union of India, [1960] 2 S.C.R. 603, relied on. In the instant case it was not obligatory on the part of the appe lant to make any requisition of its employees for providing that their wages would not be resorted to on a liberal scale, those assurances were disregarded and the practice was being followed in many cases and since, at least four persons had been employed and the correspondence between the parties on this subject showed that the policy adopted by the appellant in re employing the retired personnel was not based solely on humanitarian grounds. The fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by a third employee could not have any material bearing in dealing with the point, inasmuch as, it was presented before the Court by the respondents. Chandrai Charan Mohanty vs Union Of India, ; , referred to.

The respondent was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne addressed a letter to the Chief Accounts Officer intimating that the sanction of the General Manager for payment of special contribution to Provident Fund to Browne in French in terms of r. 1410(1) of the Railway Establishment Code was not accepted and sent them to the Reserve Bank for conversion of the amount in sterling which they were encashed. On the next day Radha Kissen Agarwalla started another execution application and applied for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money which by section 3 of the , was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The executing court overruled the objection holding that the attach issued by the Court on December 8, 1956 was perfectly in order. the moneys attached by the court lost their character as Provident Fund moneys long before they were attached and hence they were not immune from attached. The Union of India then applied to the High Court for writs quashing the attachment on ground (1) that by sending the two cheques to the respondent Bank in performance of the manner of Payment prescribed by Browne, the debt was discharged; and (2) that no order was passed directing the transfer of the money already lying with the Reserve bank. The High Court allowed the petition holding that by ordering the attachment and not to till then. HELD: 1.1 The HighCourt was in error in holding that a money in the hands of the Reserve Railway had ceased to be provident fund, and liable to be attached. [32C] 2.2 In the instant case, the Union Bank had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal, of attachment. But both the cheques drawn by the Railway Administration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3. Therefore, the order passed by the High court is set aside and there will be no order as to costs.

An employee whose services have been terminated by the management, a pump manufacturing enterprise, issuing a notice ending the employment and offering one month 's pay as authorized by the relevant Standing Orders. The appellant union protested against the order of termination as victimisation, mala fide, illegal and an act of victimisation. The Management in his written statement admitted the misconduct committed by the employee while denying the refer ence to trade union activities of the workman. It also stated that there was no proof with it for this suspicion it could not proceed against him departmentally and, in the circumstances, it was considered desirable to terminate the services of a workman as per Standing Orders the management without any stigma attached to it. The Labour Court held that the punishment of dismissal was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee, and dismissed the appellant 's writ petition upholding the order on merits. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The procedure adopted by the Management in the present case is neither colourable nor mala fide. [452 B] Where there has been no finding of victimisation, unfair labour practice or victimisation, it would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. In that case, the form of the order had no foul trace, but before the Tribunal dereliction of duty and go slow tactics were disclosed as the inarticulate reasons. The management could well have disclosed their suspicion in reply and told the Union and the workman that they resorted to an innocuous discharge avoid punitive trauma. [ 496 E F] (2) Even assuming that the loss was exalted, as a ground but the special circumstances of the case exonerated bad faith in discharge simpliciter, there being no other legal method of accompli shing their wish to remove him for misconduct. The charge levelled against the workman could not be said to have been bona fide. There is no speck of record or any hint of written material in support of the story that the management had credible information of the appellant betraying sensitive secrets of business, and therefore, the action was taken to be bonafide and the overall unsuitability led to a loss of confidence in the employee. [594 F] The direction given by the High Court to the Labour Court for holding an enquiry is one such instance , if the purpose and effect. are cogent grounds valid in law. But if such a finding is based on no evidence, or is the result of a misreading of the material evidence,or is so unreasonable or grossly unjust that no reasonable person would judicially arrive at that conclusion, it is the duty of this Court to interfere and set matters right. [498 D G] (3) The view taken by the Labour Appellate Tribunal was not correct. There was only the ipse dixit of the employer that he was suspecting since 1968 that the appellant was divulging secrets relating to his business. No such finding was made in the discharge order, or any material hint which tends to show that the workmen resorted to a innocuous discharge.

The Lions Club, Pottery Town in Uttar Pradesh arranged and conducted as part of its social service programme. The Club invited Dr. R.M. Sahay and his team of doctors to offer the surgical services. The Camp was arranged in 'Aggarwal Dharamshala ' at Novelty Road, Khurja (U.P.). The Camp ' was arranged 'Aggi lant Dharamshala Station ' at NOvelty road, Chaurasia Nagar. Dr. P.R. Singh and his associate doctors were put up for trial before the Court. Dr R. M. Sahay were also examined in the proceedings. Similarly, the inquiry report dated 8.6.1986 conducted by Dr. Anil Kumar Sinha, Chief Medical Officer, Buland Sahar District (U .P.) and the recommendation of the subcommittee of the Indian Medical Council do not deny this kind of propaganda or lack of institutional post operation care. Dr S.R Mankul submitted that persuant to the results of inquiries conducted by the Deputy Director (Eye Care) and the Sub Divisional Magistrate, appropriate follow up action is contemplated by the Government against persons concerned and that, indeed, a criminal case has been regis tered against Dr. S. R .M. underwear and he has been admitted to bail. Any process by which the answering Respondent would be compelled to disclose, in advance, his defence at the Criminal trial by replying to specific allegations in the Writ Petition would be violative of article 20(3) of the Con stitution of India, in so far as it concerns the Answering respondent. The petitioners filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the vires of these guidelines mainly on the ground that the victims of this medical mishap were given expert rehabilitatory treatment and appro priate compensation; that the Government do conduct a thorough investigation as to the conditions which rendered an medical misadventure of such a scale possible and evolve proper guide lines which will prevent recurrence of such tragedies; and that the appropriate legal action be com mended against Dr RM.248 The High Court dismissed the petition in limine on the view that the petitioners have failed to ensure obedience to the norms. Allowing the Special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 It is not merely that the unfortunate patients did not derive any benefit from the surgery but were greatly worse of than they were before the surgery owing to the post operative intra ocular medical negligence that damaged the operated eyes beyond redemption. Apart altogether from the casual connection between the widespread infection and medication or surgical procedures, as the case may be, applied or employed, it is really undisputed that such a general and unusual postoperative infection did occur. [8 C] 1.2 The learned doctor 's description of what happened to the victims is somewhat of an over simplification. The almost universal post operative hours left behind in its trial, the doctor says: "It may be mentioned that on the morning of 22nd April, 1986, Dr. Kalyan Ghosh and his associates and assistants a large number of patients could not regain their vision in the Khurja Camp". [8 G] 1 2.1 As to the devastation the almost universal Post operative infection left behind at its trial the doctor observed that despite every care taken by the Answer ing Respondent and his par ties, and assistants, a large quantity of patients cannot be restored despite every effort. On humanitarian consideration, the victims should be afforded some monitary relief by the State Government. [89 G; 890 A B] 2.2 In regard to the quantum of relief, the learned counsel submitted that the injured victims otherwise satisfy the conditions of those schemes. The causes of serious misha pation are not such as to fall in the category of discrimination.

On the basis of a resolution passed by the Bihar Legislative Assembly, under the Asom Hindi Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984, the first Chief Minister of Assam directed the Managing Committee to prepare a select list of successful candidates to be called for interview. The list was published in which the names of the successful candidates were shown. The petitioner society filed a writ petition challenging, inter alia, the vires of the Asam Rashtrabhasha Prachar sam Suchar Samiti Act, 1983 and also the validity of the order passed by him under the Pre sentication issued under Section 3 of the Act as ultra vires. The said writ petition was contested by the petitioner society mainly on the ground that (i) it violated the fundamental right of the peti tioners; and (ii) the procedure laid down in Section 16(Gha), Rules 15 to 17, which required that the amendment should reach the head office within the month of January every year. The Governor of Assam promulgated an Ordinance called the As samajubi Sabha (Taking Over of Management) Act 1984 and Section 1 sub clause (ii)(via) of this Ordinance provided that in the event of any amendment to Section 16 of the Bidhan Act or to Section 3, the Government may constitute a Board for the purposes of taking over the management and control of the Samiti consisting of not more than 9 members. The D.A. directed the State to restore back all assets and properties of the Samajuba Sabha and appoint a fresh constitution to be held in accordance with the Constitution to elect a Byabasthapika Sabha, which was originally enacted as Assam Rashtra bhasha prachar Samiti with its head office at Gauhati. The first meeting of the Board was held on 10.8.82 wherein the first meeting was held, wherein the petitioner No. 1 had a membership of about 164 22,000 persons scattered all over the States and Union Territories of North Eastern part of India. The Samiti passed resolutions for 167 amendment of the provisions of the the Bidan Act in pursuance of which the peti tions were made. By this Resolution all persons except the respondent No. 11 and Respondent No. 12 who had the principal members, filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the validity and validity of both the earlier statutes as well as the orders passed by them. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that (1) the amendments were not justified; (2) there was no violation of natural justice inasmuch as the procedure for taking over of the management temporarily, amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity, which resulted in discrimination to Respondent No 11 and (3) all the earlier actions taken under the Act taken over by the Board must be set aside. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment of the High court, this Court HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 16 sub clause(ii)(iii) are mandatory in character and not directory in nature. [179H; 180A] 2.1 The Act of 1984 and a Board nominated or appointed under Section 4 of the said Act is con trolled by the provisions contained in Section 3. Therefore, it was only for an eye wash and by this process the State Government intended to deprive the members of the society their right under Article 19(1) (c) for all times to come. [180B] 2(i)(ii) The contention that even after 1984 when the Act talks of a temporary measure in fact, the Act does not provide for as to how when the temporary measures comes to an end, the elected Byabho Prachar Sabha and Karyapalika would be restored is incorrect.

Where a widow gave her daughter in marriage and at the time of the marriage negotiations at Deoghar, the terms of the settlement included a promise by Sumitra Devi that she would arrange for the gift of ornaments worth about Rs. 20,000. The deed was not executed within the time prescribed by section 122 of the . Held, further, that the gift was not made at the 'time of the ' marriage and it was not intended to be a valid gift. The donor had authority to make such a gift. But in this case where a widow giving her daughter did not execute any deed of gift, section 123 did not apply as it stood prior to the enactment of the Indian Succession Act. In Churaman Sahu vs Go pi Sahu ([1959] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 938), Adren guments vs Manickuri (A.I.R., , Toron vs Cendworth [1878] 3 A.C., referred to. Held further, also that the respondent was not entitled to the declaration made by her in pursuance of section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act which lays down that for the purpose of making a gift of immoveable property, the transfer must be effected by a registered instrument signed by or on behalf of the donor, and attested by at least two witnesses. In the case of essential or obligatory acts, if the income of the property or the property itself is not sufficient to cover the expenses, she was entitled to sell the whole of it. But for acts which are pious and which conduce to the bliss of the deceased husband 's soul she can alienate a reasonable portion of the Property. (6) If a promise is made of such a gifts for or at the instance of the grantor, and it is not essential to make a gift at the date of the interview, that in this ease, the acceptance by the grantee subsequent to the marriage might be supported upon the ground that the admission when made fulfils that moral or religious obligation.

The appellant, who had secured 62594 votes for the respondent and the other candidate 's election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, secured 25694 votes whereas Avtar Singh (appellant) secured 9595 votes. The margin between the votes secured by Tej Singh (respondent) and L (RP) was only 123 votes. On appeal, the High Court set aside the election of the first respondent as being an unsuccessful candidate. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is imperative to defeat the dictatorial Congress in these elections. [419C] 2. The appellant had been clearly admitted by him that no election symbol was issued and he had no connection with the same. In other words, Tej Singh has not disputed that the payment of vouchers .(Ex P 5 and P 6) were made by him and the vouchers were appended by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign which was verified by him to be a true and correct statement. [416D G] 2:1. From the evidence both oral and documentary adduced by the parties, it is clear that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters. Tej Singh further admitted that Bhum Raj was incharge of his election office at Moga and that L ( RW 2) had no account with the money payable to him. It is also clear from his evidence that in view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to the appellant (Aaboratories Singh). [417E F] 2 :2. In view of these very narrow limits of votes to which the voters of Baghapurana Constituency should be ruled out, and as the margin of election was very small viz. 123 votes if such a misrepresentation was not made in all probability the votes would have went to the appellants (Aatrix Singh) and, therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered. The result is that the appeal is allowed, the judgment of the High court is quashed and the election petition of the appellant.

The respondent, the Chief Minister of the State filed a writ petition in the High Court complaining of interference by the respondent with due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. After hearing the parties and after considering the facts and circumstances of the case, the learned Single Judge dismissed the application and discharged the rule netio nation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as no punishment was imposed by the High Courts in exercise of its jurisdiction under section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, a writ of certiorari could be issued for quashing the order of Assessment on the ground that the authority concerned had erroneously exercised its jurisdiction by not granting exemption to the petitioner. On behalf of Respondent it was urged that as the jurisdiction to punish for contempt includes also the jurisdiction, to dispose of the cases either by punishing the contemnor or by acquitting him, and in any case, a judgment passed in exercise thereof could be challenged collaterally or on an application for certiorari but were binding until reversed on appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A proceeding between the court and the alleged contemnor is not one of criminal contempt as defined in section 2(c) of 'the Act. When no punishment is imposed by a High Court, it is difficult to say that the High COurt has exercised its power or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution.

The respondent obtained a permanent lease of both these properties for a period of ten years and the appellant who was one of the heirs, was recognised as the lessee for the period 18th August, 1870. It also agreed to pay monthly rent of Rs. 80 per mensem. The appellant thereafter sold his tenancy rights to one Girdhari Balaram Lodhi for Rs. 7999 and after her death a yearly payment equal to the assessment of the two lands to the heirs ofaswami. The lease provided that in default of payment of rent the tenant 's right would come to an end: On 18th September, 1870 Ladha Ibrahim sold his leasehold rights to another person for Rs, 799 and soon thereafter Ladha heard the respondent 's attempt to terminate this tenancy. This was turned down by the respondent and he filed a suit out of which this appeal arises for possession on the ground that since no rent was fixed in respect of the suit property and also because it was for the appellant to approach the respondents and not for the defendants to go to the plaintiff, and pay it, the appellant had failed to do so. The trial court dismissed the suit but passed a decree in favour of another person against which he obtained possession on forfeiture on 28th January, 1941, and his share. On appeal by special leave: Held (per Sinha, C. J., Gajendragadkar and Ranganathan, jj.) that section III(g) of the Transfer of Property Act makes no difference between a lease and a lease which is executed in 1870, and if it were so express to provide a wide discretion, meaning, no doubt, to prevent one man from forfeiting what in fair dealing belongs to some one else. It does not mean that the rule does not apply where there is a forfeiture by denial of the landlord 's title, a notice in writing determining the lease was necessary and it could be said that there was no real discretion. The distinction between a "sale" and a "reconveyor" has been thinly stated as one of discretion, and its application to leases executed prior to 1929, and the rule must be held to govern even agricultural leases. The English law on the subject is well settled. Where the statute does not require them, the ordinary rule would be that it should be applied only where statutory provisions contained in it cannot stand together. The principle of equity and good conscience are not such a variable commodity. The general rule (of equity) must necessarily be applied to leases granted under sections 114 and 115 of the , as well as in other sections of the Act, since the law stands today under the Act and the rules in force at the time and the only rule applicable is that a tenant cannot by his unilateral act or by his own wrong determine the lease unless the lessor gives an indication by some unequivocal expression of intention on his part of taking advantage of the breach. But if the purpose of the rule as to notice was to indicate the intention of the lessor to determine the leased lease and to avail himself of the tenant, the court has no discretion in the matter and must grant relief to the tenant irrespective of the conduct of the parties. [1024 B] Fulsara Savla Sudrik vs Yeshwanta Kondiba Mulay ([1932) 59 I.A. 21, referred to. There can be no doubt that when the Act is so express or by analogy it has not been made applicable to leases of prior to 1930 or even prior to the coming into force of the . [1025 E G] Case law reviewed. Where there was a forfeiture for non payment of Rent, or for non compliance with covenants in the lease. The rule as framed by the Master of the Rolls in the present case is not relied upon and it is not open to consider whether the Court must and will lean to relieve a tenant against forfeiture on every occasion particularly when he was warned by the court of appeal on a previous occasion.
