The appellants were tenants of a private forest. The lands which were occupied by the appellants had no lawful origin in their way. In such circum stances the High Court took the view that the benefit of section would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurveyed lands had a lawful origin and not to persons m unlawful occupation based on trespass or forcible entry. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to those persons whose posses sion had a subsisting origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons who were competent to grant such leases or had come into possession with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. It was not within the contemplation of the Legisla tor to confer the benefit Of protection on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. [113B C] The intention was to give protection only if those persons were in occupation of land in which they went bona fide believing that such land was Government 'S 's land of which the appellants could later obtain assignment or have taken the land on lease for from persons whom they bona fide believe to be competent to granting such leases. [114D F] The expression "in occupation" occurring in Section 7D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation".

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. The value of 7200 cigarette lighters was stated as Rs. 14400/ and of 250 tins of flints as Rs 15,000/ on which customs duty of Rs. 15,840/ and Rs 10500/ respectively was alleged to be payable. In the complaint filed on 30 10 1968 the Assistant Collector of Central Excise had admitted the production of keys from his possession. The seized articles were made over to the inspector of Central excise and Customs, Marine and Prevention Division Bombay, on 24 4 1967 under section 110 of the . The value was stated in the complaint that the cigarettelighters and flints were imported into India without an import licence and in contravention of provisions of Government of India Act, Ministry of Commerce & Industry Import Control Order No. 17/55 dated 7 12 1955, which was to be deemed to be an order passed under section 11 of the Act. The appellant 's explanation had been disbelieved by the trying Magistrate as well by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: lighters and Flints were notified as provided in the section 123(2) in the official Gazette of 26 8 1967. However, as the provisions of section 123 (1) of the , only lay down a procedural rule, they could be applied when the case came up for trial before the Presidency Magistrate who actually decided it on 15 7 1969. Indeed, the complaint itself was filed on 25 10 1968. It is immaterial that the appellant was not only in possession but knew something about the incriminating nature of their contents. Otherwise why should he, at first, have refused to produce the key he had ? Furthermore, the appellant had not given any evidence to show that his sub tenants had placed the boxes there or that there was a reason why he should allow them to use the portion reserved by him for himself. His case rested on his bare assertions in a written statement. Of course no one had come forward to state or allege that the goods found, in the circumstances stated above had been imported without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory; and, (2) that, even if the appellant is deemed to have been in possession with full knowledge of what the goods actually were, the Court could not go further and assume them to be smuggled or imported into the country from another country of their assumed origin after a time before when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. [541 C F] In any case there was some evidence to enable the Courts to come to the conclusion that the Goods must have been known to the appellant to be smuggling even if he was not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty.

(i) The provisions of a public statute which no Court can exclude from its consideration, are not held to be valid, and therefore would not only apply to the proceedings in respect of contracts which the law declares to be illegal, (ii)where a plaintiff comes to court on allegations which on the face of them show that the contract of partnership on which he sues is illegal was the only course for the courts to pursue was to say that he is not entitled to any relief on the allegations made as the courts cannot adjudicate in respect Of contracts which, the law declared to be unconstitutional (Senaji Kapurchand vs Pannaji Devichand ([1924) L.R. 52 I.A. 126), 128 E. R. 345 and Sartron vs Dunwood (1867) L.,R. 76 I. A. 129) referred to. The question is whether under the section, an unregistered firm is not illegal and if it does not comply with the provisions of the Act or any other law, it is competent for A to require B to hand back the money if B has not already parted with it and the illegal purpose has not been carried out. see Greenberg vs Cooperstein ; and In re Banarsi Das (I I.L.R , referred to and distinguished.

The respondents, who were accused in two special leave petitions before the High Court, applied for anticipatory bail alleging that on 8.6.1986 at 2 a.0 P.M., they along with another named in the complaint shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 13 of Kundurugutu Range Forest and removed the ivory tusks of the elephant. On 25.6 .1986, the Range Officer lodged a written complaint with the Judicial Magistrate alleging offences against respondents under sections 51, 52 of Wild Life Protection Act, 1972. The Magistrate took cognisance of this offence and ordered issue of process to the accused. In appeal, the High court quashed the proceedings against the respondents holding that the offences envisaged by section 9(1) read with section 50(1)(l) do not constitute the offence. It was also observed that a case to which section 210(1), Code of Criminal Procedure was attracted was pending and that as an investigation by the police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and calling for a report in the matter from the police; and that, therefore, she acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offences and ordering issue of summons. The High Court accepted the contention of the respondents and quashed the proceeding against the accused holding that as the investigation by Police was in complete progress in respect of the same offences, the Magistrate would not be required under section 210, Cr. P.C., 1973 before taking cognizance against the appellants when for the same allegation the investigation was being proceeding and pending, and that the learned Sessions Judge acted without jurisdic tion in taking congnizance of the offence and ordering issuing process against the respondent, it did, in passing an order dated 1.7.1986, and quashed proceedings against respondents. The State filed special leave petition before this Court.

In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner (i) The power of the Supreme Court to enlarge a person during the pendency of a Special Leave Petition or of an appeal is very wide; as order 21 Rule 27 of the Code discloses. in that sense, a consideration of the question (1) Report of the Legal Aid Committee appointed by the Government Of Gujarat (2) Report on legal Aid Processual Justice to the People, May 1973. 345 HELD: In the light of the guidelines which prevail with the Supreme court when granting suspension of sentence must, in a broad sense, have relevance to what the Code indicates except where special circumstances call for a different course. Moreover, the advocates who participated many of them did covered the wider area of release under the Code, whether with or without sureties, and that is why the Court consider the relevant provisions of the code in some detail. A semantic smog over frivated Kuamr the provisions of bail in the Code and prisoners rights, when cast in ambiguous language became precarious. Konjalgi the face of the poorest and the weakest man whom you may have seen, and ask yourself, if the step you contemplate is going to be of any use of him. There is no definition of bail within the meaning of section 2(oo) as including release on one 's own recognizance unless it is shown that there is substantial risk it is appearance or there are circumstances justifying imposition of conditions on release. If a Magistrate is Satisfied after making an enquiry into the condition and background of the accused that the accused has his roots in the community and is nor likely to abscond, he can safely release the accused on order to appear or on his own recognization.

In the assessment year 1951 52, the assessee claimed exemption from tax in respect of 6% of its capital employed in 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the capital so employed. The Income tax Officer held that in the assessment for 1950 52, he could not be regarded as a separate entity because in his view there were in these two undertakings the same eight partners with a share of /2(two annas) each, and that the constitution of both the undertakings being the same, 'Castle ' could not therefore be regarded, as a distinct entity. The Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed the Income tax authorities to state the case and refer it to the High Court. Commissioner appealed to this Court. Held:(i) The finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the income tax Officer in the earlier years and not in the year of assessment 1951 52. [436B C] (ii) Non inclusion of the income of 'C Packaging ' in the relevant assessment of the assessee may have been a relevant circumstance, but its effect had to be considered in the light of other circumstances on which the Appellate Assistant Commissioner relied. The finding that in a previous year to the year 1951 51 the income from 'Condastle was carried on business and had earned income cannot be regarded because a question of law arises out of the order of the tribunal. A question may arise out of an 'decision of the Appellate Tribunal, and also if the Tribunal has misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding, and in refusing to require the Tribunal to state a case for its opinion of the High court on the view that a question Of law arises from the order, it is not open to the Court to discard the Tribunal 's finding of fact, if there is some evidence to support the finding of Tribunal on a questionof fact, even if on a review of the evidence the Court might have arrived at a different conclusion. It must however be held that non inclusion of income of "Castoorle" in the assessments of the assessees may have also been a material circumstance, though its effect has to be consider in the 'castle".

The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was directed to file his personal affidavit. The Minister concerned thereafter heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The respondent challenged the subsequent order of February 18.1975 on the grounds inter alia that he had deviated from the normal procedure while passing the impugned order dated February 18; that in view of the High Court 's direction for impleading him as a party and the High court was in error in directing that the Minister be impleaded as a necessary party. The High Court allowed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that looking to the facts of the case if the High Courts came to the conclusion that the Government could not have interfered with the order made by the High COurt in so far as it directed that the Secretary be impleaded and he should file an affidavit in regard to the allegations made in the petition, it would be contrary to the directions given by the Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The direction for the impleading of the Minister as a respondent was given by tho High Court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations contained in the writ petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper, it is not necessary or proper party. [97C D] 2. The order whereby the Minister concerned was directed was to file the personal affidavit was set aside. [98D E] 3.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application for realisation of arrears of rent under section 259 of the , was made on January 7, 1960, for realisation from the respondent under section 258 of the Act on the ground that the amount due as arrears of land rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent had been due as arrear of rent on an annual rent. The magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of movable property of the defendant on June 13, 1961. Thereupon, the respondent went in revision to the Sessions judge. He held that section 259 was not applicable because it provided for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board to recover rent due under a lease. The High Court dismissed the reference holding that rent under a a lease could not be recovered under section259 and that the proceedings before him were not one under the Code of Criminal Procedure. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Section 259 does not bar the right of the Board as an owner or holder of land and buildings to take action for recovery of rent thereof by suit against a tenant who was liable under an express provision of the landlord. Therefore, section 259 cannot be applied to a simple case of money due to the Board on contract of lease. It follows therefore that section259 will apply; but where the liability to pay rent arises purely on the footing that it could not he said to be payable under any express provision Of the Act or the Rules to pay Rent to the board. [345 E G] (2) The right of a Board to claim the rent on land and building does not arise from these provisions under the , it is in such cases where the Act does not provide for claim of rent by the Board. Under that section the tenant 's liability to rent arises only when the liability arises to pay money arises against a person by reason of something done by the Chairman or the Military Estates Officer in exercise of a power or the performance of duty under the Act that liability can be enforced by the authority concerned either by instituting the suit or by making an application to a Magistrate. The section does not prevent any other provision which may have effect retro spectively from it.

The appellant was appointed as a section salesman in the respondent company on the basis of an unauthorised absence since 13th January 1973 and was con tinued to have left his service of his own account. At the instance of the respondent, Government referred to the Labour Court/or adjudication the question whether the termination of services of the appellant by the respondent Company was legal and justified. The Tribunal held that the appellant was not a "workman" and that, therefore, the reference was incompetent. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that: (1) Section salesmen and local salesmen are employed by the company in order to canvass and promote the sales of the company 's product in his area; and (2) The sections of the Industrial Disputes Act were not ap plicable and the reference therefore was incompetent, and it should be upheld. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1(a) It is seen from the facts found that the appeli lant was employed to do canvassing and promot ing sales for the company. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study following of the market condition. He was also required to suggest about the publicity in markets and melas, advertise ments including the need for posters, holders and cinema slides. These duties do require the imaginative and creative mind which could not be termed as either manual, skilled, unskilled or clerical in nature. [ 475A B] (b) The supervising work of the other local sales men was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the area of his operation. Such a person cannot be termed "workman". The section salesmen & local salesman and local trav elling salesmen who are appointed for certain number of districts and in the areas of his operations are employed on the shop of wholesaler or any retail dealer to sell them to collect the amount of sale. [475C] Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Company vs Burmah Corporation & Ors., 1976 II LLJ 974, followed. Burmah Insurance Storage & Distributing Co. vs Burma Shrad & Sons; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J. Dechane Distributor vs State 476 of Kerala and Ors., 1974 11 LLJ 971, referred to. (c) The Labour Court has given findings in favour of the ap pellant on the question as whether the appellant is a workman. [474C] 2(a). It was not the duty of the appellants to procure orders for the Company. None of the salesmen were employed to sell the product of the Company in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company; but it was only incidental ting to his primary function of canvassing, and promotion, in the four districts allotted to him. On these facts found, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the chal lant cannot be held to be a "sales promotion employees" for manual, unskilled and/or clerical nature and that the provisions of theIndustrial Disputes Act was not ap pelicable. [476D] 3(b) No interference is called for with the decisions of the Labour Courts on the ques tion whether the appei lant is a person workman. It is apparent from the records found that there was employed. to do canvass and promoting sales for 'the company. None, the salesman were employed by tile company inorder to canvass or promote the sale of the products of the companies in the 4 districts allotted by him. There were seven other local Salesmen and Local Trav eling Establishments were employed in the shop.

The respondent No. 1, the Madhya Pradesh Agricultural Lands (Vesting of Right to Property) Act, 1950, initiated proceedings against three respondents, the Gwalior Dairy Limited for eviction of the Company from its land. The Additional Collector issued a notice to the Company and the Company under section 182(2)(i) of the Code of Civil Procedure and the company filed a suit for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. It was contended by the Company that the land in question was held by the company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the land was not a `pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a ' Gair Maurusi ', and that it had not become a 'pakkha ' tenant under section 54(vii) of Part II of the Act. The High Court dismissed the Company 's appeal holding that the Company was not an occupancy tenant or as such under Section 185 of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959 and was, therefore, not liable to be proceeded against in terms, of Section 182 and, therefore since they were already held by it when that came into force, they had become a land 'Pakka Tenant" under section 181 of the Madhya Bharat Pradesh Land Revenue Act, Samvat 2007. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the High Court that the company was not "a pakka tenant" is totally unjustified and opposed to law. [180C] 2.

Section 1(3) of the Orissa Land Reforms Act, 1960 provided that where any law made any provision for the acquisition by the State of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire or requisitioning property, notwithstanding that it deprives any person of his property. By section 1(4) the Government was authorised to grant exemption from the operation of the ceiling in respect of certain classes of land, and section 52 imposed a ceiling on future acquisitions. Section 47 provided for the preparation and publication of final statement of ceiling and surplus lands after hearing objections if any received and after making enquiries as the Revenue Officer may deem necessary. By a notification issued on September 25, 1968, certain provisions of the Act other than those contained in Ch. III and IV were brought into force. The appellants challenged the authority of the Commission to investigate the cases which they challenged under the Act, by filing writ petitions before the High Court. They contended that the Travancore Act 14 Of 1124 (M.E.) not being a law in force when the United State was formed, the notification bringing the Act into force was ineffective and therefore the law must provide for the transfer of ownership or right to possession of any property to the State or to a corporation owned or controlled by the state; The High Court rejected that contention and held that section 47 incorporated by Act 13 of 1965 which provided for compensation not based on the market value, but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent was in consistent with article 3 1 A proviso 2 to article 31 A. HELD: Per Shah, J: (i) While Ch. IV of the principal Act was repealed by the Amending Act 15 of 1965, it was clearly enacted that under any law which provides for the acquisi tion of any land in an estate under the personal cultivation of the holder, compensation shall not only be less than the marketvalue thereof but at the fifteen times, the fair, and equitable rate. The expression "law in force" must be "construed only in the constitutional sense and not in the sense of its actual operati possessing".

The appellant, who was the widow of a Hindu widow, filed a suit against the respondents in respect of her rights to property belonging to the last male owner during the lifetime of the widow 's estate. The trial Judge dismissed the suit on the ground that there was a severance of joint status by an informal partition between Mathurbhai and Kashibhai but he dismissed the plaintiff 's suit on this ground. On appeal, the High Court held that there had been acceleration of inheritance in favour of the appellant and that in any case, in case of re surrender of the property to her late husband 's heirs, the deed of surrender was invalid and even if it was valid the surrenderees could not claim possession so long as the widow was alive. Held : (i) The right of the reversioner to challenge it is no part of the estate or its interest commensurate with the period of her natural life. In deciding whether a transfer made by a Hindu wife prior to the date of surrender, acquired by adverse possession against her, the interest created is to be deemed severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow, the surrenders must take it subject to such prior interest. The law of limitation that has legalised what was originally a clear act of usurpation is not to spilt up the husband ' his estate into two parts or to give to the alienee an interest necessarily co extensive with her life. (ii) An alienation made by Hindu widow in excess of her powers, though not binding on the inheritance created by it, creates in the alience an interest commensurate With the period during which she could convey to others, is not protected by any law under which, the act of the widows could bind him; they came upon the land as trespassers with,out any right and they came after the widow had parted with her interest in the property. (iii) In order to succeed on the basis of a surrender by a person who has acquired by an adverse possession the limited interest of a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe is legally valid, but unless it is proved that he fell within one of the description of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes as defined in article 366(5)(b), and subject to any other special provisions of law, the property shall be deemed to have been severed from that of the transferee. The alienation made may defeat or affect some valuable rights which the reversioners must have had in writing on the order of transfer but not as a mere device to share the estate with the reversioner, and no acceptance by the reversioner is necessary as a condition precedent to the vesting of theestate in him. Where there was no necessity for such alienation, the interests which she himself held and which she can convey to otherless persons are not affected by any act of surrender on her part of a widow ' 's property without any justification or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by adverse Possession against her.It is therefore not correct to say that there is no principle of law under Which the acts of the wife could bind the reversioner. (iv) The fact that prior rights derived from the widow if not supported by legal necessity, could be defeated by the next heir of the husband or the adopted son as the case may be.

The respondent was the management of the affairs New Swadeshi Polytex Ltd. (the Company) and was governed by the Uttar Pradesh Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958. In 1976, the Cotton Mills Company was acquired by Mangturam Jaipuria and his family in 1946. The Mill Company acquired 10 lakhs shares of Rs. 10 each from its members. On instructions from certain members, on being given to them under Section 169 of the Act from Swadeshy Cotton Mills Co. Ltd., some of its shareholders moved the High Court for issue of a writ of Certiorari against the respondent and others, alleging mismanagement of the New Sw Spadeshi Cotton Mills. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since a Receiver had been appointed by the Collector in respect of the shares held by the Mill Company and they had also been attached, the shares should not have been taken into consideration for determining the required qualification to issue the notice under section 169 of 'the Act requisitioning the extraordinary general meeting and without the support of the shareholders of the Mills company, the remaining requisitionists would not have any voting strength to issue a notice under Section 179 of the . It further held that since the said Receiver had already been appointed as a Director in respect thereof, the attachment of the 9 lakhs shares out of the 10 lakhs with the Government of Uttar Pradesh as security for the loans advanced by it was also not invalid. Aggrieved by the High Judgment and order of dismissal of the writ application, the Mills Company came up in appeal to this Court. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The attachment of shares in the Polytex Company held by virtue of an earlier judgment in a case which was pending before this Court, would not affect the voting rights of the Cotton Mill Company. [877C] 1.2 An order made by the Central Government on April 13, 1978 under section 18 AA (1) (a) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951 taking over the management or management of any industrial unit without more cannot, therefore, have the effect of depriving the holder of the share of his title to the shares. [888C D] Kerr on Receivers (14th Edn.) at page 310: "The power of the company and its directors to deal with the property comprised in the appointment (both property subject to a floating charge and property subject thereof to a fixed charge, except subject to the charge. are paralysed" which was relied on by the appellants is not of much use to them. [879D] Kerirkar vs Attril Reddi ; , Kerr, on Receivivers (13th Edn. p. 310: applied. Kerr. vs Attari Lila Pershad; ; Kerr vs Attani trict Judge ; Kertr on receivers (19th Edn.), at page 312; Kerr and Kerr dated Receivers, (16th Edn., p. 83, referred to. In the instant case, it is to be noted that a charging order under the English Law is not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of a Receiver under the Land Revenue Act.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. They instituted a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they are the owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala district Sangrur in the State of Punjab (the Panchayat) had no sort of right in the suit lands and that the suit is liable to be dismissed. The trial Court framed an issue relating to its jurisdiction and tried it as a preliminary issue. It held that since the question involved was simply one of title to the suit property, it was not necessary to decide whether the suit had been shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlat malle deh. The plaintiffs preferred this petition before this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution of India praying for grant leave to prefer an appeal against the decision of the High Court. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contention that the land was a part of shamlat over deh conferred jurisdiction on the civil court when by virtue of Section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act 1961 (Punjab Act No. 18 of 1961), the jurisdiction of the Civil Court had not been taken away by virtue Of Section 13 read with Sections 13A and 13B of the Act which had been inserted by the Haryana Legislature into the Act. [835E] 1.2 The dispute in the instant case was whether the civil Court had decided that the question was a whole one of original title to it, and not by the civil suit. [827F G] 1:3 The above decision is clearly distinguishable from the present case since in this case the Panchayat which had originally impleaded as a defendant had raised the plea that the matter was shamlat er deh and it had been vested in it. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Courts to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamil deh or was not, and whether it belonged to the Panchayat, or not. [826F G; 835A] Bhagu & Ors., vs Ram Sarup and Ors., [1985] Punjab Law Journal Page 366 in which the suit has been held to be maintainable in a civil court even though the defendant had contended that the plaintiff had only stated in the plaint that the lands belonged to him or that it did not belong to the Gram panchayat. The crucial issue which had initially been framed in that case was, whether the lands in question over which the plaintiff asserted his right was a street or not, but whether it belongs to the gram Panchayat or no. [828B D] 1 :4. On a decision of this Court in Bhagu and Ors. vs Ram Ram Sarup & Ors. , [1985], Punjab Law journal Page 366, the suit having been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the suits land was shamat deh, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. The petitioners cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration, that they were the owners along with others of the said suit land had avoided to seek a declaration from the plaintiffs in respect of an issue which there is no ground to interfere with the judgment of the trial Court and not even by the Civil court.

The appellant Board is a commercial concern. The Electricity Board is constituted under the provisions of the Electricity Act, 1910 as also under the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948. Under clause 15.3 of the terms and conditions, in the event of delay in payment of consumption or additional consumption deposit within the stipulated period, the consumer is obliged to pay surcharge at 18%. The appellant Board was also empowered to demand electricity from a consumer of high tension electricity on credit but the rate of interest on security deposit could not be equated with the rate at which it had power to charge penal interest at 2% per month for non payment of bills within the prescribed period. In the meantime, under clause 28.6 of the conditions in the case of daily supply of electricity, there was a corresponding liability to pay to the Board any sum that may become due for payment to the appellant Board on the dates fixed for payment thereof, and the demand of security from the consumer which was in accordance with the Regulations framed by the State Electricity Board, could not therefore be said to be unreasonable merely because no interest was paid on the cash security deposited by the consumer. On appeal, the Division Bench set aside the order of the learned Single Judge insofar as it gave directions that in case the Supreme Court decided that the interest at a rate higher than 3% should be paid on such security deposit and also extended to the appellants there without the necessity of any further proceedings being taken by the petitioners. Hence these Appeals. On behalf of the appellant Electricity Board it was contended: (1) There is no legal obligation to pay interest on a deposit made by the consumers with the Board in terms of clause 20(a) & (c) of the General Conditions of Supply; (2) The Electricity Regulation Act, 1981 providing for levy of electricity at concessional rates does not contain any norm of guideline with regard to framing of terms and condition for the supply of power; (3) It is in the nature of an advance payment. (4) In the event, of failure to pay, it could be proceeded against as seen from clause 28 in the manner prescribed by Regulation 20 read with Schedule II of 252 of the Supply Act that the Board may supply electricity to any person upon such terms and Conditions as the Board thinks fit. The explanation given by the appellant was not correct because in the present case there was nothing to indicate under the scheme of the Act or schedule VI of the supply that interest must be paid at the rates prescribed by the regulations. (5) A similar provision in a general condition for supply of the Board cannot be treated as arbitrary or unreasonable and it is not arbitrary or violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. Allowing the Appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. For the purpose of achieving the desired objective and to ensure that the intention of Parliament shall not be defeated a law is enacted which operates somewhat harshly on a small section of the public, taken in conjunction with the position that without a law in that form and with that amplitude smuggling might not be possible of effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by Article 19(1)(f) &(g). [262C] 2. If there is a revision in the rate or tariff there has to be an upward revision of the consumption security deposit since it had a direct bearing on the level of supply in consumption of electricity.

The petitioners belonged to the Telecommendi nation Research Centre when they were recruited at the Entry level of Junior Class I posts of S & T.Os Grade I (Telecom negligence) Project, which is directly under the control of the P&T Board of the Ministry of Communications Government of India. The Telecommunication Research Centre is engaged in the research and development work concerning the telecommunication equipment for the use of the Depart ment and in advising the P & T Board on relevant technical matters relating to the introduction of new equipment and technology in the existing public communication net work. In pursuance of the said advertisement petitioners 2,3 and 4 applied for recruitment and they were selected for appointment to the posts of Assistant Directors or Deputy Director since 1975. Direct recruitment to the Univer sity Research Centre has been discontinued.) The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong belonged and the transferred Field Officers Group A working in the Telecommunication Technology Project is being made under the Scientif ic and Technical Officers Grade I(Telecommunications Reve Audit Centre) Regulation, 1962 framed by the President under the provi so to Article 309 of the Constitution of India with effect from 1.1.1973. In response thereto petitioners 2 and 3 applied for selec tion and they prayed for recruitment as on account of their irregular implementation of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules and the second relating to violation of Article 14 and Article 16 of the Constitu tion by not grant ing them the same special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers who are working In the Tele communication Research Centre to prevent persons of inferior caliber amongst them getting into the said centre. The direct recruit recruits to whom category the peti tioners belong are not given any Special Pay in these grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It is stated that the total number of officers who were thus getting Special Pay is of the order of 275 while only about 25 Officers who are direct recruits working in P &T Department are not give any Special pay in addition to their scale of pay which was the same as the scale of D.A. The petitioners have filed these petitions demanding payment of Special Pay to them also. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellant who was employed as a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara, challenged the order of dismissal before the Labour Court under Section 78 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act 1946. His complaint was that he did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour court and prayed that the order be set aside on that ground alone. The Labour Court after holding an enquiry took the view that the findings of the Enquiry Officer were perverse, that the orders of dismissal were passed by a person not authorised to exercise the power and consequently the Labour Appellate Tribunal directed reinstatement of the third respondent with all back wages. On appeal to the State Industrial Court it was contended for the appellant, inter alia, (i) that the third Respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he had failed. section 42 (4) could not be construed as creating a complete departure from the procedure prescribed in Ch. VIII dealing with transfers; and (ii) that no evidence was allowed or filed on behalf of the employer and that the finding was based only on his statement, and in particular his cross examination. HELD: The scheme of Chapter VIII seems to be that in regard to any "change" in an matter there must be compliance with the provision of that chapter. In other words effort must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect of matters covered by section 42.(1) or an employee desiring a change in any respect of an order passed by the management under standing orders which would, of necessity include an order of dismiss, discharge and removal, retrenchment, termination of service or suspension as the case may be.

The dispute in the appeal is about the right to contin ue in possession after 31.7.1971 in respect of certain premises in the town of Ranchi, which belongs to the appellants and in which a cinema theatre is running. The contesting respondents have been occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.07.1971. They served a notice on the appel lants on 16.7 1971 claiming the right as tenants from month to month. The appellants did not accept the claim and filed before Munsif Ranchi a case purporting to be an application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent & Evic tion) Control Act, 1947, contending that the appellants ' application under Section 12 was not maintainable. The respondents contested the application and raised several points in defence which were rejected by the trial court. The Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi agreed with the findings of the Munsif on merits and concluded that the ap peals had formed a partnership as a result of which a new month to year tenancy was created, and the parties were having the relationship of lessors and lessees and landlords respectively. No month to tenan cy had been created; and in view of the findings recorded by the courts below, it is not necessary to deal with this aspect now. The parties led full evidence both oral and documentary, on the disputed issues and after an elaborate trial the learned Munsif accepted the appellants case that they are the successors in interest of the lessor company, and they were liable to eviction after the expiry of the lease period on 31st July 1971 as per the terms of the deed of lease dated 31. 7.71971.

The appellant, a registered Society, filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the court of the District Judge Jaipur City. The counsel engaged by the appel lant were Sri Satya Narain Sharma and Sri Shyam Bihari Agarwal. The suit was later transferred to the Court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1 Jaipur City where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as the Secretary. The prayer was contested and the trial court rejected the application on the ground that the same was not maintainable, proceeded further to consider the question as to who was the duly elected Secretary of the society i.e., Hari Narain Pandit. Since no notice was given of his application for withdrawal of the Suit either to the then Secretary Laxman Das Mandir or to the learned advocates Sri Satya Narayan Sharma or Sri Shyam Sunder Agarwal, through whom he the suit had been instituted, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court. Later on in the next election another Secretary named Jeeva Nand Swami was nominated and when he learnt about the fate of the peti tion, an application was filed for recalling the withdrawal order and restoring the suit to its file. The trial court after holding that the appellant was the elected Secretary, allowed the suit for withdrawal on two grounds, viz., (i) the mistake could not be corrected in the present situation; (ii) the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Proce dure was not entertainable; and (iii) the trial Court had committed several serious errors in deciding the question. The High Court agreed with the Trial Court that only remedy of the appellant is to file a fresh suit. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: The case has to go back to the trial courts for reconsideration of the evidence on this point, but the reality of the consent cannot be so investigated. [237H; 237A B] Sadho Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483, referred to.

Section 1 (3) of the , provides that the period referred to in sub section (1) shall commence with the date of the passing of this Act and ending with such date as His Majesty may by order declare to be the end of the emergency which was the occasion of the pass of this Ordinance. The appellant who was an accused No. 1 before a Magistrate was charged along with the respondent for having transferred by sale 10 High Denomination Bank Notes, both transfer and disposal of these goods at the rate of Rs. 180 per note. He sold the goods to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi for Rs. 1,800 and thereby contravened the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with section 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court and the High Court concurrently held that the appellant had in fact transferred by transfer by sale, 10 Highenomination Bank notes which were liable to confiscation under section 7 of the Act read with sections 109 and 109 of I.P.C. as the offence committed was one alleged to have been committed after April 1, 1946, when the offence was alleged to had been committed without April 1 and consequently the prosecution was not maintainable. Held, that the Ordinance in question having been promulgated during the period between June 27, 1940, and April 1. 1946, was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed as provided by section 26 of the . The Ordinance lapsed or ceased to be in operation on July 11, 1953, the date on which the offence in question was committed by the appellant. It continued in operation even after April, 1946. Further it was not necessary, that there should be a prior ordinance for the continuance of these Ordinances and that it could not have been the intention of the legislature as the Ordinance making power of the Governor General was recognised as temporary only. In respect of all Ordinances which were thus promulgated by the Governor in exercise of the powers conferred upon him under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, and was therefore within the period. Held further, that it was clear from section 72(3) Of the Indian .s case that Ordinance having been passed during the currency of January 12, 1946 became permanently in operation notwithstanding the repeal of the previous Ordinance and the adaptation prescribed in the Adaptation of Laws Order, 1950, issued under the Constitution of India were made applicable thereto.

The appellants were convicted for offences under section 302 I.P.C., read with section 354(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the Additional Sessions Judge, on a charge of murder. The High Court confirmed the death sentences passed under section 368(a). In appeal to this Court it was contended that if death sentence be awarded or not must, in my view, he be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend upon the facts and circumstances obtaining in such case. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The correct picture in each of the three cases is the inference which the Judge draws from the direct, or perceptible facts, (ii) statements of the principles of law applicable to the legal problems disclosed by the facts; and (iii) Judgment based on the combined effect of (i) and (ii). [1070 H] 1.2 A decision on a question of conviction depending upon the circumstances of a particular case, can never be regarded as a binding precedent, much less 'law declared ' within the meaning of Article 141 of the Constitution so as to bind all courts in the country.[1072 B C] 1:3 The Court is enjoined with a duty to record 'special reasons ' in case the extreme penalty is awarded. But the question whether the death sentence should be awarded, or not is left to discretion of Judge trying an accused and t he question of punishment must depend on the facts & circumstances obtaining In such case, when a sentence of death is passed it is subject to confirmation by the High Court under section 366(1) of Cr. P.C.

The appellant was in service upto 30th April 1958 when he was prematurely retired. He was promoted to the post of Income tax Officer in 1945. His case was that he had worked to the entire satisfaction of his immediate superior officers and higher authorities and had earned a number of certificates highly appreciative of his work. He also pleaded that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by Shri A. K. Bose, Deputy Director of Investigation who held the inquiry and by the punishing authority, he was suspended on 30th September 1953 by the Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., Lucknow on the basis of a preliminary enquiry on allegations involving corruption and violation of service rules. charges were framed on 30 12 1953 by Shri R. N. Srivastava, Deputy Directors Investigation, who held an inquiry and that first charge was that the appellant had entered into partnership with others with others, under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut, in contravention of Government Servants ' Conduct Rules. The second and last charges gave particulars of thirteen assessment cases in which the appellant was alleged to be either "grossly negligent, careless efficient, inefficient or/or corrupt in the performance of his duties as Income tax officer". He was subsequently placed under suspension on 30 5 1953 by Commissioner of Incometax U. P., Lucknow, on the allegation that he made various investments in the name Of various members of his family far in excess of and disproportionate to the known sources of his income. The appellant pleaded that a fresh enquiry into the same charges was not permissible under the Departmental Rules as well as the Departmental rules and was also barred by Rule 9 by rule 9 of the Rules. All relevant facts had been examined by the officer who held that the enquiry and findings by the departmental authorities were pursuing the appellant for some unknown reason which it did not find anywhere. The two authorities cited: (1) The State of Assam and Anr. vs J. N Roy Biswas, , and R. T. Rangachari vs Secretary of State, do not help the appellant. If an inquiry is held at a particular stage, possibly to determine whether regular proceedings should be drawn up or started it does not debar a departmental trial. That was the nature of earlier enquiries, (2) The question No. 3 as to whether regular appointments should be made and tried did not arise on the ground that some material facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) There was no affidavit before this Court that any particular points argued before the Division Bench had not been referred to or dealt with by the Bench. Moreover, there was also an application before the Supreme Court for revocation of grant of special leave to appeal by this Court on the grounds that some relevant material facts had already been examined and it was not hearing an appeal against the findings in the departmental proceedings or the punishment inflicted upon the Government servant even if these were erroneous. [585F G] (b) An unreasonable delay between hearing of arguments and delivery of judgments should be considered too natural to vitiate the departmental proceeding. [584G H] 2:1 It is not uncommon for astute Govt. servants, facing such enquiries to give long lists of witnesses and documents so as to either prolong an enquiry or to prepare grounds for future litigation. Unless the exclusion of evidence is of a kind which amounts to denial of natural justice or would have affected the final decision it could not be material. [586B] Further, after all, it was for the appellant to satisfy the Departmental authorities, who had looked into the case upto its final stages, that he has suffered some injustice which could not have had that effect upon the departmental proceed in null and void, that a plaintiff in such a suit could obtain the relief he had asked. Therefore, there could be no declaration that the departmental action was null and valid.

O.B., which entered into independent contracts with their foreign foreign buyer. Under the contracts two separate contracts in the chain were to be integrated F. OC.B, contracts in a course of export. There was no privity of contract between them and the H ff.

% The appellant was employed with the respondent company. Prior to this termination, an industrial dispute having been raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" The respondent management at one stage failed to participate in the proceedings; the reference was heard ex parte; the Labour Court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs. 520 per month from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate therein in the proceeding which motion was granted. The respondent also contended that even in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 25F, the termination was not illegal nor improper nor unjustified, and that the claim of the appel lant was negatived. The Labour Court on evaluation of evidence both oral and documentary held that the termination would not constitute retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) read with Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act. Accordingly it held that termination was neither illegal nor proper and unjustified, but granted relief to the appellant for reinstatement with continuity in service and seniority. The workman filed an appeal before the High Court which allowed the appeal holding that the order terminating the services of the respondent was invalid ; and that he was not entitled to reinstatement in full, or other benefits since his termination could be terminated only by way of punishment but a discharge of a temporary servant constituted retrenchment within meaning of Section 2(20)(a) read With section 25G of the Act. On behalf of the workman it was submitted: (i) that sub section (I) of section 26F(1) provides for uninterrupted service and sub section(2) comprehends a situation where a workman is not in continuous service within the purview of sub section 2 (a) for a period of one year or six months, he shall be deemed to be in continuous serv ice for a periods of one yea; and (ii) that the word `termination of service for any reason whatsoever ' now covers every kind of termination of service except those not expressly provided for by other provisions of the act such as sections 25FF and 25FFF. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(a) The termination would constitute retrenchment and by a catena of decisions it is well settled that where pre requisite for valid retrenchment as laid down in section 25 F has not been complied with, retrenchment bringing about termination of termination service is ab initio void. In other words, it does not bring about a cessation of service of the workmen and the workman continues to bein service. According to him unless the workman has put in continuous continuous service for not less than one year his case would not be governed by section 25E. [521F G] (b) The expression `termination ' is defined in section 2 of the , as under: "2(oo)(i). "retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reasons whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way or disciplinary action but does not include (a). voluntary retirement of the employee, or (b). termination of the services.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. The appointment was on temporary basis and terminable with one month 's notice. On February 5, 1955 the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement Officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The appellant was called upon to show cause why disciplinary action should not be taken against him if the allegations in the charge sheet were proved. He submitted his explanation to the charge sheets after making a memorial and to the Minister for Revenue affairs. Having failed to obtain relief, he applied to the High Court of Pepsu for a writ under article 226 quashing the order dated March 17, 1965 on the ground inter alia that the order of dismissal from service was in contravention of article 311 as no reasonable opportunity to showcause against the order dismissing him was at all given. The petition was transferred to the Labour Court and the same was transferred by the High Courts. The High Court held that the appellant who was a temporary employee should be continued in service or should be discharged under the terms of his employment, and that the termination amounted to casting a,stigma affecting his future career. Held, that the protection of article 31 (2) of the Constitution applies as much to a temporary public servant and it applies only to a permanent public servant who is confirmed, but in principle it will make no difference whether the appellant be a probationer or a temporary post. Section 3(5)(a) of Punjab & East Punjab States Union Union vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, ; , followed. State of Orissa vs Ram Narayan Das, [1958] S.C.R. 828 and State of Bihar vs Gopi Nath, A.I.R., 1960 S. C. 689, distinguished. The case was dealing with the case of a public servant on probation whereas the appellant not being a probationer, he had been served with notice to show that he should be confirmed.

The constitutional point involved in the case relates to the interpretation of section 133(2)(b) of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir, which requires that the Commission shall be consulted on the suitability of candidates for such appointments and promotions etc. and it shall be the duty of the Commission to advise on any matter so referred to them or on any other matter which the Governor may refer to them. Although it has been urged in the written arguments of the appellant that section 133 (2)(a) was "not at all attracted" in the matters of making promotions, and transfers from one service to another, and that as this requirement of the constitution was duly complied with, the High Court erred in holding that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. The contention on behalf of the respondents is that what clause (b) requires is that the commission shall be consult ed" on the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions and transfers etc. or transfers from two service to one another, because there was no deviation from merit list prepared by the Public Service Commission. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1(a) It is not possible for the appellant to advance their arguments with reference to article 16 of the Constitu tion as the various sealed covers containing the date on which the selections were made have not been received from the High court. [872E] (b). The question whether the requirement for consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise in this case because it is not disputed, and is in fact the case of the appellants State, that the Com missioner was consulted. [775D E] (c) The question as to whether the requirements for consultation with the Commission are mandatory or whether the Public Services Commission for the State of Jammu & Kashmir have been consulted in accordance with its requirement. [74F G] (d) It would thus appear that the High Courts erred in not holding that section133(2) (b), was "procurring" on its plain language, as this could be done only by a suitable provision to meet the situation arising out of the proposed action.

The petitioner was the Chief Minister of Bihar. On May 30, 1957, there was a debate in the Bihar Legislative Assembly when M. P. N. Singh, one of the oldest members of the Assembly made speech the gist of which was that criticism of the administration of Bihar as run by Dr. section K. Sinha, Chief Minister and cited certain instances of favouritism. At this stage the Speaker held that a portion of the speech was objectionable and ordered it to be struck off and expunged. On appeal, the Committee of Privileges held that no voting was taken and no time limit was given for the presentation of the report which was required under the rules of the House. The petitioner filed an petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the proceedings on three grounds: (i) article 194(3) had been made subject to the provisions of the Constitution; (ii) even if there was no time period fixed by the Speaker for the presenting of the Report which was necessary under the Rules, the report with respect to that subject had not been sent within a month and therefore it was invalid as the House had not taken any steps on it. Held: (1) The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to reasonable restrictions made by clause (2) of article 194. The power, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House of Commons of the British Parliament at the commencement of this Constitution are, therefore, subject to public control and that they cannot be questioned in any court in respect of anything said or any vote given by him in favour of a citizen for over a century. (2)(a) On the question whether the privilege conferred under article 194 (3) is protected under article 19(1), the right under that Article was preserved despite the provisions Of article 194, and not even if it did, by reason of the fact that it infringes the fundamental right of a citizens. The law made by the Legislature in respect Of the powers, privileges, immunities and immunities of a House of the Legislature or of a state cannot be challenged on the ground of any alleged irregularity of the procedure. Sankari Prasad Singh Deo vs Union of India, ; , followed. (b)The object of section 194 is to regulate the procedure for the conduct of elections but it does not necessarily mean that it was not so subject under article, and consequently can only be that such portion thereof as are ordered to be expunged by the spe cial Assembly or a committee thereof and become void to the extent of the contravention of that clause. (c) The fact that the speech is published in pursuance of the earlier part of the article 105(3), that the petitioner was entitled to succeed, does not alter the character of individual persons who are residents of the said constituency. Nor is it correct to say that the privilege under article 105 is a power and privilege of the Parliament but as it was argued at some length, it would be as well that if it infringes article 212(1) the validity Of its proceedings cannot be quired on the grounds of no alleged irregularity or that the procedure prescribed by law has been contravened. Sankara Prasad Singh vs Union for India, [1951] S.C.R. 869, distinguished. (d)The need for the publication of the publications in accordance with the provisions made under section 49(3)(a), is to enable it to publish the said public notices and give him an opportunity to make representations as he may wish. The right conferred on a citizen under article 21(1)(a). The restrictions imposed, privileges or immunities of the Houses of Parliament must be such as may from time to time be defined by law.
