The appellants made applications to the State Transport Authority for grant of temporary permits to ply their vehicles on the route. The U.P. State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation for short) also made an application for grant, for three temporary permits for the same purpose and the application was granted while the application made by each of the applicants was rejected on the ground that once a scheme had been published in view of the provision contained in section 68 F(1 A) the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such an application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled, to obtain a temporary permit. This decision of the State Government was upheld both by the state Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1 (a) The provisions of Chapter IV A of it is undoubtedly true that the Corporation enjoys a preferential treatment in the matter of obtaining permits. The authority under the Act must not ever lose sight of the fact that the primary consideration must be The service available to the travelling public. While interpreting the provisions of the undoubtedly the competing claims between the Corporation & the other private operators may be examined with reference to the provisions. But the overall consideration namely the service is for the benefit of the travelling Public should never be overlooked for a moment, [86C D, F] (b) The expression 'any person ' would comprehend any person even other than the Corporation. One has to read section 68F(1A) and Section 68F (1 C). If the Corporation applies for all the permits it cannot grant permit to any one else if the Corporation had applied for all those permits.

The appellant, a son of the respondent, inherited the suit properties from his paternal grandfather Moti. On March 22, 1927, he executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of the said properties in favour of Shibba the ancestor of respondents I to 9 for Rs. 5,000. Subsequently on April 12, 1929, he sold the equity of redemption to the said mortgagee for Rs ' 11,000 and in suit No. 145 of 1946 filed by the appellant in the court of Sub Judge, Panipat against defendants 1 to 9, the appellant claimed a declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind his own reversionary rights, because the impugned alienations were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. The trial judge held that the property was ancestral qua the appellant 1101 and that the appellant was entitled to challenge its alienation by his father respondent 10. In appeal the District Judge affirmed this decision and dismissed the suit. The appellant came up in appeal before the High Court. By certificate, the High court took the view that the suit had abated in the trial court as a result of the death of one of the defendants pending the decision of the trial judge; but even so it did not ask respondents 1 to 8 to go back to the District Court, and condoned the delay made by the said respondents in presentation of the appeal before itself and proceeded to deal with the appeal on merits. On behalf of the appellant it was urged that: (1) the High Courts had wrongly held that under the Hindu law a son does not acquire by birth an interest jointly with his father in the estate which the latter inherits from his maternal grandfather; (2) the doctrine of stare decisis did not apply because the properties were ancestral property and, therefore, the property inherited by respondents 10 to 9 was not ancestral property qua the appellants. Held: (i) The question as to whether the property in suit could be held to be ancestral property or that such property in the hands of a daughter can be given that description. has depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. In order to determine the right, it is necessary to examine the surrounding circumstances of such a case and is not desirable or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case, but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the Court, in accordance with the principles governing the custom obtaining in the particular case. [1101 D E; 1103 A C] (ii) On the merits, it was difficult to say that the doctrine on stare decisis was inapplicable because the question as a matter of law did not arise for the decision in Lehna 's case and was applicable, and should present no obstacle in holding that the earlier cases of the Full Bench of the Punjab High Court were not correctly decided. All the decisions discussed by the Calcutta High Court must be taken to have been overruled.

The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge, Birbhum on charges under section 449 I.P.C. and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court accepted that verdict convicted the appellants at all. In appeal to this Court it was contended as follows : (i) The conviction under section 147 of the I. P.C., could not be sustained in law, because there can be no conviction under s. 449 of the IPC unless murder has actually been committed; (ii) that a charge under section 307 read with section 34 of the Penal Code is not sustainable in law; (iii) that no charge under that section can be said to have been committed "in order to the committing of an offence punishable with death," and (iv) that there could be no doubt that the words "in the order to" have been used to mean "with the purpose of", because if the purpose in committing the house trespass is the commission of an offi ness punishable with imprisonment for life, the house property trespass becomes punishable under section 450 I. Tile case was remanded to the trial Court for giving an opportunity to the appellants to place evidence before the trial court. HELD : (1) There could be nothing on record to show that the intention was actually accomplished. [979 E] 2(a) The word "in" used in the section does not mean " With the purpose" of". If the purpose was the commissionof an offence under the present section, it would be proper to say that he has committed the entire criminal act. [978 G H] (b) It was quite clear from the evidence that the murder was not actually committed and the appellants attacked Haji Ebrar Ali in furtherance of the common intention of all. But once it is decided that the act is so done by a number of persons in furtherance ' of the said common intention, each of them becomes punishable thereunder under section 500 I. On this view the act did not result in death. [980 G H, 981 A] (c) The fact that the murders were not actually com puted would not affect the applicability of section 449 Cr. P; and (d) since a charge has been framed under section 408 read with s.34 I. R. Act by the High Court the act was not sustainable.

The respondent, a Hindu, died sometime in 1927 leaving certain lands in villages Bhadroya, Kingarian and Pathankot in the district of Gurdaspur. Sometime later in 1926 the State Government passed an order under section 3(1) of the , for the distribution of the estate among the various classes of tenants on non agricultural lands and for purposes connected therewith. The respondent filed a suit out of which this appeal arises against the respondent for a declaration that he was entitled to the lands mentioned at the plaint as well as to the sum of 1194 Rs. 1,539 7 0 in preference to the respondent under the custom governing the parties. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit and ordered the parties to bear their own costs. One of the questions which arose for decision in this appeal was whether there was a custom whereby the collaterals of the parents who were the last male holder excluded from inheritance by the collateral parties up to the fourth degree with respect to ancestral as well, self acquired property of her father. Held that the question raised before the High Court must be answered against the appellant and the respondent must succeed in proving its case beyond reasonable doubt. The customary rights of succession of daughters as against the collateral 's father are stated in paragraph 23 of Rattigan 's Digest of Customary Law, Jinaj i am of 1913, that para the daughter succeeds to the self acquired properties of her mother in preference and to his daughter. There is no doubt or dispute as to whether these answers quite adequately displace the general custom and shift the burden to the daughter who is the res pondent. Further, admission of this fact on behalf of the respondent was neither found nor proved by the appellant. Ludhiana vs Mst. Subhani (1918) L.R. 44 I.A. 89, In re: Farid Mohammad Khalil vs Mohammad Bakhsh ; , relied on.

Section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 provides that any instrument so framed as to come within two or more of the descriptions in Sch. I shall, where the duties chargeable thereunder are different be chargeable with the aggregate amount of the duties with which separate instruments each comprising or relating to one such matters would be chargeable under the Act. The respondent was at the material time the Managing Director of a company registered under the Indian Companies Act and on 4 7 1949 he applied to the Collector under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney marked as Exhibit A in the proceedings which he proposed to execute. By that power he empowered Messrsldas David Chisholm Fairbairn and John James Brims Sutherland jointly and severally to act for him in his individual capacity and also as executor, administrator, trustee managing agent, liquidator or Liquidator and all other capacities. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Act to the High Court. The High Court held that the difference between the two categories was one that when two persons join in executing a power in respect of matters which are unrelated. There is nothing either in the deci sion or the observations quoted above to support the contention of the respondent that if the word 'matters ' occurring in section 5 is construed as meaning anything other than 'categories ' or in the phraseology of section 6, then there could be no conflict between the four sections and the clause in section 6 that it was "subject to the provision of the last preceding section ' would be meaningless and useless. The appellant contended that by virtue of section 5 of Indian Stamp act 1899 a separate duty payable in respect Of Government stocks under the provisions of the Bombay Stamp Act must fail as the instrument in question comprised distinct matters for purposes of section 2. Held, that the transaction was a single transaction whereby the donor constituted the donees jointly and collectively his attorneys for him and in his name and on his behalf to act as for him. There can be no doubt that when one person executes a power, of attorney in respect thereof it is open to him to deal with those properties and exercise all the powers in relation thereto though with the limitations imposed upon them by reason of the properties having vested in him in different capacities.

The assessee, M/s. Kathiawar Mills Ltd., was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State, and in 1948 Bhavnagar along with other Indian States of Kathiwar, formed themselves into a union by the name of United States of his erstwhile Ruler, including the appellant assessee company. On March 16, 1949, the Raj Pramukh of this newly formed State instituted the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949. This Ordinance was in force for one year only the assessment year 1949 50. In assessing the profits of business by the two appellant companies for the year 1949 49 the Income Tax Officer had to proceed in accordance with the provisions of that Ordinance. For the purpose of calculating the depreciation allowance to which the assessee was entitled in computing the profits or gains of the business, the written down value had to be computed by deduction from the actual cost of depreciation allowance which was allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, even though not claimed. In each of these appeals before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal, the Income tax Officer took a different view and held that this expression "or which would have been allowed to him if the Indian income tax Act had in force" in the past did not permit the Income 8 Tax Officer to make any deduction under this head. The High Court also held that the expression "actually allowed" means "allowable" under the law in force, and as the words were not "depreciation allowed", it was immaterial whether the assessee got any benefit of depreciation in any previous year. In respect of these two appeals by special leave, HELD: (1) There may be no doubt that the proviso to section 10(5)(b) of the Indian Incometax Act as amended by the Income ' tax Laws (Merged States) (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 1950, does not give effect to this intention. It is well settled that where an order can be made by the Central Government under section 12, the Central Govern ment must be satisfied that in certain cases difficulties have actually arisen which arose. [225 H] (2) Neither is there anything expressing any opinion on the question whether any difficulty had actually arise in giving effect to the Act in an area to which it so become extended can be done by the State Government under the powers conferred by section 12 of the Finance Act, 1950. Once on such satisfaction an order is made it is not again necessary for the application of the order in a particular case that difficulty must be found to have arisen.

The petitioner, a member of the Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd. was an instrumentality of the State of Karnataka in favour of the Mysore Construction Co. (M.C.). His writ petition and a further writ appeal in the Karnataka High Court having been unsuccessful, he has preferred this Special Leave Petition from the Judgment of the High Court in the Writ Appeal before this Court. It is contended on behalf of both sides that while exercising jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution it is not for this Court to reap praise the facts on merits and come to one conclusion or other with regard to those aspects of the matter. What is required to be verified is whether there is any difference between the requirements in paras I and V and whether only para I and not para V sets out the pre conditions of eligibility to submit a tender for the contract. In this connection, it is pointed that the requirements of para l(1) and (2) are fulfilled that the prequalifying conditions set out in para l of the N.I.T. and that the details called for in para V could be supplied at any time before the final award of the contract are filed. The progress of the tender process indicated that the work consisted of manufacturing and working machinery, manu facture, safety and security of the intending tenderers and that it was a clear case of failure to perform certain prequali tive requirements which, under the Notification Inviting Tenders (N.I.) had to be completed before the tenders were filed. It was pointed out that in the absence of such condition, the mistake could not have been remedied by the Respondents. Allowing the Special Leave Petitions and setting aside the award of a contract, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The stipulation of time element within which the information asked for in Para V should be supplied is also of some significance; it specifically requires the information to be supplied along with the application for tender forms. It may not, therefore, be correct to read para l in isolation and treat it as the only condition precedent for the supply of forms of tender. 1.2 If a party does not strictly comply with the requirements Of paras III, V or VI of the Tender Notice, it cannot deviate from these guidelines at all in any situation but that any deviation, if made, should not result in arbitrariness or discrimination. [234B C] 1.3 It is true that the relaxations of time schedule in the case of one party does affect even such a person in the sense that he would otherwise have had one competitor less. But, it does not deprive the appel lant of its right to be considered for the con tention for the Contract; on the other hand it has received due and full consideration.

The appellant who owned a house and in the meantime occupied it on 10th October, 1947. In pursuance of that exchange Malik Khan Noon was said to have taken possession of the said agricultural lands on the 10th Octo ber, 1947, at a time when there was no restriction against any evacuee dealing with the property He had been put in possession of these said agricultural properties in Punjab Khore presumably by way of attornment 1120 from tenants who were in actual cultivating possession ofthe lands. The appellant claimed that he was entitled under section 5A read with section 5B of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947 to be confirmed on an application made long prior to the time when the office of the Custodian General was set up and he was clothed with powers of revision and as such vested in the Custodian Special Officer under section 27. The Additional Custodian rejected this contention holding that section 5 B of East Punjab Act XIV of 1947 which has been amended by the Administration of Evacuee Property (Rural) is retrospective from 15th August, 1947 operates in respect of matters covered by it and those applications were disposed of on the 20th March, 1952, by the Additional Custodian. On appeal the Assistant Custodian General set aside the order of confirmation against which no appeal was filed on the 5th May, 1952. After the orders confirming the exchange had been passed by the Custodian on the 23rd February, 1948, the appellant filed an application for revision of his own order which was rejected under section 6B(3) and the Central Ordinance XXXI of 1950. The authorities were directed to hold a summary enquiry into an application which was not rejected under subsection (3) which may decline to confirm the transaction if it appears to the Custodian that the transaction was not a bona fide one for valuable consideration ' or was in the opinion of the prescribed objects; and on doing so the entire exercise was completed. The order of the Assistant Evacuee Commi sioner rejecting the application was confirmed by the Central Custodian which was affirmed in revision by the Deputy Custodian General on an appeal to the High Court. Held, that since the revisional power could not be exercised when there Was an appeal provided but a proper appeal and once the attribute of finality in respect Of such an order is affected by subsequent legislation it does not appear to be of consequence that it was affected first by a provision for appeal and later by provisions for appeal revision, and the application for confirmation filed in 1952 would clearly be subject to revisional power of the Administrator General under section 26.

The first respondent, a locality in the city of Bombay was studded with small hardware businesses where pipes and fittings, nuts and bolts, tools and other small products were made and/or sold. These establishments, well over a thousand, employ a considerable number of workmen in the neighbourhood of 5,000 although each unit had (barring four), less than the statutory minimum of 20 workmen. A large number of workers were getting on well in their business and in their relations with their workmen and this goodwill manifested itself in ex gratia payments to them of small amounts for a number of years prior to 1965 when trouble started. Although rooted in goodness and grace, the annual repetition of these payments ripened into a sort of right nothing surprising when we see, in words, was that which was humanistically right. Anyway, the hardware merchants of Nag Devi made of sterner stuff, in the year 1965 abruptly declined to pay the goodwill sums of the spread out past and the frustrated workmen frowned on this stoppage by setting up a right to bonus averring considerable profits for the industry (if one may conveniently use that expression for a collective coverage of the conglomeration of hardware establishments). The defiant denial and the consequent dispute resulted in appointment of a Board of Arbitrators under section 10A of the Industrial Disputes Act to arbitrate upon twelve demands put forward by the workmen. The Tribunal did not enter the merits of the claim but dismissed it in limine on the ground that the demand for bonus was barred by res judicata. In appeal, this Court HELD: The contention that before the Arbitration Board no case of customary or contract bonus was urged for the year 1956 and so, in later years, such a plea is barred by the general principles of res judicata since the claim for bonus for 1948 had been founded on tradition or custom or condition of service and in that light, the Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also does not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. [597G] In this case the claim of customary bonus based on custom based bonus for the subsequent period is again relevant. If at all, as evidence, which falls outside our consideration, at present, the dispute referred by the Government deals with bonus based upon profits and to recommend principles for computation of such bonus and methods of payment . The object and reasons of the Bonus Act indicate that the subject matter of the statute is 'the question of payment of bonus based purely on profit. It is otherwise not a speculative claim but merely an exercise of discretion between the parties which tends to advance their cause for adjudication. [605C] The real test in this case was that it relates to a case of profit bonus urged under the by two sets of workmen, employed by establishments which were either excluded or exempted from the Bonus Acts.[595F H] In the instant case, although there is no evidence to show that such claim was based on profits or the financial results of the employers but was based merely on custom and service condition not one based on profit, by implication, other distinct and different categories of bonus such as the one under an adventure. [595A C] The main question about the policy of the Parliament that was agitated in that case turned on the availability of the as an independent method of claiming profit bonus de hors the Bonus act, did not detract from the claim,of customary bonus. The effect of the arbitral board 's negation of the profit based bonus claim in 1965 on custom depends upon the effect of these relevant factors enumerated by us; and it would not be materially affected by unilateral declarations of one party when the said declarations are inconsistent with the course of conduct adopted by it, but is based on customs and service conditions not one founded on profit.[595A B] The words "

% The Additional District and Sessions Judges for two or three years prior to the appointment of Respondent 3 directly were appointed directly from the Bar to the Haryana Superior Judicial Service. Respondents 1 and 2 to those Writ Petitions were the State of Punjab and Haryana. Some of the more important grievances of the petitioners are that their seniority qua direct recruits is wrongly and unjustly made to depend upon the fortuitous circumstance of the date of their confirmation in the Superior Judicial service and, therefore, it was not open to the High Court to give an arbitrary date of confirmation to the promotees. The State of Haryana filed a writ petition in the Delhi High Court contending that the ratio of 2:1 between the promotees and direct recruits had to be maintained at all stages, that is to say, not only at the time of appointment but at the point of time of confirmation also; that even if a substantive vacancy was available, the confirmation of a promotee in that vacancy is postponed arbitrarily and indefinitely, that promotees are treated with an unequal hand qua direct recruit for example, a promotee despite his satisfactory performance and the availability of a substantive post in which he can be confirmed, is continued in an officiating capacity until after a direct recruit completes his probation and is due for confirmation, and, and that, the High court applies the principle of rotation as between promotees and promotees at the times of their appointment when, in fact, that the relevant rules provide for is the application of a rule of quota at the date Of their appointment; that seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers, shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post in the service irrespective of the dates of confirmation) when, has been the correct criterion of seniority and with another set of officers also under its control, on the basis that the length Of continuous officiation in a post is the true test of seniority; and, there is no power in the High Courts to pass a law which though rules made by the High ex cadre in exercise of power conferred upon it in that behalf may have the force of law.

Sub paragraph (2) of Para 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Public Employment (Organisa tion of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order, 1975 defines 'local area ' in relation to local cadre thus: "local area" in relation l to any local cadre, means the local area specified in para 6 for direct recruitment to posts in such local cadre and includes, in respect of posts belonging to the category of lower division clerk or to any other category equivalent to or lower than that of a lower division Clerk (Junior Assistant). [568 F G] Sub para (3) provides that "In organising a separate cadre in respect o f any category of posts in any department for any part of the State, noth ing in this order shall be deemed to prevent the State Government from organising or continuing more than one local cadre for such part of tho State". Paragraph 6 deals with local areas: (1) Each district shall be regarded as a local area the details of which are not material. Paragraph 5 declares that "local cadre is a cadre comprising the posts belonging t o a category in a Department and located within a specified part of it. The concept of the local cadre is thus related to the concept of unit of appointment under the service rules; the part of State for which a local cadre was organised in respect ly of any category will serve as a unit of appoint ment etc., for that category. No. 529 (E), dated 18th October, 1975 issued under para 3(8) of the Order, as also to the specified autho rnment, by the Cen tral Government. In struction 7 provides thus: "(1) each part of a State, for which no local cadre has been organised, in sen tance of any Category of posts" shall be organised into a separate Cadre. Sub para.(9) provides: "Insing a separate quota in respect to any category, the Government may state that there is no objection to organising or discontinuing more than two local cadres for such a part of such State". By an order, in G.O.Ms. No 1648 dated November 20, 1982, the Govern ment appointed the respondent Nos. 4 and 5 to the Ningra circle. The Ninghal circle was bifurcated into seven zones and zone V consists of the revenue districts of Adilabad, Karimnagar, Warangal and Khammam revenue dis tricts. [568 B] The 'State Government was empowered under the Presidential Order to organize class or classes of posts for different parts of the state in the manner therein provided. No doubt in common paral lence, the word 'otherwise ' is of 'wide amplitude. Therefore, the phrase "constituted otherwise" is to be understood in that context and purpose which Article 371 D and the Presidential order seek to achieve.

The question whether a mortgagor in possession might grant a lease conformable to usage in the ordinary course of management but was not competent to grant a permanent lease unusual terms or authorise the use of land in a manner, or for a purpose different from the mode in which he himself used it before he granted the mortgage. Held, that the question whether the mortgagor in occupation had power to lease the mortgaged property has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the mortgaged land in the usual course of administration of management. The true position has been stated in the following terms by this section, " As the object of the burial ground is to grant rights of burial, this being the mode, in which such property is dealt with, the mortgagee was not entitled to disturb the graves of those who had been buried the land while the mortgagor continued to hold it. The question whether there was any answer to the plaintiff 's claim and the permanent lease granted by him could not prevail against the plaintiff. Rammukund vs Motilal, (1854) 9 1 K.B. 234, Firm Manohar Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar, I.L.R. , Madan Mohan Singh v Raj Kishore Kumari, A.I.R., 1932 P.C. 188 and Banee Pershad vs Beet Bhunjan Singh, A,I. R. , referred to. Held also that the two cases decided in favour of the plaintiff are not applicable. Though a mortgagor may assign the mortgaged premises, the assignee can only take subject to the encumbrances, and if the (1) (2) (i) 868 (3) (ii) (6) 114 property is sold or foreclosed by the mortgagee, any interest which the mortgagor may have created since the mortgage will be destroyed, the mortgagor 's security does not exceed his powers in making a lease for a term.

% The petitioner executed the work within 9 months. It was his claim that while executing the work he sent the bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. For the first time he sent notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondent for referring the dispute to arbitration. On receipt thereof, the respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5 and 12 of the Act. The learned Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation and that it be an exceptional case for interference, that the award should be cancelled since it was made long after 10 years. He further held that even assuming that any claim was as a fact made in July 1979 and payment was made, the petitioner had not taken follow up action thereafter for well over 10 years and that payment was without prejudice to his rights under Article 20(1) of the Constitution. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that Clause 68 of the Contract provided for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the Respondent, the respondents are duty bound to appoint an arbitrator; and that the High Court erred in allowing the petition. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that the respondents have treated the claim as stale and barred by limitations and that Section 5 has no application to the facts of the case because, the parties should not be relieved from a tribunal they had chosen because they fear that the arbitrator 's decision may go against them. On the other hand, it was reiterated that an ordinary submission without special stipulation limiting or conditioning the functions of the arbitrator carried with it the implication that the Arbitrator must decide the dispute according to the existing law of contract, and that every defence which would have been open in a court of law could be equally proponed for the arbitrator "s decision unless the parties have agreed which is not suggested here to exclude that defence. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court discarded the arbitration clause 68 of contract in matters nos. 1326, 1364, 1365 and 1365/90 dated November 23, 1990. [365C] M/s Amarch and Lalit Kumar vs Shree Ambica Jute Mills Ltd., ; at 969; Russell on Arbitration, at page 72 and 73 it is stated thus: "The parties to an arbitration agreement may provide therein, if they wish, that an arbitration must be commenced within a shorter period than that allowed by statute. But the court then has power to enlarge the time so agreed.

The appellants obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. It included both Bakasht lands as well as other lands. On January 1, 1956 the mortgagees applied under section 14 of the Act and got determined the compensation to which they were entitled under the Act. Later on the mortgagees apply under section 13 of the , and got fixed a final decree on September 19, 1955, but that application was dismissed for default. The appellants then filed an execution petition in the executing court claiming refund of the amount paid by them as compensation. That application was rejected. The execution court came to the conclusion that the objection raised by the judgment debtors is barred on the principles of res judicata and further that the same had no merits. On appeal, the High Court reversed this decision but reversed it. In the second appeal by the appellant the question that arose for decision was whether the execution is barred under the provisions of section 4(d) of the U.P. Land Reforms (Amendment) Act. 1947. Held: The decisions of this Court in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh and Ors., [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564, that where the whole of the property mortgaged is an estate, there can be no doubt that the procedure prescribed by Chapter IV has to be followed, in order that the amount due to the creditor should be determined by the claims officer and the decision of the claims Officer or the Board has been made final by the Act [979C] The fact that the property has vested in the State under the notification issued under section 3 is not a ground for rejection of the application. In construing the words of section4(d), it would be necessary to bear in mind the object of the legislation which was merely to provide for the transference to the State of the interests of proprietors and tenure holders in land and of the mortgagees and lessees of such interest. Therefore, it is not correct to say that what vested in a State are only those interests not coming within section 6. Section 4(a) providing that "any suit shall lie in any civil court" in respect of the same claim which has been already vested in tho State. Therefore the view taken by this Court is not incorrect.

The respondents in Civil Appeals Nos. 206/89 and 61 other appeals, as common question of law arose is whether the second proviso to Rule 4 of C.S.E. Rules introduced by Notification No. 13016/4/86 AIS(1) dated 13.12.1986 (Published in the Gazette of India Extraordinary Part 1 Section 1) was ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution on the ground that it makes a discrimination be tween the successful candidates of Central Service Group 'A ' and Group B as no embargo is placed restricting the candidates of Group A ' service, as in the case of Group ' A ' Services and whether the reasons given by the Government to justify the introduction of the impugned proviso have any rational nexus to the object of the Scheme of recruitment to the All India Services or/and whether such reasons are arbitrary. Allowing Civil Appeals No. 206 of 1989, this Court, HELD: The promotion of the respondents to the I.P.S.,/ Central Serv ices, Group 'B ' and C.A ' service under the C.P., Group 'C ' is different services and, therefore, the impugned second proviso is held to be discriminatory against the candidates appointed to the CUni nal Services and 16 Group 'E ' services and as such it is violative of Article 14.

The appellant, a clearing and forwarding agent at Madras, was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short), on a charge that he had fraudulently applied to the Board for permission to assist him as a friend, and that after his release from judicial custody. The Advisory Board considered this request, held that the detenu 's request for assistance of a friend at the hearing was turned down by the Board, and the refusal of such assistance to the appellant was not justified, and directed the detention order passed in his favour on the ground that he was not a friend of the detenu and that the order of detention was confirmed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The detaining authority had the assistance of the Deputy Collector of Central Excise and a Superintendent of Central excise. The Board had no justification to refuse assistance of 793 Sundararajan to the Appellant in such circumstances. [792C D] 2. It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the detenue on account of such denial. [789A B] 3. In any case, that is not what the Constitution says and it would be wholly inappropriate to read and such meaning into the provisions of Article 22. [788D E] 4. If the detaining authority or the Government takes the aid of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser before the Advisory Board the detenu must be allowed the facility of appearing before the Board through a legal lawyer. The rule in A. K. Roy 's case made it clear that the detenue was entitled to the assistance. of a 'friend '. The word 'friends ' used there was obviously not intended to carry the meaning of the term in common parlance. One of the meanings of the word ' liquidator ' according to the Collins English Dictionary is "an ally in a fight or cause; supporter". The term 'friending ' used here was obviously meant to carry with liking, affection and loyalty. [781D E, H] 5. If a detenu makes a request for legal assistance, his request would have to be considered on its own merit in each individual case.[793E G] 6. In the instant case, if the detaining Authority or the government takes the assistance, of a lawyer and the legal advisers before the appellate Board, the detenu may have, if he was so minded, made a request to the Advisory board for permission, be represented by a lawyer. [784D E]. 7. There is no reason why the Boards should not permit the authorities to do indirectly what they cannot do directly. And no one should be enabled to take shelter behind the excuse that such officers are not "legal practitioners" or legal advisors.

The appellants were the owners of certain jute mills in Calcutta. Some of the mills moved the Government for requisition of the goods on September 30, 1946, and they were served with the notices of acquisition in May 1950. The Government by a notice under section 75 A(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1939, declared that there was no service of the orders on them and as such the property in the goods stood vested in the Government free from any mortgage, pledge lien or other similar encumbrance and that the company was not bound to serve the holders with notices of the acquisition. The High Court held that the requisition orders did not affect and intended to affect individual mills and service on the managing agents but it further held that as such were not served with a notice of acquisition, they were valid. On appeal by special leave: Held, that in view of section 18 Of the Act the property which had been requisitioned passed to the Government of India under r. 75 A (2) was not good service or and reasonable way of service in the case of notices of acquisitions. It was not sufficient if the notice of the decision to acquire was served on a corporation : Held also, further that though r. 119 did not provide for the manner of service the notice did not make it clear that it was intended to be served on the mills either in the manner provided in the Act, or in any other way. Held, further, that the notice dated September 30 1946 could not affect a valid requisition order because in the present case the receipts in respect of the notice were served by the same date and are not properly served on them. The section was therefore applicable to the case. In the instant case no service was effected as required by r. 74 A(1) but the publication of the notices in the Official Gazette did not amount to a requisition within the meaning Of the section.

The assessee company was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64, and the assessee claimed that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the aforesaid provision. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal answered in favour of Revenue and against the assessee following the decision of this Court in Metal Box Company of India Limited vs their Workmen, , held that no action can be taken against the assesse for the assessment years 1963 64. In so far as item No. 3 is concerned it held that it was a reserve. Following the said judgment, the appeal pertaining to the assessment year 1964 65 was also allowed. The assessee preferred appeals before this Court. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding it to be a provision and not a reserve, [114D] 2.1 In Metal Box Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , the distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a provision & a reserve is in commercial accountancy fairly well known. Provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and therefore to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L account, a reserve was, in appropriation of profits, the asset or assets by which it is represented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. [114C] 2:2 In Metal box on which has been followed in Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co. etc., the distinction is between provision & reserve. The distinction between an "in commercial accountancy" and "in other words is that whereas a provision is a charge against the profits to be c taken into consideration against gross receipt in the p.& L.

% All the three petitioners who were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class I) were subjected to competitive written and personality test, and in the nature of things only the very best could emerge out successfully. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that Officers were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned from the date of their absorption into the Indian Railways Service of engineers Class I, subject to a maximum weightage of five years. The Respondent Board gave its decision dated September 17, 1965 to the effect that the officers so absorbed into the Central Railway service of Engineers would be given weightage in seniority "on the basis of half the total years of continuous service in working posts in Railways prior to their permanent absorption into Class. 1 and the petitioners were appointed as temporary Assistant Officers on the basis Of the results of competitive examinations and those, which were recruited by selection. The writ Petitioners contended that Officer officers were appointed only on the strength of selection by the Union Public Service Commission and that the development of law had gone a long way so as to shed the views expressed in Katyani Dayal 's case justifying demolition of demarcation between the two services made as it was an arbitrary and cavit. Allowing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The rule of weightage also appears to be reasonable and this is a pattern which has been noticed and approved in many a service. [1025E F] 1.2 In Katyila Dayal ' 's Case this court specifically said that relief of equality was being denied to the then petitioners because of the history, origin and structure of the Services. No opinion was expressed as to the validity of the given weightage of half of the length of service to Temporary Assistant Officers. subject to the maximum of five year, because of its being questioned elsewhere. [459C D] 1:3 It is not in the interest of justice nor in the interests of service. When there has been complete absorption of personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be counted from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of one half of tho length of Service subject to prescribed maximum of 5 years. It would otherwise be imprudent now, at this point of time to dig up old issues. The rule was thus designed and carried out.

Under section 11 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949, the State Government is expected to select only such offences or classes of offences or class of cases for being tried by the Special Court and it may, by general or special order in writing, direct. " The appellant was convicted under sections 302, 307 and 392 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code on the ground that the Ordinance contravened articles 14 and 19 (1) (g) of the Constitution. The Ordinance further provided that the State Govern ment shall not take any action in respect of such offences. The appellant contended that the exemption was void as offending against article 14, because, apart from the inconsistency between section 11 and section 11, which authorised the State Govt. to direct "offences" by providing for "offenses", in a special procedure, under section 11 the use of the special procedure must necessarily be confined only to disturbed areas or those areas where adoption of public safety measures was necessary. Held, that there was nothing in the Ordinance itself to guide the State Legislature to apply the special jurisdiction not to any and every case but only to those cases or offences which have a ra tional relation to, or connection with, the main object and purpose of the Ordinance and the scheme of the Act. Benoarilal vs The State of West Bengal, ; , referred to. Held further, that in any event section 11 was violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion and there was no violation of article 19 (i)(f) as it vested in the executive Government unregulated official discretion and therefore had to be adjudged unconstitutional on grounds similar to those urged on behalf of the appellant in this Court. That portion of section 11 which authorises the State to direct the "offence" is not unconstitutional, and that the notification issued by the State of Saurashtra in so far as it authorised the Sta te Government to direct particular "cases" to be tried by Special Courts did not offend against article 31 (1)(f). A distinction between offences and punishment for distinct offences was also made out, by the fact that under section II r. 5 the State government is expected bound to select persons who were involved to be charged with offences which affect the maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in those areas as a class by themselves and one can classify them in any way they like without regard to any objective and as such the statute was open to the challenge of making arbitrary discrimination. It is not out of place that section 11 must be construed along with the other sections of the latter Act and it will be seen that the object of the legislation which was to provide for public safety, maintenance of 'public order and safety in those area as a classes by themselves would be far to say that in no case and under no circumstances can a legislature lay down a special procedures for the trial of any particular class of offences.

The workmen of the appellant corporation created under a State Act entitled the respondent Corporation for nationalisation of the transport business of the appellants ' employees. The employer terminated the services of some of its employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised challenging the legality of their termination and the State Government referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held, overruled the stand of the employer that section 25F had no application, to the effect that the discharge was invalid. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the employees before this Court that: (1) the termination of service amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo)(a), and those orders were bad for non compliance with section 25 F; (2) the conditions precedent to discharge the requirements of section 25E had not been complied with. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.(i) It is true that an artificial definition may include a meaning different from or in excess of the ordinary acceptation of the word which is the subject of definition; but there must then be compelling words to show that such a meaning differ from or any in excess Of the ordinary accepted connotation of the expression. [791 H] 1.(ii) The High Court has rightly come to the conclusion that in these cases the order of retrenchment was bad and consequently it upheld the Award of the Labour court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief. There would be one set of costs. [789 F G] 2.(i). If due weight is given to the words 'the termination by the employer of the service of a workman 'for any reason whatsoever ' are understood to mean what they plainly say, it is difficult to escape the conclusion because that the expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of the services Of a probationer. Yet the Legislature took special care to mention that they were not included within the meaning of 'termination by the employers of the Service of a probationer for any reason whatever. What is being defined is retrenchment and that is the context of the definition; it is true, that an unrecognised understanding can exist where their intention was even to include a bona fide closure of the whole business, it would be straining the sense of define what is the purpose or object of the legislation. [788 G H] (ii) Once the conclusion is reached in that case the order was bad for violation of principle of natural justice or for not following the procedure prescribed for imposing punishment. It could not be said that the termination was a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation or absence on account of continued ill health. [781 C D] (iii) The contention that the consensus of judicial opinion in later decisions is against the appellant 's stand must fail. [783 B C] 1(iv) It was not necessary to dilate on the point nor to refer to the earlier decisions of this Court in view of the later two pronouncements of this court to both of which one of us was a party, indicating that it had been "absorbed into the consensus ' and there is no scope for putting the clock back or for an anti clockwise operation. Once the decision is reached that retrenchment as prescribed in section (2oo)(c) would cover every case of termination of services except those which have been embodied in the definition, discharge from employment or termination of ' service of probationer would also amount to retrenchment. [784 D E] 2.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposing of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 4 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of registration as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941 in respect of inter alia unconnected or unclaimed goods. The Commercial Tax officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the assessee was not a " dealer". On 6 June, 1959 he made an order rejecting the application on the basis that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assesse 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The revision application before the computa tioner of Commercial Taxes was dismissed on 21 January, 1960 on the finding that the sales effected by the assessee were sales under the Act and that the asses see was a "business" within the meaning of section 2(c) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940. On 6th June 1959 he applied to th e Commercial Tax Authority for cancellation thereof as a 'dealer". The Board of Revenue held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the asses sees and therefore a sale of goods took place. In further revision before the Commis sioner of Sales Tax, West Bengal it was held that systematic and organised charac ter of business carried on by the assesses clothed him with the status of a "trade ' under the Indian Railways Act. At the instance of the assessee the Board referred the question to the High Court at Calcutta for its opinion: "Whether the petitioner Railway in each case is a " trader" for the purpose of as sessment under the aforesaid Bengal Finance(Sales Tax ) Act, 1948 and therefore liable to assessment under that Act?" By order dated 17 6 1960 the Board of Reve nue Commercial Taxes allowed the revision application. The High Court not accepted the contention of the appellant that unclaimed or uncon tected goods came into possession of the respondent but not as a result of any activity of purchase or of manufacture for sale. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. A regular feature is that when such good came into posses sion of the department it acquired rights over the said goods under section 56 of the Railways Act enabling it tO sell the goods. [780C] 2. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of Goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern Rail Railway, was a 'business for the purposes of the said Bengal Finance Act (Sales tax) Act 1941. In the other case the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Tax regu lar Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. [781F] 3. A systematic and organized charac n ter of its business carried out by the appel lant clothed himwith the status functions of a ' dealer" under tO section 2 (c) read with C1)(g) of Section 2 of the Indian Railway Act. In other case, the assessee Southern Railway disposed off scrap and scrap and waste unserviceable materials lying with the it.

The appellants were members of a company incorporated in 1896. In 1936 the Dalmia had purchased certain shares of the company and became its Director, and Chairman of the Company on March 19, 1949, when his brother, J. Dalmia resigned. He was appointed Principal Officer of the appellant company till September 22, 1955. During this relevant period, both the Chairman and Principal Officer were jointly acting as directors of the companies. The Manager who had been authorised by a Board resolution to deal with the securities, received from the Bank for meeting losses suffered by them in forward transactions in shares carried on in the name of the Bharat Union Agencies Ltd., and for other purposes not connected with the affairs of the said company. During these relevant period the company had its current account in the Chartered Bank of India Australia, which shipping documents were to be kept in Bombay. The real nature of the sale and purchase transactions of the securities did not come to the notice of the head office of the Insurance Company at Delhi as Chokhani communicated to the head Office the contracts of sale and purchases with brokers ' statements of accounts and on behalf of Bhagwati Trading Company, etc., except that they were not actually received or that the cheques in payment of purchase price were issued to each of them. In the present case, however, the names of Bhagwati trading Company as also that of Bhagwati Lorries would be known as Bhagwati Lors Company which represented the true state of affairs and Chokhani had to inform the Delhi Office of the Union Agencies about the source of the money he was receiving for the Union Agency to meet its losses. The fact that the funds of the insurance company were diverted to Union Agencies by the transactions proved by the prosecution, was not challenged by Dalmia. Held, that Dalmia 's sentence, in the circumstances of the case, to be severe as is being severe. Per Sarkar, J., dissenting), that the charge under section 409 I.P.C. was not invalid because it did not mention the name or names of any person who had supplied the office with the fictitious cash statement of the Bombay Office as alleged by the Prosecution and that he also knew that it bad suffered losses as a result of sharespeculation business in 1954 55 and that therefore Dalmia did not include those securities in this letter. The compilation in which the books of account were to come up must be presumed to have been signed by the Chairman of each company and it was not necessary for the purposes of the prosecution to lead direct evidence about Bhagwati trading company and therefore, Dalmia ' his conviction on the charge of conspiracy under section 120 read with section 409 Indian Penal Code could not be sustained. The observations in the judgment of the High Court were only obiter but must be struck down as being obiter. That decision cannot be applied where a case was made out for its opinion. It is well settled that an appeal must be dismissed from acquittal and it must be upheld if on the facts and circumstances of each particular case, no error or irregularity had been committed in the decision of that Court.

The two appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the State. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 of 1956, the new State of Bombay which included the territories of the states of Saurashtra and Kutch was formed was made. Under section 115 of the it was enacted that every person who immediately before the appointed day was serving in connection with the affairs of any of the existing States specified therein shall, as from that day be deemed to have been allotted to serve in connection With the affairs Of India, be deemed, to have become allocated to serve In connection with its affairs and for ensuring fair and equitable treatment to all persons affected by the provisions of section 115 and for proper cons sideration of any representation made by those persons. By Act 11 of 1960 called "The Bombay Reorganisation Act" the States of Gujarat and Maharashtra were carved out of the territory of the new state of Saurashtra. Under sub section (1) of section 116 it was provided that "the conditions of service applicable immediately before November 1, 1956 to the case of any person allotted to another State shall not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government". The appellant were allotted to serving in respect of the affairs and of the Secretariat of the two States at a time when r. 138 was framed by the State Government. By section 83 power was given to the Central Govern ment to give directions to any State Government that may appear to be necessary for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions, of sections 114, 115 and 116 of the , namely, (1 ) that the conditions of his service shall not he varied to their disadvantage except With the previous general approval of Central Govern mitting. (2) that the persons named therein "should be treated to have regularly appointed in the posts shown against their names in column 4 of the statement with effect from the date shown in the Departments mentioned in column 5 of the 's statement appended thereto; and (3) that, in any case, on the first day of the month immediately following month in which the posts were advertised by the Commission. of Central Government, the State Governments should obtain the concurrence of the Chief c losing Public Service Commission, before deciding the question whether the officers shown in their accompanying statement should be treated as regularly appointed and assigning them duties in the Secretariat or to fix their pay and seniority among the officers in the subordinate staff performing ministerial duties".

The State of Haryana by a law dated June 7, 1967 was authorised to levy tax on purchase of raw cotton as provided in section 5(2)(a) of the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967. By section S 5(1) it was further provided that such tax shall not be levied on the purchase or sale of declared goods at more than one stage. The first proviso to s.5(1), provided that any dealer who purchased cotton and sold it after the period provided for in section S.5 (2)(b) may, within thirty days from the date of receipt of such notice intimate in writing the assessing authority of his intention to abide by the assessment or reassessment sought to be reviewed and if he did so, submit information which was in conflict with section 15(1). The petitioners who were registered or unregistered dealers challenged this provision on the ground that there was a possibility of the tax being levied at more or less than one preceeding stage. They contended that the provisions of the second proviso notwithstanding the amendment by the Punjab Legislature and the Punjab Sales Tax Act, 1957, contravened article 14 and 19 of the Constitution inasmuch as they offended section 15 of the Central Act. The High Court held that there could be no liability for payment of tax unless it was otherwise stated in the Act or the rules thereunder. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Though under section 5 (2) (a) (vi), that party is liable to pay sales tax at more times than one point and then claim refund at a later stage there will not make the original levy valid. [549 E] (2). The effect of the amendment was to enable the State by a fresh law to impose on goods imported in the State and similar goods imported at different stages. As section 5 sets out the method for determining whether the goods were liable to tax, it is not enough for the State to say that a person, who is not liable to payment of sales tax must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claimed refund, at a subsequent stage. [548 G H] (3). Under those circumstances there is always a possibility, or even a certainty, of more persons than one having paid tax or being made liable to Pay tax in respect of the same goods at different rates. No provision, contained either in the section Act or rules on the basis of which it will be entitled to be supplied with all the material information, relevant for sustaining a request for refund cannot be said to be discriminatory, because, if particular sales or purchase are exempt from taxation altogether they can never be taken into account, at any stage, for the purpose of calculating or arriving at the taxable turnover and for levying tax.

The appellants who were the representatives of three original plaintiffs instituted a suit (being O.S. No. 30 of 1934) in the Court of the District Judge, East Tanjore, for enforcement of a mortgage against the present respondent and their minor undivided brother in a joint family business. The suit was contested by all the defendants except defendant No. 1 against whom it proceeded ex parte but there was a preliminary decree passed on May 15,1937, by which the sum of Rs. 1,08,098 was directed to be paid by defendant No I and defendants 3 to 7 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties and the suit was dismissed against defendant No 2. Against this decree, two appeals were taken to the High Court under section 47 CPC by the three appellants (second respondent) being Appeal No. 48 Of 1938 (Second appeal), under 0. XXI, r. 2, Civil Procedure Code. The High Court accepted the finding of the trial judge but held that defendants 2 to 7 were entitled to have the debts scaled down and there was no application made by defendant 1 for setting aside the ex parte decree which excluded him from the benefits of Act IV of 1938. On appeal by special leave : Held, (i) It is well settled that when a person is declared liable to pay a larger amount he should on payment or tender of a smaller amount get his property exonerated from liability but this is inherent in and arises out of the proposition established by the decision already dealt with. Therefore in cases where the mortgagor has been granted a decree against him, there is nothing in the Act to deprive him of the fruits of his mortgage debt. (ii) The decision given by the District judge was right and should not have been disturbed. (iii) A compu tation under 0.(XXVIII) C.P.C., in favour of one of the judgment debtors, while as regards others the decree is kept intact, does not make any difference in principle. The rule that a mortgage debt is one and indivisible exception to this rule are admitted in special circumstances where the integrity of the mortgage has been disrupted at the instance of the mortgagee himself; e.g., when there is severance of the interest of the mort gebted with the consent of the mortgagor or a portion of the equity of redemption is vested in the latter, is quite in accord with the scheme of the Act: The general law undoubtedly is that a mort gNMENT decree is one as a whole and indivisible exceptions to this Rule are admitted; and the Madras Agriculturists ' Relief Act is a special statute which aims at giving relief not to debtors in general but only to a specified class of debtors, viz., those who are agriculturists as defined in the .

The respondents were tenants of certain premises on which the appellants had sublet them. The first plaintiff as landlord of the premises in dispute gave notice to quit to the first appellant on December 6, 1947. After the expiry of the term of tenancy under section 13 Of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, the respondents filed a suit for possession on January 28, 1957 and again sought to evict the appellants from the premises. The Small Causes Court held that the second and third respondents were not lawful sub tenants as the provisions of section 10 of the Act had been infringed by the first plaintiff 's right to deliver the premises to them being contrary to law. It also passed a decree for eviction of all the respondents. This suit was dismissed on September 20, 1954. On February 19, 1957, another order was passed by this Court in favour of the tenants on May 31, 1956, directing that every month during which the respondents shall deliver possession of the building to the respondents the sub appellants would deliver back possession within three months from the date of the issue. The appellant 's revision petition against the decision of the High Court was summarily dismissed by the High COurt on September 25, 1954, whereupon it was urged on behalf of the appellants that : (i) suits for recovery of rent were based only on the grounds of want of such a plea and there was no lawful subletting; (ii) those suits were not one between a landlord and a tenant within the meaning of section 28 and no other could deal with them and decide the issue, (iii) the courts specified in section 28 were incompetent to entertain the suit but did not record any decision on merits of the appellant ' case. Held, that the claim of the respondents was one which arose out of the provoca tion of the Bombay Rent Control Act and not a suit between a sub tenant and a landlord under section 28. In a suit under section 29A of the court has to determine all questions relating to recovery of arrears of rent or relating to possession and all claims arising out of such Act or any of its provisions, even though they may be in the nature of a title to the premises, were to be determined by the courts 4 specified in s.28 and no others could deal With it and decide only the issues relating to eviction which arose under the provisions Of section 28 of the suit must also be determined in that way by a court specified in sec tion 28 and not by the Court specified in 's section 28, and no objection can be taken to the question as raised on behalf thereof. The provisions of sections 28 and 29A relate to suits where admittedly, one party alleges that he is the landlord and the other the tenant, section 28 would apply only to a suit where admittedly the relationship of landlord and tenant subsists between the parties, jurisdiction to entertain and try such a suit is in the courts mentioned in section 282 and no more. Held further, that it was not correct to suggest that the legislature intended, after setting up special courts under section 27 to deal with such matters, that s.29A would cover a case where in a suit one party alleged that he was the landlord or a tenant, as defined in the Act, would have to conform to the provisions which of Part 11 of the , applied and in that, if it be assumed that a claim to a right to tenancy of premises is a question of title to tile premises, is that a title which s.

The appellant had been a director of the respondent company. He was given power by a deed inter vivos or by will and codicil to appoint any person as managing director in his place and stead. The respondent who was a director in succession to him and required him to work as Managing Director, filed a suit against the appellant for declaration that he ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the directors ' meetings. He also alleged that he had been disqualified from being so appointed by the company. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the appointment of the appellant Govind as managing Director was void. On appeal, the High Court set aside the judgment of the courts below and ordered that the appellant be removed from service and directed his removal from service. Held, (per Sarkar, J.): It is well established principle of construction that when one finds a proviso to a section, the presumption is that but for the proviso the enacting part of the section would have included the subject matter of the proviso. But even if it is possible for the word "assignment" to have the meaning of "appointment", then it would have to be given both the meanings of "transfer" and "appointment" in the section. The Act contemplates an appointment by a director to the office which he previously held but did not hold at the date of the appointment; and the proviso was enacted ex abundanti cautela or it may be again, to prevent a possible argument that by the appointment "of alternate directors an evasion of the main part of section 86B was being attempted. Section 312 does not purport to prevent this. There is nothing illegal if the power is exercised in the case of the death of the director by an appointment made by his will. It may be that the proviso is enacted exask abundanti Cautela cauteli or it might be again to prevent possible argument, that by adopting the simple device of appointing a person as his successor when section 255 permits him to do that. Like section 31(b) in section 312 of the new Act. the word 'transfer ' does not mean "appointment". The fact that the power to appoint alternate directors is not given by the old Act but had to be exercised by the shareholders has no relevance.

The appellant is a partnership firm and are the ten ants of premises situate at No. 6 Kasi Chetty Street, G.T. Madras. They carry on business there. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s Adeshwar Glass Mart on the ground that the appellant had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop to the said M/ s. Adeshwar glass Mart, who had unlawfully sub leased the said premises for cultivation and had issued a notice to the appellants calling upon them to vacate the shop let out to the M/S. Adibas agreed that the rent paid by the appellants from M/o. Adrenadhi Glass Mart be adjusted in the future as they would be willing to vacate it in lieu of paying Rs. 10,000 or pay it at the time of surrender. This was followed by a notice dated September 30, 1971 calling upon the appellants to vacate after receiving the rent due on September 30. The appellants submitted their return. On September 30 the appellants submitted his return and filed an application under section 23 of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960, being the Court of Small Causes at Madras. The Trial Court held that the ground established and passed a decree for eviction as sought by the respondent. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appel lants. However, the High Court held in Chhotelal Pyarelal 's case that it was only by virtue of section 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. It was also observed that if there was any evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that had the account books and ledgers been produced, they would have shown that rent was received by the appellant from M /s. Aduneshwar Glass Shop Mart which would justify the finding, of subletting. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the Appeal, HELD: 1. The partners of the firm are before the Court though in a wrong name. [420B] 2. Section 30 of 'the Tamil Nadu Rent Control Act, 1961 is not applicable to proceedings under the said Rent Act either and hence the ratio laid down in the aforesaid decision was directly applicable to the case before us. [435F G] 3. In view of the fact that M/O. Adhar Glass Mart was carrying on trade at the premises and that firm was carried on business for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business there, the respondent cannot be said to have sublet the shop to M/D. Adimeshwar Glass stall Mart. As this plea was not raised in the Trial Court nor even in the first Appel late Court, it would have been open to the respondent to amend the eviction petition and join the partners as re spondents. [416E F] Chhotelen Pyarelal vs Shikharchand, [1964] 2 S.C.R. 156 and Chhotelhal Pyare Lal 's Case, relied upon by Mr. Nayar for the appellants is not one which would have had been fatal to the eviction Petition. Had this contention been raised in this Court or even in a first Appell late Court it would be open to him to amend it and join tain the partners who as re re sents. In the aforesaid case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to it to the appellant to raise this contention at this stage at all. [414F G; 414A] 4. It is not open for the appeli lants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. This contention must, therefore, be negatived.

A Scheme was introduced by the Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Urban Areas (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1977 to provide for imposition of ceiling on vacant land in urban agglomeration other than land which is mainly used for the purpose of agriculture. The State Government issued a notification under section 4 of the Act declaring that it was satisfied from the preamble that it had decided to impose a ceiling on urban immovable property and to implement the same with a view to preventing the concentration of urban land in the hands of persons and speculation and profiteering therein and with a direction to provide that such an order be not effective so long as the area in question is notified to be an urban agglomerations for the acquisition of such land in excess of the ceiling limit. The notification was challenged by the landholders before the Andhra pradesh High Court by way of Writ Petitions Nos. 1393, 3637 and 3973/78, which were dismissed holding that the enactment of the Central Act did not have the effect of invalidating the whole of the Andhra State Act, but since the provisions of the said Act were repugnant to the corresponding provisions of Central Act so far as the concerned land satisfies both the definition of "land" in the Andhra P. (Andhra Pradesh) Urban Area (Ceiling & Regulation) Bill 1976 and the definition was not extended to that Act, the AndhraP Act was held not applicable tovacant land" falling within the ambit of the Tamil Nadu Act. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions filed by the petitioners holding that since the provision of the A.P. Act were in conflict with the provisions contained in the Central (Andhra Areas) Urban Rent Control Order, 1956, it was void or incompetent as being outside the legislative competence of the State Legislature and so far no question arose for consideration in those writ petitions. The landholders appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : 1. A combined reading of section 2(f) and 4 of Andhra Pradesh Act (Andhra area) Urban agglomeration Act, 1976 would show that it is necessary to provide a ceiling which would be applicable if and when the area is notified as an urban precomeration under section 2 (n)(A)(ii) of the central Act. In order to fall within the exclusion, the land must be entered in the revenue or land record before the appointed day as for the purposes of agriculture and must also not have been specified in the master plan for a purpose other than agriculture. [1156 G; 1155 A] 2.1 As soon as an area is declared as an Urban agglomerated under section 3(f), the deemed to be land, that by virtue of section 4 his land whether self acquired or obtained or obtained on partition would be liable to be clubbed together with the lands of other members of the family unit not because the partition was invalid but because the land held by him otherwise howsoever acquired is liable tobe clubbed together equally with the land so held by the other members for the reason that the partition is invalid, but because of the land which he has already occupied it cannot be clubbed with that of his father and mother, the divided minor son could not be included in the family Unit and his property could not therefore be clubbed alongwith that of the appellant No. 1 and her father for the same purpose would belong to him and would not be liable under section 9 9 10 of the Mysore Act. [1109 B C] 2:2 In order, to fall outside the exclusion the land, must be shown in the government plan for vied public purposes which is a part of those areas, namely, the urban agglomation and the entire area of that area will go into the hands and there are no reasons why the State Govt. should not take such an action against the landholders who had been called upon to submit his return or to file the return under section prescribed for purposes.

In 1947 a dispute regarding an individual employee was referred by the Labour Appellate Tribunal, Calcutta to the Industrial Tribunal. The question for decision in C.A. 44 and 45 were (1) whether the workmen who turned on or before October 2, 1953, must be taken back in employment without condition, and (2) whether their discharge from the company was justified if not, to what relief they were entitled.
