In respect of all those employees one of the workmen filed an application under section 33 of the , praying for restoration of their service by directing that he should go back with the order of their reinstatement till enquiry was completed and (3) whether there was a violation of principles of natural justice in the absence of exceptional or special circumstances, the Industrial Tribunil held that the discharge and/or suspension of these workmen was justified. Held (per section K. Das J., dissenting): (i) In view of the conflicting findings by those Tribunals which had relied on C. A, 44 and C. 47, the Management could not be permitted to interfere with what really was a finding of fact. But where there is conflict between them in each case, it is necessary for the Tribunal to refer to other evidence in support of the order passed against the workman and decide whether the charges had been proved. (ii) Where both the Tribunals have misdirected themselves as to the true scope and effect of grounds of their dismissal or discharge they are not entitled to claim relief during the period of his forced unemployment consequent upon suspension, which has been held by this Court in a number of cases. Held further, that the two Tribunals below had misdirectly relied on certain oral evidence to show that C was suffering from ailments and blood pressure and the Tribunal could not have interfered with the decision of the Company unless it found that the decision is mala fide or amounted to victimisation. (iii) The appellants were reinstated in accordance with standing orders of the company and the Industrial Disputes Tribunal gave orders for reinstatement. If the two awards are read together against C, nothing turns on them.

Universities of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under Section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Nathawat for the said post, after interviewing Dr. Shiv Sharma, Dr. Sudhakar Mishra and Dr. T.N. Bhardwaj who were not selected filed a writ petition in the High Court which was allowed by a common order dated 3rd December, 1983. Though the High Courts found that there was no violation of Section 5 in the Constitution of the Selection Committee and the said finding has not been challenged before this Court on behalf of the respondents, it is well settled that in matters relating to educa tional institutions, if two interpretations are possible, the courts would ordinarily be reluctant to accept that interpretation which would upset and reverse the long course of action and decision taken by such educational authority. In matters relating lo educa tion, if a two interpretations were possible, whether the courts should lean more readily in favour of the candidates who have filed the writ petition or the other, the Courts would ordinarily endeavour to accept the interpretation which will upset and reversed the long line course of proceed ings taken by the educational authorities and would accept the interpretations made by such educa ic authorities. In the instant case Dr. Uma Kant was found suitable for the re spondents in the reserve list finding him suitable for appointment on the post as Professor in the University. Thus no fault can be found that the incumbent recommended in the reserved list by the Selection Commit tee was not selected for the concerned post of teacher. In our view, the High court is wrong in taking the view that a regular vacancy arose and therefore a Selection Committee should have been constituted afresh.

The petitioners who had all similar but separate grievances with respect to the development plan prepared and published under the Act challenged the validity of certain sections of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, on the ground that they infringed their fundamental rights under articles 14, 19(1)(f) & 31 of the Constitution. The allegations made against them were : (i) that they had applied through their architect in February 1962 for permission to change the existing user of their land by putting them to industrial use and had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for that purpose by which they proposed to construct on a portion of the land in section No. 1173 required them to do so; (ii) that the approval was given on July 2, 1964; (iii) that as soon as the plan was prepared, the question was a simple one as to whether the commencement certifi cate could be given without doing any violation to the building plan; and (iv) that such permission was necessary for their building purposes. The petitioners also alleged that the Planning Committee considered the suggestions made by the public and gave a report in respect thereof to the first respondent from time to time who finalised the plan at its meeting held on July 3, 1964. The authority responsible for drawing up of the plan had to have regard to the wishes and suggestions of the public. By the combined operation of sections 4 & 11 (3) of the Act the local authority was obliged to make a declaration of its intention to prepare such a plan and to despatch a copy thereof to be sent to the State Government along with the development plans inclusive of a report of the surveys carried out by the local author ity. The Authority, on receipt of the application for permission, made before granting or refusing a commencement certificate for building work of any land proposed to be taken up by any,, of the petitioners, cancelled the registration certificate on the grounds : (1) that there were no principles in the Act itself to guide the competent authority in the exercise of its will and pleasure to refuse permission to execute a decree for eviction violated the right to hold property under article 19(i)(f). It was further contended that even assuming that the State Legislature could pass the Act, nevertheless its provisions regarding the levy of contribution towards the cost of the scheme and all other matters relating to the working of the schemes were unauthorised. Held (per B. Sinha, C.J., Sarkar, jj.), that the powers and functions of a local authority for purposes of sections 12 and 13 of the Madras Town Planning Adhiniyam, 1954 are unguided, arbitrary and uncontrolled; (1 ) that sections 4 and 11 (2) of Act do not violate article 19 (1)(d) as they were imposed mala fide. The word 'may ' used in section 13 of Act must ordinarily be construed with reference to the words used but not on its meaning, i.e., the expression 'shall have regard also to the intention, meaning and scope of a enactment. It is, however, not correct to say that the legislature was competent to pass the impugned Act as it was not covered by any of the entries in List 11 or List 111 of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; (2 ) that the power vested in the competent autho rities at its sweet will and discretion to refuse to comply with the provisions of section 13 is no less than the Municipal Commis sioner himself or the Chief Officer of the Municipal Borough or a person exercising the power of an Executive Officer of any local authority; (3 ) that by the combined effect of sections 14, 15 & 16 it was clear that the local autho ries must be given a rea sonable time for the purpose and, the legislature thought that that a period of ten years was a sufficient one. Section 11(1) empowers the local authorities to acquire any land designated in the development Plan for a purpose specified in cls. (a) of section 7.

In Civil Appeal No. 1528 of 1968, a joint Bench of the High Courts set aside the award under section 18 of the , and directed the appellant Union of India to implement the award by exchange of letters in treating the award as an operative treaty after the boundary has been marked in this area, and the matters were referred to arbitration. Under article 1 of the agreement between the two States there was a dispute between the appellant and the Government of Pakistan inter alia, about the location of the boundary line and the operative part of that award declared the alignment of the boundaries which had under the terms of the Agreement relating to the procedure for demarcation to be filed by pillars on the Akapadam region. Disputes having arisen amongst certain States in respect of their location of these boundaries the appellant 's claim was accepted and it was resolved by arbitration to refer a dispute to arbitration, as contemplated by section 290A of the Government Of India Act, 1935. The appellant Union raised three contentions: (i) that there is no territorial dispute as there is not a well established boundary running roughly along the northern edge of the Rann of Kutch; and (ii) that, as there was no concurrent boundary running between the Ahmedabad region as shown in the pre partition maps which requires to be demarcated on the ground. Held, that the question whether in implementing the award, the executive Government is ceding territory of India or not is a matter within the competence of the Executive wing of the Govern ment and does not depend upon the circumstances of each case. The Indian Independence Act, 1947, was enacted by Parliament with a view to bringing into force laws relating to land reforms for the settlement of disputes between certain territories in relation to the settlement, settlement and enforcement of rights between the States which had been transferred to Pakistan under s. 290A. It was not necessary that both sides put forward their claims, so that the dispute related to the boundary between the Gujarat region as well as the Kutch State authorities before the State merged with the Dominion of India in 1948.

One P executed a mortgage in favour of one M on June 14, 1922 and filed a suit on July 12, 1946 for enforcement of two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties and for recovery of the amounts advanced with interest. The mortgagor 's right title and interest in M 's Mauza Bahaldih was sold on January 16, 1937, and after th sale was confirmed, possession oflla S was taken by the auction purchaser on April 7, 1937. After the two mortgages were executed no encumberance to any person but a suit to enforce payment of money charged upon immoveable property and money sued for an enforcement of the two mortgage deeds by sale was filed within 12 years after the date on which the mortgage amount as payable and prima facie it was barred by limitation. But the plaintiff sought to bring the claim within limitation relying on certain part payments towards the mortgaged dues made by the mortgagor. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that the suit in respect of the first mortgage was not barred by the law of limitation because the mortgage 'was partly simple and partly usufructuary; but even if P had been one of the credles, she could still maintain the suit relying upon the dispossession of the mortgagee on April 6, 1937 as evidenced by the endorsement on the first loan deed, which was signed by the redeem ant. On appeal the High Court held that there was a covenant for payment of the amount of the principal and interest due on or after April 14, 1925, under article 132 of the Limitation Act, 1908, a usufructuary mortgage was created on the mortgagor ' his interest in Mauza Baha; that even if an offence arose within 12 year from the date when the money sued For becomes due. Held, that section 68(1) (b), does not deal with the period of limitation for filing a suit, or extension of the period prescribed by the Limitation Limitation Act for filing an application by the mortgagee for extension of time prescribed by that period for filing the suit. The right conferred by section 68 is also a right to enforce the mortgage money on the personal covenant or to claim compensation when the mortgagee is deprived of his security.

The appellants employ as many as 7000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to its employees to come to the factories from their respective villages, the appellants provided transport facilities which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Alandi or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimpri and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly, for the transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to TLLCO factory, they were charged at the rate of Rs 5 per month. A charge of RS. 2 per months was levied on the transport company from Chinchvad Village to TALCO Factory in Pimpri & back. The appellants contended that these amounts were realised by them only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in supervisory grades. The Commissioner dismissed the appeals, but upheld the contention of the appellants that they would be liable to pay the tax as also the penalty. On second appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants: (i) That the transport provided to employees by the Company was reserved for them only and no other member of the public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle; (ii) that the transport was reserved in favour of the employees of the company, as they were not members of the Public Service Vehicles Act, 1958; and (iii) that even if a nominal Charge was realised from the employee that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger, so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act. Dismissing the appeals: ^ HELD: 1(i) Entry 2(7) of the Bombay Motor Vehicles Rules, 1939 defines 'public service carriage ' thus: "public service vehicle". A combined reading therefore of rule 2(i), and section 2(2)(7) clearly indicates that the tax would be leviable only if the passengers are carried on a public motor vehicle. It is true that the term 'public ' has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of such public can have free access on payment of the usual charges.

The second respondent filed a writ petition challenging the validity of the order granting a "no objection certificate" for a period of six months. This licence was renewed upto 30th June 1976 and there was a further renewal up to 30th September 1976. A subsequent application for renewal was turned down by the District Magistrate by his order dated 29th June 1977 on the ground that Paras Talkies with permanent cinema license which was closed, has now been functioning in the locality and therefore a renewal of the licence for a temporary cinema in the same locality would not be proper. Feeling aggrieved by this refusal the appellants filed a petition in the High Court under article 226 questioning the validity or the order of the State Government conceding inter alia that they were the residents of the locality, and that there is a mosque a madrasa and a temple in the vicinity or the place where the cinema house was to be constructed, but they were influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema licence having been re opened in the premises there was no need for a cinema house with a "temporary" licence and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the Government, the State Govern ment on being satisfied that there wasno impediment to the grant of such a licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same and therefore it is not a fit case for interference of the High Courts ' order. The appellants contended that section 3 imposes a restriction on exhibition by means of cinematograph at any place other than a licensed place under the Act in compliance with the restrictions or conditions imposed by such licence; the authority granting the no objection certificate was violative of their principles of natural justice and the order awarding the noti fication for a caste could not be sustained.

The plaintiff on September 2, 1957 wrote a letter to the plaintiffs stating that they were willing to perform the contract and that they reserved their right to file a suit for specific performance. The defendant did not accept the offer either orally or by any letters sent to them. On November 1, 1957 the plaintiffs filed a suit (O.S. No. 46 of 1957) against the defendant claiming specific performance of the contract, alleging that the said 'respondent agreed to assign to the plaintiff his leasehold interest under a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekanav, Hosadurga Taluk, and claimed specific performance thereof. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no concluded contract between the parties, as alleged in the plaint; that under a contract dated August 3, 1957, the respondent agreed to transfer his leasehold interests under a, mining lease under which the plaintiff had signed and stated that he had reserved their rights to file the suit for a specific performance; and that the agreement was concluded on September 1,1957 and that in breach of the terms of the offer by the plaintiffs, they were entitled to remain in possession of the mining area. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding (a) that there had been no concluded contracts between the two parties, and (b) that the assign ment was made on September '2, 1957 and that as the governments concerned could not be compelled to accord the necessary sanction and approval, the contract to assign the mining lease could not only be specifically performed and on this ground, the High court dismissed the suit. [584 A B] (ii) The plaintiffs have failed to establish the new case. In order that there should be no concluded 'ti fication, the plaint was not an acceptance of the offered, but it was intended to be an acceptance. It is not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint; nor is it usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint through the medium of the Court. [585 C] Bloxam 's Case turned on its own special facts that if he did not receive an answer within a certain time, he was to consider his application granted and should have amended his pleadings accordingly. In re: Pellatt 's case, , relied on. (iii) The mere filing of a bill in a suit to enforce specific performance was regarded as sufficient acceptance of it unless the offer had been withdrawn before; but that is not necessary].

The appellants challenged the validity of investigation in question on several grounds: (1) that sub rule (3) of r. 3 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1955, to be read with section 7 of the 'to be read along with s.7 of the Act, was not properly issued under section 3 of that Act; (2) that the said section cannot be used for controlling the payment of the price of food crops; it can only deal with foodstuffs; food crops are outside its scope. HELD: (i) The contention that the impugned order contravenes the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens under article 19(1)( ), for no fundamental right is conferred on a buyer not to pay the price mentioned in the section, came up for consideration before this Court, [677 E] (2)(a) Section 2(a) of the , provides that food crops including sugarcane. The next important provisions in the Act are cls. (b) and (c) of section 3(1), read with s 8 of the Essential Supplies (Control ) Order, 997, which empowered the Central Government to regulate the production, supply and distribution of essential commodities and trade and commerce therein for maintaining or increasing the supplies thereof or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. The power conferred on the State by section 3 is a "specific mandate". If the Bihar Act provides anything to the contrary the same must be held to have been altered in view of article 372 of the Constitution which provides that all laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution shall continue in force therein until altered or amended by a competent legislature or other competent authority. [674 G] Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , distinguished and followed. (3)(a). The Authority altered or modified that law is a competent one.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An order dtd 12th January, 1977 stated that the Government was committed to a policy of rapid industrialization and that in pursuance thereof, the Government had on 30th November 1966 issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. The said order dated 12th Jan. 1977 inter alia provided as under: "Consequently, the Governor of Mysore is pleased to sanction the following incentives and concessions to the entrepreneurs for starting new industry in the Bangalore State: (1) Sales Tax A cash refund will be allowed on all sales tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first 5 years from the date the industry goes into production, eligibility to the concession being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by the Department of Industries and Commerce". By an order dated 11th August, 1975, the procedure was prescribed for obtaining the concessions given under the orders referred to earlier. On 12th December, 1977 the State Government issued another Order which recited that the reasons for making the said order of 12th01 1977 were: (i) The concession of refund of sales tax on raw material used by new enterprises should be limited to 10 per cent of the cost of fixed assets per year, thus not exceeding the total of 50% over a period of five years for which the concession is available; and (ii) The concessions given by the said Order dated 30th June, 1969 were of no legal effect as there was no statutory provision under which such concessions could be granted and the order of 30th Septem ber, 1969 was ultra vires and bad in law. Hence these appeals. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government had, therefore, failed to establish the requisite ground or the basis for which it might be allowed to go back on its promise.

Sections 148 and 302 read with 149 I.P.C. deal with a combina tion of persons who become liable to be punished as sharers in the commission of offences. The non applicability of Section i49 I. P.C., is, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants under 7 1 37 under section 302 readwith section 34 I.p.C if the evidence disclosed commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of them all. PW 1, the wife of the deceased and PW 3 an adjoining land owner, are the three eye witnesses to the occurrence. It is in evidence that the accused along with some unidentified persons formed the Unlawful assembly. A 4 to A 7 having been acquitted, the remaining three appellants cannot be convicted under Sections 148 & 302 read I.I.P .C. on the ground that they formed an unlawful assembly alongwith some un unnamed persons. The Addl. Sessions Judge, however, found guilty for the offences punishable under sections 148 and 149 I P.c. and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 1 to A 3 under Sections 147 and 302 I.PC. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that after acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below, the conviction of the appel lant under Section 148 and on applying 149 I .P. C. cannot be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1. The ingredients of Section 302 read in conjunction with Section 34 I P PenalC. are, therefore: (i) They acted in furtherance the common object of tard unlawful assembly; (ii) they formed the unlawful assembly along some unified persons; and (iii) they were members of the opposite factions and there was long standing enmity between the parties. During the last 30 years, there had been murders and rioting between the two factions. The deceased was undergoing life imprisonment for the murder of one of the persons belonging to the group of the accused. He had come on parole. On the day of occurrence at about 7/00 a.m., when he was passing near the field of PW 1 he was attacked by the accused party. According to the eye witnesses, A 1 and A 3 were armed with spears, A 2, A 4 A 5 and A 6 with knives and A 7 was armed with a stick. All of them were in direc tions and there Was long standing animosity between the com pants. The occurrence had been fried out by the prose cution witnesses and the accused belonged to opposite faits and thereaf ter, there was short long standing rivalry between the ac cused persons. During these 30 years there had not been murders. In view of the manner of attack as disclosed by the eye witness and the number and nature of injuries, the appellants made the mur derous attack on the deceased. [8G H; 9A B] 1:2. It would be safe to accept the evidence of P.Ws.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam, which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500 by dividing it into five shares and five of his children. In 1965 the Income Tax officer purported to reopen the assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 for which the relevant accounting year was the calendar year 1965 was completed as the normal course and that there was admittedly no under statement A of consideration in respect of the transfer of the house and it was not possible to say that the transfer was effected by the assessee with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. 48,500 to tax as a result of the transfers. The Income Tax Officer issued a notice under Section 148 of the Act seeking to reopen assessment of assessee for 's assessment year 1967 67 and requiring him to submit a return of income within thirty days of the service of the notice. 48 354,500 and to tax because there was a admittedly no provision in statement A that there should be under statement of consideration In respect of transfer and sub section (2) of Section 52 it was pointed out that this sub section did not require as a condition precedent that there must be under statements of consideration which in respect for the transfer and it would apply only where the consideration for the transferred was under stated or in other words, the assessee has actually received a larger consideration for such transfer than what is declared or disclosed by him, sub section(2) provides that the fair market value of the capital asset as on the date of the 'transfer shall be taken to be the full value of consideration for a transfer. The assessee submitted a return showing 22 odd shares at a rental price of RS. 16500 in the series of transactions which had been written off by the Income tax Officer and a sum of Rs,87692 dated 4th April 1968. In this return under section 143(2), it was stated that there were 14 odd shares in her house immediately after the transfer by the assesee to his daughter in law and five shares respectively and that the assessee had only four odd shares of her share. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the submission made on behalf of the Revenue for the IncomeTax Officer to have drawn the conclusion reached by him and held that there could be no doubt that the transaction was perfectly honest, honest and bonafide, but in fulfilment of a contractual obligation the assessee who had sold the house should be liable to pay tax on capital gains which have not accrued or arisen to him. The Tribunal upheld the view taken by the Appellate Assistant Commissionion. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 A fair and reasonable construction of section 52 subsection(2)(b) would be to read into it a condition that it would applied only where there was under statement in respect to the transfer or to put it differently, the actual consideration received for the transferor is not truly declared or disclose by him but also that the consideration has been under stated and the assessee having actually received more than what was declared or declared by him. [653E F] 1.2 The object and purpose of sub section 2 was to avoid or reduce the liability of the asses see to tax on Capital gains. But this does not mean that in order to attract the applicability of sub s.(2) the fair value of capital asset transferred by the assesses as on that date exceeds the full price of the consideration declared by the assc tant would be applicable in all its rigour in such cases. [643D] 1:3 Section 52(1) cannot be invoked by a Revenue unless there is under statement from the consideration in regard to the transfers always rests on the Revenue.

The appellant was charged with in the Court of Presidency Magistrate, Bombay as follows: "That you on 3 12 1968 at 8 a.m. at Bandra in contravention of provisions of section 2(1)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, sold 450 grams of Til seeds to the Food Inspector and that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption, and thereby committed an offence under section 16(1) (a )(1) of . " The two witnesses produced before the Presidency Magistrate showed that there was a tall; about the actual purpose for which the Tileds were kept in the accused 's shop. spite of this information given to him, the accused sold them to him and signed the necessary papers. The prosecution case was that the plant could not be used as food and, therefore, it was essential to prove that what he had stored was not really food meant for human use but an article kept for a special use. ^ Held, (per Beg, J.): (1) that mens rea in the ordinary or usual sense of this term is not required for proving an offence defined by section 7 of the Act. It is enough if an article of adultered food is either manufactured for sale, or stored, or sold or distributed in contravention ,of any provision of the . [330G H] (2) The use the article sold was not entirely irrelevant. It was more correct to say that it is presumed from the nature of the article itself or the circumstances and manner of offering it for sale. Where circumstances raise a genuine doubt on the question whether what was kept by a seller was "food", at all, this must be resolved [330 A] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to.

Appellant Government servant of Madhya Pradesh, was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13.1.1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31.8.1966, which order was communicated to him on 19.9.1960. The plaintiff gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 17.6.1969 asking for a declaration that the order of dismissal was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed in the Courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58 of the First Schedule of the . When this appeal came up for hearing before a Division Bench reliance was placed on decision of this Court in Sita Ram Goel vs The Municipal Board Kanpur & Ors. , , and that Article 113 of the Act of 1963, corresponding to Article 120 of the old Act is a general one and would apply to suits to which no other Article in the schedule applies and the view taken by this Court was not correct to say that the suit was barred by limitation. The Division Bench reversed the order in appeal setting aside the appellate order in regard to limitation but observed as follows: "An appeal, if made, though the remedy has been availed of, a six months ' period from thedate of preferring of the appeal or making of the representation shall be taken to have first arisen." This Court accordingly directed that the Appeal should be disposed of by the trial Court for disposal in accordance with law. " The Division bench also examined as to whether when the appeal of the appellate court affirming the decree of the trial court was made, the original decree had ceased to be operative, and dismissed the suit on the ground that it has no jurisdiction. The High Court however chose to wait till the decision of the State Government on his appeal and overstepped the limit of time to his own detriment. In the meantime, a Division bench of this court held in Sitaram Sahu vs The State of Orissa & Ors., ; that Article 114 would apply if the remedy availed of has not been provided by law. Allowing the Appeal to this Court, HELD: 1. One of the three Judges Bench decision of a two judge Bench in the case of Pierce Leslie & Co. Ltd. vs Violet Ouchterlony Wapshare & Ors.[ ; , explained.

The suit property was purchased by the appellant in execution proceedings against his father and alienees from him. His case was that the alienations effected by his father were not binding on him and so his share in the properties covered by the said alienations was not affected by them. It was further alleged that the appellant 's father had executed a will of sale between themselves and his father in favour of the appellant, and this suit was decreed by the trial court. Subsequently the appellant applied for leave to appeal to the Privy Council and on his behalf it was urged that the decree sought to be appealed from was one of affirmance and there was no substantial question of law raised by the proposed appeal. Held: (i) A party aggrieved by a decree may appeal only against a part of it and is not bound to file an appeal against the whole of the decree; but in the case of a claim for interest before the date of the suit which is a part Of the dispute between the parties if the appellate court makes a variation in respect of the award, of interest that would affect the character of the appellate decree. (ii) If the judgment or decree of the High Court varies the decision of the lower court in respect to a matter in controversy in the proposed case to be brought to this Court under appeal, then such modification would not confer a right of appeal as regards matters unconnected with the matter in dispute in the present case. (iii) In considering whether an appellate decree passed by the High court affirmed the decision on the merits, the Appellate decree must be considered as a whole in relation to the decision or grounds given for it but the decision must be applied to the said subject matter alone. If there is a variation made in the judgment of the trial Court it is not a decree of affirmence and this position would not be affected either by the extent of the variation shown or by the fact that the variation is made in favour Of the intending appellant, or against him. (iv) In determining the question as to whether an Appellate decree passed in a suit should be held to be one of affirmedance, it is a matter of comparing the appellate judgment with the decision in a trial court which deals with a matter where there has been a variation and does not affect the nature of the claim or relief and so it would be inappropriate to adopt a technical or pedantic approach in interpreting the material words used. The distinction between a judgment of affirmment and an appeal by a suit is a question of fact and the decision is one of law, and not a final order of one judge of a High Court. Since there is no variation in regard to the decree as to costs, such a variation would not affect either by its nature or (if it was made in respect thereof or by a part only of the original suit.

The High Court, in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, read with section 115 of the C.P.C., held that no such revision petition was maintainable against a revisional order under section 25, Provincial Small Causes Courts Act. The District Judge held that the provisions of section 115 and section 115 were inconsistent with the main enactment as now amended. The High Court in revision dismissed the revision petitions filed by the appellant. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that a revisional power was formerly entrusted exclusively to the highest Court in the State but it had been conferred in terms enabling the High Court to exercise its revisional powers in respect of a revisional. Dismissing the appeals and setting aside the order of the High court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction under Section 115 is not amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the District Court under section115, Code, Civil Procedure. [39H; 40A] 2.1 Section 3 of the Act makes express provision barring the application of sections 96 to 112 and 115 of C. P.C. in respect, of cases decided before the 20th September, 1972 and also all cases arising out of original suits or other proceedings of any valuation, decided by the District Judge exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes was according to law, may call for the case and pass such order with respect thereto as it thinks fit. [40E] 2:2 No change in the principle was brought about merely because revisional power under section25 before the proviso was added, was now entrusted to the District judge. It must be remembered that the legislative intention behind the amendment was to relieve the High Courts of the burden of exercising revisional jurisdiction in respect off cases decided under the Provincial Small Cause Court Act. [42E] 3:3 While considering the nature and scope of the revisional juris diction, it is necessary to advert to the second question, whether a revisional application pending immediately before 1st August, 1978 of the nature in which a District Judge would exercise revisional power of revision under section 159 would vest in the High COurt. [41F] 3.1 The history of the various provisions of the Provincial Courts Act indicates that it is a self sufficient code so far as the present enquiry is concerned. For the purpose of correcting errors involving civil or criminal cases, the jurisdiction has been entrusted to highest court of the State, demonstrating that broadly the order under Section 25 would vest ' in the District court and decentralise that jurisdiction. That purpose was sought to be achieved by classifying all cases into two mutually exclusive categories depending on the valuation of the suit out of which they arose.

The respondents in C. P. No. 5972 of 1984 owned Khasra Nos. 383 area 14 bighas 16 biswas situate in village Madrampura on the outskirts of Jaipur city. On June 25, 1975 the Special Officer issued a notice to the respondents for personal hearing under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 and as to why a writ in the nature of mandamus should not be issued directing the appellants herein, the State Government and the Land Acquisition Officer, Jaipur, and the land Acquisition Officer Jaipur, to forbear from giving effect to the impugned notification dated February 8, 1984. Aggrieved by this, the respondents filed a Writ Petition before the High Court praying for issuance of an appropriate writ , direction or order restraining the appellants from taking any steps under sub section (5) of section 52 of the Act to surrender or deliver possession of the lands acquired forthwith or upon their failure to do so to take immediate steps in contravention thereof. The High Court, holding that the cause of action neither wholly nor in part arose within the territorial limits of the Calcutta High Court and hence the learned Single Judge had no jurisdiction to issue a rule nisi on the petition filed by the respondents under article 226 of the Constitution or to make the ad interim exparte prohibitory order restraining them from taking steps to take possession of those lands. The State Government preferred an appeal before this court against the said decision. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. It is well settled that in a proceeding for acquisition of land, it is a bundle of facts which taken with the law applicable to them gives the plaintiff a right to relief against the defendant. [605F G] 2.1 The expression 'cause of action ' is tersely defined in Mulla 's Code of Civil Procedure: (i) "the cause of actions" means every fact which, if traversed, it would be necessary for the plaintiff t prove in order to support his right to a judgment of the Court. [ 603A B] 3.2 The words "cause of Action ' is construed by equating all facts which took with the Law applicable to the them gives a plaintiff a locus right to be relief against a defendant. The mere service of notice under section52(2) of , on the respondents at their registered office at 18 B , Brabourne Road , Calcutta i.e., within the local territorial limits could not give rise to a cause of f action within that territory unless the service of such notice was an integral part of the cause.

The Respondent filed a suit for eviction and arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation pendent lite on the allegation that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises in suit on a monthly rent of Rs. 250 on 7/2 February, 1972, that the building in question was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to s 2(2) of the new Rent Act, and that it was covered by the new rent Act. The appellant further challenged the service and the validity of the notice terminating his tenancy, and contended that the said notice having been duly amended so as to bring the suit under the provisions of the old Rent Act the suit was barred by section 20 of the Act. B] The Additional District Judge negatived the defence and decreed the suit for ejectment. In appeal, the High Court confirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding about arrears of salary for the period between April 7, 1976 and April 25, 1977 and remanded the case to the trial Court for redetermination of the amount of rent in arrears payable by the appellant after affording opportunity to the parties to adduce further evidence in regard to this aspect. The High Court however did not endorse the finding of the Additional District Court on all points except that finding about the arrears of rents. In the opinion of the High 'Court admittedly a sum of Rs, 1000 had been paid by the Appellant to the landlord through a crossed cheque dated 16th August, 1976 which was received by the landlord on 15th September, 1976, and therefore when the plaintiff was in the witness box payment by cheque was not specifically put to him and it has not been established as to for which period the payment by cheques was made. [338C E] 128 The Court, however did never endorse the decision of the learned Additional District judge that the payment through the cheque may have been made towards rent for some period prior to April 7 1976 and held it to be manifestly erroneous and without any basis. In view of the fact that a sum in Rs. 1000 had already been paid in March 1981 instead of ten years, the building should be deemed to have been completed on the date of assessment which was 1st October, 1971.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and stores at Ranchi. Disputes arose between the parties over the bills and ultimately by an agreement dated February 6 1948, they were referred to arbitration of one Col. A. W. section Smith. The arbitrator made his award on June 4,1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under section 19 of the Act for a decree in terms of the award. The appellant contended that the agreement for reference did not comply with the requirements of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935 which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date and that it was therefore void. Held, that the copy of the order sent to the Government would have been insufficiently stamped. Unless this was done the copy could be validated on payment of the deficiency and penalty under section 35 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899. The law is no doubt well settled that a copy of an instrument cannot be validated by an executive Gazette but there is nothing in the section itself to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person; and when that was established the requirements Of section must be held to be satisfied. In the instant case the Government had failed to produce the same. Y. K. Lall, the Executive Engineer had been authorised by the Governor acting through his Secretary to execute the agreement dated Feb 6, 1948. It was a formal document executed by one Y. M. Lall. Executive Engineer who was in fact a party thereto. The subject matter of the arbitration was a claim which concerned the Government. The proposal at the earlier stages to amend cl. 23 of the original contract so as to include an arbitration shows that the intention of the parties was to treat the agreement as part and parcel of that contract. Even after the agreement was executed, the Secretary made corrections and modifications in the agreement on the basis that it Was the Government that was a party thereof.

In 1980 some complaints were received in the Department against the respondent pertaining to the purchase of sign boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged on August 27, 1985 against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act. In the meantime, the respondent retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. On September 30, 1983 he filed an application in the High Court for quashing of the First Information report on account of which challan could not be filed and it was only when the challenge to the First Report was repelled by the High court that a challan was filed on August 28, 1985 in the teeth of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume II and consequently was liable to be quashed. The plea raised by the Respondent found favour with the High 'Court which relying on an earlier decision of that Court in Des Raj Singhal vs State of Punjab, quashed the First F Information Report by its order dated February 12, 1986. Mangal Singh Minhas filed Criminal Appeal Nos. 423 24/1988 on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of signed boards in 1979 was in the colour of Rule (2.2). The State contended that keeping in view the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule 1.2, the said rule cannot be interpreted to be a rule placing an embargo on prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of a period of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein; and since the Government had the power under article 309 of the Constitution to make suitable amendments even retrospectively in Rule 2, there was no question of law involved in the appeal. Allowing the appeals by Special Leave, the Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court should be required to decide afresh the petition made against Mangal Singhirming the case on grounds, if any, other than those which have already been considered above. [919A] 1.3 In view of what has been said and keeping in mind the scope and interpretation of Rule2, there is no doubt with regard to the interpretation of the said Rule. The question whether the said Rules can be interpreted as one placing an restriction on institution of judicial proceedings as against a person referred to therein for prosecution in respect of a cause of Action which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution, [920D] 1:4 In the instant case, First Information F Report was promptly lodged on June 19, 1980. The filing of challan, however, was delayed on account by the steps taken for getting the First information quashed quashed.

The respondent company was a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. For the years 1946 to March 31, 1949, the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on the preference shares and therefore paid up capital of the company in respect thereof. On May 23, 1953, the respondent company entered into an agreement with A for paying up capital and in lieu thereof an amount equal to Rs. 7,000/ ,in addition to Rs . 7,500. The company was managed by a firm which after the death of 12 Nageswara Rao Panthulu Mavanthulu joint venture consisting of himself and three others, had been running business on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". On May 29, 1953 A notice was issued to A for reopening the assessment proceedings under section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer served a notice after obtaining the approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Income tax, inter alia, stating that the undistributed portion of the assessable income of the respondent Company as computed forincome tax purposes and reduced by the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the company to the extent it was less than sixty per cent of the amount available for distribution as computed under section 22 A. The appeal preferred by the assessee before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was dismissed, and a few contentions were raised on behalf of the Revenue authorities that the said provision was unconstitu tional or ultra vires. Held, that the Explanation to section 23 A of the Indian Income tax (1) was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which the public are substantially interested, has been held by persons other than the controlling group and none is entitled to a fixed rate of dividend. The rule which excludes from the computation of voting power holders of shares entitled to fixed rates of dividend is that section 23 of the Act imposes an obligation on the company not to whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company or to make it impossible for any shareholder to avoid payment of super tax either than in excess of twenty five per cent. Held thus, further, that where a shareholder holds or a group of shareholders acting in concert holding 50 per cent or more of the voting power which controls the working of a company it is from its very nature a company in which there is no controlling member or group and therefore the public were substantially interested. When the controlling interest i.e. a minimum of fifty one per cent was held by a single individual or a groups of individuals acting in com prising concert hold fifty one% or more share of the controlling power, it is not exercisable by the public. The proviso to section 24 A of that Act does not define "company" in which a public are materially interested, and consequently the public is substantially interested; but on a comparison of the provisions of the third proviso to s 23A (1), the order of the High Court must be con firmed. Further the Explanation and the explanation do not purport to define a company which the general shareholders may be regarded as one in which section 23 B applies. Nor can it be said that the expression "company ' in which in a public company are substantially con tended, is 'a question to which no attention was paid by the Tribunal.

The first appellant 's selling procedure was that the quota holder in respect of 13 bales was Shree Kishan & Company and the amount said to have been paid by Dwarkadas Khetan & Co. had been written on behalf of another quota holder Beharilal Bajirathi and on the back side of each printed form states. On receipt of this advice slip the first appellant despatched all the 13 bales to Dharsi Moolji for delivery in the same truck as the 13 pieces. The first appellant, however, sent a letter to the first appel lant stating that he had delivered the goods to Dhartia Moolji and had not received anything from him. He then debits Dwarkadash Khetan and Company with the price and not the purchaser. For payment it looked to Dwarkad as the person to whom delivery was made. The goods were in the Dady Seth Seth godown under the control of Dwarkada Oudh and Company sent them to Dharti Moolji C. Vora, but the first appellants retained the money for the bales from Dharsi. Held, that, the goods were not required by the terms of the contract of sale and as such the sale was a property in possession of the first plaintiff. The second clause of the portion marked "Important ' towards the head of the form states that all stocks pledged/hypothecated by manufacturers with banks or others must also be included, and Instruction No. II on the front directs that the names of the "any other person" must be entered in column 3 and that the number and date of General Or special Permission must be set out in column 2, whether this means that goods cannot be pledged without permission or that only goods allotted to quota holders can be pledged, they would not know, but whatever it means. It was a printed form and that was filled in as follows : " I hereby demand the first first appellant to have sent another letter for delivery of the goods by A ; " The second bottom marked "ore" is listed as "During the time . One does not intend to apply them but only refers to those goods which are sold under a General or special permission or order of the Textile Commissioner. There was nothing in the terms section which called for the severe strictures which are to be found in the trial court 's judgment and certainly not for the savage sentences which the learned Magistrate imposed. Dwarkadaseas Khetan could, in the circumstances, given above he described as "Imported by " ordelivery" in the sense of plain English words, which any ordinary man of average intelligence, not versed in the law would have no difficulty in understanding. The facts were truly and accurately so given according to the popular and natural meaning of the words used; nothing was hidden. The word 'physical possession ' may be generally described by stating that 108 "when a person is in such a relation to a thing that, so far as regards the thing, he can assume, exercise or resume manual control of it at pleasure, and so far, as regards other persons, the thing is under the protection of his personal presence, or in or on a house or land occupied by him or in some receptacle belonging to him and under his control. " Held further, that the goods did reach the quote quoted above from the words "called for supply" and not to the appellants but to the respondent.

The respondent was a Senior lecturer in a Government College. He was charged with offences under section 161 Indian Penal Code, and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947. The Special Judge who tried both these cases found them guilty of the offence with which they were charged. It was contended on behalf of the State that as regards section 161, Indian Penal code it was necessary that the person committing that offence must be a public servant and in that connection to his work as an Examiner of the Gujarat University which, it had been found, had no connection with his being a Government servant. HELD: (i) The word "otherwise" has wide connotation and if no limitation is placed on it, the words "corrupt" and "otherwise ' mentioned in the clause become surplusage, for on that construction every abuse of position is gathered by the clause. [327 A C] (ii)In framing a charge the court would not go into any evidence nor to determine whether there was abuse or abuse of authority. The use of the word "corruption" and its connotation are different from those mentioned in section 161 of the Indian Penal Codes. One class of cases may arise where corrupt or illegal means are adopted or pursued by the public servant to gain for himself a pecuniary advantage. [325 E F] No doubt the word 'otherwise ' has wide meaning and if that is so, the abuse of situation as a public Servant would be essential. But it would be reasonable to put on that word and that limitation is that it takes colour from the preceding words along with which it appears in the cl. that is to say something savouring of dishonest act on his part. [326 A B] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration ; , referred to. (iii)In view of the clear provisions of section 5, it was not necessary that only such persons could be appointed as Examiner who is the holder of an office but there would be no abuse of his position as a Government Servant and if he uses corrupt or unlawful means for obtaining valuable thing or pecuniary advantage he commits an offence as contemplated by section 5. [328 C] The 'porch of the University had to be looked at; but in this case there was nothing to show that the various reasons given were not sufficient to sustain the construction or interpretation of section 6 (1).

The petitioners were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of a Signal Unit in Northern Railway. All the writ petitions having disposed of by a common judgment as questions of law, and fact involved therein were similar. The petitioners alleged that notwithstanding the fact that each of them had put in continuous service for quite a long period, during which the Railway Administration was not treating them as temporary servants, they were denied to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., they are now entitled to all these privileges as applicable to open line temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. On behalf of the Administration it was submitted that there has been break in such continuity between the two categories of employees till temporary status is acquired. Allowing the writ Petitions and setting aside the order of 1st of June, 1984 passed by the Railway Board, this Court, HELD: 1. The question whether casual labour who acquire temporary status, will not, however, be brought on to the permanent establishment unless they are selected through regular Selection Boards for Class IV staff. They will have a prior claim over others to permanent recruitment and they will be considered for regular employment without having to go through employment exchanges. Such of them who join as casual labourers before attaining the age of 25 years may be allowed relaxation of the maximum age limit prescribed for Class III posts to the extent of their total service which may be either continuous or in broken periods. [144C] 2. All those casual labourers would also be granted to carry forward the leave at their credit to the new post on absorption in regulation service. [149E F] 3:1. The Railway Establishment Manual has made provisions for their protection but implementation is not P effective. Several instructions issued by the Railways Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before this Court to show that the Administration is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. [145B] 3.(i) The respondents shall have a direction to consider the claims of each of the petitioners promptly and make appropriate orders for their regularisation. For over ten years, litigations of this type have been coming to the Court. About three years back, this court directed a scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. Casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railway administration and cannot be avoided. The writ petitions are disposed of with the directions indicated above without any order for costs. [146A C] 4:2.

The appellants entered into contracts with the Central Government for settlements in February and May 1956. In fact, there was no dispute that these contracts were in accordance with the bye laws of the Association as they stood at the date when the contracts were entered into. The terms and conditions of forward contracts in cotton including "hedge contracts" and the manner of their implementation were governed by Bye law 52AA which on the date on which the appellants entered ' contracts ran as follows : "52 A.A. (1) whether or not prices at which the Cotton may be bought or sold are at any time controlled under the provisions of this Act, if the Textile Commissioner with the concurrence of the Forward Markets Commission and after consultation with Chairman (of the Board), be of opinion that the continuation of hedge trading is likely to result in a situation detrimental to the larger interests of the economy of India and so inform the Board, the Board shall forthwith cause a notice to be posted on the Notice Board to that effect and on the posting of such notice and notwithstanding anything to be contrary contained in these bye laws or in any hedges or on call contract made subject to these Bye law, the following provisions shall take effect. " The Forward Markets (Regulation) Act 1952 was enacted with a view to bring about an equitable distribution of trade produce between producers and consumers. Under section 4(f), the Central Govern ment may either on a request in writing received by it from the governing body of a recognised association or if in its opinion it is expedient so to do, make bye laws for all or any of the matters specified in section 11 or amend any bye law made by such association. " Held further that the contention that the notification issued by the Forward Market Commission was illegal and the appellants were entitled to the issue of a writ of mandamus could not be accepted. If there was an emergency the Government was competent under section 12(1) to make a bye law in respect of any matter specified in that section.

The assessee company, a shareholder of a company, was declared as dividend for each of the three years in respect of which they were received. In this group of cases, it claimed that out of the amounts set out in the Table only Rs. 8,669/ , and Rs. 21,822/ for the year 1357 B.S., Rs. 37,125/ , for the years 1358 B.E. and Rs . 21,820/ , , for 1357B, the year 1359 B. S. Rs. 28,125. The Income tax Officer referred under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, three questions to the High Court. the first two questions were referred by the assessee and the third question in issue was whether distribution of dividend out of capital gains was taxable. He brought the entire amount to tax declaring as dividend income for each one of the 3 years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of Income tax, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire amounts for each year were income in the hands of the assessee as receipt of dividends within the meaning of section 2(6A) of, 1922 was liable to be grosted up. In second appeal, he also held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for the grant of long term leases after 31st March 1948 was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assesse from "other sources". On an application made by the Commissioner for reference under section 256(1), the High court referred three questions, namely (a) whether distribution took place before 31st December 1948, which was in the nature of a receipt of income in its hands and taxable as the Income tax officer brought the whole amount to "other source", which comprised salami or premia received by it as consideration for grant of longer term mining and other leases and as compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes; (b) whether, on the facts and circumstances of the case, distribution to the assessee of the land attributable to land acquisition compensation was capital gain. The High Court held that these answers were in the negative on all questions in the affirmative. Allowing the appeals, HELD : 1.1 But as it is agreed between the parties that the answers in the positive on all the questions were subject to the final decision in appeals filed against the orders made in Income tax References Nos. 131 of 1961 and 3 of 1964. [35E G] 1.2 In cases where the High Courts below have answered the question in favour of the Revenue it is necessary to observe that in Appeals Nos. 737 to 739 of 1968 and 13 of 1968 which arose out of Reference No. 131, all such questions were to be referred. Therefore, in appeals Nos. 738 to 739, of 1968, the only question of law raised was whether any distribution of profit out of Capital gains was ' taxable. [36A B] The scope of enquiry in this group is more extensive and in cases where this Court has not recorded final answers in respect thereof, the order is subject to another infirmity.

Kustru equally in his 'Materia Medica of 504 India and theirrahin Plantations were concerned in finding out, physio chemical properties contained in wood oil and the source from which they were drawn for use in industrial purposes. The forest produce whether found in or brought from a forest or not was a forest Produce which include that is to say, the "enumerated items in Clauses 1 and 11 ",wood oil ' included tea, saw peals, creISCO oils and all other parts of wood including bamboo trees standing thereon. The Forest Conservation Act, 1980 aims to prevent depleting forests, conservation thereof and protection of wild life in the country to maintain ecological balance. By the Kerala Forest Act (Act No. 1/65) Sandalwood Oil was produced by making hole on the trunk of the living tree commonly known as "oil trees". Wood oil was gathered by heating the hole in the trunk to induce exudation of the olec resin from the tree and commercially dealt with as wood oil which is a cheap substance in the commercial world used solely for the purpose of painting planks of wood or wooden vessels floating in the sea. The physio Chemical Works and expert opinion would bring out a demonstrable distinction between wood oil &forest oil. The wood oil was being carried out as industry, either by licence by the individuals or the state government as its monopoly like Karnataka State, in a larger scale or as small scale business. It is further alleged that these technical literatures were concerned with finding out physio Industrial chemical properties mentioned in Clauses I and II of the Kerala Forests Act, 1961. The State Acts regulate preservation of forest and regulation of possession of the forest produce failing of trees in the forest area and removal from the forest or reserved forest area by transit permits etc. When Sandal wood Oil either was found in transit or in possession of manufacturers it was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under section 5 1 (1) (or contravention thereof. As said earlier, the jurisdictional question was raised on the premise that sand is a wood oil. S.2 (f) defines forest produce thus: "Section 2(f) forest produce" includes: (i)the following whether found In or brought From, a forest and not any 'forest produce including that is, to say timber, charcoal, wood oil gum resin, natural varnish bark lac, fibres and roots of bamboos and rosewood. and (ii) the following when found in and brought from afore said, that isto say, atrees and leaves, flowers and fruits and all parts or produce not here in before mentioned, of trees. " It was also contended by the aggrieved parties that inclusive definition of forest produce must receive extended meaning. The expression wood oil ' is generally used as a word of extension. When use in an interpretation clause, it seeks to enlarge the meaning of the words or pharases occuring in the body of the Statute. 64 stated the construction to be adopted to the meanings of the expressions and pharits that "the cardinal rule for the construction of Acts of Parliament is that they should be construed according to the intention expressed in the Acts themselves. If the words of the statute are themselves precise and unambiguous, then no more can be necessary than to expound those words in their ordinary and natural sense". The language of a statutory provision is not static vehicle of ideas and concepts and concepts change, as they are bound to do in any country like ours with the establishment of a democratic structure based on agalitarian values, the meaning and content of the statutory provision undergo a change. The process by which the oil is extracted is not decisive as oil may be extracted by natural process of exudies or it may be extracting by subjecting to chemical or mechanical process and Sandal Woodwood (Santalum Album) are cut into pieces.

The prosecution alleged that there was no evidence against the accused sufficient to warrant a conviction and sentence. The trial court acquitted the accused on appeal. Held, that in ascertaining the guilt or innocence of the accused differ from that of the High Court, yet where the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused was guilty this court would set aside the conviction, and the High court was wrong in accepting the testimony of the eye witness in support of the correctness of the two dying declarations nor could the statement of the deceased alleged to have been made in the circumstances of this case be considered sufficient to support a conviction of the appellant. Sundarlal vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, A.I.R. , explained and followed. It cannot be said that the opinions of these authors were given in regard to circumstances exactly similar to those which arose in the case now before us nor was this a satisfactory way of disposing of the evidence of an expert unless, the passages which are sought to discredit his opinion are put to him. [857 B C] The Sessions Judge was of the opinion that he was comparatively young and that his statement was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. But it could not be said if the opinions were given they were not sufficient for sustaining a conviction on a charge of murder. [ 860 C F] The learned Judges of the Court were, therefore, in error in accepting their testimony in support. [ 858 B].

The appellant company, engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling agents, employees, etc. of a company, was to maintain a standing union for the workmen and to attend to annual conventions of their federation, to attend in accordance with their applications dated 7 9 1963 annexed hereto. Clause 5(a) of the agreement clearly stated that the disputes agreed to be referred to were those set out in the agreement and state mented: "Whereas the Governor of Bihar is pleased to refer the said dispute " The undersigned the above mentioned reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment, "the present references enclosed with this application signed by the District Manager on behalf of the Company and the General Secretary of the said union representing the said workmen contamed inter alia, the following information: (a) Number of workmen employed in the undertaking affected 352 (d) Estimated number of workmen affected or likely to be affected by the dispute", (b) The aforesaid disputes concerned the workmen employed In the company 's factory at Jamshedpur and represented by their union the Indoxco Labour Union.
