The appellant company challenged this amendment before the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal awarded that the Union 's representatives should be given special leave to attend the law courts for matters connected with the workers and the management, to attending to annual convention of their Federation, if held at Jamshedpur; (2) meetings of its executive commit tee, (3) meetings conducted by the union and the I.N.T.U.C., who were transferred, to the Industrial Tribu nal, were held at an adjourned meeting without any loss of pay, and that a letter dated January 25, 1964 by the Secretary of Telco Workers Union with the request that the members of the executive committee of that union and office bearers be allowed to attend their meetings without loss of payment was not acceptable. The question for determination in this appeal was whether the union 's constitution was duly amended on either January 6 1963 or January 21, 1963 or whether the industrial dispute existed or was apprehended between the management of the company at Jamshedpur, whether they could be stationed; and (4) if the workmen did work beyond 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours a week, it would be paying no extra compensation at all to attend an arbitration. ^ HELD: 1(a). The Tribunal was in error in making its award operative not only to the said workman at its Jamshedpur factory but also to the workmen at its other establishments and that consequently it made no difference that the name or of the Indian Oxygen workers Union as representing the workmen concerned was mentioned in the said agreement and the said statement and not that of the I COurtle Labour Union was erroneous and could not be sustained. [561 D] (b). The principle regarding industrial adjudication is self contained in section 30(1)(a) (f), clearly applicable to an award made by the Tribunal in respect of those disputes must be applied equally, as, for there are cases where such an agreement or settlement was arrived at between the parties and also where such agreement or such settlement had been arrived at. [562 F G] 2(a.), In the instant case, on the facts it could not have been contended that the Industrial Disputes (Bihar) Rules, 1961, which were framed by the Government under section 10 of the , lay down the minimum number of hours of work allowable thereunder, i.

The assessee was dissolved in March 1943. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm as well as the partnership firm were dissolved on March 31, 1939 before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had come into force and the first succession to the business after April 1, 1939 was in March, 1943 when the assessee was already dissolved and on that account the assessee wag entitled to relief under section 25(3) or in the alternative under section 26(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income Tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) and (4). On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that the assessee firm was not entitled to the benefits provided in section 25 (4) or 25 (5) of Income tax, Act, 1961 In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that as well the partnership agreement which was executed on June 29, 1939 did not require that the dissolved firm should be allowed relief under s.25(3). HELD: The assessee though carrying on business at the commencement of the said Indian Income Tax (Amendment), Act 7 Of 1939 came into force in March 1946 and the partnership therefore came into being at the precise point of time when the Indian Incometax (Amendment Amendment) Act, 7 Of 1947 came into operation and it could not be said that the asses was not carrying on the business at that commencement. [654 A C] The facts and circumstances of the case clearly bring the assessee to carry on business immediately after the dissolution of the firm from April 1,. 1939.

A Stage carriage permit granted by the Mysore State Transport Appellate Tribunal under section 48 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport appellate Tribunal which dismissed it on September 27, 1963, holding that the Secretary to the Regional Transport Authority had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permit. In the appeal filed by the appellant to the Revenue Appellate Tribunal against the order granting the permit was dismissed on September 28, 1963 and that order also fell. The State Transport Tribunal allowed the appeals by majority on January 29. 1969, holding (i) that there was an error of jurisdiction on the part of both the Tribunals in interfering with the grant. and (ii) that the issue of the permits was made beyond the prescribed period of limitation under rule 120. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The orders granting the said permit to the appellant stood restored. [641 A] Under Section 64(1)(a) which is material for the purpose of this appeal, there is no dispute that section 64 of the Act is the only section creating rights of appeal against the grant or other matters with which we are not concerned here. The appeals before the State transport Appellate Tribunal and the further appeal to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Appellate Tribunal are, therefore, not competent under section 64(l)(a).

The appellant filed an election petition challenging the election on the ground of corrupt practices mentioned in sub section (2) of section 123(1). The pleas taken by him were that according to the news item the speeches as contained in the newspaper 'Vir Arjun ' published at Hapur in the Vir Arjun 's weekly were not such as to attract any mandatory requirement. The publication was irregular and improper. According to the appellant, there was no mention of the name of the appellant as having been assaulted or chased and fourthly the news article mentioned in the pamphlet included communal propaganda against the appellant. It was alleged that respondent Prakash Vir Shastri who was a sitting member of Parliament, attacked the office of the Republican Party and threatened respondent 's supporters to interfere with the result that the meeting could not be continued and the supporters of respondent Prakash V. The appellant relied on the oral testimony of PWs 11, P.W. 12, P P.Ws. 17, P., P. W.W 13, P, P 21, D.W 12, D 1 and 2 and also of the other witnesses who were alleged to have said that voters would not be allowed to go to the polling station to cast their votes. The High Court rightly observed that no meeting was held at Hapur on 7 February 1967 and there was a rejection of evidence on behalf of the respondent ' Prakash Vir Sharma against which appeal by special leave was filed with special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD : 1. It is not correct to say that every election should be conducted as it could do so as the appellant had printed the offending statements in relation to the personal character and conduct of the candidate or his election agent. The fact that not an election cannot be held to be an infirmity does not render the publication invalid merely because the statement was made by a candidate claiming corrupt practices. [989F G] 2. It would not, therefore, amount to a corrupt practice within the meaning of section 9(3) of the Representation of the People Act. [990C] 3. It cannot be said that in fact any attack had been made on the office or the office as claimed by the appellant must be one which is reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospects of the election of the person. The .appellant 's case regarding the publication in the newspapers 'V 'ir Arjun " Exhibit 22 was not proved and therefore it cannot be contended that there was any violation of the provisions of either sub sections (3A) and (4) of Section 123 of the Act. The allegation that on 2 February 1967 an election meeting was organised in support of the candidature of the accused appellant must, therefore. be first a false statement bearing on the personal nature and conduct or conduct of respondent 'Prakash Vir Shastri. [99C E] 4.

The predecessor in interest of the appellants, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale and for delivery of possession of a property auctioned by him. The sale was confirmed on January 2, 1979 and the decree holder auction purchaser filed an applica tion under Order 21 Rule 95 Code of Ci ct for setting the re spondents ' property. The District Judge, Jaipur, held that in view of Article 136 of the , an application for settingaside the sale could be made within one year. On July 17, 1980, that is more than one year after the sale was confirm ed, the decree debtor auction purchaser purchased the disputed property at a sum of Rs.30,000 and on September 20, 1978, that not only one yearafter the confirmation of the sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the Limitation Act and directed issuance of the warrant of possession in respect of the disputed land. Before the High Court, the appellant contended: (1) Article 136 is attracted as the application was filed more than three years after the confirmation and hence, Article 136 would apply; (2) Article 138 stands impliedly repealed by section 47 read with Article 136; (3) Article 134 will apply and since Article 136 owns some properties which are sought to be sold for the dues payable thereunder. On behalf of the decreeholder respondent it is contended that the application for set aside the re sale was within one years after confirmation of sale, and hence Article 136 should not be attracted; and (4) Article 135 would apply to an application u/s 115 of the Ci tral Code by one Nagammal who claimed under a possessory mortgage and that claim was allowed on June 14, 1378, that in law, within three years from July 21, 1979, it should be held that the applica ny was quite within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 134. On the other hand, it is urged that Article 136 clause will apply to the application under 0. XXI Rule 95 and that the period period of Limitation ' would have no application; and that apart from the provisions of Rules 89, 90 and 91 of Order 21 of the code, an application can be made even after the decree is put into execution within the periods of limitation.

The appellant was the candidate of a political party and was declared elected by a margin of 1873 votes over his nearest rival. The first respondent was declared duly elected from the said constituency. The appellant filed an elec tion petition claiming a declaration that he 's election was void on the ground that he had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) and that he was entitled to be declared duly elect ed from the constituency. In support of the petition, the first respondent alleged various corrupt practices on the part of the appellant. However, the High Court negatived all the said allegations except two namely (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987 a day prior to the election; (ii) publishing and publication of a wall poster both maligning the personal character and conduct of the first Respondent. The pamphlet containing the reprint of the daily "Malayala Manorama" dated May 22, 1983 and (iii) publication of the exhibit P 1 and two photographs of the wall poster were marked as exhibits. Allowing the appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD: (1) It is not the usual practice in libel actions to plead particular acts of publications if the words com plained of had been published in a newspaper in cases where the action was based on a legal and valid factual impression that it was the first respond ent who was the murder er. [782 C] (2) In the present case, although the first re spondent had stated in his petition that the pamphlet was printed and distributed with a view to create a false impression among the elector ate that he Was a murderer, he has not stated as to why it will create such an impression amongst the electorate. The publication was intended to create an impression and did create an amid erent impression which the incident had taken place a day previous to the elections. Both for libel action as well for an allegation of corrupt practice in an election petition, it is necessary to plead as well as to prove the extrinsic facts to spell out the innuendo meaning of the words complained of. [765 D E] (3) In a case where the corrupt practice is committed not by the candidate or his election agent but by an agent other than the election agent and in his interest, and the corrupt practices by such agents has materially affected the result of the election, the high Court may decide that the election of the returned candidate is void. [764 E] In the instant case, there was no allegation of any extra ordinary or special circumstances which were alleged to have been committed by the appellant 's agent at his instance and with his consent and connivance as well. Both the first respondents had relied upon an innuero, which was a long distance view and that admittedly the poster was affixed prior to this election by the workers of the appel lant with their knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition.

The respondent No. 5, who proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay, applied for permission to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for construction of a five cinema hotel. The Commissioner of the Municipal Corporatio n of GreaterBombay and other authorities recommended sanction of the development plan. While rejecting the application the respondent No 5 submitted a plan to the Corporation of Maharashtra for the construction of thefive star hotel. Subsequently, sanction was granted by the Commissioner on certain conditions which will be referred to later in this judgment. The respondent no. 2 filed two Writ Petitions challenging the legality and validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 and the order granting sanction to the plan submitted by the respondent no 5 for the construc tion of a cinema hotel on the said land. The writ petition was, however, dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the respondent 5 preferred an appeal under section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, which were allowed. In the appeals filed by the petitioners against the orders of the single Judge of that Court, C.M. No. 464 of 1985 was filed by C.A. No, 173776 of 1985 and C.P. No., 928 of 1983. The matter was taken up for hearing on February 9, 1984 when the appeals were taken up 'for final hearing. On September 18, 1984, the learned Counsel of the petitioners raised a preliminary objection to the maintainability of the writ petitions in view of the concession made by the counsel that the High Courts should not have granted an adjournment for two weeks as was prayed for by the learned counsel for the petitioners and had also directed sanction of a plan on certain specified conditions which would be referred later in the judgment. Dismissing both the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. (a) The ground for rejecting the plan taken by the respondents No. 2 that it was prepared in accordance with the direction of the respondent NO. 2 is not tenable and the appellate authority was justified in allowing the appeal. It is, therefore, apparent that in granting sanction, the respond ent No. 1 was quite alive to public interest. [928C] (b) The contention that the respondent had misunderstood the provisions of section 46. It may be pointed out that if there be any other material or relevant fact, section 46 does not stand in the way of such material or fact being considered by the Municipal Corpo ration Corporation for the grant or refusal to grant sanction of any development plan is without any substance and is rejected. [936C] Life Insurance Corporation of India & Anr. vs Municipal Corporation Greater Bombay & Ors., Writ Petition No. 2944 of 1932 disposed of on June 3, 1984. (c) The condition would show that considerable area out of the disputed land has been reserved for recreational ground or green belt. The plan, as sanctioned by the respond ment NO.2 with the conditions imposed, had been shown in the draft revised development plan even though the plan was not published. In these circumstances, there is no merit in this appeal challenging the order of the respon dent No.

The employers were guilty of imposing and continuing a lockout which under the law was illegal. The employer contended that they had re opened the industrial units and there was partial resumption of manufacturing process. The Industrial Court accepted these contentions and dismissed the complaints. The Union thereupon filed two special civil applications in Bombay High Court under article 226 of the Constitution questioning the correctness of the decision of the Industrial Court. Both the applications were dismissed in limine. After hearing the parties, the learned Judge answered the issue in negative and dismissed all the complaints by observing that it was not necessary to call for any fresh decisions pointed out by Mr. M. K. Ramamurthy on the point of lock out and closure since now it is well established that in case of a lock out there is only closure of the place of business where as in case the closure had been brought about malafide and whether it could have been avoided, are matters irrelevant and what is to be seen is whether in fact and in effect there is a closure or not. The High Court also dismissed the appeals filed by the Union. 66 In these appeals by special leave, it was contended for the employers that there was a closure of a industrial undertaking and it was never a case of lockout. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. A lock out has been defined in Section 2(L) of the 1947 Act to mean the closing of a place of his business or the suspension of work or the refusal by an employer to continue to employ any number of persons employed by him. In lockout the employer refuse to continue. to employ the workmen employed by it even though the business activity was not closed down. The impact of closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides of the employer at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter [67 F] 2. It is not necessary that when it is claimed that the employer has resorted to closure bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device or pretence. Therefore, the correct approach ought to be that when a lock Out from the employer refuses to continue, he can cannot do so upon the pain because that the dismissal would be found a device to terminate services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of theemployer.

The assessee company purchased shares of the value of Rs. 1,33,930. During the assessment years 1943 44 to 1948 49, no purchases were made with the exception of a few shares of Loyal Mills Ltd., taken over from the staff of E.D. Sassoon & Co., which ceased to be a stock in the year 1930 and ended 30th June, 1940, and when the assessee company had failed to get the return filed for the assessment year 1943 44, the Central Board of Revenue, by its order dated August 18, 1943, accepted the plea of the assessee Company that it was not a 49 dealer but merely an investor. The Income tax Officer rejected this contention and held in favour of the assesses assessee company and treated it as a dealer in shares, securities and immoveable properties and assessed it on that basis. For these years and for the assessing year 194344 the assessee firm made its return in that basis and so on that ground the Income tax Department accepted the claim of the asses see Company and taxed it on the basis of being an investor but that was upheld by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Central Board, on a reference under section 66(1) of the Act held that the assessee was an Investment Holding Company and accordingly an amended return of total income under section 22( 1 ) of the Indian Income tax Act was submitted on which the assessment for 1943 44 may be based as on this particular question the company obviously could not have one status for Excess Profits Tax and another for Income taX.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge and on June 19, 1950 he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District, and subsequently transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Vellore, West Godavari District. On August 22, 1950, when judgment was still pending, she was in charge of the Sub Court, Amalapuram, such as that he had delayed delivering judgments in the suits and appeals for an unreasonable time, that he made false returns to the District Court and that to cover his defaults he had altered the records of the court so as to be consistent with those returns. On April 28, 1954, the appellant filed in the High Court a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of suspension dated January 28,1954 on the grounds (i) that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal), Rules 1953 which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953, the enquiry into the conduct of Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above could be held only by a Tribunal to which the Government might refer the same; (ii) that on the one hand there was force in the contention of the appellant that having regard to its setting, the proviso should more properly be read as qualifying sub rule (2) but since under the proviso to Rule 4 of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services Rules, enquiries against subordinate judicial officers could not be referred to a Tribunal under Rule 4 (1)(a) and (2), the proceedings in the present case were without jurisdiction and were consequently void. Held also that on a consideration of the material with respect to the charge against the appellant, there was no force in his contention that having view to its taking, the Proviso should be more properly read as qualify sub rule(2). Rule 4 provides that the amendment shall be deemed to have come into force on October 1 and it expressly provided that the amendments shall be retrospective in character.

The respondent a registered holder of 2674 shares of the appellant company, acquired in British India his share certificates with transfer deeds duly executed were delivered to the legatees in respect of those shares and no question arose in this appeal in regard to those shares. The order made by the Income tax Officer under section 23A gave rise to a notional income: it merely created a fiction about distribution and consequential receipt of dividend. The Tribunal held that only 2124 undistributed parts of the assessable income of the company shall be deemed to have been distributed as dividends amongst the shareholders as at 31st March 1949, and since such dividend was deemed to be distributed in respect thereof under section 18(5) included it in the total income of Anderson and levied tax thereon at the appropriate rate. The High Court answered the first question in the negative. It held that when the registered share holder of a company acquires shares with his own name in the company, he does not acquire in all cases the rights of a shareholder of a Company in respect o shares of which the name of the deceased was registered as holder; (2) whether the Act contains machinery for assessing dividends deemed to had been distributed by virtue of an order under section 25A of the Income Tax Act, 1922, and under section 24B for enforcement of liability against the legal representative of a deceased person to pay tax which would have been payable if such person had not died, has a limited application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) even if after the expiry of the year of account receipts which if the person earning had not death would have acquired by the death of the shareholder his executor or administrator may enforce the rights Of the shareholders or incur liability in respect Of the shares to the company: and (ii) that when an order made under section23A was passed by the Incometax Officer pursuant to which the income was to be deemed so distributed, then the legal personality of the dying representative of the estate of the late person must be regarded as extended to the end of the assessment year in which such notional income must be deemed for the purpose of assessing his total income. HELD: (i)(a) The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) is substituted by the Indian Income tax Act, 1939, and it does not warrant the application of two different interpretations in the matter of extension of the legal entity according as the income is actual or notional. [528 C E] (b) There is no special machinery devised by the Act enabling assessment and levy of tax in respectof such deemed income from the estate to the detriment of public revenue. But if the Legislature has failed to set up the procedure to assess such income, the courts cannot supply it. The expression 'assessee ' in section 24A does not contemplate any special machinery for assessment of income receivable by the estate or of the loss sustained by him or of tile amount of refund due to him. [596 G] (c) The Legislature not having made any provision generally for assessment and imposition of tax by the 'Income Tax Officer, the expression "Tribunal" cannot be deemed 'to have supplied the machinery for taxation of income received by a legal representative to the estate after the expiration of the period of the accounting year inwhich such person died. It is then argued that apart from section 24 B, the legal representatives of a registered shareholder also represent his estate in the matters of taxation of Income and it is competent to the taxing authorities to assess them on income received on behalf of the body of the representation alone.

The appellant, a Ruler of the State of Baster, entered into an agreement with the Dominion of India for carrying on the business in estates, mahals alienated and alienated lands. After the passing of the Indian Independence Act 1947, the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion ' of India whereby he ceded the State to the Government of India. The Act was passed by the Legislature of the state of Madhya Pradesh and it received the assent of the President of India on January 22, 1951. Before the High Court the appellant contended that his rights had been recognised and guaranteed under the agreements entered into by him with the Government as required by the second and third paragraphs of the Merger Agreement, the High court was not correct in holding that the appellant was an ex Ruler for the purposes of the Act. Held, that the contention on behalf of the appellant must fail. It is impossible to accept this contention on his behalf that the burden was on the appellant to prove this fact which he never attempted to discharge. Naufidar 's case, (1947) L. R. , referred to. The "maufidar" as defined in article 366(22) of the Constitution of India is "a holder of rent free land, a grantee". It was common ground in the High 978 Court that the villages in question were exempt from payment of rent or tax. In view of the provisions of article 362(1), any dispute arising out of the ' Merger Agreements or the Instrument of united covenant) is beyond the competence of the courts to enquire into.

The respondent who was working in Shillong since the year 1979, approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal questioning the order of his transfer. He submitted that his wife is also employed at Shillong and off ice of the central Government, that his children are studying there and also because his health had suffered a setback some time ago. The respondent approached the Tripura Bench of Central Administrative Tribu nal (Original Application No. 33 of 1991) questioning the said order of transfer. The Tribunal quashed the order on the following reasoning: that the decisions of courts establish that power of transfer is not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued 430 by the Government. An order of Transfer can be interdicted if it is discriminatory. The said principles are applicable to the case of the respondent. Further, 'in matters of considering transfer of an individual officer, the Office Memorandum dated 3.4.1986, educational dislocation of children and health ground, if all present, deserve special consideration not to pass the order '. On a perusal of the judgment, it is clear that the guidelines require the two spouses to be posted at one pi" as far as practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental Authorities should consider this aspect along with the exigencies of administration and enable the two branches to live together at one station if it be possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. [419A B, 431C] Bank Of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta [1992] 1 S.C.C., 307; Bank of India vs Jagir Singh Mehta ; ; Bank of 14rs. ; Bank Of Indus trial Haja vs Jagjit singh Mehta , referred to.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them. A7 was charged under Section 302 read with Sections 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murders. The second charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A5 and A6 armed with sticks, A3 armed with aruval (bill hook) and A4 armed with two axes with sticks (corn rods), attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2, 8, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the Trial Court. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended that keeping in view the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case, the offence committed by the appellants came within the purview of Section 325 read with 34, IP. C. and not under section 302 read a/w Section 34, IPC; that the participation of the appel lant in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of A2 was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence com pany committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 324 I.

The appellant Bank, a nationalised Bank, entered into a Loan Agreement with the respondent bank, a Cooperative Housing Society, for the repayment of its loan and other moneys advanced by it to the firm under cash credit account. The respondent firm was running its business on a monthly basis in Madras, which had two partners namely one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased. The father of the respondent No. 3 and the respondent nos. 4 to 12, mortgaged certain motor vehicles in favour of the bank under cash Credit Account on 28 11 1967 and 17 2 1972 respectively, and it was revealed therein that the appellant Bank had created an equitable mortgage in favour thereof by way of loan from the Bank after its nationalisation. The firm and its partners contended before the Trial Court that section Dorna Choudhury, being a `special Indian law ' which authorised the bank to recover the amount claimed by it on account of the loan together with interest due thereon; and that the respondent Nos. 4 & 12 created equitable mortgage and the appellant bank was bound by the alienations and transfers made in their favour of properties alleged to be under mortgage. The Bank contested the suit contending inter alia that it had created a equitable mortgage, in favour Of the Bank on December 22 1969, in respect of C schedule properties of the plaint, and that even assuming that the expression `special I law ' meant a law enacted by the British Parliament, ,and that the Banking Companies Act was such a law, still the provision of section 4(e) of the Act will not apply insofar as they direct the scaling down of the debt in accordance with the provisions of the Madras Agriculturists Relief Act. The Trial Court decreed the suit against the appellant and its partner and decreed the Bank 's suit instituted by the bank. In appeal the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court, holding that no equitable mortgage was created in favour or of the Bank and, accordingly, dismissed the suit filed by the Bank. It also held that the claim of the respondents, except to the extent of Rs.1,00,418.55 was barred by limitation. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even if assuming that section 4 (e) Of the Act applied in the absence of any such pleading, such a plea could not be entertained at all; and as the High court negatived the contention relying upon a Division Bench decision in Indian Bank, Alamuru vs Krishna Murthy, [1984] 3 Andhra Pradesh 347. Dismissing the appeal, this Court. 967 HELD: 1.1 The words `special ' mean a special Indian law enacted under the Indian , that is to say, a Special Indian law by the Indian Legislature. The expression `Special Indian law" has a clear and unambiguous meaning and there is no need for its interpretation. There is no reason why the expression 'special Indian Law ' should be interpreted in the light of the setting in which the words are placed may be taken into consideration, but that does not mean that even though the words which are to be construed convey a clear meaning still a different interpretation or meaning should be given to them because of the set. [947D E] 1.2 The expression 'Special Indian Law " has a definite and uniform meaning and it is well settled that in construing the words of the provision, the setting of the words may sometimes be necessary for the interpretation of the specified words of statute but that has not been ruled by this Court to be the only and the surest method of interpreting.

Section 3 of the Sugar (Control) Order, 1955 empowered the Central Government to pass orders under the Act in respect of any essential commodity or for securing their equitable distribution and availability at fair prices. No legislation was therefore placed before the Parliament by which the impugned notification fixed ex factory prices and provided inter alia for controlling the prices of sugar. The Central Government promulgated the Sugar Export Promotion Ordinance, 1958, as follows : " By section 3 of this Act power is given to the Central government to fix the retail price, i.e., the price or minimum price fixed for sugarcane, (ii) manufacturing cost, and taxes, (iii) reasonable margin of profit for producer and/or trade, and (iv) any incidental charges". The petitioners challenged before the High Court the validity of this notification on various grounds and contended that (1) the impugned order was not beyond the authority conferred on the CentralGovernment under section 3 Of the , it was discriminatory because it fixed exfactory prices only for factories in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar and not for factories within other parts of India. Held: The object of the Act is to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in essential commodities in the interests of the general public so that the Central Govt. must give consideration to the relevant factors mentioned therein before fixing the price; (2) the Act and the Order so far as they are concerned with the fixation of price are valid and not beyond its authority and must therefore be struck down as invalid on the ground that it had merely fixed ex factories prices at all stages, the Act requires that prices for the consumer only should be fixed. The Act and section 3(2) (c) of the , are different from those in other parts.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956, transferred the dispute between the parties to the Second Industrial Tribunal under section 10 Of the , with effect from July 1, 1957. However, on April 9, 1956 the Government made an order transferring the said dispute from the file of the Second industrial Tribunal to that of the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. The Fifth IndustrialTribunal after making the necessary inquiry, made the award on August 26,1957 and it was duly notified in the Calcutta Gazette on September 29, 1957, and as a mistake had crept in. the award was modified by the Tribunal by its Order dated September 29 1951, an amended award was published in the High Court on September 26. The Company preferred an appeal against that order to the Labour Appellate Tribunal and a review petition also failed. But the Tribunal again fixed the basic wages and the rate of dearness allowance payable to the employees. The High Court allowed the Company 's appeal by special leave and set aside the award giving rise to 25 per cent increase on the basis of the rise in cost of living index, as provided under section 19(6) of the Act. In appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union that (1) the award dated June 21, 1951, was not terminated in accordance with law; and (2) the previous award made by the Labour Tribunal between the same parties on April 26, 1951 and confirmed by the Industrial Appellate Tribunal by the order dated August 30, 1951 had not been terminated in compliance with the provisions of section 19 (6), for making out a new award. HELD: The question is what did the parties intend to agree by the aforesaid clause in the agreement. [144 B] Pritam Singh vs The State of Madras, ; , and New India Assurance Co. Ltd. vs Their Workmen, [1960]1 S.C.R. 324, followed. Section 19(7) which says that "The appropriate Government may, by notified order, transfer the proceeding pending before a tribunal constituted under the . , as in force on such commencement, as if this Act had not already been passed". The amended definition is a provision giving power for the first time to transfer a proceeding pending in a tribunal to another Tribunal. or in the case of a proceeding under section 33 or 33A pending before any tribunal to a Labour Court. There is no reason why the agreement should prevail unless there is a substantial change in the working class cost of live index in the year 1957 and that circumstance cannot have any bearing on the impact of the amendment of the definition of " ' Tribunal ' in section 33B of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1948. [145 F H] Pritam singh vs State of Punjab, ; explained. The replacing these words does not in terms impair what is an arbitration award and has to be interpreted along with the definition as a whole. Section 30 of the Amending Act, expressly saves a pending proceeding before a Tribunal constituted under section 7A of the , before it came into force, otherwise than by any other statute. Section 31(5)(b) of which says " Notwithstanding the expiry of the period of operation under sub section (3), the award shall continue to be binding on the parties until a period of two months has elapsed from the date on which notice is given by any party bound by the award to the other party or parties intimating its intention to terminate the award". [145 A C] In regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date of the agreement is the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change. The appellant, a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism, was established under the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act XIX of 1951 which prescribed the proper administration of the Mutt. Under section 103(d) of the , after consultation with the Mathad Govindaraja Rajendraswami Temple, the Board stood dissolved and its endowments were to be settled and so, it provided that any scheme settled or modified by a Court under the earlier Act shall be deemed to have been settled or modification under any other law in force under this Act and shall have effect accordingly. The Executive Officer, after consulting the Matad withdral of the Math, filed a suit challenging the legality of the scheme on the ground that they contravened the appellant 's fundamental rights guaranteed by article 1 9(1)(f) of India. It was contended inter alia on his behalf that the principles of natural justice were not violated in any way and that he had the right to object the scheme, because, as such, no effective steps could be taken to implement the scheme and its properties, under the scheme. Held: (i) that section 103 (d) clearly brings out the fact that where the legislature wanted the con stitution of the action taken under the provisions of the earlier Acts only if the said action was consistent with the relevant pro visions of the latter Act, it had so provided. The fact that the order was not implemented did not make any difference to this legal position. (ii)The scheme contemplated an examination of the schemes before they were allowed to be continued in the interest of proper administration and was in accordance with the provisions under section 62(3 )(a).

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha M.E. school (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools), on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. Even after this period, he remained absent from duty for a certain period of time during all these years. The appellant filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 121982. The only argument raised before the High Court was that the appellant was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989 (hereinafter called 'the Act 'the validation Act '). The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appel lant was not entitled to the benefit of the validation Act on the aforesaid reasoning. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 There are neither enough schools nor teachers to teach. Insecurity is writ large on the face of the teaching community because of nebulous and unsatisfactory conditions of service. [994C] 1.2 The High Courts erred in denying the benefit to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. The validation Act covers the field upto December 31, 1984. The State of Orissa will do well to consider the cases of all those who have completed one year or more as ad hoc teachers after December 31.1984 and come out with a scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise their services.[994D E] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana ; followed.

The appellant, who was a member of the Punjab State Legislature and whose Chairman. who was elected as a Sarpanch, assailed the election of the respondent on the ground that he had been disqualified from being chosen as a member despite the fact that he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The High Court dismissed the petition but did not express any opinion on the third question relating to the validity of the Ordinance and passing an order dismissing the petition with costs. Hence this appeal: Allowing the appeal, HELD : (1) In construing a statute the intention is clear that the Legislature has intended that the benefit conferred by the statute should be given to the legislature. The Act was enacted for furtherance of the welfare of the State. [437 B C] (2) The fact that the right to receive it accrues only when the journey is outside the district is made manifest by laying down that the receipt of this daily allowance is to be subject to the provisions of r. 3. 'Me allowances are also meant to ensure that he does not have to incur expenditure from his own pocket for the purpose of discharging his duties. [427 C] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, A.I.R. 1954 SC. 653 at p. 656 applied. (3) The payment made is not salary and remuneration but is a part of what the person concerned would have to incurred for the expression ' profit ' in order to discharge his official duties. There are, however, certain limitations, such as that no travelling allowance was to be drawn by a Member if the journey was performed for attending a meeting held within a radius of five miles from his place of residence or he performed journey in a transport provided at the expense of the Zila Parishads/Panchayat Samiti or any other local authority or Government. There were also limitations on the right of each other.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appel lant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. On a suit for eviction the appellant filed. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later, they filed a suit claiming that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. It was not necessary to refer to other grounds as the sole ground which survived for the decree of eviction relates to the material alterations made in the tenanted premises without obtaining the permission of the landlord. The disputed construc tions include a partition wall in a hail converted the same into two portions and tin sheds shown by letters ABHG and CDGH. The trial Court held that the partition wall constituted 'material alteration ' and it further held that since the constructions had been made with out permission of t he respondent, the tenant was liable for eviction. It also held that there was no dispute that the demised premises is sub ject to the provisions of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act 10 of 1952. On second appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the appell lant 's order and dismissed the respondents suit on the findings that none of the construc tion constituted material alteration justifying eviction under sec. 14(c). The High Court also found that the tin shed had been constructed by the appellant without obtaining permission of P.W. No. 9, which materially altered the accommodation and on that finding allowed the appeal filed by the respond ents holding that the entire building constituted ' material alteration. Hence the appeL lant has preferred this appeal after obtaining Special Leave. Dismissing the Appeal, the Court HELD: 1. A permanent construction tends to make changes in the accommodation on a permanent basis, while a temporary construction is on temporary basis which does not ordinarily affects the form or structure of the building, as it can easily be removed without causing any damage to the building. [873C] 2. The Legislature intended that only those constructions which bring about substantial change in the front and structure of tho building should provide a ground for tenant 's eviction, it took care to use the word 'materially altered the accommo dation. The material alterations contemplate change of substantial nature affecting the form and character of the build ings.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree on account of non delivery of certain goods. Summons in the suit was sent to the registered office of the Company in Calcutta and was said to have been served on one Shri Navlakha on 17 3 1975 asking the company to appear at Indore on 25 3 1975 for settlement of issues. Since the company did not appear in the Court on that date, eventually 1030 the ex parte proceedings were passed by the trial court on 22 4 1975. According to the case of the appellant the company came to know about the exter parte decree for the first time when its constituted attorney Shri Section K Jhunjhunwala received a notice from the respondent by registered post demanding the decretal dues. Thereupon the company remained in dark and, as stated above, learnt for the second time on 29 7 1975 about the passing of the exparte decree. N. section Pareek was the only witness examined on behalf of the respondent. The Trial Court held: (1) that handing over of summons to Navlakh who was only an Office Assistant working in the Company and who was not an officer duly authorised to accept summons on behalf for the company, did not amount to valid service of summons on the applicant company; (2) that the summons could be left anywhere uncared for in the registered offices of the company. The High Court allowed the revision set aside the judgment of the trial Court and upheld the passing passed ex parte decrees. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, it was, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by the Trial Court setting aside the decree was correct. [1031E] 2.1 The judgment by the High Court setting down the decree has been correct. In any event no error of jurisdiction was committed by it. [ 1031F] 2(a) Rule 17 of Order 5 of C.P.C. is headed "Suits by or against Corporations". There are only three Rules in it. The first part of clause (b) has got to be understood with reference to the other provisions of the Code, and in other words, if the serving peon or bailiff is not able to serve the summons on a Secretary or any Director or any other Principal Officer of the Corporation because either he refuses to sign the summons or is not to be found by the serving person even after due diligence then he can leave the summons at the registered Office of the corporation and make a report to that effect. [931A C] 2.(b) The meaning of clause(b) had got to he understood in the background of the provisions of Code in order 5 which is meant for issue and service of notice on natural persons. [1000E] 3.2 Rule 17, C. P.C., confers a valuable right upon the defendant to defend his case against ex parte suit. It has agreed to continue the same till the disposal of the suit. This Court cannot add an error of law entitling the High court to interfere with it. Order 29 of the C.p. is in the form of Order 1 which deals with only modes of service on the defendant in the sense as to what is meant by service of summon on the Secretary, Director or Principal Officer in Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd., and another vs The Union of India and others ; , referred to. In view of the plain language of clause 3(a), it has got scope for re consideration. [1002C F] 4.3 It is not necessary that the plaintiff must prove affirmatively that the defendant had knowledge or could have intimated the receipt of summons so called bosses. Without prejudice it is submitted that the Madhya Pradesh amendment in Order 9 Rule 13 C.A.P., may kindly be perused.

A preliminary order was passed by the Magistrate, recording a finding that there was an apprehension of breach of the peace in which he had already taken part under section 145(5) Cr. P.C., and that it was not necessary for him to repeat what he had said in the preliminary order in the final order also. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code for quashing the order of the Magistrate on the ground that there were no clear findings by the magistrate in the Final order that there had been an apprehension that breach existed even in thefinal order. The question was whether the final orders were vitiated as contemplated under section145(5). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Under section 145 it is for the Magistrate to be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach of a peace and once he records his satisfaction in the main order, he can continue the proceedings. Once that was done the magistrate is thereafter expected to call upon the parties concerned in such dispute to attend their court in person or by pleader and put in written statements of their respective claims as respects the fact of actual possession of the subject of dispute. [92D E] (2) A finding of existence of breach does not bring the case within the ambit of sub section (5) of section 145 nor is such a case set up by any party before the Magistrate or before the High court. [96C, 96A B] R. H. Bhutani vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , referred to. In the instant case, there was no question of the dispute having ended so as to lead to cancellation of the order under sub section(5)(6) of s 145 nor was such a ease set up in by any of them before the magistrate or before High Court. [97A] R D. H, Bhutliani vs State of Bombay & Ors, ; , applied. Hari Ram and Ors. vs Banwari Lai Lal & Others., ; followed.

Held, that sections 42(1) and 42(3) applied only to nonresidents but not to non resident doctors. Such a determination was open to review by the court only on the ground that it was not supported by any evidence or perverse. The finding of the Commissioner was final as required by section 66(1). Although there is no provision in the Act which lays down how the profits are to be disposed of, such as distribution of dividends or adding to the reserve and until that was done there was no accrual of income or of profits under the statute. Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai & Co., (1960) 60 section C R. 215, relied on. In the present case the question whether a particular amount is liable to tax is one of fact and not of law according as the point for determination in the present proceedings was one of pure fact or mixed question of law and fact, and that the finding of fact given by the Tribunal in favour of the assessee was binding upon the tribunal to which the case is referred unless it appears from the previous findings that there are facts which support it. Commissioner Of Income tax Bombay vs Ahmadbhai Umarabhai Umarbhai and Co., , and Commissioner of Incometax vs Ahmed Ahmedabadbhai Umarubhai and Co. ([1964] 60 section Rep.C.R. 288) distinguished.

The appellant carried on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to General Manager and the Income tax Officer determined a sum of Rs, 5,000 as a reasonable amount payable as commission. The first Appellate Tribunal upheld the view of the Income Tax Officer and took the view that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after his death, the General Manager.Tiffs post carried a remuneration of Rs 18,000 plus Rs. 6,000 per annum as remuneration and Rs. six,000 for its accounting year 1947 48. The second Appellate Tribunal in appeal held that the rate of commission paid by the assessee was not fixed on account of business considerations but there was some collateral reason. But considering the practice in similar business concerns, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner expressed the view, that the rates of commission payable to Shri Vaish were not fixed and therefore the commission paid, increased from Rs. 5,00,000 and also awarded a reasonable sum payable as compensation. In appeal before this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the circumstances of this case the amount claimed by the assesseee was an amount laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of business of the assessee within the meaning of section 10(2)(xv) of the Incometax Act, 1922. HELD: (i) The question must be answered in the manner indicated and this appeal is accordingly allowed with costs.

The appellant was a workman in a factory. On January 13, 1954, the management served him with a charge sheet alleging that he had been doing anti union activities inside the factory during the working hours and so was guilty under section 12B(1) of the Standing Orders and Rules of the company. Thereupon he filed a petition before the High Court praying for an issue of appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order of February 26, 1957, by which the Tribunal had rejected his prayer for representation by a person of his own choice in place of Fateh Singh. The High Court dismissed the application summarily. On appeal to this court it was contended that the order passed by the High court was without jurisdiction because the respondent could not take up his cause. Held: An individual workman is at no stage a party to the industrial dispute independently of the Union. A dispute between an employer and a single employee cannot be an industrial dispute but it may become one if it is taken up by an union or a number of workmen. In the present case there were no such exceptional circumstances which justify the Tribunal to permit other representation of the workman concerned. The respondent could have also urged that the petition was collusive and mala fide.

Under section 240(3) of the Indian Penal Code, he may dismiss or remove from service any person who has been informed of charges against him any penalty which is proposed to be taken in regard to him. But under clause (2) of article 311, the Governor must be satisfied that, in the interest of the security of the State, it was not expedient to give him a reasonable opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to he taken in respect to him in regard, to him, unless the order is passed by him. The satisfaction recorded by the Governor under sub clause (c) of cl. (3) on the basis of materials before him that the Governor had stated that it was expedient to do so, was not a sine qua non for making any such representation. In matters where the Governor himself passes an original order imposing the penalty of dismissal on a public servant, the procedure laid down in sub clause 5 of article 320(3)(c) is that if the President or the Governor, as the case may be, is satisfied that in the interests of the public it was necessary to give that person an opportunity. The first step is to direct that an enquiry be held against him and the second is that, if it is proposed (i) for imposing on him any such penalty; (ii) where the President and the Governor as the ease may be are satisfied that he had not been guilty of any misconduct to merit any punishment at all and also that the particular punishment proposed to to be given was much more drastic than he deserves. The second step is that in a enquiry, the person has to be informed of the charges against it and given such an opportunity as he can only do if he is told what the charges levelled against him are and the allegations on which such charges are based .(c) an opportunity to defend himself by cross examining the witnesses produced against him. Sub clause (d), which deals with cases where the consultation has not been dispensed with, nor does it affect the power of the Governor to pass an order of dismissal without holding an inquiry, without informing the Government servant of the charge against him, and without giving him a opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges, and provided for an opportunity of making a representation against the penalty proposed. It further provides that the consultation with the Public Service Commission in cases where a Governor himself pass an original orders imposing the penalties of dismissal, removal or reduction in rank, any one of them can lay down such procedure as it deems fit. The proviso to clause (3)(C) of section 320 was in effectuating the words "it is not expedient t to give the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity for showing cause by cross examine the witnesses examined against him by a court of law, vide Khem Chand vs The Union of India and Others [1969] Vol. VI Assam Law Reports 192; Khemchand vs The State of U.P. ; and Khem Chand V.
