The respondent company disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10,200 but claimed set off of capital loss incurred by it during the assessment year 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. It was maintained by the assessee that the loss was sustained in the previous year rele vant to the assessment years 1957 58 and the same should be set off against the capital gains in the assessment order in question. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the asses see 's assessment year 1947 58, the loss had been claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal by holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim of set off to be admissible had to be notified by the Income tax Officer u/s 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. This view having not been done, the appellant approached this Court for relief by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. Section 80 of the 1961 Act cannot apply to a case where in law a return could not have been filed under section 139 because in that year this Section was not on the Statute Book. But if section 80 is construed to mean that a return filed u/ s 139 is also within its purview then in our opinion, the requirement of this section was equally fulled because the assessee has for his as sessment year 1957 filed a return of loss which loss had not been determined as required under section 24(2) of Income tax Act, 1922. [1164A B] 2.1 A bare reading of the provisions of Section 74(1)(b} and section 80 together shows that it is con tended that a Return filed under Section 139 is within its province then in my opinion the requirement, of this Section is equally applicable because the assesee has for the as sorsment year to 1957 58 filed a ' return of Loss which loss has been determined by the income tax Officer in the assess ment order. When the assessee had made the claim and he took note of it, his failure to comply strictly with the requirement contained in sub section (3) should not be permitted to be taken advantage of by the Revenue nor should it be used to the prejudice of the assessee.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted at the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DSS & P). On the basis of an Office Memorandum dated April 24,1985, the Central Government issued instructions to all the three Defence Science Services Rule, which had been quoted above, namely, "Other conditions of service: (i) The conditions of serv ers belonging to the three units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were identical and those applicable would also retire at the age of 60 years provided they had been promoted to the grades they were holding at the time of attaining the age Of 58 years within the preced ing five years. Later, by another Office Memorandum No. 7(3)85 D(R & D) dated 10.2.86, the said decision was extended to all 23 Scientific and technical personnel of the DRDO i.e.,DRDS as listed in the Appendix 'A of that Memo. By virtue of Rule 12 quoted above; this benefit given to the members of the JTS was also available to the Members of DAQAS, since the said condition of service was not expressly provided for in the Service Rules. The Tribunal held that though respondent belonged to another unit viz. DAQ, he was entitled to the said benefit and held that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the said age of 58 years his superannuation being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with Rule 12 of the Rules in DAQ Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution.

In a meeting of the Muslim workers held on 29 4 1967 at the Madina Masjid Hall under the presidentship of M. Shaikh it was resolved unanimously that in the place of Shaikh Usman Abdul Bidiwale the Congress ticket should be given to Umar Shaikh, who had the backing of Muslim community and that he did great public service in the past. The appellant made an application before the Judge for issuing summons on these two persons as his witnesses but the Judge rejected this application because the appellant had not been examined during the course of the evidence led by him. The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine holding that there was no evidence to show that the charge against the appellant could be found guilty and the order of dismissal having been made on the basis of the oral and documentary evidence led in the case it became quite clear that the two persons who were called as court witnesses were fully conversant with the engagement of motor vehicles and the Court therefore examined them as court witness and, on the ground that there had been no material to come to the conclusion that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practice. In appeal by special leave: HELD : (1) The trial judge had jurisdiction to call these two respondents as witnesses under the provisions of the Act. [976 B] (2) If the two candidates have not been produced and when the trial Judge accepted the evidence with regard to the distribution of pamphlet by the appellant, the High Court may well have decided the issue in the first instance. But the Act certainly gave him the power to do so and no exception can be taken to the course adopted by the Judge although it must be recorded that his earlier order refusing to issue summonses to them in the second instance when asked to do it on the 21st August was hardly justifiable. [946 E F] R. In this case, if the two people had not not been examine, the Judge might well have ruled the issue and found out why there were two Gazette Publications and which was the publication to be taken into account for computation of the period of limitation prescribed by section 21(1) of the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965 it would have been very difficult.

The U. P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, was passed by the State Legislature validating certain sales effected between April 1, 1956 and July 31, 1956, but it provided that on a true construction of sections 3 A and 4, the whole of sub section (2) of section 3 A as it then stood was deleted and the following substituted: " This Act shall be deemed to have effect on and from the first day of April. New Section 3 A was inserted in U.P. Sales tax Act, 1910, with effect from March 31, 1957, and came into force on May 28, 1956. The appellant contended that there were subsequent amendments to it in 1948, but they were not material for the present discussion. Held, that the validity of the Validation Act, was valid as it operated retrospectively, and the validation Act was not ultra vires the powers of the State legislature under Entry 54 or List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. Consequently, the law passed by respondent No. 1 in U P., a tax on agreement to sell was not validly authorised by the entry, and in consequence the said notification stood validated by it. Held further that the Validation acts were intra vires articles 31(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution as the impugned notification did not contravene article 14 or r. 23 of the U. Pradesh Sales Tax Rules. The contention of the appellant in support of his contention was that the validation Acts were ultra vires on the ground that it operates retrospectively, as a result of a notification under section 3A on March 31. 1956 and after. an amendment in 1957, they continued to be null and void and that, therefore, the validity Act must be held to be within the saving of the validation. The fact that the Act had introduced a new rule for realising the tax which became payable did not affect the competence of the legislature under entry 54 of List II in the Seventh schedule, and an amendment made by Act 43 of 1957 was validated by fresh legislation on December 30, 1958.

The appellant who was a 'habitual ' and had no vicious antecedents except this fugitive, barbaric kirana. The screaming victim complained to her mother working in the field; thereafter a first information, prosecution and conviction ensued, a sentence of 4 years R.I. was imposed by the Sessions Court and the High Court affirmed it in appeal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. An offence is not brutal but fulfill with violence, the offender is in his early twenties and signs of repentance are seen. The victim and her parents have forgiven the molester who is a first cousin, says Counsel. An affidavit from the father in law of the woman has been filed and, if needed, counsel is ready to produce the victim 's statement that she has forgiven tho criminal. While it is possible that the accused may procure such condonation from unwilling victim, the fact remains that the two families being close cousins are ready to take a lenient view of the situation. [592E F] Sunil Batra vs Delhi Administration, ; ; Sunil Batra V. Batra 's case and later followed. [593F G] 2. The special circumstances of this case defected to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. The task is not done by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method, in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits Of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a new form leaf. The unconvicted deviants in society are demoralisingly large and the State has, as yet, no convincing national policy on female flesh and sex sanity.

The respondent, a limited company dealing in land, owned its accounts on the mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with Section 19 of the Act certain plots of land belonging about 19.17 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the assessee were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5, Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952. The respondent claimed that the amount of compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was therefore a trading receipt of business carried on by the company. The Income tax Officer, treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the respondent on the date of the award and not when the land remained taken over by the government. In second appeal the Appellate Tribunal accepted the contention and held that the compensation received to the assesee related to acquisition of lands which was a stock in the trade of assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipts of the business carried out by the Company. The High Court allowed the Tax Revision Application filed by the Revenue. Hence this appeal by certificate granted by the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 On the date when the Collector awarded the compensation, it is only that amount which had accrued or deemed to accrue, whether in fact paid or not. But by no stretch of the words in section 4(1)(b)(i), could it be said that the right to enhanced compensation which has not yet been accepted by the proper forum, namely, the court, has become payable on the dates when the original compensation became payable, for being included in that year of assessment. The enhanced compensation accrues only when it becomes payable i.e., when the Court accepts the claim. As has been stated earlier, a mere claim by the appellant, after taking of possession of the land, at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation. [396 B C] Naresh Narain Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd. and others vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, followed. [397 E F] 1.2 In the present case though the award was made by the Arbitrator on July 29, 1955 enhancing the amount payable to the appellant assessee, the entire amount was in dispute in the appeal filed by it Government. Indeed, the dispute was regarded by the Court as real and substantial, because the assessee was not permitted to withdraw the sum of Rs.7,36,691 deposited by the State Govt on April 25, 1956 without furnishing a security bond for refunding the amount in 394 the event of the appeal being allowed.] [397 F] Kedarnath Jute Mex Co. Limited vs Commissionerof Income Tax Gujarat,Poddar & Anr., [1962] 1 SCR 676; Topandas Kundanmal (supra) were relied on by this Court in Additional Commissioner of Incometax, Gujarat vs New Jehangir Vakil Mills Co.

On the failure of the appellants to do so in accordance with the terms of the compromise decree, the respondents were tried for eviction and other reliefs. The trial court accepted the respondents ' contention that the compromise was void being non est and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. The Additional District Judge rejected the appellants ' objection on the ground that the suit which was filed in 1966 proceeded to trial in October 1967 and some evidence was adduced. But eventually, the parties entered into a compromise whereunder one of them had withdrawn all his defence to the application filed by the landlord and submitted to a decree for eviction unconditionally. The appellants objected to the execution on the grounds that the dispute was an admission in respect of only the first part, namely, the positive aspect of clause (f) and not of the second part, viz., that the landlord had no other reasonably suitable nonresidential accommodation. The respondents contended that paragraph 1 of the agreement was an admitted admission in a respect of both the second and the negative aspects of clause(f). Both were denied in para 3 of the written statement of the appellant. Paragraph 2 of the compromised petition says: "That due to necessity of the plaintiffs for their own business opening grocery shop, decree for ejectment may be granted to them against the defendants." In the appeal the appellants contended that paragraphs 1 and 2 of compromise petition indicated that the parties shall vacate the shop in dispute by 31 12 1970. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that paragraph I of the plaint was an admissions in respect only the second, namely the positive aspects of cl.(f) of section 12(1). The order so recorded in the present case was in full compliance with the requirement of Order 23, Rule 3 of Code of Civil Procedure. [864 A] In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordancewith the provisions Of the Act.[864 C E F] The provision relating to the filing of the suit only. No suit can be filed for eviction of a tenant except on one or more of the grounds enumerated in section 12 (11). It is too late in the day to contend that the provisions in Order 23 Rule 3, Rules 3 of Civil Code could not apply to eviction suits governed by the special statutes. [874 D G] The suit was contested the issue went to trial.

The assessee is a limited company doing business as selling agents of a Textile Mill. For the assessment year 1955 56 the assessee was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 69,973/ leaving a distributable balance of Rs 49,116/ . In appeal, the Asstt. Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss and he cancelled the orders of the Income Tax Officer under section 23A (1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner took an erroneous view of the scope of s.23 A(2) of the Act. On appeal by the department, the Tribunal agreed with the conclusions reached by the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner. On a reference made to it, the High Court answered that question in favour of the assessee. Allowing the appeals by certificate, HELD: 1.1 The expression "property" is used not only to denote only losses previously incurred by and to the smallness of the profits made. No answer which can be said to be in any measure adequate can be given to the question "unreasonableness" considering these two matters only. Their Lordships are of the opinion that the Statute by the words used while making sure that "losses and smallness do not never lost sight of require all matters relevant to the quage of unreasonableness to be considered capital loss, if established is one of them. [85 D G] Commissioner of Income tax West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee & Co., , relied on. The question is whether the Directors of a company had reasonable grounds for not declaring any dividend. [86 E F] Commissioner Of Income Tax, West Bengal, vs Gangadhar, , distinguished.

The appellants filed objections before the Civil Judge on September 8, 1956, modifying the award and in modification of the award ordered by the District Judge. The District Judge modified the award only to the extent that it allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Civil Court modifying the rate of compensation payable to the appellants. On appeal by special leave the appellants urged that section 37 of the Act applies only as far as procedure is concerned, and section 39 of the provides for appeals does not apply because the appellant had apparently applied under section 15 of the to the Court to modify the award made by a person and they had succeeded in getting an order modified. HELD: (i) The effect of section 37 must be inter distinguished from that applicable to villages not under consolidation, and there is thus discrimination which offends article 14 of the Constitution. [68 C] Attar Singh vs The State of U.P. and Attar singh vs The Union of India, ; , relied on. (ii) The consequence of section 46 and section 47 was that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holdings Act. [69 F] Shri Attar Sing Singh vs State of Uttar Pradesh, ; followed. (iii) Apart from the question of appointment of an arbitrator in all other respects, the matter referred to, i.e., the question whether section 39 applies to arbitration proceedings under the U. P. Consolidation of Holding Rules, 1954, but that does not mean that it makes the applicable to proceedings before the Arbitrator in the matter of procedure only. The effect Of section 46 is that all sections of the .except sub section(1) Of section 6 which apply to an arbitration proceeding under the Act shall be determined in accordance with the provisions Of the .

The respondent Corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. The petitioner who was junior to respondent NO. 2 would have been promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer on 31st October, 1990. However, since respondent No.2 was a degree holder, he got the said resolution and was promoted to that post on that date, i.e., 31st December, 1990, and therefore, since Respondent No. 2 was a Degree holder, who got the same resolution and been promoted in that year, he would have be promoted to Respondent NO.2. The promotion which was challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court was dismissed. Allowing the Writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. For the purpose of promotion, a valid classification can be made among the members holding the same post on the basis of their qualification. In State of Jummu & Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors., ; , a Constitution Bench of his court has clearly held that such a classification is permissible and does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [718G] 2. The Court, while dealing with the relief claimed, do support the petitioner: " Prayer No. 4 is to declare the petitioner Graduate Engineers as a separate category amongst Junior Engineers and give them equal quota like Diploma holder Junior Engineer`s out of 50% quota for promotion a Assistant Engineers. This cannot be done except by carving out two classes in the same category of junior Engineers othe basis merely of their qualifications which is not permissible in law though the creation of selection grade in the different categories on the date of merit and on seniority is well known and permissible. The proposition that in the absence of rule or regulation, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [Emphasis supplied].

These applications filed under Article 32 of the Constitution, seeking a direction to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme Court and the various High Courts of the country and ancil lary orders of directions in regard to the same. The main prayer in this application was for directing the Union Government to fill the vacancies in the Bombay High Court and several High Courts. In reply, the Union contended that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancies should be in violation of Article 124(1) of the Arti cle Constitution as also under Article 14 or Article 16 of the Constitu tion. The Advocate General withdrew the objection regarding this Court 's jurisdiction and made a statement that he was of the view that it was the constitutional obligation of the Union to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the superior courts and the default, if any, was a matter exclusively within the domain of the constitutional schemeand concern of the concerned constitutional functionaries. These petitions were clubbed together and heard from time to time, following the concession made by the Attorney General. The Court recorded its reasons for holding that it had proceeded on the basis that there had been a change in the personnel of the Chief Justice of India or the Chief Minister of the State concerned, and that the provision of Article 14 was not applicable to private parties, including the petitioners, who had raised their grievance before this Court. The petitioners contended that (i) for Sikkim has adequate judge strength; (ii) the petitions are dismissed as being not maintainable; (iii) even if there is difference of opinion amongst the constitutional functionaries required to be consulted, the opinion of the Division Bench in S.P. Gupta 's case did not recognise the special and pivotal position of the institution of the learned Chief Jus tice of India; (iv) the Court 'tou is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government; (v) the power to appoint solely vests with the executive and that, the executive after bestowing such consideration on the result of consultations with the judicial organ of the state, would be at liberty to take such decision as it may think fit in the matter of appointments, is an over simplification of a sensitive and subtle constitutional sentence and, if allowed foul play, would he subversive of the doctrine. Allowing these applications, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The principle which the three Judges shared, in Gupa 's Case, does not recognise that the Special and pivotal provi sions of theRecommendations finalised by the Chief Judge of India unless for any particular reason and unconnected with the mere change of the chief Justice or the cabinet justifying the same should not be reopened and if in a given case the Union is of the opinion that the matter requires to be looked into again a reference should be made, to the Chief sesy of the High Court. [462C D] 1.2.

The respondent Bank brought a departmental enquiry against the respondent Bank by a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978, which was followed by a departmental inquiry. The Enquiry Officer conducted the departmental enquiry and submitted his report on January 14, 1980, but during the pendency of the departmental proceedings he retired from service on January 31, 1979. Not withstanding the retirement he continued to function as an Enquiry Officer and concluded the enquiry against him by the end of 1979. He then gave an opportunity to the respondent to be heard on the question of punishment and thereafter passed the impugned order discharging him on January 19, 1980. The respondent filed a writ petition in this Court against the aforesaid order of discharge in the High Court. A Single Judge of the High COurt held that the de facto doctrine could have no application because of absence of mala fides, prejudice or mala fides; since the said order was without jurisdiction and void, therefore null and void. The Division Bench directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned orders were bad in law. Hence this appeal by special leave. During the pendency and till the disposal of the Departmental Relieving Envi sion proceedings he ap pointed an Enquiry Offi cer was retired from serv ice on January 30, 1979, but the respondent was served with a Memo dated August 1, 1978 by the Divisional Office of the Bank calling for his expla nation. The said Enquiry Officer submitted his Report on January 3, 1979 and apprais ing the report as given by him to be called "Pursuant to the powers vested in the Executive Director by the Chairman & Managing Director". In the meanwhile, the respondent filed an appeal before the Division Bench against the order of dismissal in a writ Petition No. 18140/80, which came to be dismissed by a single member on his view that the departmental inquiry held against the respond ent Bank was incompetent and without jurisdiction since the impugned Order of discharge got merged in the appellate order, the initial defect, if any, stood removed, was repelled by the learned Judge. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the order passed by the Single member bench, this Court HELD: 1.1 A non official cannot act as a matter of mere partici pation but is merely a bank employee, for that matter an ex employee. [200G; 200A] 1.2 The doctrine of acts of officers de jure performed within the sphere of their assumed official authority, in the interest of the public or third parties and not for their own interest are generally held valid and binding as if they were performed by a de facto Officer. This doctrine has two requisites namely (i) the possession of the office and the performance of the duties attached thereto, and (ii) colour of title, that is, apparent right to the office, and acquiescence in the posses sion thereof by the public. [201G; 202A] 2.1 The respondent did not attribute any bias or mala fide to the Enquiry Officer nor did he com plain that he was in any manner prejudiced on account of the said Enquiry Envi dence Officer conducting him domestic enquiry but that will not cure the defect as to his compensat ence.

Certain buildings were being constructed as per the Master Plan prepared by the Authority for Delhi which has statutory force, had come into operation under the Development Act. Under section 342(2)(a) of the Corporation Act the Commissioner is entitled to refuse sanction of a building or work if the building or works or use of the site for building or for work would contravene any of the provisions of that sub section. The respondent who was the owner of the building applied for execution of a work and filed an affidavit stating that a Zonal Development Plan had not been prepared for the area in question, but simultaneously informed the appellant that their application for execution had been refused on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW. The Commissioner rejected this contention and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The Master Plan is a Master plan and is prepared by him under section 8 of the Development act. Under sections 10, 11, 12 and 14 "the Authority shall, while submitting the Master plan, proceed with the preparation of the Master plans or as soon as may be thereafter, , accordwith the procedure" mentioned therein. In order to sustain the validity of the assessment on both sides it is certainly not the scheme of the Act that the moment a Master Plan has come into force and if it contains a proposal regarding the width that a road should have, all use of land adjoining that road is prohibited for an indefinite period. The reasonable interpretation to be placed on section 14 will be that if any particular and definite use of such land is indicated in a Masterplan, a different use of that land cannot be permitted. Similarly, if a Zonal development Plan provides for a certain user of any land or building otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Development plan, then section 14 would quite naturally stand attracted, because any user of a land orbuilding otherwise than as in conformity With the Zonal development plan will be hit by that section. [171 E F G] In order that to sustain validity of a order of rejection passed by the Commissioner the appellant has to establish, as it seeks to, that the proposed building or the use of it for building by the respondents would contravene the provisions contained in any other law '. If the proposed build or use is indicated elsewhere in a master plan, section 14 may not have applied whatsoever. [172 H] The Master plan drawn up by the appellant shows the approximate location and extents. of land uses proposed in a zone for roads; further, under sub cl. (d) of section 8 the said Zonal Development Plans will also contain provision regarding the allotment or reservation of land for roads. If such an indication is made available by the Zonal Building Plan then section 15 will not be attracted. [173 D E] The development Act is an Act to provide for the development of Delhi according to plan and for matters ancillary thereto. Section 1 A provides for the Authority and the Central Government making modifications in the Master DeLhi as well as the Zonal Planning Plan. Section 17(1) provides that after the commencement of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Amendment) Act, 1964 no development of land shall be undertaken or carried out in any area by any person or body including a department of Government) except in the manner provided therein. After coming into operation of any of these plans in a Zone no person shall use or permit to be used any land without the previous sanction of the Commissioner under section 33(2) or section 340. The permission accorded by the authority is intended to have a width of 60 feet and on the two maps annexed to the Master Plans which, according to him would show the lay out of the proposed road.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No 1 intimated that he would come back on his own but that he did not talk over the matter with the appellant. The Dy. District Magistrate who tried the case convicted both the appellants under sections 120 B, 161 and 466 I.P.C., and still confirmed them. The State appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the respondent that (i) the statements made to the two witnesses in regard to the statement made by the appellant were not recorded as required by section 164 of the Code, and therefore inadmissible in evidence; (ii) there were circumstances which would clearly lead to the conclusion that the appellants had committed an offence under section 161 I. P.C. In support of his contention he relied on the statements of the two persons made to them before they were made to their witness, and the statements were admissible under section 164 Of the Code; and (iii) although there was a serious lacuna in the evidence the accused could not be allowed to be put up for trial. Held, that the statement of the accused as to recovery of the sums of money by the police Authorities to the tune of Rs. 1,000 from his own sources was inadmissible in itself, and was admissible under rule 17 Of the Criminal Rules. The statements made on behalf 'and given to them were admissible in evidence in proof of the criminal liability incurred by the accused. Per section R. DAS J. (dissenting) (per K. C. Das Gupta, C.J., p. 1115) and a decision of this Court in Gokul Chand Jain vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, [1955] 2 S.C R. 836, relied on.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the plaintiff along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge against the respond ent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. He was convicted under section 325 read with section 34 I.P.C. and several other sections, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months each. The conviction was maintained up to the Supreme Court stage. Pursuant thereto, the respondent filed a Criminal Miscellaneous Petition before the High Court against the decree of the first appellate court which was dismissed at the admission stage itself by merely saving: "HEARD. . [825E F] In the instant case, it has been asserted on oath before this Court and not denied by the res pondent that the charge was made with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. Both the issues were decided by the learned 824 Subordinate Judge against the plaintiff and the suit was accordingly decreed. On appeal by the State, it was contended that there was no limitation on the ground of reasonableness and, therefore, the bar of limitation would not apply. It was further submitted that in the case of another member of the Police force a mistake was committed; that since there was an order of dismissal passed against the respondent, his service stands terminated. The trial court held that the order of dis missal was void on the plea of limita tion and, there fore, the period of limitation could not be applied in the present case, which is the old one.

The appellant company entered into certain transactions in jute. On the question whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that the transactions were not speculative, and as there were no speculation profits in that year he held that loss would be carried forward and set off against speculation profits. The department took an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who held that the transaction amounted to speculative transfers within the meaning of section 24(1) read with Explanation 2 and restored the order of income tax Officer. On reference the High Court answered the question in the affirmative and against the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The question referred to the High court in the present case has been correctly answered. There is no connection with sec 24 of the Income Tax Act. [186B] The Madras General Sales tax Act, 1939, as it stood on the relevant date was correctly stated in D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal. ; It is well settled that where there are two separate transactions of sale by one between the mills and the original purchasers, and the other there is a long line of dealings which is not otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual delivery of the commodity or the scrips has taken place; on the other hand, a transaction which is otherwise speculative would not be a speculative transaction within the mischief of Explanation 2 if it is not necessary that the transfer in question should be followed up by actual delivery and having regard to the mischief which was sought to be averted by the promulgation of the ordinance to prevent persons who dealt in differences only and never intended to take delivery under any circumstances it was held that such intendment of the Ordinance was that actual delivery must be actual delivery as also symbolic or constructive delivery. [187E F] The contention that the assessee relied on an English decision cannot be accepted. In D.M. Wadhwaiwana vs Commis sioner of Income Tax, Calcutta and State of Andhra Pradesh vs Kolla Sreeramurthy, ; , applied.

The first respondent was the candidate for the reserved seat in Pun jab Legislative Assembly. The appellant who was a candidate for general seat and Ram Prakash filed his election petition challenging the rejection of his nomination papers by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage. He contended that the nomination papers were invalid because the signature of the proposer and seconder did not amount to "attestation" but were merely sign by way of attesting the candidate 's signature to the nomination form; they were invalid and so rejected them. Held per KANIA, that the attestation in the prescribed manner was required in the case of proposers and seconders who were not signed " either in one way or the other, then it was clear that the words " subscribing " imports a "signature" and "subscribe" meant the same thing and whether they could be taken to include the placing of a mark. The nomination papers are intended to help the candidates for filling the nominations and the Returning Offi cerates have found themselves in order and to decide objections, and it was not necessary to reject any nomination paper on the ground of any technical defect which is not of a substantial character but he could not remedy the defect. He must leave it as it is. If the Returning officer had omitted to the attestation because of some slip on his part and it could be proved that he was satisfied at the proper time, the matter might be different because the element of his satisfaction at the time of making _a mark in place of writing a signature. The fact that the sign has to be incorporated into any provision of the Act would not have been rejected as technical and unsubs tantial. The words " subscribe " must be construed in the sense of making a signature and as the Act tells us quite clearly how the different types of signatures are to be made, they were bound to give effect to them, to ft. In the case Of illiterate persons unable to write their names it is necessary to guard against misrepresentation and fraud by requiring that their signatures should be formally authenticated in a particular way.

In the proceedings before the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication of a dispute, 344 workmen of the Company including the appellants went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to an strike notice given to the Company by their registered union calling upon them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names were struck off from the muster rolls of the company. In case No. 336 of 1972 before the Second Labour Court, Bombay for adjudication, 344 persons of the workmen went on strike with an unmishedulent strike with a view to terminate this strike notice by appellants. The Company sent separate communications to the appellants indicating that they had not abandoned service and there was no abandonment of services. On October 23, 1972 the union made a formal demand calling upon the company to re instate the appellants and others who had been removed from service on the ground that they bad abandoned their service. In May 1973, the appellants made the aforesaid complaints before the Labour Court with the result that their names had been struck off on August 30.1972. The appellants then made the said complaints before it against the Company in respect of this industrial dispute concerning the re instated approval of the discharge notice and for reinstatement as well as other striking workmen who had not only by their letters dated September 21, 1972 and September 26, 1972 unequivocally intimated to the company that they did not intend to abandon the service but also returned the cheques sent by the Company on account of their leave salary gratuity etc. The company returned the aforesaid sums which were the amounts due to him on account from January 19, 1973 and October 23. 1972. On December 18,1972 the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the action of the respondent company in removing them from service and asserting that the said action was by way of victimization for their participation in the strike. The learned Single Judge of the High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the termination of the services of the appellants was illegal and arbitrary and that the appellants had not in any event terminated the services even on the plea that they were absent in connection with the notified strike; that the action was therefore illegal and invalid. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the decisions of this Court in Express Newspapers (P) Ltd. vs Michael Mark & Anr., ; ; , relied upon by the High Courts fell squarely within the ambit of the expression 'abandonment of service ', that the discharge of the statutory duties under section 33(A) is not a change in the conditions of service of the employees during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the labour court which adversely affected them and could not be countenanced; and that even if there had been a voluntary abandonment or relinquishment of service by the workmen, there can be no question of abandonment of employment by them. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The intention may be inferred from the acts and conduct of the party, and is a question of fact. Temporary absence is not ordinarily sufficient to constitute an abandonment of office '. From the connotations reproduced above it clearly follows that to constitute abandonment, there must be total or complete giving up of duties so as to indicate an intention not to resume the same. In Buckingham Co. vs Venkatiah & Ors., , this Court has held that under common law an inference that an employee has abandoned or relinquished service is not easily drawn unless from the length of absence and from other surrounding circumstances an inference to that effect can be legitimately drawn and it can be assumed that the employee intended to abandon service.

The trustees of a public trust, styled "Shri Tricumraiji" and started the present suit for a declaration that under decree, and in default of three instalments the entire amount remaining unpaid shall become due and recoverable from the mortgagee property. The trial court passed an order disposing of the execution application and directed that Rs. 250 out of the deposit, by the trustees be paid over to the appellant. The District Court issued an order directing that a sum of Rs.250 out of amount deposited by the Trustees be paid to the auction purchaser. In revision, the High Court set aside the sale held in execution of the decree holding the sale in execution and directed the delivery of the certificate. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) under section 36(a), the Court had no power to set aside a sale as section 56B did not exclude a sale in exercise of authority derived from the trustees ' e.g. a covenant for sale under an English mortgage executed by the trustee or a sales in terms of a consent decree attract the application; and (ii) that in view of the precedent, the decision of the High court would be regarded as binding on the District Court. HELD: (i). The words "sale" occurring in section 36 must be construed according to their ordinary meaning, and not by the facts of that case. [461 C] (ii). It is true that every Judge of a High Court before he enters upon his office takes an oath of office that he will bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India as by law established and that he would duly and faithfully and to the best of his ability, knowledge and judgment perform the duties of office without fear or favour, affection or illwill and that when he enters on his office take an oath in office that the office he will have no bias, but there is nothing in the oath of Office which warrants a Judge in ignoring the rule relating to the binding nature, of the precedents which is uniformly followed. [463 H] (iii) A judgment delivered by a single judge after due consideration of the points before it is liable to be regarded if the District Judge was of the view that every judge is entitled to take such view as he chooses of the question of law arising before him as Venkatarama Aiyar, J., would not embark upon that enquiry sitting as a single Judge. [458 A] (iv) The proper and traditional way to deal with such matters and it is founded on healthy principles of judicial decorum and propriety. It has been held time and again by counsel for the auctionpurchaser that in the absence of a provision in ' the Constitution and the character of a reference made by a Judge or a Bench of Judges or to a larger Bench, when it appears to a Single Judge or Division Bench that there are conflicting decisions of the same Court. or there are decisions of other High Courts in India which are strongly persuasive and take a view different from the view which prevails in his or their High Court. [459 G] (v) Under section 36, the expression "sale ' in section 35(a) includes a sale of the property of a Public trust in execution thereof or a proceeding to enforce a mortgage decree against property belonging to a public Trust. The section imposes a fetter upon the power of the trustees: it is not intended thereby to confer upon the Charity Commissioner an overriding authority upon actions of the Civil Court in execution cf decrees. In the present case, the Trustees had deposited Rs. 25 for payment to the appellants and deposited Rs 3.20 towards the mortgage dues from the auction purchasers. They also invested Rs. 63 for payment after being released. They did not pay the instalments due under the decree.

Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950, which permits the Central Government to retire a government servant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service, confers unguided powers in the Govern ment and as such is ultra vires Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The object of this Rule is to chop off the dead wood, because Rule 2(1) of pension Rules permits the Government to prematurely retire a Government servant at anyone time after completion of 30 years ' qualifying service although he has a right to continue till the age of superannuation which is 58 years. Rule 2 (2) provides no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Govern ing authority, and there is no requirement under the rule to act in 'Public Interest '. A person who joins Government service at the age Of 21 years can be retired prematurely under F.R. 56(j) only on the ground of 'public interest ' whereas another Government servant who is only 51 and has completed 20 years of qualified qualifying service can be retiring at anytime at the discretion of the Govern mment under Rule 2.(2). The object,of this Rule being to chind off the life wood. Rule 56(J) lays down that the retirement under rule 2(i) should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. The instructions are supplementary to the Rule, according ly, the order of retirement has to be in Public Interest ' and as per r.2(2). Such instructions can only supplement and not supplant the rule. Shri Anil Dev Singh then placed reliance on Ministry of Home Affairs Memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and argued that the same, having been issued in the name of President of India, is statutory and has the effect of amending Rule 2 of Pension Rules. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 From the memorandum dated November, 1961, it could not and did not add anything to Rule 2.2 of the Pension Rules that the power to retire under para 6 was in addition to the power already contained in the Pension rules. [800G] 1.2 The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the Constitu tion of India and as is such cannot be stat ed with the support of executive instructions. [ 800A B] Union of India & Ors. vs R. Narasimhan, ; Union of lndia & Ors., [1981] 1 SCR p. 205; referred to. 1.3 The memorandum of November, which inter alia incorporated Rule 56 (j) into Fundamental Rules is a statutory rule and is identical to Fundamental Rule 56.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable account ing period of accounting in question was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1944, falling in the financial year ending 31st Decem ber, 1941, sales were effected from April 1, 1944 to April 4, 1944. These sales were conducted between 26th July, 1943 to 29th September, 1941 and 9th November, 1942 respectively for the purpose of extraction of Katechu from October, 1940 to March 31, 1945. The sales in this case were effected between 26st July,1943 to March 30, 1946, failing in the Financial year ending March 31st, 1944 failing in terms of its respective sales during the chargeable accounting period namely 31st January, 1943 and March 31rd, 1943. Sales took place from May 30, 1941 to September 29th July 1942. The assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of business transaction was maintained in the books of M/s Biharilal Balkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". It had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose and had extracted Katechoo from October 1940 to September, 1942. It was alleged that according to the terms of the agreement between the assessee firm and its partners the sale of Katech ure at their shops in Kanpur, accused or arose at Raichur and that such profits were not liable to be taxed under section 13(1) (e) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940. The Excess Profit Tax Officer rejected these claims on the ground that business carried on during the said chargeable accounting periods was not separate to and distinct from the business carried out in 1940 41 and the corresponding counts were maintained in itam language; that the same business of manufacturing Katech la could under takings in Nepal; that since there was no sale during the financial years ending 31 st March, 1941 & 31st December, 1941 these sales took place between 26rd July, and 3rd November, 1944 and therefore, while there was manufacturing activity there were no sales at all during the relevant accounting periods, although there were sales effected, yet profits accrued to the assessee; and that there could be no profit or loss during the accounting period ending on 31st Mars, 1943, and as such there could also be no deficiency of profits during those years. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order. On further appeal by the assessee before the Appellate Tribunal the High Court held that it was not disputed before them that the assessee was carrying on the same 'business from 28th October 1940, to 4th April, 1944; and therefore there could he no profit and loss during these two chargeable accounting years although there had been no sale in the , financial years ended 31st July 1946, and 23rd November 1942, failing which there could arise no deficiency or loss in profits pertaining to the chargeable income period. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the manufacturing activities were carried on for the purposes of the Act and as provided in the provi sions of the E.P.T. Act, 1947 was applicable to every business of which any part of profits was made during the income tax year and that the intention of the legislature was to tax the profits of certain business in excess of a certain limit as provided under that Act; and the provisions of the impugned Act would apply to every 'business of which section 13 and section 21 were applicable and accordingly the assessment should be made on the basis of the 'accounting period ' and after that set off carried forward to be set off during the proce dure period. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the KPSC Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). Similar qualification was prescribed in the examination held by the Public Service Com mission. The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the K PSC and there after, in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained in category I, questions in C Engineering and in Category II, questions ( Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineering) applicants who were qualified in Civil engineering had to answer the questions in Category 1 on the one hand and those who had qualified in Mechanical Engineering but answered questions indicated in Category I on the two hand and the those who qualified in civil engineering had not yet been appointed. The Kerala Public Services Commission invited application for filling 131 expected vacancies. However, some of the aggrieved respondents in the Writ Petitions filed appeals before the Division Bench of the High Court, al lowed the Appeals with a direction to the Government to prepare "two lists, namely, one for the Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". It was also contended that the applicants who had held a Mechanical Engineering degree, were one of the Special Leave Petitioners before the Supreme Court. The High Court allowed the Writ Appeals filed by the respondents holding Civil Engineering degrees.

The respondent, a partnership firm in 1979 was created on 15.1.1979 to be effective from 1.11979 in which the plaintiff had no interest. The business was under the control of Abdul Samad and the defendant Nos. 1 and 2, besides denying the plaint allegations made by the plaintiff, challenged the valuation given by the defendant as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The claim of the plaintiff respondent was rejected by the trial Court on the ground that the court was powerless to challenge the valuation put by the appellant on the relief claimed in the suit. The High Court dismissed the defendant 's revision application holding: (i) The suit is governed for the purpose of Court Fees by section 7(iv)(f) of the Court Fees Act and not by section7(iv) (f). (ii) Where the valuation fixed by the respondent appears to be arbitrary and unreasonable, the court may reject it and leave the plaintiff to correct the valuation or have the suit rejected. [505D E] Smt. Tara Devi vs Sri Thakur Radha Krishna Maharaj, AIR 1936 Cal 948, applied. In a suit for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose; (iii) The valuation put was arbitrary and unacceptable. [511F G] (iv)(a) It is the sweet will of the respondent to choose any figure he likes and thus decide finally the Court which shall have jurisdiction to entertain the suit without reference to the subject matter of the litigation, the nature and extent of relief claimed or any other factor; (b) The Court has no jurisdiction to examine the matter further and remit this question to be reconsidered by the Trial Court.] [511E] (c) The interpretation put by this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. None of the two cited judgments relied upon by the learned counsel helps him. It is true that in a suit, for accounts, the plaintiff has been ousted from the partnership business.

The assesses ' claim for exemption from sales tax for certain periods in question was accepted by the High Court, and following its decision in G.S. Dhall & Flour Mills and, following it, in the case of Peti tions, the State submits that C.A. 2211/87 should be allowed and that the assesses 's S.L.Ps should be dismissed in limine. The assesses ' s claim for exemptions from sales Tax was accepted, by the State Government on the ground that they did not comply with (a) above or that they had opted for the scheme of deferring the pay ment of tax under the rules framed for this purpose; and (b) that they were eligible for exemption under the notification and that they should be rejected in limine, but without assigning any reason. In these appeals by special leave, the assessee contended before this Court that C .A. 1911/1987 should be granted and that, in view of this and the fact that the Government had already issued ted an incentive to some one who set up a new industry in the State so that the industrial units did not get any benefit, the notification presently under consideration was issued with the object of industrialising the backward areas of the State and so it was immaterial what type of industry went in there and whether the industry proposed to be set up was a "tradition al" one or not. On behalf of the asses see, on the basis of the instruc tions of 12.1.1983 which were issued on January 13, 1983, C 's application for Scheme of deferred payment of tax, etc., had been rejected and it was contended that since the notification did not set out the conditions on which, and the procedure in accordance with which the Director of Industries was to issue the eligibility certificate, that earlier scheme and provi sions could be read into the Notification, C should have granted them a certificate to this effect. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object for exemption has to be and are set out in the notification itself and all that the Director, of Industries has to do is to satisfy himself that those condi tions are fulfilled; he cannot travel beyond the terms of the Notification. But, here: "as pointed out earlier, column 3 of the 1981 notification is capable of a wider meaning, it would appear that these words govern only the immediately preceding words; rules envisaged are not in relation to the grant of exemption certifi cate and condi tion therefore, but in respect of the circum stances in which the assesses can exercise the option between exemption and deferment of sales tax.
