Section 31 of the Income Tax Act, 1922, provides that where as the result of an appeal, any change in the assessment of a firm or association of persons is ordered to be made the Appellate Assistant Commissioner may authorise the Income tax Officer to amend accordingly any assessment made on any partner of the firm or any member of the association. All the returns have been filed by Debi Parshad but in the present appeals by Debi, their assessments depend upon the assessment depends on the assessment and the liability of the former. The said instances are only illustrative. Held, that where persons other than the appealing, might be affected by orders passed under an order passed by the Appellate re spondents for a particular year may affect the assessment for the said year on a partner or partners of the latter firm. Commissioner off Income tax, U.P., vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; and Commissioner off lncome Tax, U .P. vs Kanpur coal Spring Supply Co., A.I.R. 1965 S.C. 881 referred to. Shri Debi Parhshad was not a stranger to the assessment proceeding. The income earned by the assessee was assessed in the hands of the family of Debi Parl lath and he was liable to be assessed personally in respect of the income. The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner had directed that the income in the three assessment years be assessed in his hands in respect Of the Income. 'showment in the said assessment years should be assessed as the income of the undivided family ofri lath, apparently on the view that Debi Parathshad represented the Hindu Undivided Family.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his joint family properties and an account in respect of the joint family assets managed by him. The plaint was valued at Rs, 4,00,000, under section 7(iv)(f) of the Madras Code of Civil Procedure. After the institution of the suit, the Court fees were paid on applications made by the appellant. The application for amendment was rejected, and a memorandum of appeal filed in the High Court was rejected. Held that as the plaint did not fall under article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act. It cannot be disputed that as a result of this rule, section 7 (iv)(a) (b), (c) and (f) applied to suits filed on the Original Side of the High Courts in Madras even though they were consolidated in respect thereof they could be included only under the provisions of sections 7(v) of that Act. Per section K. Das, J., The appellant 's case was that though the plaint was properly referred by the Master under section 5, the appellant was not heard; he did not state the amount at which he values the relief sought for the purpose of court fees and the valuation for jurisdiction alone is; therefore, no question about the adequacy of the court fees leviable on the appellant ' s memorandum of Appeal could be said to have been extended. The order made by him on October 4, 1951, was final under section 6, sub section (4) of section 7, sub els 10 and 11 and was final in character as between the parties.

Section 9 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 requires the location of 'refuge areas ' for a group of floors as specified therein. The first respondent obtained permission from the Land Devel opment Officer to erect a high rise building of an area of 1,62,000 square feet and paid Rs.63,40918 towards betterment levy. On 4.5.1982 it applied for and on 29.8.1980, sanction from the Rent Controller of the Authority was revalidated for a further period of two years. The NDMC challenged the said decision before the High Court by way of Writ Petition before the Delhi High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of building plans on or before 5th May, 1989 and accordingly conveyed its formal approval of the building plan on or after 6th May 1988. Against this order of the High court, the New Delhi Municipal Committee moved this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.01. The permission given to the land Development Officer was an indispensable condition for eligibility for sanction for accord ing of sanction by the NDMC is not in substitution of the requirement of compliance with the objec tive prescriptions of those bye laws. [508E F] 1.02. There is no reservation or change in the procedure adopted by the DDA in this behalf, though entitled to weight, would not be binding on the NDMC. The clearance from the Chief Fire Officer envisaged by Bye law 16.4.8 was an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the NDMC under Article 16. [609B C] 1:03. The requirement of bye law 16 is an additional essential condition and, not a limitations on the powers of the chal lenged authority to satisfy itself that the building plans provide for adequate fire safety precaution in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure.

The joint family carried on joint family business of a grocery shop, liquor shops and also moneylending under the name of "Sontakke Brothers". The family also Possessed immovable and movable property. Balkrishna sontakke was the eldest of the brothers and was the plaintiff respondent in the present appeal. He will be referred to hereafter as the plain tiff. It is common ground that up to 1944 the brothers were living together and messing together and the income from the said businesses or properties. The parties tried to have partition effected between them through arbitrators but the attempt failed failed. On June 29, 1945 all the five brothers filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all joint family properties including the accounts of all the businesses. The application was made on November 22, 1947 and he alleged that during this period his business had been stopped by some members of a family their position was analogous to that of a partner carrying on partnership after dissolution and applying the principle underlying section 37 of the Partnership Act he held that the two brothers carrying on the motor business were liable to account. Accordingly they passed a preliminary decree directing accounts of the motor transport business to be taken from March 31, 1946 up to the date on which a final decree for payment was made. A Commissioner was appointed to take the accounts to ascertain the profits earned by the use of the capital belonging to his share of the profits and assets of the Motor business carried on by them separately to determine the amount due upto that date. Each of the five names of all members was to get one sixth share in the cash balance as found on March 31 1946. On September 30, 1945, all the 5 brothers filed an application before the Civil Judge praying for a final judgment and order. The Civil Judge held that though the motor 'business carried on after the partition had ceased to be a joint family property yet as it was carried on, by some of the members of the family their right to account would be entirely stopped after the 31st March 1946, or would be run either by the arbitrators or the Commissioners and the profits accruing therefrom would be deposited in Court for distribution among the parties according to their shares. The plaintiff appealed to the High Court against this judgment and decree. On appeal it was urged on behalf of the appellant that the cause of action in a suit is the desire and intention of the Family to separate that the causes of action were identically identical and not separate and distinct and that, the cause for action Was different from the cause. cause of actions in the two suits being the same, the suit was barred under Order II, rule 2(3), of the Code of Civil Procedure; Held: (i) It is well settled that a consent decree is as binding upon the parties thereto as a decree passed by invitum and is binding on the parties therein as a final order passed by the invitamour. [106 C D] (ii) A consent decree obtained in respect of a motor business only is anything but honest. The compromise having been found not to be vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, misunderstanding or mistake the decree passed thereon has the binding force of res judicata.

Under the Bombay Salt Works Act, 1947 "the word " factory" includes " any premises in which certain type of work is carried on by way of trade or for purposes of gain. The word "premises " is defined to mean any premises and includes precincts thereof (1) wherein ten or more persons are employed in any manufacturing process is being carried on without the aid of power; or (2) whereon twenty or less workers are working, or were working on any day of the preceding twelve months, and in any part of which a manufacturing process Is being carried On or within the Prec DURING of which such water is brought within the definition Of " manufacturing process ", the Salt Works, 1946, was amended by the Bombay Legislature with effect from April 1, 1950 which Act came into force on April 1. It also provided that "the factory ' shall be taken to mean all building and premises situated within any part Of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland wherein or within tho limits or jurisdiction of Salt Works is being worked on by means of trade; and the words " factories, in which " certain type goods are carried on with the aid Of power, or is ordinarily so carried on notwithstanding certain matters mentioned in the section. The appellant was working as a Company carrying on business in the said Salt Works and was maintaining regular managing its business and running a factory without obtaining a licence under section 6 of the Act read with r . 4 of the Rules framed thereunder. An application for the issue of a warrant of arrest against the company for allegedly attempting to carry on the manufacturing process of treating the salt works as a " manufacturing industry in making or not including any building which would make it necessary that this process should be carried on in a building ". in contravention of r .4 of the Bombay Act read. The High Court held the appellant 's Salt Works attracted the provisions Of section 7 of the Salt Act and convicted them for the offence under section 92 of the Indian Factories Act, and acquitted them. On appeal by special leave: Held (per Hidayatullah, J., dissenting) that the expression " premises " in section 2 of the , includes factories and factories and that the appellant was rightly convicted of the offence of working the factory without complying with its provisions, and the finding of the High Court were correct. The process of converting sea water into salt carried on the appellant Salt Works comes within the meaning of the definition of " manufacturing " in el. (k) of section 2. The words " premises" include factories or factories and buildings, which are covered by the Factory Act of 1833 were such which could function only in buildings, the conception grew that nothing would come within the expression ' factory ' unless it had a building and unless the factory itself provided for the application of the Factories to it. The Act was for the welfare of the workers and dealt with matters connected with the health, safety, welfare, working hours of the workmen; employment of young persons and leave to be granted to workers and that therefore the Legislature could not have intended to discriminate between the workers who were engaged in a manufacturing processes in a buildings and those who 'are engaged in such a process on open land.

The respondent was a national scale officer in the Department of Public Instructions. In 1949, three occupational Institutes (Polytechnics) were started in the State. The respondent was sent on deputation to serve in the Polytechnic at Devangere as Instructor in Tailoring and he joined duty there on December 1, 1949. While so, the respondent was reverted by the Directorate and appointed as Tailoring Instructor under the rules then in force and as his reversion at this distance of time for no fault of his would cause a great hardship to him, the Commission were of the opinion that he may be absorbed as tailoring Instructor from the date of his appointment as such as has been ordered in the case of Sri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty. Thereafter, the Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960, made these recommendations in favour of the respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director (Appropriatement) which was the Unit officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Sri Srinivasa Murthy who was fully qualified as Tailored Instructor in the Technical Education Department and there was no need to classify the vacancy post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. Along with him Sri K Narayanaswamy C: Chetty, who was junior to him in the parent Department and came on deputation in that Department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to 1949 and he be given the benefit of revisions of pay scales of pay. " The respondent continued tp serve on deputation from other departments to the Polytechnics and all of them except the respondent, were absorbed permanently in the department by Government in consultation with the Public Services Commission. Later, his services were allotted to and absorbed in the same department by order dated June 11, 1956. In 1955, he was again posted on deputation as Instructor (in tailoring) in the Ministry of Defence. He contended that this principle of policy was ignored in his case. The Government held that: (1) the temporary reversion of the Respondent to his parent department in 1955 56 was not justified because he had been invidiously discriminated against in the matter of absorption and appointment, while his junior K. N. Chetty who was senior to him were similarly placed absorbed in that wing; (2) the respondent had no legal right to be absorbed in service of the Department with effect from a particular anterior date, or to be given revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in service, because he could not claim as of right; and (3) if he was found suitable for absorption in the other department, his case was identical in all respects. ^ HELD: (i) Articles 14 and 16 do not apply to enforce a mere concession. The appellant had no right to claim such promotion under article 14 or Article 16 of the Constitution. [259 B C] (ii) It is an undisputed fact that sit other employees, who were similarly situated, were appointed from the dates on which they initially joined duty, after deputation to the polytechnics, and, therefore, it was clear that this rule was ignored when he originally resumed duty on deputation, to the Junior Division Branch of the Poly technics. [260 C] K. V. Rajalakshmiah Setty vs State of Mysore ; , followed. (iii) The High Court has held that his "impermissible reversion" for a short while in 1955 to the parent department was no ground to hold that he was not similarly situated as K. niliyar Gounder Chetty.

The petitioner an advocate practising in this court complaining of malpractices indulged by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents. The letter referred to a press report based on "empirical investigation carried out by the staff of a reputed foreign magazine" called "the Mail". On behalf of the petitioner it was contended that (a) the procedure adopted by the court in Bombay, Delhi and Gujarat, was discriminatory as inasmuch as there were social organisations licensed or recognised by the Government and if any such adoption will provide moral and material security to the child with an opportunity to grow into the full stature of its personality in an atmosphere of love and affection; (b) the scheme for giving notice to the Indian Council of Social Welfare or the Indian Presidential Council for Child Welfare or any other independent, reputed and publicly recognised social welfare agency was obviously to ensure that the application of foreign parents for guardianship of the child alongwith a view to their eventual adoption is properly and carefully scrutinised and evaluated by an expert body having experience in the area of child welfare with a view not to its adoption or the making by that person of any arrangements for such adoption. Allowing the writ petition, the Court, HELD: (1) The adoption of children by foreign parents need not wait until social or child welfare agencies are recognised by Government as directed in this order, but pending recognition of social or Child welfare agencies for the purpose of inter country adoptions, which interregnum, is not the only way in which a foreign parent can take an Indian child in adoption is by making an application to the Court in which the child ordinarily resides for being appointed guardian of the person of the children with leave to remove the child out of India and take it to his own country for the purposes of adopting it in accordance with the law of that country can be followed. [801 G] (2) It would not make any difference that if an application of a foreigner for taking a child in adopt is required to be routed through a recognised social orchild welfare agency and the necessary steps for the proper management of the adoption would also be taken only through a recognized social or family welfare agency, so that one copy can be filed in Court and the other could remain with the social or children welfare agency in India.

% The company employed workmen numbering over 5000. It is branches in Bombay, Madras, New Delhi, , Kanpur and Bangalore (In addition to insulated cables, the Company manufactures Aluminium Rods, Radio Aerials, Fuse Wires and other products.). Its paid up capital is Rs. 2,48,65,450. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year amounts to Rs. 1,0532,880. Its accounting year is from Ist April to 31st March of succeeding year. For the accounting year 1964 65, the company declared and paid bonus at 20% to all employedes in accordance with the provisions of the (hereinafter to be referred as the Act). For the assessment year 1965 66 it calculated a sum of Rs. 23,68,785 as available surplus. This amount represented 13 51% of the wage bill. The workmen were dissatisfied with this offer of bonus at 1351% and demanded payment of bonus for the accounting years 1964 65 to employees drawing emoluments exceeding Rs. 22 lakhs. Consequent upon the agreement between the parties to refer the claim for additional bonus for adjudication, the workmen received the bonus at 108 rate of 13.51% offered by the Company. The Union, however, maintained that it has kept proper accounts which have been audited by a reputed firm of auditors. The Unions further alleged that the Company has spent large amounts for payment of liability for future years with a view to reduce the available surplus and allocable surplus, which in consequence had resulted in reduction of percentage of bonus. The company on the other hand maintained that the computation of allocable balance had been properly arrived at having due regard to the provisions Of the Act. The Tribunal computed the available available surplus at Rs. 47 lakhs, after deducting therefrom the prior charges for payment in accordance With section 6, but not the bonus payable to its workmen, and directed the payment of balance 6.49% within a period of two months. On appeal by the Union, the High Court held that the amounts claimed by the workmen should be deducted from the gross profits for calculation of direct tax or alternatively rebate for bonus found payable has to be calculated and 60% of this rebate had to be added back as allocable available surplus, and the Tribunal directed the said payment within a further period. The Company appealed to this Court on special leave. HELD : (i) The Tribunal was justified in disallowing deduction of certain items from the net profits for purposes of computing the available and alloca tionable surplus. [128E] (ii) The workmen will be entitled to bonus at 14.02% of their total salary or wages and the amount will be Rs. 14,76606 and not Rs. 20% as awarded by the Tribunal.

The appellant, who was working as Commercial Tax officer in 1954, was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes at the instance of Vigilance and Anti Corruption Department, he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal which, by its order dated November 29, 1974, held that the charges against him were not substantiated in the enquiry made by the Directorate of Vigilance, Anti Corruption and Anti corruption. The Government accepted the view of the Full Board and dropped the charges making the following order on November 29. 1974: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Director of Vigilance & Anti Corruption but out of eleven allegations levelled against Thiru D. Ramaswami, seven allegations were not proved in the inquiry made by Directorate of Enforcement and Anti. The government accepted the views of the Board and drop the charges framed against ThiruD. Ramaswami on November 28, 1974. " The Government"s order dated 11.1.73 was to grant absolution to the appellant from the repercussions of the note of the Deputy Commissioner, Commercial Taxes made in 1969. If there was any ambiguity about the effect of the Government order, it was cleared by the circumstance that within a few months, on May 7, 1975 he was promoted and posted as Deputy Director of Commercial taxes in 1971. On being informed by the appellant that within one month, on June 7,1975 he was not promoted to a selection post, he accepted his views on November 30, 1974 and dropped all charges made against him. The order was challenged before the High Court, which held that all the charges made were not established in the departmental enquiry and proved and so the Government accepted his view that all of the charges may be dropped. The appeal filed by the State was allowed by the Division Bench, and a direction was issued to frame charges afresh as for a major penalty against Thiruigmathnam on the basis of allegations levelled and after obtaining their explanation, if any, made in the disciplinary proceedings, were initiated against him after giving him an opportunity of being heard. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The promotion of the appellant just a few month earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter was impossible to sustain the order of the government retiring the appellant. [80G] 2. It is indeed odd to retire a Government servant a few years after promoting him to a Selection post. In the instant case, there were some stray mild and hildly deprecating entries such as the one in 1964 which said: "He is sincere and hardworking". He had no longer prosperent relationship with public.

The appellants who had been operating motor transport operators whose permits are liable to be modified or cancelled under the provisions of the Schemes on their coming into force filed objections to the scheme before the State Government under section 68 D(2) and (3) of the . The appellant contended that they were responsible for the delay in implementing the schemes, that the Government considered the desirability of nationalisation of transport services in the interests of the citizens and had passed a resolution with an objective object to fill up certain routes and submitted it to the Chief Minister who was the head of one of them and that as such there was no proof that the Transport Minister who heard the objections raised by him to the schemes was influenced by the Chief Mini tive, in order to carry out his behest. Held: (1) The scheme framed by the Corporation was not valid on the ground that it contravened the provisions contained in section 68 C of the Act and rules made thereunder, because the Regional Transport Authority which is specifically mentioned in section 69 F(1) was empowered to issue the permit to the transport undertaking " notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Ch. No doubt as in Andhra Pradesh there was a admit tedly a Regional Transport Officer, but there was some other authority which functions as the Regional Authority for tile purposes of the Art, such an Authority might be that which would be comprehended by section 68 F( 1 ) but where as in A. P. No. 2191/1963, a State where there is no Regional Transport authori ties for the purpose of the Article, such Authority might he that which function and which would he comprehended by the section 68F(I) not be bound to give effect to it. [353 C] (2) The provisions of those schemes were vitiated by non compliance with the requirements of section 68C and the rules made under them. [354 C E] Dosa Satyanaraya namurty etc. vs The Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corpora tion, ; , applied.

The appellant company was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The assessee made various attempts to get duplicate forms of declaration from the dealers and on account of circumstances over which it had no control and because of the unhelpful and hostile attitude of the Commercial Tax Officer within whose jurisdiction the said dealers functioned, it was not able to furnish the duplicate forms for all the declarations that were lost. The Commercial Tax officer by notice dated April 22, 1955 fixed August 4, 1955 for hearing the assessee in respect of its return but he did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. He then flied an application under article 226 of the Constitution to the High Court for issuing a writ directing the respondents, i.e., the Commercial tax Officer and the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes to implement the assessment order. The said application came up for hearing before Sinha J. who dismissed the same. On appeal by certificate granted by the High court, Held: (i) In view of Ss. 5(2)(a)(ii), 4 and 9 of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1947, which are similar in terms to section 5(1)(a) (ii), the Proviso cannot be construed as laying down a condition for giving the exemption, but only as a directory provision to subserve the substantive provision in a reasonable way. If so construed, a dealer is not precluded from producing other relevant evidence to prove that the sales to the registered dealers were for the purposes mentioned in the said sub clause. This conclusion is sought to be supported on the basis of the expression "on demand". In the nature of things, in view of innumerable transactions between dealers it will well nigh be impossible for the taxing authorities to ascertain in each case whether a dealer has sold the specified goods to another for the purpose mentioned in section. Therefore, presumably to achieve the twofold object namely prevention of fraud and ' facilitating administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration form in the manner prescribed under the section. The liberal construction suggested will facilitate the commission of fraud & introduce administrative inconveniences, both of which the provisions of the said clause seek to avoid. [627C D] In the present case the object of section 5 (2)(b) of the Act and the rules made thereunder is self evident. While the two sections are obviously intended to give exemption to a dealer in respect for sales to registered dealers of specified classes of goods, it seeks also to prevent fraud, collusion, in an attempt to evade tax.

The appellant, who was the landlord and the respondent filed an application for possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The tenant objected and claimed benefit of the third clause of subs. (2 A), and the question that arose for determination was whether the tenant was entitled to the protection contained in cl. (b) of section 34(1). Held, further, that the notice given by the landlord under s.34(1) is merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention to terminate the tenancy and not a further proceedings may be taken by the land lord in consequence thereof it was open to the landlord not to carry out his intention. If the landlord failed to comply with the condition, the Amending Act came into force and the amendment provided that a tenant would be liable to ejectment on one year 's notice by the landlords. Accordingly, the provisions of the Amending Acts which came into effect before the tenancy stood terminated by the notice will have to be taken into consideration in determining the right of the landlord arising out of the notice of termination of the tenancy, for the Amending, Act put certain fetters on this right of termination. In the circumstances, the proviso to section 34 (2A) was introduced and the amending Act provided that the tenant would therefore be liable under ejectment on two years ' notice by his landlord. The amendment permitted a tenant to terminate tenancy from one year "s notice" by the tenant. The proviso was not retrospective in operation because of any misapprehension about the meaning of sub section (2) A). Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai, ; and Jee bankrishna Chakrabarti vs Abdul Kader Chaudhuri, I.L.R. LX Cal. 1037, referred to.

The petitioners purchased the houses by a notification under section 7 of the , and were in possession thereof. The buildings vested in the Custodian under the provisions of section 8 of the Act, and they took possession, but these houses were not declared evacuees. Thereupon they moved this Court by way of a petition challenging the validity of section 7 Of the Act on the ground that it had been filed beyond time prescribed for it, and that no notice had been issued to them under section 9(2) of the . Held, that the acts of the Custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. The exercise of such a power is a judicial one. It is well established and not disputed that no property can be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 10(2). It is also well established that the peti tioners did not maintain this petition, because, in any event, there was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting Zafar Ali 's right in the houses. [707 C E] The order of January 10, 1952, was without jurisdiction so far it affected the rights of the petitioners in the properties concerned. In view of the decision of this Court inENabhai Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, ; , and that where no notice under s.10(2), had been served to the petitioners within a reasonable time, their interest in the two houses never vested in Custodian, it was not open to them to contend that they had not been wrongly deprived of their rights in the house by the action of the custodian.

The assessee company had two Departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool, and (2) for weaving yarn from imported wool tops by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The plant went into production in September 1952. The assessee Company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents for the worsted yarn on payment of 2% commission. Subsequently on December 15, 1953 the assessee company entered into an agreement with Mis Saligram Premnath under which the latter were appointed as the agency selling agents on certain specified conditions, the important of which being that the agent were to finance the assessee Company to the extent of Rs 2,50,000/ and the assessee agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to Pay 2% Commission on the net proceeds of sales of goods in India. Before expiry of this agreement another agreement was entered into by the assessee with Mis saligram agree ing to share losses which were a provision peculiar to the present transaction and was not at all covered by any authority cited before the Tribunal or the High Court that itself was proof positive of the fact that the transaction amounted to a joint venture with a view to division of profits; and (3) The assessee company, however, entered into a joint agreement with M/S. Murlidhar Ratilal Premnath Woollen Mills, Kharar, while the other one was known as M/ s. Navin Woollen Mill and others who were known as Drivers Chiranjrakashilal, agreed to finance this business by giving him a loan Of Rs. 6 lakhs from Industrial Finance. The sale agents were to get 6% commission on net sales and 50% commission On December 15 the assessee issued two show cause notices to the assessee for failure to furnish return of turnover in accordance with the provisions of section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer disallowed the deduction claimed under section 10 (2)(XV) of that Act but held that the sum in question was not a valid deduction under section 5(2) (xv) and as such could not be claimed as a valid allowance under the provisions Of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner however allowed the appeal, and held that payment was a permissible deduction as it was incurred for the purpose of the assessee 's trade in order to facilitate the business. In reference the High 836 Tribunal held against the Revenue. ^ HELD: (1)(a) This Court cannot go behind an agreement like a contract of agency. [841C] Dharamvir Dhir vs Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., ; , followed. (b) The ratio laid down by the Calcutta High Court in Dharam Vir Vir Nath Dhir 's case is not applicable to the facts of this case. (c) The agreement was a sort of a joint partnership or a joint adventure rather than a contract for payment of a share of profits simpliciter and a payment of remuneration which is deductible in truth from the profits divisible. It was on the peculiar facts of the present case that this Court could not go behind the commercial expediency which had to be deter mined from from the point of view of a businessman. [881D F] (d) The question whether the transaction was a joint arrangement or a partnership agreement is a matter of agency simpliciter and has been given the form and appearance of a contract by which the agents agreed to share the losses to the amount paid to the selling agents would be quite consistent with a remuneration in lieu of services lent and would certainly amount to an expenditure incurred by the assesses wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business which was conducted by the asses see.

The respondent assessee maintained an accounts pertaining to him in its books. The Income tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2(6A)(e) could not be construed as including current profits but it rejected the claim of the appellant. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order and determined a sum of Rs. 25,107 as dividend under Section 2( 6A)(c) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and remitted the case to the Appellate Tribunal to determine whether the accumulated profits amount was included within the accumulated profit of the company for the assessment year 1959 60 60 58 on a total income of Rs 43,407. The Revenue applied for a reference to the High Court of Kerala, and at its instance the Tribunal referred the following question to the Supreme Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of this case the Appellate tribunal was right in holding that Rs. 18,950 constituted accumulated profits for the purpose of section 2 (6A) of Income tax 1961 Act, which had been held that the expression "accuumulated profit" in Section 2 (4A)(C) could mean profits which had accumulated prior to the accounting year of which the income profits and gains were being assessed, while current depreciation would mean the profits of the accounting years in a recent case. The High Court answered it against the Revenue.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the suits out of which the present appeals arise were instituted by him to recover possession of various plots of land in the occupation of the defendants or in the alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. It was alleged in the plaints that the suit lands formed part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, but the suit properties formed part Of the permanently settle estate of Calcutta and were Malla lands assessed to revenue and that more than 200 years previously there had been a permanent Mokarrari grant of those lands by Maharaja of Burdwan to the Rajgunaj Asthal. Held, that when the land in an estate is assessed it must follow that they could not have been held on the date of the permanent settlement as Lakheraj grant. The entries in the record of rights relied on by the defendants as containing assertions that they held under a Lakhearaj grant were not shown to relate to the suit land, and that what all had been established was non payment of rent for a considerable length of time, but it has not been established precisely for how long. In respect of this plea, it must be established that the grant was one which could have legally been made by him. Since the defendants omitted to produce any revenuefree grant they could be said to have asserted a hostile title, and they could only be said clearly to have stated a hostile right. Held further, that even in 1931 there was no rent free grant in favour of the predecessors of the respondents, that grant to be presumed must have been made within time from that date. The mere fact that the defendants claimed to hold under a rents free grant would not make their possession adverse. In the present case, the suit property had been settled on the Raj Pramukh or by the Rajmangunj Prad Asthal more than 300 years ago, and as there was neither premium paid nor rent reserved but a Lakhisraj grant unsupported by any consideration, they were clearly within time. They could not be said so clearly to be in eluding the application of section 36 of the Regulation No. 8 of 1793 to reopen the question of limitation.

The appellant had been in possession of certain agricultural land. The respondent plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of contract. The appellant pleaded that the land which was the subject matter of contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, for short) and as the intending purchaser, the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act section 63 of the Tenancy Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and, therefore. as the agreement was contrary to the provisions contained in section 70(a), he could not sell the land in dispute except by way of damages etc., for short period. The trial Court found that the certificate was not valid and dismissed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that after framing the scheme of sections 70 and 85A, the Mamlatdar had jurisdiction to decide these issues. In an appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that any change in the scheme would be inconsistent with the provisions and the result was that where in a civil suit properly instituted before the Civil Court an issue arose whether specific performance should be granted or not, civil court will have jurisdiction to determine the same, and the jurisdiction of the civil court is ousted. Dismissing the appeal ^ HELD: 1.1 It would thus appear that even when a properly constituted suit is brought to the Civil court having jurisdiction to try the same prima facie on a contention being raised by an issue may arise which the Civil Judge would not be competent to try and the legislature stepped in to avoid the conflict of jurisdiction by introducing section 85A making it obligatory upon the civil Court to refer such an issue to the competent authority under the Tenancy ' Act. [595B C] 1.2 A person intending to purchase agricultural land files a suit requesting that his rights should be settled, decided or dealt with by the competent authorities under the Land Reforms Act and if section 85 of the Factories Act and sections 85A and 85C were attracted, he would be governed by the said provision in the Tenancy Acts. The Mamlatdar had exclusive jurisdiction to deal with the question set out in section 68 read with sections 85 and 85 A. The civil Court was of the view that the jurisdiction as provided under section 70 to decide objections to be raised thereunder should alone be barred under section 85. It would, therefore, have jurisdiction under the said Act. Even when a proper construction had been made in the context of the provisions relating to the rights of parties under an Tenancy Act and which is required to be settled decided or deal with by any competent authority, it was obligatory for the civil Courts not only to arrogate jurisdiction to itself to decide the same treating it as a subsidiary or incidental issue but also to refer the same to the Mamlatdar and on such decision being brought before the civil courts, it would have exclusive jurisdiction under that Act.

In June, 1957, the appellant assessee company was manufacturing boilers, wagons etc. and for that purpose, the assessee started the Jute Mill Division where the parts made out of raw material supplied by the Boiler division by machining and forging them were given to the Boiler Division of the Company. The Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held under takings as expansion and reconstruction of the business already existing and hence the asses see was not entitled (1) to exemption under section 15C(2)(i) on the ground that they formed part of the erstwhile business already in existence, namely, the business of heavy engineering. On appeal by the assessee to this Court it was contended for the Revenue that setting up of a separate unit to do something in the course of pre existing manufacturing process to aid the production of the same article as was being produced by the pre existing industrial undertaking would not amount to starting of a new industrial undertakings and that, therefore, there could be no doubt on the part of it that the two industrial undertakings were formed out of the original business of the assessee. Dismissing the appeals and remanding the case to the Income Tax Tribunal, HELD: 1.1 Section 15C is applica ble to an absolutely new industrial undertaking for the first time started by an assessee. The new activity may produce the same commodities of the old business or it may produce some other distinct marketable products, even commodities which may feed the old concern. Such a new Industrially recognisa ble unit of an asses see cannot be said to be reconstruction of his old business since there is no transfer of any assets of the existing business to the new undertaking which takes place when there is reconstruction of tile old busi ness. [773B C] 1.2 Even if a new business is carried on, but by piercing the veil of the new business it is found that there is employment of the assets of old business, the benefit will be not available. The words "the capital employed" in the principal clause of section 15 C are significant for fresh capital must be employed in the new industrial trans portment undertaking claiming exemption. [778D E] Commissioner of Income tax vs Naya Sahitya, ; , referred to.

In the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, a personal inam was granted to an office holder as remuneration for his services connected with a math or temple. The inams were confirmed by the British Government. For over 80 years, the inams were in the enjoyment of alienees from inamdars and were granted as inams. In 1863 Sri Madurai Temple was abolished and during April 1953, the inam lands were resumed in the possession of the hereditary office holder then rendering services. The Inam Commission confirmed the grants of the inams in favour of the holder of the ancient deity that the inamdars were entitled to the kudiwaram and the melwaram. In view of the abolition of the inam by the inamer, it was not possible for the High Court to hold that the inams comprised both melwarmam and kudi motti rights in the land. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the said inams were personal inams burdened with services and were not resumable under section 44 B(2)(a) of the Act, that the High court had no jurisdiction to consider the question whether section 44B was ultra vires the powers of the legislature. [544 D] In the present case, there could be no doubt that section 44D(2) (a)(i) allowed resumption even in cases where there has been an alienation of the Inam either before or after 1934. Even apart from section 44A any inam whatever its nature could be resumed for failure to perform the conditions of the grant. The object of the section was to define and enlarge the grounds on which the inams could be taken de firmed and to devise a proper procedure for the resumption. On general grounds of public policy, the legislature declared that the Inam may be resumed on any of the three grounds mentioned therein. The words "has failed" in sub section (2)(b) of section 44 A must be for a term exceeding 5 years. In the plaint in suit O.S. No. 4 of 1954 the plaintiffs claimed title to the lands under a grant from the inamdar before 1861. The plaintiffs did not prove that the lands were being enjoyed by the Inamdars and that they they were holding under a cowle lease. The only direct evidence as to how Kunjanna Ayyar came into possession of them was furnished by exhibit A 2, a statement made by the temple holders to the Madurai District Collector on August 14, 1868. It shows that in 1863 the inam was being enjoyed for the service of Sree Padam Thangi which was being then rendered, that it was being earlier rendered, and that in consequential periods the inam comprised both the melbaram and melwarams. The title deeds acknowledged their title to Devadayan or pagoda service inam to 11.47 acres of land held for the serv ice of Sree Meenakshi Padam Thanigi (the temple). They made the following statement: "For taking the deities in procession round the village during the festival in the temple of Tirumulanathaswami and Akilandeswari Ammanai, the aforesaid land has been grant ed as inam. The rights were granted to the office holders as remuneration of the services to be rendered by them in connection with the temple. " The lands were enjoyed by Sri Padam Thanjivayam and his successors in title were lessees of the other inam lands under the inam Tenants. When the inams came into force, the Inam lands were shown to be in their enjoyment in equal shares.

Section 21 of the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909 authorised a Municipality to impose taxes set out therein including the tax on houses, buildings or lands or both. The appellant 's case was that under the 1954 Act the tax could be assessed on the basis of gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of cost of repairs or on any other account whatsoever and therefore it was not bound to deduct the 10% allowance provided by sec. 73(2) from such gross annual rental value. HELD: (1) Under section 77 read with section 69 of the Act, if it is assessed on net and not the gross annual rent after deducting 10% of the gross letting value, i.e., the value arrived at after deducting 5% of gross monthly letting value. The word "if" appearing in sub sec. 2 of sec. 79 is obviously a mistake and must be read as "as if " because the word "is" standing by itself makes no sense at all. 79 therefore has to be construed to mean that though a Municipality need not prepare a fresh assessment list every year the owner or occupier of the building would be deprived of the right to object to the valuation or the annual letting values or the tax assessed thereon for at least 4 years even though the valuation and the annual hearing value thereof may have decreased for one reason or the other. [132 E G] (2) Section 73(1) read with sec. 69 provides that such assessment list when authenticated becomes conclusive evidence of the valuation of the amount of tax leviable on such buildings or land or both in any official year in which such list is in force. The Municipal tax is an annual tax leviable for a particular official year and the assessment list on the said basis of which the tax is assessed is for each such official year. This is supported by the words "such assessment list" and "of the amount" of tax assessed on 'the basis of 'annual letting value as also for the amount or tax assessed upon such buildings and lands or either both in others, or even in others or in others. [133 A C] (3) The Municipality had to prepare a new assessment list each every year. Under sections 75 and 76 when the assessment lists are prepared the assessees have to invite objections and has to have to be authenticated in the manner prescribed by secs. 76(6).

The respondent was a company carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling textiles, which were contemplated by cl. (3) of the Memorandum of Association as future sales in respect of the years 1941 to 1946, which covered its sale of assets the assessee Company had purchased from the purchaser Sri Sahib Natesa Iyer for Rs. 5, 75,000 and a sum of Rs. 7,35,000 was paid as earnest money, and the sale included chemicals and paper for manufacture which had not been sold in the first instance. In a confidential report made on August 1, 1944, to the shareholders the company stated that the price obtained had shown a capital appreciation of about six times the cost price, and that the sale of these chemicals had also resulted in a substantial profit. The assessee Company filed a suit for a declaration that the aforesaid sale was not a 'business ' within the meaning of section 2(7) of Indian Income Tax Act. The High Court found an incometax authorities to tax the company on a profit of Rs, 36,498 6 4 as its business had terminated since 1947 and that its business was wound up, but they were assessed at a profit. On appeal by special leave: Held (Per Gajendragadkar, C. J., Hidayatullah and Wanchoo, jj.), that there can be no question of an activity in respect to capital assets of the assessee company. The distinction between a sale of the entire stock as a part of trading and a sale for the purpose of selling wool is quite true because the skill of the transaction is not merely one which is buying and selling, but is also one which can fairly be regarded as the stock in trade. If this test is applied to the present case, then, the true answer would be the one given by the High Court in the judgment under appeal. The decision under appeal must be set aside and the assessee was directed to be restored to its original position on the evidence in the light of what has been stated above.
